:question/math-academy-id "q-346173" :question/problem "Express ${\int }_{1}^{5}(\operatorname{arctan}⁡(x)+2)\,\text{d}x$ as the limit of a left Riemann sum.

*Hint: Write down the missing expression in terms of $i$ and $n.$*

${\int }_{1}^{5}(\operatorname{arctan}⁡(x)+2)\,\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}[(\operatorname{arctan}⁡($

$)+2)\cdot \frac{4}{n}]$" :question/worked-solution "The definite integral can be defined in terms of the limit of a left Riemann sum as

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}f({x}_{i})\cdot Δx,
$$

    

where $Δx=\frac{b-a}{n}$ and ${x}_{i}=a+iΔx.$

In the definite integral

$$
{\int }_{1}^{5}(\operatorname{arctan}⁡(x)+2)\,\text{d}x,
$$

the function is $f(x)=\operatorname{arctan}⁡(x)+2,$ the lower bound is $a=1,$ and the upper bound is $b=5.$ So, we have

$$
Δx=\frac{5-1}{n}=\frac{4}{n},
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{5}(\operatorname{arctan}⁡(x)+2)\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}f({x}_{i})\cdot Δx \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}[f(1+i\cdot \frac{4}{n})\cdot \frac{4}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}[f(1+\frac{4i}{n})\cdot \frac{4}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}[(\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\,1+\frac{4i}{n}\,)+2)\,\cdot \frac{4}{n}].\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-f2252516-11cb-503e-94e5-fbb51ee360c4"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-f2252516-11cb-503e-94e5-fbb51ee360c4" :answer-field/id #uuid "f2252516-11cb-503e-94e5-fbb51ee360c4" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-2c9696ed-0cf7-51a5-ab03-f99476ed2805" :answer-field/choices ["answer-2c9696ed-0cf7-51a5-ab03-f99476ed2805"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-2c9696ed-0cf7-51a5-ab03-f99476ed2805" :answer/id #uuid "2c9696ed-0cf7-51a5-ab03-f99476ed2805" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "1+\frac{4i}{n}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186233960 :question/worked-solution "The definite integral can be defined in terms of the limit of a left Riemann sum as

In the definite integral

$$
{\int }_{1}^{10}{x}^{1/2}\,\text{d}x,

and therefore

$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-5b26923d-aa9d-5c1e-919b-9d716067cb9d" :question/id #uuid "5b26923d-aa9d-5c1e-919b-9d716067cb9d" :question/math-academy-id "q-113883" :question/problem "What is ${\int }_{1}^{2}{x}^{4}\,\text{d}x$ expressed as the limit of a left Riemann sum?" :question/worked-solution "The definite integral can be defined in terms of the limit of a left Riemann sum as

:question/math-academy-id "q-346192" :question/problem "Find the function $f(x)$ and the value of $b,$ given that

$$
{\int }_{1}^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=0}^{n-1}[7{(1+\frac{2k}{n})}^{-3}\cdot \frac{2}{n}].
$$

{{field-2}}" :question/worked-solution "A definite integral can be defined as the limit of a left Riemann sum as follows:

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=0}^{n-1}f({x}_{k})\cdot Δx
$$

where $Δx=\frac{b-a}{n}$ and ${x}_{k}=a+kΔx.$

Notice that we're given that the lower limit $a=1.$ 

Comparing the given summation with the general expression above, we see that $Δx=\frac{2}{n}.$ Therefore, 

$$
\frac{2}{n}=\frac{b-1}{n}\,⟹\,b=3.
$$

Consequently, ${x}_{k}=1+\frac{2k}{n}$ and $f({x}_{k})=7{x}_{k}^{-3}.$

Hence,

$$
{\int }_{1}^{3}7{x}^{-3}\,\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=0}^{n-1}[7{(1+\frac{2k}{n})}^{-3}\cdot \frac{2}{n}].
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is 

$$
f(x)=7{x}^{-3}\,\text{and}\,b=3.
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-a295c97d-d2d9-5a3d-9891-87fc0cfd77f6" "answer-field-02fa8ffe-84d7-5a81-9584-e9e83fe39768"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-a295c97d-d2d9-5a3d-9891-87fc0cfd77f6" :answer-field/id #uuid "a295c97d-d2d9-5a3d-9891-87fc0cfd77f6" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-e9b4387d-0850-5ada-aa3a-96062914b732" :answer-field/choices ["answer-e9b4387d-0850-5ada-aa3a-96062914b732"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-e9b4387d-0850-5ada-aa3a-96062914b732" :answer/id #uuid "e9b4387d-0850-5ada-aa3a-96062914b732" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "7x^{-3}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-02fa8ffe-84d7-5a81-9584-e9e83fe39768" :answer-field/id #uuid "02fa8ffe-84d7-5a81-9584-e9e83fe39768" :answer-field/key "field-2" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-80e91b06-f9f7-58e7-9b93-fa4bf08254ae" :answer-field/choices ["answer-80e91b06-f9f7-58e7-9b93-fa4bf08254ae"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-80e91b06-f9f7-58e7-9b93-fa4bf08254ae" :answer/id #uuid "80e91b06-f9f7-58e7-9b93-fa4bf08254ae" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "3" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-368aa1bb-68dd-5e11-83de-3c6725fca7d6" :question/id #uuid "368aa1bb-68dd-5e11-83de-3c6725fca7d6" :question/math-academy-id "q-346198" :question/problem "Find the function $f(x)$ and the value of $b,$ given that

{{field-2}}" :question/worked-solution "A definite integral can be defined as the limit of a left Riemann sum as follows:

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=0}^{n-1}f({x}_{k})\cdot Δx
$$

where $Δx=\frac{b-a}{n}$ and ${x}_{k}=a+kΔx.$

Notice that we're given that the lower limit $a=3.$ 

Comparing the given summation with the general expression above, we see that $Δx=\frac{4}{n}.$ Therefore, 

$$
\frac{4}{n}=\frac{b-3}{n}\,⟹\,b=7.
$$

Consequently, ${x}_{k}=3+\frac{4k}{n}$ and $f({x}_{k})={log}_{2}\,(5{x}_{k}).$ By replacing the sample point ${x}_{k}$ with the variable $x,$ we find the original function.

Hence,

$$
{\int }_{3}^{7}{log}_{2}⁡(5x)\,\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=0}^{n-1}[{log}_{2}\,(5(3+\frac{4k}{n}))\cdot \frac{4}{n}].
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is

$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-d284849d-09d1-59ac-a76f-00d1db75563f"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-d284849d-09d1-59ac-a76f-00d1db75563f" :answer-field/id #uuid "d284849d-09d1-59ac-a76f-00d1db75563f" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-f116d16e-87ef-5163-a0be-ec090d753eb4" :answer-field/choices ["answer-f116d16e-87ef-5163-a0be-ec090d753eb4"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-f116d16e-87ef-5163-a0be-ec090d753eb4" :answer/id #uuid "f116d16e-87ef-5163-a0be-ec090d753eb4" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{2i}{n}+2" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186097910 :tutorial/content "Suppose that we want to approximate the area $\mathcal A$ bound by the curve $y= x^2+1$ and the lines $x=0,$ $x=1,$ and the $x$-axis. We can do this using a left Riemann sum with $n=4$ subintervals, as shown below:

![](images/1b/1b25a722d5527db77cd7dd5fb581c0ffed9b9324913d390e2633211360b6a8ab.png)

A better approximation can be found by taking more subintervals. For instance, taking $n=8$ subintervals gives:

![](images/17/17f6c8e458b2e6fbd887728cbbcc7cb64a670598256f76cad69d9e5a9c3cf7b5.png)

As we continue to increase $n,$ our approximation gets better and better. In fact, we can get an *exact* value for the area by taking the limit of the Riemann sum as $n\to\infty.$

Let's write down that limit. First, we need to express the left Riemann sum using sigma notation. Using $n$ subintervals between the endpoints $a=0$ and $b=1,$ we express

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ≈{\sum }_{k=0}^{n-1}f({x}_{k})Δx \\  & ={\sum }_{k=0}^{n-1}f(0+k\cdot Δx)Δx \\  & ={\sum }_{k=0}^{n-1}f(k\cdot Δx)Δx \\  & ={\sum }_{k=0}^{n-1}({(k\cdot Δx)}^{2}+1)Δx \\  & ={\sum }_{k=0}^{n-1}({k}^{2}\cdot \frac{1}{{n}^{2}}+1)\cdot \frac{1}{n} \\  & ={\sum }_{k=0}^{n-1}(\frac{{k}^{2}}{{n}^{2}}+1)\cdot \frac{1}{n}.\end{aligned}
$$

In the above, we used the fact that $x_k = 0 + k\Delta x = k\Delta x$ and $\Delta x = \dfrac{1 - 0}{n} = \dfrac 1 n,$ as we've seen before.

The exact area is found by computing the limit as $n\to\infty.$ So instead of using an approximation symbol $(\approx),$ we can now use an equality symbol and write

$$
A = \lim_{n\to\infty}\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\left(\dfrac{k^2}{n^2} + 1\right)\cdot \dfrac{1}{n}.
$$

The formula above is a bit clunky, so instead of writing it using limits and sigma notation, we introduce a new notation called the **definite integral**, defined as

$$
\mathcal{A} = \lim_{n\to\infty}\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\left(\dfrac{k^2}{n^2} + 1\right)\cdot \dfrac{1}{n}= \int_0^1 (x^2 + 1)\, \textrm{d}x.
$$

In our example, 

$$
\displaystyle \int_0^1 (x^2+1)\, \textrm{d}x
$$

can be interpreted as the exact area under the graph of $y = f(x) = x^2+1$ between $x=0,$ $x=1,$ and the $x$-axis." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186097911 :tutorial/content "In general, for a function $f(x)$ defined on $[a,b],$ the **definite integral** of $f(x)$ between $x=a$ and $x=b$ can be defined using the limit of a left  Riemann sum as

$$
\int_a^b f(x)\textrm{d}x = \lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\sum_{k=0}^{n-1} f(x_k)\Delta x,
$$

    

where $\Delta x = \dfrac{b-a}{n}$ and $x_k = a + k\Delta x.$

The limit $x=a$ is referred to as the **lower limit**, whereas $x=b$ is called the **upper limit**." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186096875 :activity/expected-seconds 960.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id 17592186097447 :step/math-academy-id 631552 :db/ensure [:step/validate]} {:db/id 17592186097449 :step/math-academy-id 631553 :db/ensure [:step/validate]} {:db/id 17592186097448 :step/math-academy-id 631554 :db/ensure [:step/validate]} {:db/id 17592186097450 :step/math-academy-id 631557 :db/ensure [:step/validate]} {:db/id 17592186097451 :step/math-academy-id 631560 :db/ensure [:step/validate]} {:db/id 17592186097452 :step/math-academy-id 631563 :db/ensure [:step/validate]} {:db/id 17592186097453 :step/math-academy-id 631564 :db/ensure [:step/validate]} [:db/retract 17592186127711 :answer-field/choices 17592186127712] [:db/retract 17592186127711 :answer-field/choices 17592186127713] [:db/retract 17592186127711 :answer-field/choices 17592186127714] [:db/retract 17592186127711 :answer-field/choices 17592186127715] [:db/retract 17592186127711 :answer-field/choices 17592186127716] {:db/id 17592186129089 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-3f8dfca9-4caa-51a0-a26a-4299455440e3" "question-c798fdda-953e-5d91-a2f9-32a46093ebbe" "question-b8d4049d-0cbf-5d7d-aff8-ae877201f7a7" "question-f32b0e13-9234-5f0f-8ec6-055e7e55ffd4"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186128903 :question/worked-solution "The function has discontinuities due to vertical asymptotes at $x=\pm 1.$ Note that

To find the vertical asymptotes, let's start by factoring the expression in the denominator. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{1}{{x}^{2}-5x+6} \\  & =\frac{1}{(x-3)(x-2)}.\end{aligned}
$$

There are no common factors in the numerator and denominator, so we can find the vertical asymptotes by setting the denominator to zero:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{{x}^{2}+x-6}{{x}^{2}-4} \\  & =\frac{(x-2)(x+3)}{(x-2)(x+2)} \\  & =\frac{\cancel{(x-2)}(x+3)}{\cancel{(x-2)}(x+2)} \\  & =\frac{x+3}{x+2}.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the vertical asymptotes, we set the denominator equal to zero and solve:

$$

![](images/2b/2b1f430a78861fce15c689843d0e4af5376e0f600b650b0a614257d86365cd29.svg)" :question/worked-solution "Infinite discontinuities coincide with the vertical asymptotes of $y=f(x).$ The only possible way that $y=f(x)$ can have vertical asymptotes is if either $\dfrac{1}{x-5}$ or $\dfrac{1}{x-4}$ grow without bound within their respective subdomains.

- We first compute the asymptotes of $\dfrac{1}{x-5}.$ Setting the denominator equal to zero, we get

$$
x-5=0\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad x=5.
$$

Although this branch of the function is defined for $x < 5$, we do have that

$$
\lim_{x\to 5^{-}}\left(\dfrac{1}{x-5}\right) = -\infty,
$$

and therefore we conclude that $x=5$ is indeed an infinite discontinuity.

- Next, we compute the asymptotes of $\dfrac{1}{x-4}.$ Setting the denominator equal to zero, we get

$$
x-4=0\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad x=4.
$$

However, this branch of the function is defined for $x \geq 5,$ which does not contain the neighborhood of $x=4.$ So $x=4$ cannot be a vertical asymptote, and therefore $x=4$ cannot be an infinite discontinuity.

Therefore, the function $f(x)$ only has a single infinite discontinuity, and it is at $x=5.$

$$

$$

$$
f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{5-x}, & x<5 \\ \frac{1}{8-x}, & x\ge 5,\,x\ne 8\end{aligned}
$$

 has an infinite discontinuity are

{{field-1}}$\,$ and $\,$ $x=$
{{field-2}}." :question/worked-solution "Infinite discontinuities coincide with the vertical asymptotes of $y=f(x).$ The only possible way that $y=f(x)$ can have vertical asymptotes is if either $\frac{1}{5-x}$ or $\frac{1}{8-x}$ grow without bound within its respective subdomain.

- We first compute the asymptotes of $\frac{1}{5-x}.$ Setting the denominator equal to zero, we get

$$
5-x=0\,⟹\,x=5.
$$

Although this branch of the function is defined for $x<5,$ which excludes $x=5,$ we have that

$$
{lim}_{x\to {5}^{-}}(\frac{1}{5-x})=+\infty ,
$$

and therefore we conclude that $x=5$ is an infinite discontinuity.

- Next, we compute the asymptotes of $\frac{1}{8-x}.$ Setting the denominator equal to zero, we get

$$
8-x=0\,⟹\,x=8.
$$

Although this branch of the function is defined for $5\le x<8$ and $x>8,$ which excludes $x=8,$ we have that

$$
{lim}_{x\to {8}^{-}}(\frac{1}{8-x})=\infty \,,\,{lim}_{x\to {8}^{+}}(\frac{1}{8-x})=-\infty ,
$$

and therefore we conclude that $x=8$ is an infinite discontinuity.

Therefore, from left to right, the function $y=f(x)$ has infinite discontinuities at 

$$
x=5\,\text{and}\,x=8.
$$

This matches up with what we see in the graph of $y=f(x),$ shown below.

![](images/ed/ed2cae2a50cb15f86ead5831990366db2048c100d71dc9d1b681b890da38844f.png)" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-a5a17e3a-0fbe-5957-845d-21ab2cabc3a9"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-a5a17e3a-0fbe-5957-845d-21ab2cabc3a9" :answer-field/id #uuid "a5a17e3a-0fbe-5957-845d-21ab2cabc3a9" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-25291edd-4784-5a6b-bca1-a12e8664f92a" :answer-field/choices ["answer-25291edd-4784-5a6b-bca1-a12e8664f92a" "answer-4afab431-d446-53d4-92fd-4a3980b1aff2" "answer-1c0cd33a-fca9-5c78-8f3b-efa5df68b680" "answer-f2286a1f-5879-59e5-8aba-c9d1177ea0c6" "answer-59b19465-a919-5d91-b4bb-f487a9c859aa"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-25291edd-4784-5a6b-bca1-a12e8664f92a" :answer/id #uuid "25291edd-4784-5a6b-bca1-a12e8664f92a" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "x=-8" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-4afab431-d446-53d4-92fd-4a3980b1aff2" :answer/id #uuid "4afab431-d446-53d4-92fd-4a3980b1aff2" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "x=8" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-1c0cd33a-fca9-5c78-8f3b-efa5df68b680" :answer/id #uuid "1c0cd33a-fca9-5c78-8f3b-efa5df68b680" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "$x=-4$ and $x=\frac{1}{2}$" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-f2286a1f-5879-59e5-8aba-c9d1177ea0c6" :answer/id #uuid "f2286a1f-5879-59e5-8aba-c9d1177ea0c6" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "$x=-8$ and $x=-4$" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-59b19465-a919-5d91-b4bb-f487a9c859aa" :answer/id #uuid "59b19465-a919-5d91-b4bb-f487a9c859aa" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "No infinite discontinuities" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186130330 :tutorial/content "Let's take a look at the function $y=\dfrac 1 x$ below.

![](images/cc/cc9593860b0c134d0d99635b37eeac4f16a712a7af9e1c6474fcf1f885e8451e.png)

The function has a vertical asymptote at $x=0.$ There is also a discontinuity in the function at $x=0,$ since we cannot draw the points on the curve without taking our pen off the paper to cross the asymptote.

So, we say that $y = \dfrac 1 x$ has a **discontinuity due to a vertical asymptote** at $x=0.$ Discontinuities due to vertical asymptotes are also called **infinite discontinuities**.

Notice that here, both one-sided limits are infinite:

$$
\lim_{x\to 0^-} \left(\dfrac 1 x\right) =-\infty\qquad\text{and}\qquad\lim_{x\to 0^+} \left(\dfrac 1 x \right)=\infty.
$$

In general, a function $y=f(x)$ has a discontinuity due to a vertical asymptote at $x=c$ if either one-sided limit is infinite:

$$
\lim_{x\to c^-} f(x) =\pm \infty\qquad\text{or}\qquad\lim_{x\to c^+} f(x) =\pm \infty.
$$

Note that we only need a single limit to become infinite to conclude that there is an infinite discontinuity at $x=c.$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186129349 :activity/expected-seconds 540.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id 17592186184238 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-779dfcc0-3a36-5636-a5d6-b4ea61af4fcc" "question-81d25b33-02da-5a6a-a064-091425605527" "question-275cbf3f-d183-51d1-83d2-3cab6277b499" "question-2ac5902a-7a9e-53bd-a352-8c43204e3720"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186184239 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-d32420f7-bf1c-5010-9d26-1f698469ec0b" "question-d0a1a56f-e520-52c2-bfca-2937cd7b17ca"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186184240 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-55ce71ca-d33d-5c8b-9d05-07e0dca2765b" "question-78505148-e7b2-516b-80ad-17e7629d4193" "question-cdfb619c-431d-5983-938b-5503bb7b30f1"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-779dfcc0-3a36-5636-a5d6-b4ea61af4fcc" :question/id #uuid "779dfcc0-3a36-5636-a5d6-b4ea61af4fcc" :question/math-academy-id "q-339135" :question/problem "Evaluate the following limit:

$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-b0fcb170-b0cc-55d0-ae9f-7fe8d73132e7"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-b0fcb170-b0cc-55d0-ae9f-7fe8d73132e7" :answer-field/id #uuid "b0fcb170-b0cc-55d0-ae9f-7fe8d73132e7" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-7ad20156-2882-5a14-94a6-b4ce02519922" :answer-field/choices ["answer-7ad20156-2882-5a14-94a6-b4ce02519922"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-7ad20156-2882-5a14-94a6-b4ce02519922" :answer/id #uuid "7ad20156-2882-5a14-94a6-b4ce02519922" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "3\pi" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-55ce71ca-d33d-5c8b-9d05-07e0dca2765b" :question/id #uuid "55ce71ca-d33d-5c8b-9d05-07e0dca2765b" :question/math-academy-id "q-152891" :question/problem "${lim}_{x\to \,3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3}{2}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{x}{\sqrt{3}}))=$" :question/worked-solution "First, let's sketch the graph of  $y=\frac{3}{2}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\frac{x}{\sqrt{3}}):$   

![](images/4a/4abceba56f404b0b39fbde4b1f7da0ec36e69a496c4ef52d3bebfbcb8c7d3380.png)

$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-65db8db6-731c-5056-8281-d2ccd26fd053"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-65db8db6-731c-5056-8281-d2ccd26fd053" :answer-field/id #uuid "65db8db6-731c-5056-8281-d2ccd26fd053" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-c141ccd2-2281-55be-a7bc-e600a17abbd9" :answer-field/choices ["answer-07850059-ddb8-59d8-9ab0-8177d5206ad1" "answer-c969f3b4-9799-57d4-a8f4-6cf2a9b701dd" "answer-c141ccd2-2281-55be-a7bc-e600a17abbd9" "answer-f5168c4d-1a9d-5db6-b1eb-f2e01f7135ac" "answer-4d11d421-27fe-5c53-897b-17c35864bd3f"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-07850059-ddb8-59d8-9ab0-8177d5206ad1" :answer/id #uuid "07850059-ddb8-59d8-9ab0-8177d5206ad1" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-\frac{1}{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-c969f3b4-9799-57d4-a8f4-6cf2a9b701dd" :answer/id #uuid "c969f3b4-9799-57d4-a8f4-6cf2a9b701dd" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-c141ccd2-2281-55be-a7bc-e600a17abbd9" :answer/id #uuid "c141ccd2-2281-55be-a7bc-e600a17abbd9" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "1" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-f5168c4d-1a9d-5db6-b1eb-f2e01f7135ac" :answer/id #uuid "f5168c4d-1a9d-5db6-b1eb-f2e01f7135ac" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-4d11d421-27fe-5c53-897b-17c35864bd3f" :answer/id #uuid "4d11d421-27fe-5c53-897b-17c35864bd3f" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{\pi }{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-78505148-e7b2-516b-80ad-17e7629d4193" :question/id #uuid "78505148-e7b2-516b-80ad-17e7629d4193" :question/math-academy-id "q-302680" :question/problem "Evaluate the following limit:

${lim}_{x\to \,\sqrt{3}/2}\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{3}{4}\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(x))=$
{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "![](images/24/24f07da42a537ded7916fc2440dcf3ee1ccdfc81c7b027b47e97814fec059f5a.png)

 

The domain of $\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(x)$ is $x\in [-1,1].$

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \,\sqrt{3}/2}\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{3}{4}\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(x)) & =\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{3}{4}\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2})) \\  & =\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{3}{4}\cdot \frac{\pi }{3}) \\  & =\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}) \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-d1fc9040-4cdf-577b-b242-fcc38c2ab2bd"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-d1fc9040-4cdf-577b-b242-fcc38c2ab2bd" :answer-field/id #uuid "d1fc9040-4cdf-577b-b242-fcc38c2ab2bd" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-20c2c4de-610f-51d5-844f-c2ff3be490af" :answer-field/choices ["answer-20c2c4de-610f-51d5-844f-c2ff3be490af"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-20c2c4de-610f-51d5-844f-c2ff3be490af" :answer/id #uuid "20c2c4de-610f-51d5-844f-c2ff3be490af" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "1" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-cdfb619c-431d-5983-938b-5503bb7b30f1" :question/id #uuid "cdfb619c-431d-5983-938b-5503bb7b30f1" :question/math-academy-id "q-339480" :question/problem "Evaluate the following limit:

${lim}_{x\to \,\frac{1}{2}}\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{3}{4}\operatorname{arccos}⁡(x))=$
{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "![](images/85/85a182aabfe64c27eaafde94e3bdbede9409b02cfd87395cb2fc5543b09c4e05.png)

The domain of $\operatorname{arccos}⁡(x)$ is $x\in [-1,1].$

Now, substituting $x=\frac{1}{2}$ directly into the limit, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \,\frac{1}{2}}\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{3}{4}\operatorname{arccos}⁡(x)) & =\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{3}{4}\operatorname{arccos}⁡(\frac{1}{2})) \\  & =\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{3}{4}\cdot \frac{\pi }{3}) \\  & =\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}) \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-8dc400da-c09d-518f-b91a-2b22630e2790"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-8dc400da-c09d-518f-b91a-2b22630e2790" :answer-field/id #uuid "8dc400da-c09d-518f-b91a-2b22630e2790" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-a10c49bb-a853-5a0a-96ce-acd212343d3b" :answer-field/choices ["answer-a10c49bb-a853-5a0a-96ce-acd212343d3b"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-a10c49bb-a853-5a0a-96ce-acd212343d3b" :answer/id #uuid "a10c49bb-a853-5a0a-96ce-acd212343d3b" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "1" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186185359 :tutorial/content "In this lesson, we will learn how to deal with limits involving inverse trigonometric functions. 

Let's begin by recalling the graph of $y=\arcsin(x).$

![](images/df/df22eea4331c47da3047381ca672fd80ebf75118054316fe88c0e2d96dae0d34.png)

Using the graph, we note the following:

- The domain of $\arcsin(x)$ is $x \in [-1,1].$

- For every value $a \in (-1,1),$ we have

$$
\lim_\limits{x\to a} \arcsin(x) = \arcsin(a).
$$

 
In other words, we can evaluate the limit using direct substitution. For example,

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 1/2}\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(x) & =\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

- For any value $a$ that does *not* lie in the domain of $\arcsin(x),$ the limit

$$
\lim_\limits{x\to a} \arcsin(x)
$$

 
does *not* exist.

- At the point $x=-1,$ the limit does *not* exist because the left-sided limit does not exist. However, the right-sided limit *does* exist and is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (-1)^{+}}\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(x) & =\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(-1) \\  & =-\frac{\pi }{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Similarly, at the point $x=1,$ the limit does *not* exist because the right-sided limit does not exist. However, the left-sided limit *does* exist and is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {1}^{-}}\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(x) & =\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(1) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

The limit properties of $y=\arccos(x)$ are similar. Let's discuss them briefly." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186185363 :tutorial/content "Let's recall the graph of $y=\arccos(x).$

![](images/9d/9dcc5a116c2a564547283783a7df7b1cd3a9ab3b76ac24dc2695c4cb367796d5.png)

From the graph, we note the following:

- The domain is $x \in [-1,1].$

- For every value $a \in (-1,1),$ we have

$$
\lim_\limits{x\to a} \arccos(x) = \arccos(a).
$$

- For any value $a$ that does *not* lie in the domain of $\arccos(x),$ the limit

$$
\lim_\limits{x\to a} \arccos(x)
$$

 
does *not* exist.

- The right-sided limit at $x=-1$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (-1)^{+}}\operatorname{arccos}⁡(x) & =\operatorname{arccos}⁡(-1) \\  & =\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

- Similarly, the left-sided limit at $x=1$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {1}^{-}}\operatorname{arccos}⁡(x) & =\operatorname{arccos}⁡(1) \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, let's deduce the limit properties of $y = \arctan x.$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186185362 :tutorial/content "The graph of $y=\arctan x$ is shown below.

![](images/fc/fc06a4e63f38a315dd3944f65f871cca2dbdddee26ec268e857f79e5f4ab8848.png)

From the graph, we note the following:

- The domain is $x \in (-\infty, \infty).$

- For every value $a,$ we have

$$
\lim_\limits{x\to a} \arctan(x) = \arctan(a).
$$

- The limit as $x\to-\infty$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to -\infty }\operatorname{arctan}⁡(x) & =-\frac{\pi }{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

- The limit as $x\to\infty$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \infty }\operatorname{arctan}⁡(x) & =\frac{\pi }{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can use the algebra of limits to evaluate expressions involving inverse trigonometric functions. Let's see some examples." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186185360 :tutorial/content "We can deduce limits at infinity of transformed inverse trigonometric functions by sketching their graphs.

For example, let's consider the following limit:

$$
\lim_\limits{x \to \, \infty} \dfrac{2}{\pi}\arctan \left(x-\pi\right)
$$

To evaluate this limit, we first sketch the graph of  $y =\arctan \left(x-\pi\right){:}$  

![](images/51/51a0b9a210147b3791ce20a2f65320e20618826671ea6c7c31a27f8647595079.png)

The domain of   $\arctan \left(x-\pi\right)$ is $(-\infty,\infty).$   Moreover, from the graph, we see that 

$$
\lim\limits_{x\to \infty} \arctan \left(x-\pi\right)=\color{blue}{\dfrac{\pi}{2} }  .
$$

Therefore, by the algebra of limits, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \,\infty }\frac{2}{\pi }\operatorname{arctan}⁡(x-\pi ) & =\frac{2}{\pi }\cdot {lim}_{x\to \,\infty }\operatorname{arctan}⁡(x-\pi ) \\  & =\frac{2}{\pi }\cdot (\frac{\pi }{2}) \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Limits at infinity involving the inverse sine and cosine functions usually do not exist. Let's see an example." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186184398 :activity/expected-seconds 540.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id 17592186124459 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-93366598-9424-5753-a6aa-f85435a0ef2f"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-93366598-9424-5753-a6aa-f85435a0ef2f" :question/id #uuid "93366598-9424-5753-a6aa-f85435a0ef2f" :question/math-academy-id "q-130279" :question/problem "In what direction does the function $f(x,y)={e}^{2y}\operatorname{tan}⁡({x}^{2})$ increase most rapidly at the point $(\frac{\sqrt{\pi }}{2},0)?$" :question/worked-solution "At a given point, a function $f(x,y)$ increases most rapidly in the direction of its gradient at that point.

So, we compute $∇f(x,y)$ and evaluate it at the point $(1,-1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({e}^{2y}\operatorname{tan}⁡({x}^{2}))\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({e}^{2y}\operatorname{tan}⁡({x}^{2}))\,j \\  & =2x{e}^{2y}{sec}^{2}⁡({x}^{2})\,i+2{e}^{2y}\operatorname{tan}⁡({x}^{2})\,j \\ ∇f(\frac{\sqrt{\pi }}{2},0) & =2(\frac{\sqrt{\pi }}{2}){e}^{0}{sec}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})\,i+2{e}^{0}\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})\,j \\  & =2\sqrt{\pi }\,i+2\,j\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the function increases most rapidly in the direction of $2\sqrt{\pi }\,i+2\,j.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields "question-540d859a-8179-5e53-b6ff-389c30bf0b61"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186128997 :question/worked-solution "The tangent plane to a surface is horizontal if and only if the normal vector to the tangent plane is vertical. So, let's first find the general expression of a normal vector to the surface.

Remember that the Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the surface $z=f(x,y)$ at the point $(x_0, y_0, z_0)$ on the surface can be written as

$$
z - z_0 = (x-x_0)\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}(x_0,y_0) + (y-y_0)\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}(x_0,y_0)
$$

where $\left\langle \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}(x_0,y_0), \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}(x_0,y_0), -1 \right\rangle$ represents a normal vector to the tangent plane.

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({y}^{2}+xy) \\  & =y \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{2}+xy) \\  & =2y+x\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, a normal vector to the tangent plane is 

$$
\left\langle y, \: 2y+x, \: -1 \right\rangle.
$$

We want to find where this normal vector is vertical. This means that the $x$- and $y$-components of the vector must be $0\mathbin{:}$

![](images/ec/ec631b90dd9a037263e163bc32ebd982de5f60ee813622ae7b4f1a6b153fe856.svg) 

From the first equation, we get $y=0.$ Substituting this into the second equation, we obtain 

$$
2(0) +x = 0 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad x = 0.
$$

Finally, substituting $x=0$ and $y=0$ into our function, we get

$$
z = 0^2+(0)(0)= 0.
$$

Therefore, the point where the tangent plane is horizontal is $(0,0,0).$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-bbe6eb83-f049-5d99-ba2d-54fe9f07632a" :question/id #uuid "bbe6eb83-f049-5d99-ba2d-54fe9f07632a" :question/math-academy-id "q-129449" :question/problem "Determine the equation of the tangent plane to the surface $z={y}^{2}-{x}^{2}y$ at the point $(1,0,0).$" :question/worked-solution "The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the surface $z=f(x,y)$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ on the surface can be written as

$$
z-{z}_{0}=(x-{x}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}).
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({y}^{2}-{x}^{2}y) \\  & =-2xy \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{2}-{x}^{2}y) \\  & =2y-{x}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

 

Hence, the normal vector to the tangent plane is 

$$
⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡y,\,\frac{x}{y},\,-1⟩.
$$

Note that the tangent plane is horizontal if and only if the normal vector is vertical. This means that the $x$- and $y$-components of the vector must be $0:$

$$

$$

$$

:question/problem "At which points on the surface $z=xy-3x+2y-5$ is the tangent plane horizontal?" :question/worked-solution "The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the surface $z=f(x,y)$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ on the surface can be written as

$$
z-{z}_{0}=(x-{x}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),
$$

where $⟨\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),-1⟩$ represents a normal vector to the tangent plane.

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(xy-3x+2y-5)=y-3 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(xy-3x+2y-5)=x+2\end{aligned}
$$

 

Hence, the normal vector to the tangent plane is 

$$
⟨y-3,\,x+2,\,-1⟩.
$$

Note that the tangent plane is horizontal if and only if the normal vector is vertical. This means that the $x$- and $y$-components of the vector must be $0:$

$$
\{\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=0 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y}=0\end{aligned}\,⟹\,\{\begin{aligned}y-3=0 \\ x+2=0\end{aligned}
$$

 

From the second equation we get $x=-2,$ while the first equation gives $y=3.$ 

Finally, substituting $x=-2$ and $y=3$ into our function, we get

$$
z=(-2)(3)-3(-2)+2(3)-5=1.
$$

Therefore, the point where the tangent plane is horizontal is $(-2,3,1).$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186130386 :tutorial/content "Similar to tangent lines for single variable functions, we can think of the **tangent plane** to a surface at a point as the plane that "touches" the surface at that point.

The equation of the tangent plane to a surface $z=f(x,y)$ at the point $(x_0,y_0,z_0),$ where $z_0=f(x_0,y_0),$ can be found using the formula

$$
z - z_0 = (x-x_0)\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}(x_0,y_0) + (y-y_0)\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}(x_0,y_0).
$$

For example, consider the surface 

$$
z = 4-x^2-y^2.
$$

Let's find the equation of the tangent plane to the surface at the point $(0,\sqrt{2},2),$ as shown below.

![](images/03/03df90a94615238e2126338f64d1f51fcefc379068a8cdc366b33b998cd69f45.png)

 

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(4-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2})=-2x \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(4-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2})=-2y\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the partial derivatives at $(x,y) = (0,\sqrt{2})\mathbin{:}$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}(0,\sqrt{2}) & =-2(0)=0 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y}(0,\sqrt{2}) & =-2(\sqrt{2})=-2\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write down the equation of the tangent plane:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-2 & =(x-0)\frac{∂f}{∂x}(0,\sqrt{2})+(y-\sqrt{2})\frac{∂f}{∂y}(0,\sqrt{2}) \\ z-2 & =0(x-0)-2\sqrt{2}(y-\sqrt{2}) \\ z-2 & =-2\sqrt{2}y+4 \\ 2\sqrt{2}y+z-6 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So, we get that the Cartesian equation of the tangent plane is $2\sqrt{2}y + z - 6 = 0.$

![](images/d5/d51bdbe8820472334f7e1d942c027b6ad8164eaece58220f3f2e5cdb51544f05.png)" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186130382 :tutorial/content "Earlier, we claimed that function $f(x)$ is differentiable at $x_0$ *if the function admits a unique tangent line* at $x_0.$ Let's now justify this claim.

Recall that a function $f(x)$ is differentiable at $x=x_0$ with derivative $f'(x_0)$ if and only if the following limit exists:

$$
f'(x_0) = \lim_{x\to x_0}\dfrac {f(x) - f(x_0)} {x-x_0}
$$

We can rewrite this limit as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {x}_{0}}(\frac{f(x)-f({x}_{0})}{x-{x}_{0}})-{f}^{′}({x}_{0}) & =0 \\ {lim}_{x\to {x}_{0}}(\frac{f(x)-f({x}_{0})}{x-{x}_{0}}-{f}^{′}({x}_{0})) & =0 \\ {lim}_{x\to {x}_{0}}\frac{f(x)-f({x}_{0})-(x-{x}_{0}){f}^{′}({x}_{0})}{x-{x}_{0}} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

In order for the above limit to hold true, the numerator must approach zero. So, near $x_0,$ we must have

$$
f(x) - f(x_0) - (x-x_0)f'(x_0) \approx 0,
$$

which can be rewritten as

$$
f(x) - f(x_0) \approx (x-x_0)f'(x_0).
$$

This corresponds to the following equation of the tangent line at $x_0\mathbin{:}$

$$
y -y_0 = (x-x_0)\dfrac{\textrm d f}{\textrm d x}(x_0)
$$

From here, we can say that a function $f(x)$ is differentiable at $x_0$ *if the function admits a unique tangent line* at $x_0.$

We'll now use a similar idea to define the differentiability of a multivariable function at a point $P$ in terms of tangent planes." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186129328 :activity/expected-seconds 1260.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id 17592186192842 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-b0992f95-7b13-5c5a-ba7a-568131e59eaa" "question-f0b7f966-d726-5db3-885d-bd379b62b2e1"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186192539 :question/problem "Solve the inequality $10x - 4 > 16.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we apply the addition principle, adding $4$ to both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}10x-4 & >16 \\ 10x-4+4 & >16+4 \\ 10x+0 & >20 \\ 10x & >20\end{aligned}
$$

Second, we apply the multiplication principle, dividing both sides by $10{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}10x & >20 \\ \frac{10x}{10} & >\frac{20}{10} \\ \frac{\cancel{10}x}{\cancel{10}} & >2 \\ x & >2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x> 2.$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186192843 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-0822285c-ebb1-578e-9679-e7a486cbcc58" "question-a80bc2bf-80f4-5f0b-bce9-f8d616688e2c"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186192540 :question/problem "Solve the inequality $-2x + 3  > -1.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we apply the addition principle, subtracting $3$ from both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}-2x+3 & >-1 \\ -2x+3-3 & >-1-3 \\ -2x+0 & >-4 \\ -2x & >-4\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we apply the multiplication principle, dividing both sides by $-2.$ 

Remember, when multiplying or dividing an inequality by a negative number, we need to flip the inequality sign:

$$
\begin{aligned}-2x\,\, & >\,\,-4 \\ \frac{-2x}{-2}\, & <\,\,\frac{-4}{-2} \\ \frac{\cancel{-2}x}{\cancel{-2}}\, & <\,\,2 \\ x\,\, & <\,\,2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x<2.$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186192844 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-6bd147ae-a22b-5420-b57b-dd219e2ccfea" "question-a7f55f36-a99e-57a6-94a7-d395d5c39a69"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186192541 :question/problem "Solve the inequality $-11 \le     -8y + 5.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we apply the addition principle, subtracting $5$ from both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}-11 & \le -8y+5 \\ -11-5 & \le -8y+5-5 \\ -16 & \le -8y+0 \\ -16 & \le -8y\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we apply the multiplication principle, dividing both sides by $-8.$ 

Remember, when multiplying or dividing an inequality by a negative number, we need to flip the inequality sign:

$$
\begin{aligned}-16\,\, & \le \,\,-8y \\ \frac{-16}{-8}\, & \ge \,\,\frac{-8y}{-8} \\ 2\, & \ge \,\,\frac{\cancel{-8}y}{\cancel{-8}} \\ 2\, & \ge \,\,y\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, let's swap the left and right-hand sides so that the variable is on the left-hand side. Remember, we also need to flip the inequality.

$$
y \le   2
$$

Therefore, the solution is $y \le   2.$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-b0992f95-7b13-5c5a-ba7a-568131e59eaa" :question/id #uuid "b0992f95-7b13-5c5a-ba7a-568131e59eaa" :question/math-academy-id "q-6275" :question/problem "Solve the inequality $4x+2\le 10.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we apply the addition principle, subtracting $2$ from both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}4x+2 & \le 10 \\ 4x+2-2 & \le 10-2 \\ 4x+0 & \le 8 \\ 4x & \le 8\end{aligned}
$$

Second, we apply the multiplication principle, dividing both sides by $4:$

$$
\begin{aligned}4x & \le 8 \\ \frac{4x}{4} & \le \frac{8}{4} \\ \frac{\cancel{4}x}{\cancel{4}} & \le 2 \\ x & \le 2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x\le 2.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-ad88ce2c-c0b4-5896-8791-c75ff580324c"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} $-7t+2\le -5$ is $t${{field-1}}{{field-2}}." :question/worked-solution "First, we apply the addition principle, subtracting $2$ from both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}-7t+2 & \le -5 \\ -7t+2-2 & \le -5-2 \\ -7t+0 & \le -7 \\ -7t & \le -7\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we apply the multiplication principle, dividing both sides by $-7.$ 

Remember, when multiplying or dividing an inequality by a negative number, we need to flip the inequality sign:

$$
\begin{aligned}-7t\,\, & \le \,\,-7 \\ \frac{-7t}{-7}\, & \ge \,\,\frac{-7}{-7} \\ \frac{\cancel{-7}t}{\cancel{-7}}\, & \ge \,\,1 \\ t\,\, & \ge \,1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is $t\ge 1.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-a485e9b9-1f0c-5b82-a657-2123599d4351" "answer-field-659a3cf2-555b-5d99-8f3e-501ecab03101"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-a485e9b9-1f0c-5b82-a657-2123599d4351" :answer-field/id #uuid "a485e9b9-1f0c-5b82-a657-2123599d4351" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-1f537108-5876-58bc-8818-e7077c20c274" :answer-field/choices ["answer-1f537108-5876-58bc-8818-e7077c20c274"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-1f537108-5876-58bc-8818-e7077c20c274" :answer/id #uuid "1f537108-5876-58bc-8818-e7077c20c274" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\ge" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-659a3cf2-555b-5d99-8f3e-501ecab03101" :answer-field/id #uuid "659a3cf2-555b-5d99-8f3e-501ecab03101" :answer-field/key "field-2" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-d847024f-d453-512d-88af-bc347ca62fad" :answer-field/choices ["answer-d847024f-d453-512d-88af-bc347ca62fad"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-d847024f-d453-512d-88af-bc347ca62fad" :answer/id #uuid "d847024f-d453-512d-88af-bc347ca62fad" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "1" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-a80bc2bf-80f4-5f0b-bce9-f8d616688e2c" :question/id #uuid "a80bc2bf-80f4-5f0b-bce9-f8d616688e2c" :question/math-academy-id "q-177679" :question/problem "The solution to the inequality $-5y+16\le -4$ is $y${{field-1}}{{field-2}}." :question/worked-solution "First, we apply the addition principle, subtracting $16$ from both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}-5y+16 & \le -4 \\ -5y+16-16 & \le -4-16 \\ -5y+0 & \le -20 \\ -5y & \le -20\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we apply the multiplication principle, dividing both sides by $-5.$ 

Remember, when multiplying or dividing an inequality by a negative number, we need to flip the inequality sign:

$$

$$
2x + 6 < 12.
$$

An inequality like this one can be solved just like an equation, using the addition and multiplication principles.

First, we apply the addition principle, subtracting $6$ from both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}2x+6 & <12 \\ 2x+6-6 & <12-6 \\ 2x+0 & <6 \\ 2x & <6\end{aligned}
$$

Second, we apply the multiplication principle, dividing both sides by $2{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}2x & <6 \\ \frac{2x}{2} & <\frac{6}{2} \\ \frac{\cancel{2}x}{\cancel{2}} & <3 \\ x & <3\end{aligned}
$$

The solution is $x < 3$ In other words, any value less than $3$ satisfies the inequality.

Let's see another example." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186192903 :activity/expected-seconds 420.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id 17592186119796 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-445c4dee-b549-5e10-93bb-06205e66703c"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186119795 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-d4f26408-d253-562e-8b0f-c05af2f72107" "question-dbe20736-69a2-5914-aaf4-587bd8fc1776"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-d4f26408-d253-562e-8b0f-c05af2f72107" :question/id #uuid "d4f26408-d253-562e-8b0f-c05af2f72107" :question/math-academy-id "q-32688" :question/problem "Suppose that a $3\times 3$ matrix $C$ is reduced to row echelon form using the following elementary row operations, applied in the order in which they appear:

:answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "radii, chord $\overset{―}{AB}$" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186176967 :tutorial/content "Let's consider yet more important parts of a circle:

- The **circumference** of a circle is used to describe the perimeter of the circle, as shown in the left diagram below.

- An **arc** is a part of the circumference which is enclosed between two points on a circle. In the right diagram below, we have the arc $\overset{\frown}{AB}.$

![](images/5c/5c918b32007a68beecfdef486e9cd5d0818a2122ad672415608f761f7f7953e7.png)

If an arc is denoted using only two letters, we are referring to the *shortest* arc. However, to avoid ambiguity, we can use three letters. For example, in the diagram below, $\overset{\frown}{ACB}$ is the arc to the left and $\overset{\frown}{ADB}$ is the arc to the right.

![](images/f6/f6329cc70c467e968628d2d82a0839253ee443881371893d6d7721724e9ae02a.png)" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186176974 :tutorial/content "Finally, we have two more elements of a circle to remember:

- A **circular sector** is the region bounded by an arc of the circle and two radii which connect the center of the circle with the endpoints of the arc. In the left diagram below, we have the circular sector $OCD.$

- A **circular segment** is the region bounded by an arc of the circle and the chord that connects the endpoints of the arc. In the right diagram below, we have the circular segment $PQ.$

![](images/84/848e64be2b80b78d88da42473f6778d4012f7ec52ae6950f4ca3635b5b154ca6.png)" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186176115 :activity/expected-seconds 420.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id 17592186161998 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-328730e5-b32c-5f55-aef8-1fdf6d6f55ce"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-328730e5-b32c-5f55-aef8-1fdf6d6f55ce" :question/id #uuid "328730e5-b32c-5f55-aef8-1fdf6d6f55ce" :question/math-academy-id "q-94622" :question/problem "Find the median of the random variable $Y$ if the probability density function of $Y$ is given by

$$
f(y)=\{\begin{aligned}{e}^{-y},\, & y\ge 0, \\ 0,\, & \text{otherwise.}\end{aligned}
$$" :question/worked-solution "The median of a random variable $Y$ is the number $m$ such that

$$
P(Y\le m)=\frac{1}{2}.
$$

In our case, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(Y\le m) & ={\int }_{0}^{m}{e}^{-y}\,\text{d}y \\  & =-{e}^{-y}{|}_{0}^{m} \\  & =1-{e}^{-m}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the median is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}1-{e}^{-m} & =\frac{1}{2} \\ {e}^{-m} & =\frac{1}{2} \\ -m & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{2}) \\ -m & =-\operatorname{ln}⁡2 \\ m & =\operatorname{ln}⁡2.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-a0c67064-cabf-594b-8138-f2a53ecff042"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "e2b4a0b2-77c3-5ed8-8555-0cfe3f01b758" :question/math-academy-id "q-94668" :question/problem "Find, to three decimal places, the interquartile range of the random variable $X$ if the cumulative distribution function of $X$ is given by

$$
F(x)=\{\begin{aligned}0, & x<0, \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{16}, & 0\le x\le 4, \\ 1, & x>4.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/worked-solution "To find the interquartile range, we first need to find the lower quartile and the upper quartile.

The lower quartile of a random variable $X$ is the number ${q}_{1}$ such that

$$
P(X\le {q}_{1})=\frac{1}{4},
$$

and the upper quartile is the number ${q}_{3}$ such that

$$
P(X\le {q}_{3})=\frac{3}{4}.
$$

First, we find the lower quartile:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\le {q}_{1}) & =\frac{1}{4} \\ F({q}_{1}) & =\frac{1}{4} \\ \frac{{q}_{1}^{2}}{16} & =\frac{1}{4} \\ {q}_{1}^{2} & =4 \\ {q}_{1} & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we find the upper quartile:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\le {q}_{3}) & =\frac{3}{4} \\ F({q}_{3}) & =\frac{3}{4} \\ \frac{{q}_{3}^{2}}{16} & =\frac{3}{4} \\ {q}_{3}^{2} & =12 \\ {q}_{3} & =2\sqrt{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the interquartile range is

$$
IQR={q}_{3}-{q}_{1}=2\sqrt{3}-2≈1.464
$$

rounded to three decimal places." :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-cdc675dd-7a38-5eec-ad05-1b9e422a82c4"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} random variable $Y$ if the probability distribution function of $Y$ is given by

$$" :question/worked-solution "The $100p$th percentile of a random variable $Y$ is the number ${y}_{p}$ such that

$$
P(Y\le {y}_{p})=p.
$$

In our case, we want to find the $60$th percentile, which corresponds to the decimal $p=0.6.$ We have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(Y\le {y}_{0.6}) & ={\int }_{1}^{{y}_{0.6}}\frac{1}{{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={-\frac{1}{y}|}_{1}^{{y}_{0.6}} \\  & =1-\frac{1}{{y}_{0.6}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the $60$th percentile is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}1-\frac{1}{{y}_{0.6}} & =0.6 \\ \frac{1}{{y}_{0.6}} & =0.4 \\ {y}_{0.6} & =\frac{1}{0.4} \\ {y}_{0.6} & =\frac{5}{2}.\end{aligned}

$$" :question/worked-solution "The $100p$th percentile of a random variable $X$ is the number ${x}_{p}$ such that

$$
P(X\le {x}_{p})=p.
$$

In our case, we want to find the $72.9$th percentile, which corresponds to the decimal $p=0.729.$ We have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\le {x}_{0.729}) & ={\int }_{0}^{{x}_{0.729}}\frac{3}{16}\sqrt{x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\frac{{x}^{\frac{3}{2}}}{8}|}_{0}^{{x}_{0.729}} \\  & =\frac{{x}_{0.729}^{\frac{3}{2}}}{8}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the $72.9$th percentile is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{x}_{0.729}^{\frac{3}{2}}}{8} & =0.729 \\ {x}_{0.729}^{\frac{1}{2}} & =\sqrt[3]{(8)(0.729)} \\ {x}_{0.729}^{\frac{1}{2}} & =(2)(0.9) \\ {x}_{0.729} & =(1.8)^{2} \\ {x}_{0.729} & =3.24.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-4d9539fc-eb18-57bd-a7aa-1b80040b3b7f"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-4d9539fc-eb18-57bd-a7aa-1b80040b3b7f" :answer-field/id #uuid "4d9539fc-eb18-57bd-a7aa-1b80040b3b7f" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-1aed5558-3986-50d7-b1f2-81753d74b873" :answer-field/choices ["answer-9a4f0b16-dcc0-5510-825c-f040ca9cf4a6" "answer-92f9b85f-813a-5ae6-862a-7c2bae09fbfa" "answer-3978a119-ff81-5c74-849d-d9dd5d8e9158" "answer-1aed5558-3986-50d7-b1f2-81753d74b873" "answer-8b6cb7e1-9231-5421-81e5-f17c6d73d937"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-9a4f0b16-dcc0-5510-825c-f040ca9cf4a6" :answer/id #uuid "9a4f0b16-dcc0-5510-825c-f040ca9cf4a6" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "1.8" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-92f9b85f-813a-5ae6-862a-7c2bae09fbfa" :answer/id #uuid "92f9b85f-813a-5ae6-862a-7c2bae09fbfa" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "2.56" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-3978a119-ff81-5c74-849d-d9dd5d8e9158" :answer/id #uuid "3978a119-ff81-5c74-849d-d9dd5d8e9158" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "3.14" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-1aed5558-3986-50d7-b1f2-81753d74b873" :answer/id #uuid "1aed5558-3986-50d7-b1f2-81753d74b873" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "3.24" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-8b6cb7e1-9231-5421-81e5-f17c6d73d937" :answer/id #uuid "8b6cb7e1-9231-5421-81e5-f17c6d73d937" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "7.29" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-c3057bfc-a8d8-5a19-9075-be23799b04aa" :question/id #uuid "c3057bfc-a8d8-5a19-9075-be23799b04aa" :question/math-academy-id "q-125715" :question/problem "Find the interquartile range of the random variable $X$ if the cumulative distribution function of $X$ is given by

$$" :question/worked-solution "To find the interquartile range, we first need to find the lower quartile and the upper quartile.

The lower quartile of a random variable $X$ is the number ${q}_{1}$ such that

$$
P(X\le {q}_{1})=\frac{1}{4},
$$

and the upper quartile is the number ${q}_{3}$ such that

$$
P(X\le {q}_{3})=\frac{3}{4}.
$$

First, we find the lower quartile:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\le {q}_{1}) & =\frac{1}{4} \\ F({q}_{1}) & =\frac{1}{4} \\ 1-\frac{1}{{q}_{1}^{6}} & =\frac{1}{4} \\ \frac{1}{{q}_{1}^{6}} & =\frac{3}{4} \\ \frac{1}{{q}_{1}} & =\sqrt[6]{\frac{3}{4}} \\ {q}_{1} & =\sqrt[6]{\frac{4}{3}}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we find the upper quartile:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\le {q}_{3}) & =\frac{3}{4} \\ F({q}_{3}) & =\frac{3}{4} \\ 1-\frac{1}{{q}_{3}^{6}} & =\frac{3}{4} \\ \frac{1}{{q}_{3}^{6}} & =\frac{1}{4} \\ \frac{1}{{q}_{1}} & =\sqrt[6]{\frac{1}{4}} \\ {q}_{1} & =\sqrt[6]{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the interquartile range is

$$
\begin{aligned}IQR & ={q}_{3}-{q}_{1} \\  & =\sqrt[6]{4}-\sqrt[6]{\frac{4}{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-87f1f10e-3dae-5b47-be1d-ec0989a80ffb"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186064143 :question/problem "Find the derivative of the function $y = x^{x^3}.$" :question/worked-solution "We have the function 

$$
y = x^{x^3}.
$$

First, we take the natural logarithm of both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{{x}^{3}}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & ={x}^{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to $x{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡x) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =({x}^{3})^{′}\cdot (\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+({x}^{3})\cdot {(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)}^{′} \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =3{x}^{2}\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡x+{x}^{3}\cdot \frac{1}{x} \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =3{x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡x+{x}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve for $y'{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =y(3{x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡x+{x}^{2})\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $y=x^{x^3}{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & ={x}^{{x}^{3}}(3{x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡x+{x}^{2}) \\  & ={x}^{{x}^{3}}({x}^{2}(3\operatorname{ln}⁡x+1)) \\  & ={x}^{{x}^{3}+2}(3\operatorname{ln}⁡x+1)\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186064307 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-73c29bd9-9c93-5235-9a81-b902322f8bb3" "question-9798e200-13a6-549b-86eb-d44d6cb98aeb" "question-22063a8c-2673-5c08-b0b7-4fcd50355c5f" "question-cdcbfec1-c9f8-5550-af44-736f646a25ea"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186064144 :question/problem "Find the derivative of the function $y = (x^2-1)^x.$" :question/worked-solution "We have the function 

$$
y = (x^2-1)^x.
$$

First, we take the natural logarithm of both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(({x}^{2}-1)^{x}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}-1)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to $x{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}-1)) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x)\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}-1)+x\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}-1)) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =1\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}-1)+x\cdot (\frac{1}{{x}^{2}-1}\cdot 2x) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}-1)+\frac{2{x}^{2}}{{x}^{2}-1}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve for $\dfrac {\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x}{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =y(\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}-1)+\frac{2{x}^{2}}{{x}^{2}-1})\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $y = (x^2-1)^x{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =({x}^{2}-1)^{x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}-1)+\frac{2{x}^{2}}{{x}^{2}-1}) \\  & =({x}^{2}-1)^{x}(\frac{({x}^{2}-1)\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}-1)}{{x}^{2}-1}+\frac{2{x}^{2}}{{x}^{2}-1}) \\  & =({x}^{2}-1)^{x-1}(({x}^{2}-1)\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}-1)+2{x}^{2})\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186064308 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-965ab36a-7265-52be-bed3-0fcb25681407" "question-650ff22d-86ac-5784-9e2d-04a2cd40b0db" "question-a8502904-ea72-54be-8bde-7a62b1b58e76"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186064145 :question/problem "Find the derivative of the function $y = (\sin x)^{\cos x}.$" :question/worked-solution "We have the function 

$$
y = (\sin x)^{\cos x}.
$$

First, we take the natural logarithm of both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡((\operatorname{sin}⁡x)^{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to $x{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)^{′}\cdot (\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{sin}⁡x))+(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)\cdot {(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{sin}⁡x))}^{′} \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =(-\operatorname{sin}⁡x)\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)+\operatorname{cos}⁡x\cdot (\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡x) \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\operatorname{cot}⁡x-\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve for $y'{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =y(\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\operatorname{cot}⁡x-\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{sin}⁡x))\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $y = (\sin x)^{\cos x}{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)^{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}(\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\operatorname{cot}⁡x-\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{sin}⁡x))\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-e9eb4864-b21d-5e66-84e3-4be25804889c" :question/id #uuid "e9eb4864-b21d-5e66-84e3-4be25804889c" :question/math-academy-id "q-341713" :question/problem "Given that $y=5e{x}^{1/x}$, find ${y}^{′}.$

{{field-1}}$)$" :question/worked-solution "We have the function 

$$
y=5e{x}^{1/x}.
$$

First, we take the natural logarithm of both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(5e{x}^{1/x}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(5e)+\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{1/x}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(5e)+(\frac{1}{x})\operatorname{ln}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(5e)+(\frac{1}{x})\operatorname{ln}⁡x) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =0+{(\frac{1}{x})}^{′}\cdot (\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+(\frac{1}{x})\cdot {(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)}^{′} \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =(-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}})\operatorname{ln}⁡x+(\frac{1}{x})\cdot \frac{1}{x} \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =-\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{{x}^{2}}+\frac{1}{{x}^{2}} \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}(1-\operatorname{ln}⁡x) \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & ={x}^{-2}(1-\operatorname{ln}⁡x)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve for ${y}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =y[{x}^{-2}(1-\operatorname{ln}⁡x)]\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $y=5e{x}^{1/x}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =5e{x}^{1/x}[{x}^{-2}(1-\operatorname{ln}⁡x)] \\  & =5e{x}^{1/x-2}\cdot (1-\operatorname{ln}⁡x)\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-8cbd0b0a-4f04-5099-bf6e-7a48a06d53ff"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-8cbd0b0a-4f04-5099-bf6e-7a48a06d53ff" :answer-field/id #uuid "8cbd0b0a-4f04-5099-bf6e-7a48a06d53ff" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-5de69524-b32f-529b-907d-70d9251c90c0" :answer-field/choices ["answer-5de69524-b32f-529b-907d-70d9251c90c0"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-5de69524-b32f-529b-907d-70d9251c90c0" :answer/id #uuid "5de69524-b32f-529b-907d-70d9251c90c0" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "1-\ln x" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-3fe57972-490a-52da-b89f-179c602b71c5" :question/id #uuid "3fe57972-490a-52da-b89f-179c602b71c5" :question/math-academy-id "q-138749" :question/problem "Consider the function $y=6{x}^{x}.$ Its derivative is given by

Find the function $g(x).$" :question/worked-solution "We have the function 

$$

$$

First, we take the natural logarithm of both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(6{x}^{x}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡6+\operatorname{ln}⁡{x}^{x} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡6+x\operatorname{ln}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡6+x\operatorname{ln}⁡x) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & ={(\operatorname{ln}⁡6)}^{′}+(x)^{′}\cdot (\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+(x)\cdot {(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)}^{′} \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =0+1\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡x+x\cdot \frac{1}{x} \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡x+1\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve for ${y}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =y(\operatorname{ln}⁡x+1)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $y=6{x}^{x}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =6{x}^{x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡x+1)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $g(x)=\operatorname{ln}⁡x+1$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-4723771a-307d-5638-bcc4-3cc4b09d18e9"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} $$
y={x}^{\operatorname{sec}⁡x}.
$$

First, we take the natural logarithm of both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{\operatorname{sec}⁡x}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{sec}⁡x\,\operatorname{ln}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{sec}⁡x\operatorname{ln}⁡x) \\ \frac{1}{y}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =(\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}\operatorname{sec}⁡x)\operatorname{ln}⁡x+\operatorname{sec}⁡x(\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}\operatorname{ln}⁡x) \\ \frac{1}{y}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =(\operatorname{sec}⁡x\operatorname{tan}⁡x)\operatorname{ln}⁡x+\operatorname{sec}⁡x\cdot \frac{1}{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve for $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =y(\operatorname{ln}⁡x\,\operatorname{sec}⁡x\operatorname{tan}⁡x+\frac{\operatorname{sec}⁡x}{x})\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $y={x}^{\operatorname{sec}⁡x}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & ={x}^{\operatorname{sec}⁡x}\cdot (\operatorname{ln}⁡x\,\operatorname{sec}⁡x\operatorname{tan}⁡x+\frac{\operatorname{sec}⁡x}{x}) \\  & ={x}^{\operatorname{sec}⁡x}\cdot \frac{\operatorname{sec}⁡x}{x}\cdot (x\operatorname{ln}⁡x\,\operatorname{tan}⁡x+1) \\  & ={x}^{\operatorname{sec}⁡x-1}\operatorname{sec}⁡x\cdot (x\operatorname{ln}⁡x\operatorname{tan}⁡x+1).\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-a32a9416-0150-598e-ac86-6202b9e0f123"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-a32a9416-0150-598e-ac86-6202b9e0f123" :answer-field/id #uuid "a32a9416-0150-598e-ac86-6202b9e0f123" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-016328d0-e890-5f0f-acd5-5481d9b4f783" :answer-field/choices ["answer-016328d0-e890-5f0f-acd5-5481d9b4f783"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-016328d0-e890-5f0f-acd5-5481d9b4f783" :answer/id #uuid "016328d0-e890-5f0f-acd5-5481d9b4f783" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "1+x\tan x\ln x" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-73c29bd9-9c93-5235-9a81-b902322f8bb3" :question/id #uuid "73c29bd9-9c93-5235-9a81-b902322f8bb3" :question/math-academy-id "q-138837" :question/problem "Consider the function $y=(\operatorname{tan}⁡x)^{x}.$ Its derivative is given by

$$
y=(5{x}^{2}+2x)^{x}.

First, we take the natural logarithm of both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡((5{x}^{2}+2x)^{x}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡(5{x}^{2}+2x)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x\operatorname{ln}⁡(5{x}^{2}+2x)) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x)\cdot (\operatorname{ln}⁡(5{x}^{2}+2x))+(x)\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(5{x}^{2}+2x)) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =1\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡(5{x}^{2}+2x)+x\cdot (\frac{1}{5{x}^{2}+2x}\cdot (10x+2)) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(5{x}^{2}+2x)+\frac{10{x}^{2}+2x}{5{x}^{2}+2x}\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-e5ec8274-52d3-526d-accb-2a89c9a62542"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-e5ec8274-52d3-526d-accb-2a89c9a62542" :answer-field/id #uuid "e5ec8274-52d3-526d-accb-2a89c9a62542" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-19cbcd6f-25b2-5cce-957b-c04f39806845" :answer-field/choices ["answer-19cbcd6f-25b2-5cce-957b-c04f39806845"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-19cbcd6f-25b2-5cce-957b-c04f39806845" :answer/id #uuid "19cbcd6f-25b2-5cce-957b-c04f39806845" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "(5x^2+2x)\ln(5x^2+2x)" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-22063a8c-2673-5c08-b0b7-4fcd50355c5f" :question/id #uuid "22063a8c-2673-5c08-b0b7-4fcd50355c5f" :question/math-academy-id "q-138809" :question/problem "Consider the function $y=(\sqrt{x})^{x}.$ Its derivative is given by 

$$
{y}^{′}=\frac{1}{2}{(\sqrt{x})}^{x}\cdot g(x).
$$

Find the function $g(x).$" :question/worked-solution "We have the function 

$$
y=(\sqrt{x})^{x}.
$$

First, we take the natural logarithm of both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡((\sqrt{x})^{x}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡(\sqrt{x})\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x\operatorname{ln}⁡(\sqrt{x})) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =(x)^{′}\cdot (\operatorname{ln}⁡(\sqrt{x}))+(x)\cdot {(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\sqrt{x}))}^{′} \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =1\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡(\sqrt{x})+x\cdot (\frac{1}{\sqrt{x}}\cdot \frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}}) \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\sqrt{x})+\frac{1}{2} \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)+\frac{1}{2} \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)+1)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve for ${y}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =\frac{1}{2}y(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)+1)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $y=(\sqrt{x})^{x}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =\frac{1}{2}(\sqrt{x})^{x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)+1)\end{aligned}
$$

Find the function $g(x).$" :question/worked-solution "We have the function 

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡((2x)^{x}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x)\end{aligned}

Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x)) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =(x)^{′}\cdot (\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x))+(x)\cdot {(\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x))}^{′} \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =1\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡(2x)+x\cdot (\frac{1}{2x}\cdot 2) \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x)+1\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =y(\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x)+1)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $y=y=(2x)^{x}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =(2x)^{x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x)+1)\end{aligned}

Therefore, $g(x)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x)+1.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186061945 :answer-field/correct "answer-458cddab-14fc-5f26-9c92-145cd90d2727" :answer-field/choices ["answer-27f2940b-1ddc-59bd-aa4d-a19c8dfaf251" "answer-6d6767d3-90fd-55f9-99ca-5116679ff0b1" "answer-458cddab-14fc-5f26-9c92-145cd90d2727" "answer-430fa093-d180-5fb7-8644-1b06f135536c" "answer-07651916-0973-556a-b9c6-a20002d3cbf6"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-27f2940b-1ddc-59bd-aa4d-a19c8dfaf251" :answer/id #uuid "27f2940b-1ddc-59bd-aa4d-a19c8dfaf251" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "2+\operatorname{ln}⁡x" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-6d6767d3-90fd-55f9-99ca-5116679ff0b1" :answer/id #uuid "6d6767d3-90fd-55f9-99ca-5116679ff0b1" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x)" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-458cddab-14fc-5f26-9c92-145cd90d2727" :answer/id #uuid "458cddab-14fc-5f26-9c92-145cd90d2727" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x)+1" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-430fa093-d180-5fb7-8644-1b06f135536c" :answer/id #uuid "430fa093-d180-5fb7-8644-1b06f135536c" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "x\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x)+1" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-07651916-0973-556a-b9c6-a20002d3cbf6" :answer/id #uuid "07651916-0973-556a-b9c6-a20002d3cbf6" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "x\operatorname{ln}⁡x" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-cdcbfec1-c9f8-5550-af44-736f646a25ea" :question/id #uuid "cdcbfec1-c9f8-5550-af44-736f646a25ea" :question/math-academy-id "q-138840" :question/problem "Consider the function $y=({x}^{2}+3x)^{x}.$ Its derivative is given by 

$$

$$

Find the function $g(x).$" :question/worked-solution "We have the function 

$$
y=({x}^{2}+3x)^{x}.
$$

First, we take the natural logarithm of both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(({x}^{2}+3x)^{x}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+3x)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+3x)) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x)\cdot (\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+3x))+(x)\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+3x)) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =1\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+3x)+x\cdot (\frac{1}{{x}^{2}+3x}\cdot 2x+3) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+3x)+\frac{2{x}^{2}+3x}{{x}^{2}+3x}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve for $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =y(\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+3x)+\frac{2{x}^{2}+3x}{{x}^{2}+3x})\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $y=({x}^{2}+3x)^{x}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =({x}^{2}+3x)^{x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+3x)+\frac{2{x}^{2}+3x}{{x}^{2}+3x}) \\  & =({x}^{2}+3x)^{x}(\frac{({x}^{2}+3x)\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+3x)}{{x}^{2}+3x}+\frac{2{x}^{2}+3x}{{x}^{2}+3x}) \\  & =({x}^{2}+3x)^{x-1}(({x}^{2}+3x)\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+3x)+(2{x}^{2}+3x)).\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, $g(x)=({x}^{2}+3x)\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+3x)+(2{x}^{2}+3x).$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields
