{{field-1}}$)$" :question/worked-solution "We have the function 

$$
y=(\operatorname{sec}⁡(x))^{\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)}.
$$

First, we take the natural logarithm of both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡((\operatorname{sec}⁡(x))^{\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)\,\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{sec}⁡(x))\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{sec}⁡(x))) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =(\operatorname{sin}⁡(x))^{′}\cdot (\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{sec}⁡(x)))+(\operatorname{sin}⁡(x))\cdot {(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{sec}⁡(x)))}^{′} \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{sec}⁡(x))+\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)\cdot (\frac{1}{\operatorname{sec}⁡x}\cdot \operatorname{sec}⁡(x)\operatorname{tan}⁡(x)) \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)\,\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{sec}⁡(x))+\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)\operatorname{tan}⁡(x)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve for ${y}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =y(\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)\,\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{sec}⁡(x))+\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)\operatorname{tan}⁡(x))\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $y=(\operatorname{sec}⁡(x)^{\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =(\operatorname{sec}⁡(x))^{\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)}\cdot (\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)\,\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{sec}⁡(x))+\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)\operatorname{tan}⁡(x))\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-d1418ec4-9e2c-5aec-b01d-aff904f686c2"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-d1418ec4-9e2c-5aec-b01d-aff904f686c2" :answer-field/id #uuid "d1418ec4-9e2c-5aec-b01d-aff904f686c2" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-b71b8dc8-607f-5822-afac-e0d10c462052" :answer-field/choices ["answer-b71b8dc8-607f-5822-afac-e0d10c462052"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-b71b8dc8-607f-5822-afac-e0d10c462052" :answer/id #uuid "b71b8dc8-607f-5822-afac-e0d10c462052" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\sin(x)\tan(x)" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-650ff22d-86ac-5784-9e2d-04a2cd40b0db" :question/id #uuid "650ff22d-86ac-5784-9e2d-04a2cd40b0db" :question/math-academy-id "q-341951" :question/problem "Find the slope $m$ of the tangent line to the curve $y=(\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x))^{{x}^{2}}$ at $x=\frac{e}{3}.$

$m=$
{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "The slope of the tangent to the curve at $x=\frac{e}{3}$ equals the function's derivative at the corresponding point.

We have the function 

$$
y=(\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x))^{{x}^{2}}.
$$

First, we take the natural logarithm of both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡((\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x))^{{x}^{2}}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & ={x}^{2}\,\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x))\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}\,\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x))) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =({x}^{2})^{′}\cdot (\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x)))+({x}^{2})\cdot {(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x)))}^{′} \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =2x\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x))+{x}^{2}\cdot (\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x)}\cdot \frac{1}{x}) \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =2x\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x))+\frac{x}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x)}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve for ${y}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =y(2x\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x))+\frac{x}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x)})\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $y=(\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x))^{{x}^{2}}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =(\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x))^{{x}^{2}}(2x\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x))+\frac{x}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x)})\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of $y=(\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x))^{{x}^{2}}$ at $x=\frac{e}{3}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}m={y}^{′}{|}_{x=e/3} & =(\operatorname{ln}⁡(e))^{(e/3)^{2}}(2(\frac{e}{3})\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡(e))+\frac{(\frac{e}{3})}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(e)}) \\  & =(1)^{(e/3)^{2}}(2(\frac{e}{3})\operatorname{ln}⁡(1)+\frac{(\frac{e}{3})}{1}) \\  & =1\cdot (0+\frac{e}{3}) \\  & =\frac{e}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-36d45e39-f71d-51b2-ae6d-2faee3a34b79"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-36d45e39-f71d-51b2-ae6d-2faee3a34b79" :answer-field/id #uuid "36d45e39-f71d-51b2-ae6d-2faee3a34b79" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-9bdcbb96-5ec9-5007-b256-214fc5f8397c" :answer-field/choices ["answer-9bdcbb96-5ec9-5007-b256-214fc5f8397c"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-9bdcbb96-5ec9-5007-b256-214fc5f8397c" :answer/id #uuid "9bdcbb96-5ec9-5007-b256-214fc5f8397c" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{e}{3}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-a8502904-ea72-54be-8bde-7a62b1b58e76" :question/id #uuid "a8502904-ea72-54be-8bde-7a62b1b58e76" :question/math-academy-id "q-138863" :question/problem "Find the slope of the tangent to the curve $y=(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)^{5x}$ at $x=e.$" :question/worked-solution "The slope of the tangent to the curve at $x=e$ equals the function's derivative at the corresponding point.

We have the function 

$$
y=(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)^{5x}.
$$

First, we take the natural logarithm of both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡((\operatorname{ln}⁡x)^{5x}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =5x\,\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(5x\,\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =(5x)^{′}\cdot (\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x))+(5x)\cdot {(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x))}^{′} \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =5\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+5x\cdot (\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}\cdot \frac{1}{x}) \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =5\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+\frac{5}{\operatorname{ln}⁡x} \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =5(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡x})\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve for ${y}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =y(5(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}))\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $y=(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)^{5x}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =5(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)^{5x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡x})\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of $y=(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)^{5x}$ at $x=e$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}{|}_{x=e} & =5(\operatorname{ln}⁡e)^{5\cdot e}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡e)+\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡e}) \\  & =5(1)^{5e}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(1)+\frac{1}{1}) \\  & =5.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-ba9151a4-b3b8-572e-a482-a0acf45515d6"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-ba9151a4-b3b8-572e-a482-a0acf45515d6" :answer-field/id #uuid "ba9151a4-b3b8-572e-a482-a0acf45515d6" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-958860f4-6bc6-5bdf-97ca-7bb1fc4df790" :answer-field/choices ["answer-8b404956-da94-552b-947d-159dfaef39dd" "answer-958860f4-6bc6-5bdf-97ca-7bb1fc4df790" "answer-7035e9b8-2a3c-533d-bcf2-3bfb073ccc28" "answer-6fd19c25-5aab-572e-808f-2654216bf71a" "answer-a0be53dd-9f2c-5eb8-a506-84c246e69f71"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-8b404956-da94-552b-947d-159dfaef39dd" :answer/id #uuid "8b404956-da94-552b-947d-159dfaef39dd" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-958860f4-6bc6-5bdf-97ca-7bb1fc4df790" :answer/id #uuid "958860f4-6bc6-5bdf-97ca-7bb1fc4df790" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "5" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-7035e9b8-2a3c-533d-bcf2-3bfb073ccc28" :answer/id #uuid "7035e9b8-2a3c-533d-bcf2-3bfb073ccc28" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "5e" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-6fd19c25-5aab-572e-808f-2654216bf71a" :answer/id #uuid "6fd19c25-5aab-572e-808f-2654216bf71a" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "6" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-a0be53dd-9f2c-5eb8-a506-84c246e69f71" :answer/id #uuid "a0be53dd-9f2c-5eb8-a506-84c246e69f71" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "e" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186065395 :tutorial/content "**Logarithmic differentiation** is a technique to compute derivatives that are difficult to find using the usual rules of differentiation, such as the product, quotient, and chain rules.

Let's consider the following function.

$$
y = x^x
$$

We aim to compute $\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d x}.$ However, in this case, we note the following:

- Both the base and the exponent are functions of $x.$

- This means we cannot apply the power rule since the exponent is not a fixed number.

- We also cannot apply the rules for differentiating exponentials since the base is not a fixed number.

So instead, we'll use logarithmic differentiation. We proceed as follows:

**Step 1.** We take the natural logarithm of both sides and apply the power rule for logarithms:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & ={x}^{x} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡{x}^{x} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2.** We differentiate both sides of the above equation with respect to $x$ using implicit differentiation and the product rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x\operatorname{ln}⁡x) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x)\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡x+x\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡x) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =1\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡x+x\cdot (\frac{1}{x}) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡x+1\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3.** Now, we solve for $\dfrac {\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x}.$ This gives

$$
\dfrac {\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} =  y\left( \ln x + 1 \right).
$$

**Step 4.** Finally, we substitute back our original expression for $y=x^x{:}$

$$
\dfrac {\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} = x^x \left( \ln x + 1 \right)
$$

III. $A$ is indefinite" :question/worked-solution "Given a quadratic form $Q(x)={x}^{T}Ax,$ we have the following theorem:

- $Q$ is positive-definite if and only if all the eigenvalues of $A$ are positive,

- $Q$ is positive semi-definite if and only if all the eigenvalues of $A$ are non-negative (note that positive semi-definite quadratic forms include all positive-definite quadratic forms),

- $Q$ is negative-definite if and only if all the eigenvalues of $A$ are negative,

- $Q$ is negative semi-definite if and only if all the eigenvalues of $A$ are non-positive (note that negative semi-definite quadratic forms include all negative-definite quadratic forms), and

- $Q$ is indefinite if and only if $A$ has both positive and negative eigenvalues.

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. Computing the characteristic equation of $A,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}|A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}2-\lambda  & 7 \\ 7 & 2-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (2-\lambda )(2-\lambda )-49 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-4\lambda -45 & =0 \\ \lambda  & =-5,\,9.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is false, while statement III is true. Since $A$ has both positive and negative eigenvalues, the quadratic form ${x}^{T}\,A\,x$ (as well as the matrix $A$) is indefinite.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only."" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-cf1da4cf-719f-5bbd-9c32-cdb26adbbe05"] :db/ensure $$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}^{′}{(\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x))}^{′}+{u}_{2}^{′}{(\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x))}^{′}=6\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ {u}_{1}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)+{u}_{2}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)=0\end{aligned}\,⟹\,\{\begin{aligned}-3{u}_{1}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)+3{u}_{2}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)=6\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ {u}_{1}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)+{u}_{2}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)=0\end{aligned}\end{aligned}

$$
y_c(x) = Ae^x + Be^{2x}
$$

where $A$ and $B$ are constants, and the fundamental solutions $y_1(x)$ and $y_2(x)$ are

$$
y_1(x) = e^{x}, \qquad y_2(x) = e^{2x}.
$$

Note that the Wronskian 

![](images/e5/e5fd444b69d4c3b0e7acc93217dc44dd3b6c4042da7fda41b6bb38d1b36336ba.svg)

is nonzero for all $x,$ and so the set 

$$

$$

 
is a linearly independent set of fundamental solutions. 

Now, suppose we wish to seek a particular solution using variation of parameters. By allowing the constants $A$ and $B$ to vary, we can introduce new functions $u_1(x)$ and $u_2(x),$ and seek a particular solution of the form

$$
y_p(x) = u_1y_1+ u_2y_2.
$$

But we have a problem! Differentiating $y_p=u_1y_1+u_2y_2,$ we get terms involving $u'_1$ and $u'_2.$ Substituting into the ODE produces a single equation involving both $u'_1$ and $u'_2,$ so we need a second equation.

To help with this issue, we will seek a solution that satisfies the following constraint:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}^{′} & ={u}_{1}{y}_{1}^{′}+{u}_{2}{y}_{2}^{′}\end{aligned}
$$

This constraint for $y_p'$ does **not** come from differentiating $y_p.$ Rather, it is a condition that we force so that we obtain a solvable system of equations. We'll go over its justification in more detail at the end of the lesson.

- **Step 1**: To ensure the expression for $y_p'$ above is valid, we must first impose the condition $u_1' y_1 + u_2' y_2 = 0.$

- **Step 2**: Next, we differentiate $y_p'$ to find $y_p'',$ substitute it into the differential equation, and simplify. This yields the second condition $u_1' y_1' + u_2' y_2' = f(x).$

- **Step 3**: We solve the resulting system of two equations for the derivatives $u_1'$ and $u_2',$ then integrate to find $u_1$ and $u_2.$

\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}^{′} & ={({u}_{1}{e}^{2x}+{u}_{2}{e}^{-3x})}^{′} \\  & ={({u}_{1}{e}^{2x})}^{′}+{({u}_{2}{e}^{-3x})}^{′} \\  & ={u}_{1}^{′}{e}^{2x}+{u}_{1}({e}^{2x})^{′}+{u}_{2}^{′}{e}^{-3x}+{u}_{2}({e}^{-3x})^{′} \\  & ={u}_{1}^{′}{e}^{2x}+2{u}_{1}{e}^{2x}+{u}_{2}^{′}{e}^{-3x}-3{u}_{2}{e}^{-3x}.\end{aligned}

$$

which finally gives

$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186148652 :tutorial/content "Now, we’ll apply the method of variation of parameters from start to finish to see the full picture.

Consider the differential equation

$$

for which the corresponding homogeneous equation has the fundamental solutions $y_1 = e^{2x}$ and $y_2 = e^{-2x}.$ 

Let’s work through this example using the method of variation of parameters.

We seek a particular solution of the form

$$
y_p = u_1 y_1 + u_2 y_2
$$

subject to the standard constraints:

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}^{′}{y}_{1}^{′}+{u}_{2}^{′}{y}_{2}^{′}=4{e}^{2x} \\ {u}_{1}^{′}{y}_{1}+{u}_{2}^{′}{y}_{2}=0\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

First, let's verify that the fundamental solutions $y_1$ and $y_2$ are independent by computing the Wronskian:

$$
\begin{aligned}W({y}_{1},{y}_{2}) & =|\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} & {y}_{2} \\ {y}_{1}^{′} & {y}_{2}^{′}\end{aligned}| \\  & ={y}_{1}{y}_{2}^{′}-{y}_{1}^{′}{y}_{2} \\  & =({e}^{2x})({e}^{-2x})^{′}-({e}^{2x})^{′}({e}^{-2x}) \\  & =({e}^{2x})(-2{e}^{-2x})-(2{e}^{2x})({e}^{-2x}) \\  & =-2-2 \\  & =-4 \\  & \ne 0\end{aligned}
$$

Since $W \neq 0,$ the functions are linearly independent. 

Substituting $y_1, y_2$ and their derivatives into our constraints gives the system:

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}^{′}{({e}^{2x})}^{′}+{u}_{2}^{′}{({e}^{-2x})}^{′}=4{e}^{2x} \\ {u}_{1}^{′}{e}^{2x}+{u}_{2}^{′}{e}^{-2x}=0\end{aligned}\,⟹\,\{\begin{aligned}2{u}_{1}^{′}{e}^{2x}-2{u}_{2}^{′}{e}^{-2x}=4{e}^{2x} \\ {u}_{1}^{′}{e}^{2x}+{u}_{2}^{′}{e}^{-2x}=0\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

We start by solving for $u_2'$ from the second equation to get

$$
u_2' = -\dfrac{u_1'e^{2x}}{e^{-2x}}=-u_1'e^{4x}.

Substituting this into the first equation, we get

$$

Thus, we have

\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\int {u}_{1}^{′}\,\text{d}x=\int 1\,\text{d}x=x, \\ {u}_{2} & =\int {u}_{2}^{′}\,\text{d}x=\int -{e}^{4x}\,\text{d}x=-\frac{1}{4}{e}^{4x}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our particular solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p} & ={u}_{1}{y}_{1}+{u}_{2}{y}_{2} \\  & =(x){e}^{2x}+(-\frac{1}{4}{e}^{4x}){e}^{-2x} \\  & =x{e}^{2x}-\frac{1}{4}{e}^{2x}.\end{aligned}
$$

The general solution is $y = y_c + y_p,$ where $y_c = C_1 e^{2x} + C_2 e^{-2x}.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =({C}_{1}{e}^{2x}+{C}_{2}{e}^{-2x})+(x{e}^{2x}-\frac{1}{4}{e}^{2x}) \\  & =({C}_{1}-\frac{1}{4}){e}^{2x}+{C}_{2}{e}^{-2x}+x{e}^{2x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, replacing constants $C_1 - \dfrac{1}{4}$ with $A$ and $C_2$ with $B,$ we get

$$
\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{y(x) = A e^{2x} + B e^{-2x} + xe^{2x}}
$$

where $A$ and $B$ are arbitrary constants." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186148655 :tutorial/content "In variation of parameters for a second-order linear equation, we seek a particular solution of the form

$$
y_p = u_1y_1 + u_2y_2,
$$

where $y_1$ and $y_2$ are linearly independent solutions of the corresponding homogeneous equation, and $u_1$ and $u_2$ are unknown functions.

At first, it may seem natural to differentiate $y_p$ directly:

$$
y_p' = (u_1y_1+u_2y_2)' = u_1'y_1 + u_1y_1' + u_2'y_2 + u_2y_2'.
$$

This expression contains the *extra terms* $u_1'y_1$ and $u_2'y_2,$ which will also appear (after differentiating again) in the expression for $y_p''$.

If we substitute $y=y_p$ into the differential equation, we will obtain *one* equation involving *two* unknown derivatives $u_1'$ and $u_2',$ so we need a second equation to determine them.

To create a second equation, we *choose* to impose the condition

$$
u_1'y_1 + u_2'y_2 = 0.
$$

This is not a property of $u_1$ and $u_2$ that we already know, but it is an additional constraint that we enforce to make the system solvable.

Now, observe what happens to the formula for $y_p'.$ Starting from the product rule expansion,

$$
y_p' = u_1'y_1 + u_1y_1' + u_2'y_2 + u_2y_2',
$$

and using the constraint $u_1'y_1+u_2'y_2=0,$ we obtain

$$
y_p' = u_1y_1' + u_2y_2'.
$$

So, the commonly stated "derivative condition"

$$
y_p' = u_1y_1' + u_2y_2'
$$

is simply the product-rule derivative of $y_p$ *after* we impose $u_1'y_1+u_2'y_2=0.$

This constraint has two key benefits:

1\. *It produces a solvable system.* Substituting $y_p$ into the differential equation gives one equation in $u_1'$ and $u_2'.$  The constraint $u_1'y_1 + u_2'y_2=0$ gives a second equation.

2\. *It simplifies the computation of $y_p''.$* Since the $u_1'y_1$ and $u_2'y_2$ terms vanish, the expression for $y_p''$ becomes simpler, and the final system for $u_1'$ and $u_2'$ is easier to solve.

This is why variation of parameters uses the constraint $u_1'y_1 + u_2'y_2 = 0,$ and why it leads to the simplified expression $y_p' = u_1y_1' + u_2y_2'.$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186147706 :activity/expected-seconds 480.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id 17592186064275 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-e241dd2f-cf9d-55b1-810e-b45db1f40880" "question-3bf93bdf-40a6-507b-8e4d-2fa269000a75" "question-354ae055-47d1-5393-8d47-099f76806cac" "question-c4cdcaf7-2982-5947-b7f9-f0933f5cb1a5" "question-6b9e1a36-03a5-51c4-becb-f3f4b938141f"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186064118 :question/problem "The function $f(x)$ is defined for every real number $x$ and is given by

$a=$ {{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "To calculate the limit, we multiply the numerator and the denominator by the conjugate of the denominator. We get

f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{x}{\sqrt{x+k}-\sqrt{k}}, & x\ne 0, \\ 18, & x=0.\end{aligned}
$$

If $f(x)$ is continuous at $x=0$, what is the value of $k?$" :question/worked-solution "From the definition of $f(x),$

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 0}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{x}{\sqrt{x+k}-\sqrt{k}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}(\frac{x}{\sqrt{x+k}-\sqrt{k}}\cdot \frac{\sqrt{x+k}+\sqrt{k}}{\sqrt{x+k}+\sqrt{k}}) \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{x(\sqrt{x+k}+\sqrt{k})}{x+k-k} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{\cancel{x}(\sqrt{x+k}+\sqrt{k})}{\cancel{x}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}(\sqrt{x+k}+\sqrt{k}) \\  & =\sqrt{0+k}+\sqrt{k} \\  & =2\sqrt{k}.\end{aligned}
$$

In order for $f(x)$ to be continuous at $x=0,$ we must have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 0}f(x) & =f(0) \\ 2\sqrt{k} & =18 \\ \sqrt{k} & =9 \\ k & =81.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-fe2b2c06-359a-556f-b20c-5c316319fefe"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-fe2b2c06-359a-556f-b20c-5c316319fefe" :answer-field/id #uuid "fe2b2c06-359a-556f-b20c-5c316319fefe" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-331d3ba3-7d70-552c-9017-a789e832ecce" :answer-field/choices ["answer-a1847f87-ec08-58e3-8324-c070554a3699" "answer-059675b4-5317-52c5-9e12-a825b02e678a" "answer-ffa20eb0-d1e6-5ca7-86c5-1fe41e49f4b3" "answer-9d3dc435-4333-5003-b8cf-c80d000a682d" "answer-331d3ba3-7d70-552c-9017-a789e832ecce"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-a1847f87-ec08-58e3-8324-c070554a3699" :answer/id #uuid "a1847f87-ec08-58e3-8324-c070554a3699" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "25" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-059675b4-5317-52c5-9e12-a825b02e678a" :answer/id #uuid "059675b4-5317-52c5-9e12-a825b02e678a" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "27" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-ffa20eb0-d1e6-5ca7-86c5-1fe41e49f4b3" :answer/id #uuid "ffa20eb0-d1e6-5ca7-86c5-1fe41e49f4b3" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "34" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-9d3dc435-4333-5003-b8cf-c80d000a682d" :answer/id #uuid "9d3dc435-4333-5003-b8cf-c80d000a682d" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "64" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-331d3ba3-7d70-552c-9017-a789e832ecce" :answer/id #uuid "331d3ba3-7d70-552c-9017-a789e832ecce" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "81" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-1326dade-f2c7-5d3e-a020-cedd74fc345f" :question/id #uuid "1326dade-f2c7-5d3e-a020-cedd74fc345f" :question/math-academy-id "q-342648" :question/problem "The function $g(x)$ is given by

$$
g(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{x}{\sqrt{x-b}-\sqrt{2{x}^{2}-b}}, & x\ne 0, \\ 10, & x=0.\end{aligned}
$$

For what value of $b$ is the function continuous at $x=0?$

$b=$
{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "To calculate the limit, we multiply the numerator and the denominator by the conjugate of the numerator. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 0}g(x) & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{x}{\sqrt{x-b}-\sqrt{2{x}^{2}-b}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}(\frac{x}{\sqrt{x-b}-\sqrt{2{x}^{2}-b}}\cdot \frac{\sqrt{x-b}+\sqrt{2{x}^{2}-b}}{\sqrt{x-b}+\sqrt{2{x}^{2}-b}}) \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{x(\sqrt{x-b}+\sqrt{2{x}^{2}-b})}{(\sqrt{x-b})^{2}-(\sqrt{2{x}^{2}-b})^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{x(\sqrt{x-b}+\sqrt{2{x}^{2}-b})}{x-2{x}^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{x(\sqrt{x-b}+\sqrt{2{x}^{2}-b})}{x(1-2x)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{\cancel{x}(\sqrt{x-b}+\sqrt{2{x}^{2}-b})}{\cancel{x}(1-2x)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{\sqrt{x-b}+\sqrt{2{x}^{2}-b}}{1-2x} \\  & =2\sqrt{-b}.\end{aligned}
$$

In order for $g(x)$ to be continuous at $x=0,$ we must have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 0}g(x) & =g(0) \\ 2\sqrt{-b} & =10 \\ \sqrt{-b} & =5 \\ -b & =25 \\ b & =-25.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, setting $b=-25$ removes the point discontinuity." :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-77bbd51e-5904-5d45-8bc3-de4505ff154f"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-77bbd51e-5904-5d45-8bc3-de4505ff154f" :answer-field/id #uuid "77bbd51e-5904-5d45-8bc3-de4505ff154f" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-24ede090-0e98-526f-95c9-95e8850bcb72" :answer-field/choices ["answer-24ede090-0e98-526f-95c9-95e8850bcb72"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-24ede090-0e98-526f-95c9-95e8850bcb72" :answer/id #uuid "24ede090-0e98-526f-95c9-95e8850bcb72" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-25" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186065391 :tutorial/content "Consider the function $f(x)$ below.
![](images/20/20b2fd99ae051c3447e4c3530fee053b248393147a8295d3a9451524d7534f52.svg)

The function $f(x)$ seems to have a point discontinuity at $x=4.$ However, by selecting a particular value for $a,$ we can remove the point discontinuity and make the function continuous.

We can find this value of $a$ by forcing the limit of the function to be equal to the value of the function at $x=4\mathbin{:}$

$$
\lim\limits_{x\to 4} f(x) = f(4)
$$

Remember that $\lim\limits_{x\to 4} f(x)$ represents the value that $f(x)$ approaches as $x$ gets closer and closer, but not equal, to $4.$ So, when evaluating $\lim\limits_{x\to 4} f(x),$ we need to use the function definition for $x \neq 4.$

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 4}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to 4}(3x+a) \\  & =3(4)+a \\  & =12+a\end{aligned}
$$

At $x=4,$ the function is defined as $f(x)=13.$ So $f(4)=13,$ and we can solve the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 4}f(x) & =f(4) \\ 12+a & =13 \\ a & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, to make $f(x)$ continuous at $x=4,$ we need to choose $a=1.$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186064432 :activity/expected-seconds 540.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} [:db/retract 17592186189604 :answer-field/choices 17592186189605] [:db/retract 17592186189604 :answer-field/choices 17592186189606] [:db/retract 17592186189604 :answer-field/choices 17592186189607] [:db/retract 17592186189604 :answer-field/choices 17592186189608] [:db/retract 17592186189604 :answer-field/choices 17592186189609] {:db/id 17592186192627 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-8301710f-dfbb-5680-866d-b67f486e14d7" "question-a4783dad-574a-5127-8f16-79c4f5746713"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186192581 :question/worked-solution "The inequality $x \geq 1$ corresponds to all numbers greater than or equal to $1.$ A number line for this inequality is shown below:

![](images/82/829c0bd7c365ef7e5b1d3bee70a632b34cd644349a7528b688abdfd57575a1ab.png)

From the segment on the number line, we have the following:

- The left endpoint $1$ *is* included in the interval.

- There is no right endpoint - it continues forever. So, we write the interval with infinity as the right endpoint, not included.

Therefore, using interval notation, we represent $x \geq 1$ as

$$
x \in [1,\infty).
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186192628 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-df8b3cd8-e582-5e68-8862-832cf8d8a7f7" "question-05484b4a-57a2-55c2-9049-f423ce09e86a"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186192582 :question/problem "What inequality corresponds the interval $x\in\left[5, \infty\right)?$" :question/worked-solution "The statement $x\in\left[5, \infty\right)$ means that $x$ lies between $5$ and $\infty,$ where 

- the left endpoint $5$ *is* included, and

- the right endpoint $\infty$ is *not* included.

Therefore, the inequality represented by this interval is 

$$
5 \leq   x <     \infty.
$$

However, since all numbers are smaller than infinity, it suffices to write 

$$
5 \leq   x
$$

or, equivalently, 

$$
x \geq 5.
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186192629 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-7495bbc7-a548-574a-82ac-70b0b5806589" "question-0b34c9dd-15c6-517b-a545-622b3797f82a"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186192583 :question/worked-solution "The inequality $x \leq 1$ corresponds to all numbers less than or equal to $1.$ A number line for this interval is shown below:

- The right endpoint $1$ *is* included in the interval.

Therefore, using interval notation, we represent $x \leq 1$ as

$$
x\in(-\infty, 1].
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186192630 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-ca3bed50-c15f-520c-b7d3-e53cd1fcae8f" "question-6d843358-b3f1-509e-8689-eba95475d008"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186192584 :question/problem "What inequality corresponds to the interval $x\in\left(-\infty, 9\right)?$" :question/worked-solution "The statement $x \in \left(-\infty, 9\right)$ means that $x$ lies between $-\infty$ and $9,$ where

$$
x > 0
$$

We can represent this inequality using a number line as follows:

![](images/79/79664d125db14d5b8534d592d232839659a6d0efbd527379207b50d71f9e7454.png)

How do we represent this inequality using interval notation?

Note the following:

- The left endpoint $x=0$ is *not* included. Therefore, we use a parenthesis $($ for this endpoint.

- The interval continues forever in the positive direction. To denote this, we must introduce the **infinity** symbol $\infty.$ Infinity is not a number but a concept that means *larger than any number*.

- We use a right parenthesis $)$ in conjunction with the $\infty$ symbol.

Therefore, we can express the inequality $x > 0$ in interval notation as follows:

$$
x \in (0, \infty)
$$

**Watch Out!** Whenever $\infty$ appears in an interval, it is *always* associated with a right parenthesis. Infinity is *never* associated with a bracket, even if the other endpoint is." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186193940 :tutorial/content "Now, consider the following inequality: 

$$
x \lt 0
$$

We can represent this inequality using a number line as follows:

![](images/52/52be4b1ae3d32f2d3bb1dbf9f4faa1f288cff5736870064533b958ac89a76dad.png)

To represent this inequality using interval notation, we note the following:

- The right endpoint $x=0$ is *not* included. Therefore, we use a parenthesis $)$ for this endpoint.

- The interval continues forever in the negative direction. To denote this, we use the **negative infinity** symbol $-\infty.$ We use a left parenthesis $($ in conjunction with the negative infinity symbol.

Therefore, we can express the inequality $x < 0$ in interval notation as follows:

$$
x \in (-\infty, 0)
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186192906 :activity/expected-seconds 420.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id 17592186124608 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-dfe98e1c-3b93-5422-932b-6229fbfa5965"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186124610 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-adb4921d-df66-5c35-baf2-cc613e0cb3d4"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186124451 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-d66b6ff3-5c30-5d09-a1a7-0b4d573341bb"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186125256 :question/problem "Let $f(x,y)$ be a differentiable function such that

$$
f(1,1)=1,\,{f}_{x}(x,y)=3{x}^{2}{y}^{4},\,{f}_{y}(x,y)=4{x}^{3}{y}^{3}.
$$

Using a linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(1,1),$ estimate the value of $f(1.02,0.97).$" :question/worked-solution "The linear approximation of the function $f$ at the point $(a,b)$ is given by

$$
f(x,y)≈f(a,b)+∇f(a,b)\cdot ⟨x-a,y-b⟩.
$$

So, the linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(1,1)$ is:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ≈f(1,1)+∇f(1,1)\cdot ⟨x-1,y-1⟩ \\  & ≈f(1,1)+⟨{f}_{x}(1,1),{f}_{y}(1,1)⟩\cdot ⟨x-1,y-1⟩ \\  & ≈1+⟨{f}_{x}(1,1),{f}_{y}(1,1)⟩\cdot ⟨x-1,y-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we find ${f}_{x}(1,1)$ and ${f}_{y}(1,1)$ using the given partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(1,1) & =3(1)^{2}(1)^{4}=3 \\ {f}_{y}(1,1) & =4(1)^{3}(1)^{3}=4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
f(x,y)≈1+⟨3,4⟩\cdot ⟨x-1,y-1⟩
$$

Finally, we can estimate $f(1.02,0.97)$ by evaluating the linear approximation at $x=1.02$ and $y=0.97,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(1.02,0.97) & ≈1+⟨3,4⟩\cdot ⟨1.02-1,0.97-1⟩ \\  & =1+⟨3,4⟩\cdot ⟨0.02,-0.03⟩ \\  & =1+0.06-0.12 \\  & =0.94\end{aligned}

$$

Using a linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(-1,0),$ estimate the value of $f(-1.01,0.01).$" :question/worked-solution "The linear approximation of the function $f$ at the point $(a,b)$ is given by

$$
f(x,y)≈f(a,b)+∇f(a,b)\cdot ⟨x-a,y-b⟩.
$$

So, the linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(-1,0)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ≈f(-1,0)+∇f(-1,0)\cdot ⟨x-(-1),y-0⟩ \\  & ≈f(-1,0)+⟨{f}_{x}(-1,0),{f}_{y}(-1,0)⟩\cdot ⟨x+1,y⟩ \\  & ≈2+⟨{f}_{x}(-1,0),{f}_{y}(-1,0)⟩\cdot ⟨x+1,y⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we find ${f}_{x}(-1,0)$ and ${f}_{y}(-1,0)$ using the given partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(-1,0) & =4(-1)=-4 \\ {f}_{y}(-1,0) & =6(0)=0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
f(x,y)≈2+⟨-4,0⟩\cdot ⟨x+1,y⟩.
$$

Finally, we can estimate $f(-1.01,0.01)$ by evaluating the linear approximation at $x=-1.01$ and $y=0.01,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(-1.01,0.01) & ≈2+⟨-4,0⟩\cdot ⟨-1.01+1,0.01⟩ \\  & =2+⟨-4,0⟩\cdot ⟨-0.01,0.01⟩ \\  & =2-4(-0.01)+0(0.01) \\  & =2+0.04+0 \\  & =2.04\end{aligned}

$$

the linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(1,0,2).$" :question/worked-solution "The linear approximation of the function $f$ at the point $(a,b,c)$ is given by

$$
f(x,y,z)≈f(a,b,c)+∇f(a,b,c)\cdot ⟨x-a,y-b,z-c⟩.
$$

So, the linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(1,0,2)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & ≈f(1,0,2)+∇f(1,0,2)\cdot ⟨x-1,y,z-2⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

From the definition of $f,$ we have that $f(1,0,2)=2.$ Computing the partial derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x} & =2xz\,⇒\,{f}_{x}(1,0,2)=4, \\ {f}_{y} & =-2y\,⇒\,{f}_{y}(1,0,2)=0, \\ {f}_{z} & ={x}^{2}\,⇒\,{f}_{z}(1,0,2)=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the gradient of the function at the point $(1,0,2)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(1,0,2) & =⟨{f}_{x}(1,0,2),{f}_{y}(1,0,2),{f}_{z}(1,0,2)⟩ \\  & =⟨4,0,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the linear approximation of the function $f$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & ≈f(1,0,2)+∇f(1,0,2)\cdot ⟨x-1,y,z-2⟩ \\  & ≈2+⟨4,0,1⟩\cdot ⟨x-1,y,z-2⟩ \\  & ≈2+4(x-1)+0(y)+(z-2) \\  & ≈-4+4x+z.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-531515dc-d792-550d-b5bf-9db7ffa81bdf"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-531515dc-d792-550d-b5bf-9db7ffa81bdf" :answer-field/id #uuid "531515dc-d792-550d-b5bf-9db7ffa81bdf" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-47f1f736-9ce9-5cac-950e-771e037ad90b" :answer-field/choices ["answer-9d9e6cd4-918b-5fdf-8fab-439839fcb9fa" "answer-3b911150-117d-5354-83c0-6cdaf5fb85a2" "answer-47f1f736-9ce9-5cac-950e-771e037ad90b" "answer-6f0da771-d211-5e7f-9eb1-b6339fde5443" "answer-1205b66d-2ea8-57c6-8f6d-0b9c7514c512"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-9d9e6cd4-918b-5fdf-8fab-439839fcb9fa" :answer/id #uuid "9d9e6cd4-918b-5fdf-8fab-439839fcb9fa" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "f(x,y,z)≈-1+x-y+z" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-3b911150-117d-5354-83c0-6cdaf5fb85a2" :answer/id #uuid "3b911150-117d-5354-83c0-6cdaf5fb85a2" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "f(x,y,z)≈-2+4x-y" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-47f1f736-9ce9-5cac-950e-771e037ad90b" :answer/id #uuid "47f1f736-9ce9-5cac-950e-771e037ad90b" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "f(x,y,z)≈-4+4x+z" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-6f0da771-d211-5e7f-9eb1-b6339fde5443" :answer/id #uuid "6f0da771-d211-5e7f-9eb1-b6339fde5443" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "f(x,y,z)≈3+x+2y-z" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-1205b66d-2ea8-57c6-8f6d-0b9c7514c512" :answer/id #uuid "1205b66d-2ea8-57c6-8f6d-0b9c7514c512" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "f(x,y,z)≈4+2y-z" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]}]

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}f({x}_{i})\cdot Δx,
$$

    

where $Δx=\frac{b-a}{n}$ and ${x}_{i}=a+iΔx.$

In the definite integral

$$
{\int }_{1}^{5}(\operatorname{arctan}⁡(x)+2)\,\text{d}x,
$$

the function is $f(x)=\operatorname{arctan}⁡(x)+2,$ the lower bound is $a=1,$ and the upper bound is $b=5.$ So, we have

$$
Δx=\frac{5-1}{n}=\frac{4}{n},
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{5}(\operatorname{arctan}⁡(x)+2)\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}f({x}_{i})\cdot Δx \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}[f(1+i\cdot \frac{4}{n})\cdot \frac{4}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}[f(1+\frac{4i}{n})\cdot \frac{4}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}[(\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\,1+\frac{4i}{n}\,)+2)\,\cdot \frac{4}{n}].\end{aligned}

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=0}^{n-1}f({x}_{k})\cdot Δx
$$

where $Δx=\frac{b-a}{n}$ and ${x}_{k}=a+kΔx.$

Notice that we're given that the lower limit $a=1.$ 

Comparing the given summation with the general expression above, we see that $Δx=\frac{2}{n}.$ Therefore, 

$$
\frac{2}{n}=\frac{b-1}{n}\,⟹\,b=3.
$$

Consequently, ${x}_{k}=1+\frac{2k}{n}$ and $f({x}_{k})=7{x}_{k}^{-3}.$

Hence,

$$
{\int }_{1}^{3}7{x}^{-3}\,\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=0}^{n-1}[7{(1+\frac{2k}{n})}^{-3}\cdot \frac{2}{n}].
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is 

$$
f(x)=7{x}^{-3}\,\text{and}\,b=3.

the function is $f(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x),$ the lower bound is $a=0$ and the upper bound is $b=\pi /6.$ So, we have

$$

$)^{\,3}\cdot \frac{2}{n}]$" :question/worked-solution "The definite integral can be defined in terms of the limit of a right Riemann sum as

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}f({x}_{i})\cdot Δx,
$$

where ${x}_{i}=a+iΔx$ and $Δx=\frac{b-a}{n}.$

In the definite integral

$$
{\int }_{0}^{2}(x+2)^{3}\,\text{d}x,
$$

the function is $f(x)=(x+2)^{3},$ the lower bound is $a=0$ and the upper bound is $b=2.$ So, we have

$$
Δx=\frac{2-0}{n}=\frac{2}{n}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2}(x+2)^{3}\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}f({x}_{i})\cdot Δx \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}[f(0+i\cdot \frac{2}{n})\cdot \frac{2}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}[f(\frac{2i}{n})\cdot \frac{2}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}[{(\,\frac{2i}{n}+2\,)}^{\,3}\cdot \frac{2}{n}].\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-d284849d-09d1-59ac-a76f-00d1db75563f"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-d284849d-09d1-59ac-a76f-00d1db75563f" :answer-field/id #uuid "d284849d-09d1-59ac-a76f-00d1db75563f" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-f116d16e-87ef-5163-a0be-ec090d753eb4" :answer-field/choices ["answer-f116d16e-87ef-5163-a0be-ec090d753eb4"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-f116d16e-87ef-5163-a0be-ec090d753eb4" :answer/id #uuid "f116d16e-87ef-5163-a0be-ec090d753eb4" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{2i}{n}+2" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186097910 :tutorial/content "Suppose that we want to approximate the area $\mathcal A$ bound by the curve $y= x^2+1$ and the lines $x=0,$ $x=1,$ and the $x$-axis. We can do this using a left Riemann sum with $n=4$ subintervals, as shown below:

![](images/1b/1b25a722d5527db77cd7dd5fb581c0ffed9b9324913d390e2633211360b6a8ab.png)

A better approximation can be found by taking more subintervals. For instance, taking $n=8$ subintervals gives:

![](images/17/17f6c8e458b2e6fbd887728cbbcc7cb64a670598256f76cad69d9e5a9c3cf7b5.png)

As we continue to increase $n,$ our approximation gets better and better. In fact, we can get an *exact* value for the area by taking the limit of the Riemann sum as $n\to\infty.$

Let's write down that limit. First, we need to express the left Riemann sum using sigma notation. Using $n$ subintervals between the endpoints $a=0$ and $b=1,$ we express

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ≈{\sum }_{k=0}^{n-1}f({x}_{k})Δx \\  & ={\sum }_{k=0}^{n-1}f(0+k\cdot Δx)Δx \\  & ={\sum }_{k=0}^{n-1}f(k\cdot Δx)Δx \\  & ={\sum }_{k=0}^{n-1}({(k\cdot Δx)}^{2}+1)Δx \\  & ={\sum }_{k=0}^{n-1}({k}^{2}\cdot \frac{1}{{n}^{2}}+1)\cdot \frac{1}{n} \\  & ={\sum }_{k=0}^{n-1}(\frac{{k}^{2}}{{n}^{2}}+1)\cdot \frac{1}{n}.\end{aligned}
$$

In the above, we used the fact that $x_k = 0 + k\Delta x = k\Delta x$ and $\Delta x = \dfrac{1 - 0}{n} = \dfrac 1 n,$ as we've seen before.

The exact area is found by computing the limit as $n\to\infty.$ So instead of using an approximation symbol $(\approx),$ we can now use an equality symbol and write

$$
A = \lim_{n\to\infty}\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\left(\dfrac{k^2}{n^2} + 1\right)\cdot \dfrac{1}{n}.
$$

The formula above is a bit clunky, so instead of writing it using limits and sigma notation, we introduce a new notation called the **definite integral**, defined as

$$
\mathcal{A} = \lim_{n\to\infty}\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\left(\dfrac{k^2}{n^2} + 1\right)\cdot \dfrac{1}{n}= \int_0^1 (x^2 + 1)\, \textrm{d}x.
$$

In our example, 

$$
\displaystyle \int_0^1 (x^2+1)\, \textrm{d}x
$$

can be interpreted as the exact area under the graph of $y = f(x) = x^2+1$ between $x=0,$ $x=1,$ and the $x$-axis." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186097911 :tutorial/content "In general, for a function $f(x)$ defined on $[a,b],$ the **definite integral** of $f(x)$ between $x=a$ and $x=b$ can be defined using the limit of a left  Riemann sum as

$$
\int_a^b f(x)\textrm{d}x = \lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\sum_{k=0}^{n-1} f(x_k)\Delta x,
$$

    

where $\Delta x = \dfrac{b-a}{n}$ and $x_k = a + k\Delta x.$

The limit $x=a$ is referred to as the **lower limit**, whereas $x=b$ is called the **upper limit**." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186096875 :activity/expected-seconds 960.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id 17592186097447 :step/math-academy-id 631552 :db/ensure [:step/validate]} {:db/id 17592186097449 :step/math-academy-id 631553 :db/ensure [:step/validate]} {:db/id 17592186097448 :step/math-academy-id 631554 :db/ensure [:step/validate]} {:db/id 17592186097450 :step/math-academy-id 631557 :db/ensure [:step/validate]} {:db/id 17592186097451 :step/math-academy-id 631560 :db/ensure [:step/validate]} {:db/id 17592186097452 :step/math-academy-id 631563 :db/ensure [:step/validate]} {:db/id 17592186097453 :step/math-academy-id 631564 :db/ensure [:step/validate]} [:db/retract 17592186127711 :answer-field/choices 17592186127712] [:db/retract 17592186127711 :answer-field/choices 17592186127713] [:db/retract 17592186127711 :answer-field/choices 17592186127714] [:db/retract 17592186127711 :answer-field/choices 17592186127715] [:db/retract 17592186127711 :answer-field/choices 17592186127716] {:db/id 17592186129089 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-3f8dfca9-4caa-51a0-a26a-4299455440e3" "question-c798fdda-953e-5d91-a2f9-32a46093ebbe" "question-b8d4049d-0cbf-5d7d-aff8-ae877201f7a7" "question-f32b0e13-9234-5f0f-8ec6-055e7e55ffd4"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186128903 :question/worked-solution "The function has discontinuities due to vertical asymptotes at $x=\pm 1.$ Note that

$$
\lim_{x\to (-1)^{+}} f(x) = -\infty,
$$

which is enough to conclude that there is a discontinuity due to a vertical asymptote at $x=-1.$ Similarly

$$
\lim_{x\to 1^{-}} f(x) = \infty,
$$

which is enough to conclude that there is a discontinuity due to a vertical asymptote at $x=1.$

There is also a discontinuity at $x=-2,$ but this is a point discontinuity, not a discontinuity due to a vertical asymptote." :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186129090 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-c899081f-aaf3-5d73-a009-6354d1a2e255" "question-e2b2de31-2e08-55fe-906d-b2e8d713411d" "question-51bf4893-7d23-5880-bdd4-7c570a118b95" "question-5f60286b-a701-5a91-9733-7afc68b9ba06" "question-d79ab0ee-343a-572d-8ea7-20c9b4a3405e"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186128904 :question/worked-solution "Infinite discontinuities coincide with the vertical asymptotes of $y=f(x).$ 

To find the vertical asymptotes, let's start by factoring the expression in the denominator. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{1}{{x}^{2}-5x+6} \\  & =\frac{1}{(x-3)(x-2)}.\end{aligned}
$$

There are no common factors in the numerator and denominator, so we can find the vertical asymptotes by setting the denominator to zero:

$$
(x-3)(x-2) = 0 \qquad \Longrightarrow\qquad x=2,3.
$$

Therefore, the function has infinite discontinuities at $x=2$ and $x=3.$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186129091 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-cdf00b6e-c9c6-53a7-abba-5979171f25e7" "question-a3713990-073a-5c59-933e-791d16a2c49e" "question-a9115fbc-4fac-58df-8796-79802b979ca7" "question-adf0b53d-c3e9-5c25-81fa-45a5c95eb4da" "question-f55b2c6c-0d34-5876-a0ba-01591a852f5d"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186128905 :question/worked-solution "Infinite discontinuities coincide with the vertical asymptotes of $y=f(x).$

To find the vertical asymptotes, we set the denominator equal to zero and solve:

Therefore, the function has an infinite discontinuity at $x=-2.$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186129092 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-bccf9705-1345-5b91-b48e-5b2d9522eb17" "question-28d2bedc-f4b0-58dc-80a4-886e3d716859" "question-af7b8af8-e50c-5536-8725-7ed61d38a3dd" "question-57542381-13e5-59f8-9ea4-61779c51f267" "question-fdd8bd57-2d2f-5ace-b80e-0473ac5a0a46"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186128906 :question/problem "Find all of the points where $f(x)$ below has infinite discontinuities.

![](images/2b/2b1f430a78861fce15c689843d0e4af5376e0f600b650b0a614257d86365cd29.svg)" :question/worked-solution "Infinite discontinuities coincide with the vertical asymptotes of $y=f(x).$ The only possible way that $y=f(x)$ can have vertical asymptotes is if either $\dfrac{1}{x-5}$ or $\dfrac{1}{x-4}$ grow without bound within their respective subdomains.

- We first compute the asymptotes of $\dfrac{1}{x-5}.$ Setting the denominator equal to zero, we get

$$
x-5=0\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad x=5.
$$

Although this branch of the function is defined for $x < 5$, we do have that

$$
\lim_{x\to 5^{-}}\left(\dfrac{1}{x-5}\right) = -\infty,
$$

and therefore we conclude that $x=5$ is indeed an infinite discontinuity.

- Next, we compute the asymptotes of $\dfrac{1}{x-4}.$ Setting the denominator equal to zero, we get

$$
x-4=0\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad x=4.
$$

However, this branch of the function is defined for $x \geq 5,$ which does not contain the neighborhood of $x=4.$ So $x=4$ cannot be a vertical asymptote, and therefore $x=4$ cannot be an infinite discontinuity.

$$

$$

$$
(2x+1)(x-2)=0\,⟹\,x=-\frac{1}{2},2.
$$

 has an infinite discontinuity are

{{field-2}}." :question/worked-solution "Infinite discontinuities coincide with the vertical asymptotes of $y=f(x).$ The only possible way that $y=f(x)$ can have vertical asymptotes is if either $\frac{1}{5-x}$ or $\frac{1}{8-x}$ grow without bound within its respective subdomain.

- We first compute the asymptotes of $\frac{1}{5-x}.$ Setting the denominator equal to zero, we get

$$
5-x=0\,⟹\,x=5.
$$

Although this branch of the function is defined for $x<5,$ which excludes $x=5,$ we have that

$$
{lim}_{x\to {5}^{-}}(\frac{1}{5-x})=+\infty ,
$$

and therefore we conclude that $x=5$ is an infinite discontinuity.

- Next, we compute the asymptotes of $\frac{1}{8-x}.$ Setting the denominator equal to zero, we get

$$
8-x=0\,⟹\,x=8.
$$

Although this branch of the function is defined for $5\le x<8$ and $x>8,$ which excludes $x=8,$ we have that

$$
{lim}_{x\to {8}^{-}}(\frac{1}{8-x})=\infty \,,\,{lim}_{x\to {8}^{+}}(\frac{1}{8-x})=-\infty ,
$$

and therefore we conclude that $x=8$ is an infinite discontinuity.

Therefore, from left to right, the function $y=f(x)$ has infinite discontinuities at 

$$
x=5\,\text{and}\,x=8.
$$

has an  infinite discontinuity at $x=${{field-1}}." :question/worked-solution "Infinite discontinuities coincide with the vertical asymptotes of $y=f(x).$ The only possible way that $y=f(x)$ can have vertical asymptotes is if either ${x}^{2}-1$ or $\frac{2}{x-1}$ grows without bound within its respective subdomain.

$$
x-1=0\,⟹\,x=1.
$$

Although this branch of the function is defined for $x>1$, we have that

$$
{lim}_{x\to {1}^{+}}(\frac{2}{x-1})=\infty ,
$$

and therefore we conclude that $x=1$ is indeed an infinite discontinuity.

![](images/cc/cc9593860b0c134d0d99635b37eeac4f16a712a7af9e1c6474fcf1f885e8451e.png)

The function has a vertical asymptote at $x=0.$ There is also a discontinuity in the function at $x=0,$ since we cannot draw the points on the curve without taking our pen off the paper to cross the asymptote.

So, we say that $y = \dfrac 1 x$ has a **discontinuity due to a vertical asymptote** at $x=0.$ Discontinuities due to vertical asymptotes are also called **infinite discontinuities**.

Notice that here, both one-sided limits are infinite:

$$
\lim_{x\to 0^-} \left(\dfrac 1 x\right) =-\infty\qquad\text{and}\qquad\lim_{x\to 0^+} \left(\dfrac 1 x \right)=\infty.
$$

In general, a function $y=f(x)$ has a discontinuity due to a vertical asymptote at $x=c$ if either one-sided limit is infinite:

$$
\lim_{x\to c^-} f(x) =\pm \infty\qquad\text{or}\qquad\lim_{x\to c^+} f(x) =\pm \infty.
$$

Note that we only need a single limit to become infinite to conclude that there is an infinite discontinuity at $x=c.$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186129349 :activity/expected-seconds 540.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id 17592186184238 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-779dfcc0-3a36-5636-a5d6-b4ea61af4fcc" "question-81d25b33-02da-5a6a-a064-091425605527" "question-275cbf3f-d183-51d1-83d2-3cab6277b499" "question-2ac5902a-7a9e-53bd-a352-8c43204e3720"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186184239 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-d32420f7-bf1c-5010-9d26-1f698469ec0b" "question-d0a1a56f-e520-52c2-bfca-2937cd7b17ca"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186184240 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-55ce71ca-d33d-5c8b-9d05-07e0dca2765b" "question-78505148-e7b2-516b-80ad-17e7629d4193" "question-cdfb619c-431d-5983-938b-5503bb7b30f1"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-779dfcc0-3a36-5636-a5d6-b4ea61af4fcc" :question/id #uuid "779dfcc0-3a36-5636-a5d6-b4ea61af4fcc" :question/math-academy-id "q-339135" :question/problem "Evaluate the following limit:

$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-d1fc9040-4cdf-577b-b242-fcc38c2ab2bd"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-d1fc9040-4cdf-577b-b242-fcc38c2ab2bd" :answer-field/id #uuid "d1fc9040-4cdf-577b-b242-fcc38c2ab2bd" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-20c2c4de-610f-51d5-844f-c2ff3be490af" :answer-field/choices ["answer-20c2c4de-610f-51d5-844f-c2ff3be490af"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-20c2c4de-610f-51d5-844f-c2ff3be490af" :answer/id #uuid "20c2c4de-610f-51d5-844f-c2ff3be490af" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "1" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-cdfb619c-431d-5983-938b-5503bb7b30f1" :question/id #uuid "cdfb619c-431d-5983-938b-5503bb7b30f1" :question/math-academy-id "q-339480" :question/problem "Evaluate the following limit:

${lim}_{x\to \,\frac{1}{2}}\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{3}{4}\operatorname{arccos}⁡(x))=$
{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "![](images/85/85a182aabfe64c27eaafde94e3bdbede9409b02cfd87395cb2fc5543b09c4e05.png)

The domain of $\operatorname{arccos}⁡(x)$ is $x\in [-1,1].$

Now, substituting $x=\frac{1}{2}$ directly into the limit, we have

$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-8dc400da-c09d-518f-b91a-2b22630e2790"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-8dc400da-c09d-518f-b91a-2b22630e2790" :answer-field/id #uuid "8dc400da-c09d-518f-b91a-2b22630e2790" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-a10c49bb-a853-5a0a-96ce-acd212343d3b" :answer-field/choices ["answer-a10c49bb-a853-5a0a-96ce-acd212343d3b"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-a10c49bb-a853-5a0a-96ce-acd212343d3b" :answer/id #uuid "a10c49bb-a853-5a0a-96ce-acd212343d3b" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "1" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186185359 :tutorial/content "In this lesson, we will learn how to deal with limits involving inverse trigonometric functions. 

Let's begin by recalling the graph of $y=\arcsin(x).$

![](images/df/df22eea4331c47da3047381ca672fd80ebf75118054316fe88c0e2d96dae0d34.png)

Using the graph, we note the following:

- The domain of $\arcsin(x)$ is $x \in [-1,1].$

- For every value $a \in (-1,1),$ we have

$$
\lim_\limits{x\to a} \arcsin(x) = \arcsin(a).
$$

 
In other words, we can evaluate the limit using direct substitution. For example,

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 1/2}\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(x) & =\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

- For any value $a$ that does *not* lie in the domain of $\arcsin(x),$ the limit

$$
\lim_\limits{x\to a} \arcsin(x)
$$

 
does *not* exist.

- At the point $x=-1,$ the limit does *not* exist because the left-sided limit does not exist. However, the right-sided limit *does* exist and is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (-1)^{+}}\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(x) & =\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(-1) \\  & =-\frac{\pi }{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Similarly, at the point $x=1,$ the limit does *not* exist because the right-sided limit does not exist. However, the left-sided limit *does* exist and is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {1}^{-}}\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(x) & =\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(1) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

The limit properties of $y=\arccos(x)$ are similar. Let's discuss them briefly." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186185363 :tutorial/content "Let's recall the graph of $y=\arccos(x).$

![](images/9d/9dcc5a116c2a564547283783a7df7b1cd3a9ab3b76ac24dc2695c4cb367796d5.png)

From the graph, we note the following:

- The domain is $x \in [-1,1].$

- For every value $a \in (-1,1),$ we have

$$
\lim_\limits{x\to a} \arccos(x) = \arccos(a).
$$

- For any value $a$ that does *not* lie in the domain of $\arccos(x),$ the limit

$$
\lim_\limits{x\to a} \arccos(x)
$$

 
does *not* exist.

- The right-sided limit at $x=-1$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (-1)^{+}}\operatorname{arccos}⁡(x) & =\operatorname{arccos}⁡(-1) \\  & =\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

- Similarly, the left-sided limit at $x=1$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {1}^{-}}\operatorname{arccos}⁡(x) & =\operatorname{arccos}⁡(1) \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, let's deduce the limit properties of $y = \arctan x.$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186185362 :tutorial/content "The graph of $y=\arctan x$ is shown below.

![](images/fc/fc06a4e63f38a315dd3944f65f871cca2dbdddee26ec268e857f79e5f4ab8848.png)

From the graph, we note the following:

- The domain is $x \in (-\infty, \infty).$

- For every value $a,$ we have

$$
\lim_\limits{x\to a} \arctan(x) = \arctan(a).
$$

- The limit as $x\to-\infty$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to -\infty }\operatorname{arctan}⁡(x) & =-\frac{\pi }{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

- The limit as $x\to\infty$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \infty }\operatorname{arctan}⁡(x) & =\frac{\pi }{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can use the algebra of limits to evaluate expressions involving inverse trigonometric functions. Let's see some examples." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186185360 :tutorial/content "We can deduce limits at infinity of transformed inverse trigonometric functions by sketching their graphs.

For example, let's consider the following limit:

$$
\lim_\limits{x \to \, \infty} \dfrac{2}{\pi}\arctan \left(x-\pi\right)
$$

To evaluate this limit, we first sketch the graph of  $y =\arctan \left(x-\pi\right){:}$  

![](images/51/51a0b9a210147b3791ce20a2f65320e20618826671ea6c7c31a27f8647595079.png)

The domain of   $\arctan \left(x-\pi\right)$ is $(-\infty,\infty).$   Moreover, from the graph, we see that 

$$
\lim\limits_{x\to \infty} \arctan \left(x-\pi\right)=\color{blue}{\dfrac{\pi}{2} }  .
$$

Therefore, by the algebra of limits, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \,\infty }\frac{2}{\pi }\operatorname{arctan}⁡(x-\pi ) & =\frac{2}{\pi }\cdot {lim}_{x\to \,\infty }\operatorname{arctan}⁡(x-\pi ) \\  & =\frac{2}{\pi }\cdot (\frac{\pi }{2}) \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

"question-540d859a-8179-5e53-b6ff-389c30bf0b61"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186128997 :question/worked-solution "The tangent plane to a surface is horizontal if and only if the normal vector to the tangent plane is vertical. So, let's first find the general expression of a normal vector to the surface.

Remember that the Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the surface $z=f(x,y)$ at the point $(x_0, y_0, z_0)$ on the surface can be written as

$$
z - z_0 = (x-x_0)\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}(x_0,y_0) + (y-y_0)\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}(x_0,y_0)
$$

where $\left\langle \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}(x_0,y_0), \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}(x_0,y_0), -1 \right\rangle$ represents a normal vector to the tangent plane.

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({y}^{2}+xy) \\  & =y \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{2}+xy) \\  & =2y+x\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, a normal vector to the tangent plane is 

$$
\left\langle y, \: 2y+x, \: -1 \right\rangle.
$$

We want to find where this normal vector is vertical. This means that the $x$- and $y$-components of the vector must be $0\mathbin{:}$

![](images/ec/ec631b90dd9a037263e163bc32ebd982de5f60ee813622ae7b4f1a6b153fe856.svg) 

From the first equation, we get $y=0.$ Substituting this into the second equation, we obtain 

$$
2(0) +x = 0 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad x = 0.
$$

Finally, substituting $x=0$ and $y=0$ into our function, we get

$$
z = 0^2+(0)(0)= 0.
$$

Therefore, the point where the tangent plane is horizontal is $(0,0,0).$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-bbe6eb83-f049-5d99-ba2d-54fe9f07632a" :question/id #uuid "bbe6eb83-f049-5d99-ba2d-54fe9f07632a" :question/math-academy-id "q-129449" :question/problem "Determine the equation of the tangent plane to the surface $z={y}^{2}-{x}^{2}y$ at the point $(1,0,0).$" :question/worked-solution "The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the surface $z=f(x,y)$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ on the surface can be written as

$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({y}^{2}-{x}^{2}y) \\  & =-2xy \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{2}-{x}^{2}y) \\  & =2y-{x}^{2}\end{aligned}

Next, we evaluate the partial derivatives at $(x,y)=(1,0):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}(1,0) & =-2(1)(0)=0 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y}(1,0) & =2(0)-{1}^{2}=-1\end{aligned}

$$
z-{z}_{0}=(x-{x}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),

where $⟨\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),-1⟩$ represents a normal vector to the tangent plane.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x\operatorname{ln}⁡y)=\operatorname{ln}⁡y \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(x\operatorname{ln}⁡y)=\frac{x}{y}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡y,\,\frac{x}{y},\,-1⟩.
$$

Note that the tangent plane is horizontal if and only if the normal vector is vertical. This means that the $x$- and $y$-components of the vector must be $0:$

$$
\{\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=0 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y}=0\end{aligned}\,⟹\,\{\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y=0 \\ \frac{x}{y}=0\end{aligned}
$$

 

From the first equation we get $y=1,$ while the second equation gives $x=0.$ 

Finally, substituting $x=0$ and $y=1$ into our function, we get

$$
z=0\operatorname{ln}⁡1=0.
$$

Therefore, the point where the tangent plane is horizontal is $(0,1,0).$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-ad0c27f9-210c-5ce2-b084-7092323ef65b"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-ad0c27f9-210c-5ce2-b084-7092323ef65b" :answer-field/id #uuid "ad0c27f9-210c-5ce2-b084-7092323ef65b" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-fd721e99-b5b7-5a4e-b1d8-811769a3048d" :answer-field/choices ["answer-b25d1249-7c51-5c00-b1c9-b4a6458d9224" "answer-fd721e99-b5b7-5a4e-b1d8-811769a3048d" "answer-701f9bb7-1a2b-56ef-93cd-483643dbc08a" "answer-d4c9af82-218f-589b-95f5-eb090db2877c" "answer-ec215226-6805-52c4-aba1-c30628fbeff7"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-b25d1249-7c51-5c00-b1c9-b4a6458d9224" :answer/id #uuid "b25d1249-7c51-5c00-b1c9-b4a6458d9224" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "(-1,{e}^{-1},1)" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-fd721e99-b5b7-5a4e-b1d8-811769a3048d" :answer/id #uuid "fd721e99-b5b7-5a4e-b1d8-811769a3048d" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "(0,1,0)" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-701f9bb7-1a2b-56ef-93cd-483643dbc08a" :answer/id #uuid "701f9bb7-1a2b-56ef-93cd-483643dbc08a" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "(1,e,1)" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-d4c9af82-218f-589b-95f5-eb090db2877c" :answer/id #uuid "d4c9af82-218f-589b-95f5-eb090db2877c" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "(2,1,0)" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-ec215226-6805-52c4-aba1-c30628fbeff7" :answer/id #uuid "ec215226-6805-52c4-aba1-c30628fbeff7" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "(2,e,2)" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186342097 :question/worked-solution "The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the surface $z=f(x,y)$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ on the surface can be written as

$$
z-{z}_{0}=(x-{x}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),

where $⟨\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),-1⟩$ represents a normal vector to the tangent plane.

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}-2x+{y}^{2}+6y+10) \\  & =2x-2 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}-2x+{y}^{2}+6y+10) \\  & =2y+6\end{aligned}
$$

 

Hence, the normal vector to the tangent plane is 

$$
⟨2x-2,\,2y+6,\,-1⟩.
$$

Note that the tangent plane is horizontal if and only if the normal vector is vertical. This means that the $x$- and $y$-components of the vector must be $0:$

$$
\{\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=0 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y}=0\end{aligned}\,⟹\,\{\begin{aligned}2x-2=0 \\ 2y+6=0\end{aligned}
$$

 

From the first equation, we get $x=1$ while the second equation gives $y=-3.$ 

Finally, substituting $x=1$ and $y=-3$ into our function, we get

$$

$$

Therefore, the point where the tangent plane is horizontal is $(1,-3,0).$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186403710 :question/worked-solution "The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the surface $z=f(x,y)$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ on the surface can be written as

$$

where $⟨\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),-1⟩$ represents a normal vector to the tangent plane.

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{3}-3x+{y}^{2}+2y) \\  & =3{x}^{2}-3 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{3}-3x+{y}^{2}+2y) \\  & =2y+2\end{aligned}

Hence, the normal vector to the tangent plane is 

$$

Note that the tangent plane is horizontal if and only if the normal vector is vertical. This means that the $x$- and $y$-components of the vector must be $0:$

$$
\{\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=0 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y}=0\end{aligned}\,⟹\,\{\begin{aligned}3{x}^{2}-3=0 \\ 2y+2=0\end{aligned}
$$

 

From the first equation, we get $x=\pm 1$ while the second equation gives $y=-1.$ 

Finally, substituting $x=-1$ and $y=-1$ into our function, we get

$$
z=(-1)^{3}-3(-1)+(-1)^{2}+2(-1)=1.
$$

Substituting $x=1$ and $y=-1$ into our function, we get

$$
z=(1)^{3}-3(1)+(-1)^{2}+2(-1)=-3.
$$

Therefore, the points where the tangent plane is horizontal are $(-1,-1,1)$ and $(1,-1,-3).$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-8c4b6aea-97fe-50e3-9ab8-7b3e7d7d950a" :question/id #uuid "8c4b6aea-97fe-50e3-9ab8-7b3e7d7d950a" :question/math-academy-id "q-73855" :question/problem "At which points on the surface $z={e}^{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}$ is the tangent plane horizontal?" :question/worked-solution "The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the surface $z=f(x,y)$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ on the surface can be written as

z-{z}_{0}=(x-{x}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),

where $⟨\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),-1⟩$ represents a normal vector to the tangent plane.

$$

 

Hence, the normal vector to the tangent plane is 

$$
⟨2x{e}^{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}},\,2y{e}^{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}},\,-1⟩.
$$

Note that the tangent plane is horizontal if and only if the normal vector is vertical. This means that the $x$- and $y$-components of the vector must be $0:$

$$

:question/problem "At which points on the surface $z=xy-3x+2y-5$ is the tangent plane horizontal?" :question/worked-solution "The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the surface $z=f(x,y)$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ on the surface can be written as

$$
z-{z}_{0}=(x-{x}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),
$$

where $⟨\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),-1⟩$ represents a normal vector to the tangent plane.

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(xy-3x+2y-5)=y-3 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(xy-3x+2y-5)=x+2\end{aligned}
$$

 

Hence, the normal vector to the tangent plane is 

$$
⟨y-3,\,x+2,\,-1⟩.
$$

Note that the tangent plane is horizontal if and only if the normal vector is vertical. This means that the $x$- and $y$-components of the vector must be $0:$

$$
\{\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=0 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y}=0\end{aligned}\,⟹\,\{\begin{aligned}y-3=0 \\ x+2=0\end{aligned}
$$

 

From the second equation we get $x=-2,$ while the first equation gives $y=3.$ 

Finally, substituting $x=-2$ and $y=3$ into our function, we get

$$
z=(-2)(3)-3(-2)+2(3)-5=1.
$$

Therefore, the point where the tangent plane is horizontal is $(-2,3,1).$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186130386 :tutorial/content "Similar to tangent lines for single variable functions, we can think of the **tangent plane** to a surface at a point as the plane that "touches" the surface at that point.

The equation of the tangent plane to a surface $z=f(x,y)$ at the point $(x_0,y_0,z_0),$ where $z_0=f(x_0,y_0),$ can be found using the formula

$$
z - z_0 = (x-x_0)\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}(x_0,y_0) + (y-y_0)\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}(x_0,y_0).
$$

For example, consider the surface 

$$
z = 4-x^2-y^2.
$$

Let's find the equation of the tangent plane to the surface at the point $(0,\sqrt{2},2),$ as shown below.

![](images/03/03df90a94615238e2126338f64d1f51fcefc379068a8cdc366b33b998cd69f45.png)

 

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(4-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2})=-2x \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(4-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2})=-2y\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the partial derivatives at $(x,y) = (0,\sqrt{2})\mathbin{:}$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}(0,\sqrt{2}) & =-2(0)=0 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y}(0,\sqrt{2}) & =-2(\sqrt{2})=-2\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write down the equation of the tangent plane:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-2 & =(x-0)\frac{∂f}{∂x}(0,\sqrt{2})+(y-\sqrt{2})\frac{∂f}{∂y}(0,\sqrt{2}) \\ z-2 & =0(x-0)-2\sqrt{2}(y-\sqrt{2}) \\ z-2 & =-2\sqrt{2}y+4 \\ 2\sqrt{2}y+z-6 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So, we get that the Cartesian equation of the tangent plane is $2\sqrt{2}y + z - 6 = 0.$

![](images/d5/d51bdbe8820472334f7e1d942c027b6ad8164eaece58220f3f2e5cdb51544f05.png)" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186130382 :tutorial/content "Earlier, we claimed that function $f(x)$ is differentiable at $x_0$ *if the function admits a unique tangent line* at $x_0.$ Let's now justify this claim.

Recall that a function $f(x)$ is differentiable at $x=x_0$ with derivative $f'(x_0)$ if and only if the following limit exists:

$$
f'(x_0) = \lim_{x\to x_0}\dfrac {f(x) - f(x_0)} {x-x_0}
$$

We can rewrite this limit as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {x}_{0}}(\frac{f(x)-f({x}_{0})}{x-{x}_{0}})-{f}^{′}({x}_{0}) & =0 \\ {lim}_{x\to {x}_{0}}(\frac{f(x)-f({x}_{0})}{x-{x}_{0}}-{f}^{′}({x}_{0})) & =0 \\ {lim}_{x\to {x}_{0}}\frac{f(x)-f({x}_{0})-(x-{x}_{0}){f}^{′}({x}_{0})}{x-{x}_{0}} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

In order for the above limit to hold true, the numerator must approach zero. So, near $x_0,$ we must have

$$
f(x) - f(x_0) - (x-x_0)f'(x_0) \approx 0,
$$

which can be rewritten as

$$
f(x) - f(x_0) \approx (x-x_0)f'(x_0).
$$

This corresponds to the following equation of the tangent line at $x_0\mathbin{:}$

$$
y -y_0 = (x-x_0)\dfrac{\textrm d f}{\textrm d x}(x_0)
$$

From here, we can say that a function $f(x)$ is differentiable at $x_0$ *if the function admits a unique tangent line* at $x_0.$

We'll now use a similar idea to define the differentiability of a multivariable function at a point $P$ in terms of tangent planes." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186129328 :activity/expected-seconds 1260.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id 17592186192842 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-b0992f95-7b13-5c5a-ba7a-568131e59eaa" "question-f0b7f966-d726-5db3-885d-bd379b62b2e1"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186192539 :question/problem "Solve the inequality $10x - 4 > 16.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we apply the addition principle, adding $4$ to both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}10x-4 & >16 \\ 10x-4+4 & >16+4 \\ 10x+0 & >20 \\ 10x & >20\end{aligned}
$$

Second, we apply the multiplication principle, dividing both sides by $10{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}10x & >20 \\ \frac{10x}{10} & >\frac{20}{10} \\ \frac{\cancel{10}x}{\cancel{10}} & >2 \\ x & >2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x> 2.$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186192843 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-0822285c-ebb1-578e-9679-e7a486cbcc58" "question-a80bc2bf-80f4-5f0b-bce9-f8d616688e2c"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186192540 :question/problem "Solve the inequality $-2x + 3  > -1.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we apply the addition principle, subtracting $3$ from both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}-2x+3 & >-1 \\ -2x+3-3 & >-1-3 \\ -2x+0 & >-4 \\ -2x & >-4\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we apply the multiplication principle, dividing both sides by $-2.$ 

Remember, when multiplying or dividing an inequality by a negative number, we need to flip the inequality sign:

$$
\begin{aligned}-2x\,\, & >\,\,-4 \\ \frac{-2x}{-2}\, & <\,\,\frac{-4}{-2} \\ \frac{\cancel{-2}x}{\cancel{-2}}\, & <\,\,2 \\ x\,\, & <\,\,2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x<2.$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186192844 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-6bd147ae-a22b-5420-b57b-dd219e2ccfea" "question-a7f55f36-a99e-57a6-94a7-d395d5c39a69"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186192541 :question/problem "Solve the inequality $-11 \le     -8y + 5.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we apply the addition principle, subtracting $5$ from both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}-11 & \le -8y+5 \\ -11-5 & \le -8y+5-5 \\ -16 & \le -8y+0 \\ -16 & \le -8y\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we apply the multiplication principle, dividing both sides by $-8.$ 

Remember, when multiplying or dividing an inequality by a negative number, we need to flip the inequality sign:

$$
\begin{aligned}-16\,\, & \le \,\,-8y \\ \frac{-16}{-8}\, & \ge \,\,\frac{-8y}{-8} \\ 2\, & \ge \,\,\frac{\cancel{-8}y}{\cancel{-8}} \\ 2\, & \ge \,\,y\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, let's swap the left and right-hand sides so that the variable is on the left-hand side. Remember, we also need to flip the inequality.

$$
y \le   2
$$

Therefore, the solution is $y \le   2.$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-b0992f95-7b13-5c5a-ba7a-568131e59eaa" :question/id #uuid "b0992f95-7b13-5c5a-ba7a-568131e59eaa" :question/math-academy-id "q-6275" :question/problem "Solve the inequality $4x+2\le 10.$" :question/worked-solution "First, we apply the addition principle, subtracting $2$ from both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}4x+2 & \le 10 \\ 4x+2-2 & \le 10-2 \\ 4x+0 & \le 8 \\ 4x & \le 8\end{aligned}
$$

Second, we apply the multiplication principle, dividing both sides by $4:$

$$
\begin{aligned}4x & \le 8 \\ \frac{4x}{4} & \le \frac{8}{4} \\ \frac{\cancel{4}x}{\cancel{4}} & \le 2 \\ x & \le 2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x\le 2.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-ad88ce2c-c0b4-5896-8791-c75ff580324c"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} $$

Second, we apply the multiplication principle, dividing both sides by $2:$

$$
\begin{aligned}2x & >-12 \\ \frac{2x}{2} & >-\frac{12}{2} \\ \frac{\cancel{2}x}{\cancel{2}} & >-6 \\ x & >-6\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}-7t+2 & \le -5 \\ -7t+2-2 & \le -5-2 \\ -7t+0 & \le -7 \\ -7t & \le -7\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}-7t\,\, & \le \,\,-7 \\ \frac{-7t}{-7}\, & \ge \,\,\frac{-7}{-7} \\ \frac{\cancel{-7}t}{\cancel{-7}}\, & \ge \,\,1 \\ t\,\, & \ge \,1\end{aligned}
$$

:question/worked-solution "First, we apply the addition principle, subtracting $14$ from both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}-1 & \le 5x+14 \\ -1-14 & \le 5x+14-14 \\ -15 & \le 5x+0 \\ -15 & \le 5x\end{aligned}
$$

Second, we apply the multiplication principle, dividing both sides by $5:$

$$
\begin{aligned}-15 & \le 5x \\ -\frac{15}{5} & \le \frac{5x}{5} \\ -3 & \le \frac{\cancel{5}x}{\cancel{5}} \\ -3 & \le x\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, let's swap the left and right-hand sides so that the variable is on the left-hand side. Remember, we also need to flip the inequality.

$$
x\ge -3
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x\ge -3.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-4f90a6ab-67eb-52cc-8691-87196f6365e4"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-4f90a6ab-67eb-52cc-8691-87196f6365e4" :answer-field/id #uuid "4f90a6ab-67eb-52cc-8691-87196f6365e4" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-0cf264f3-eda3-5c7d-b91e-05b943df2dd7" :answer-field/choices ["answer-0cf264f3-eda3-5c7d-b91e-05b943df2dd7" "answer-023bbc6a-3c52-5565-bf3a-b9068e2f0a1d" "answer-2a356c0a-5c85-5ef6-89f7-71357f55c704" "answer-51d31921-a1aa-55dd-9c26-0657fbe6c246" "answer-fd30a97e-f59d-55a7-a079-e8fc6782015c"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-0cf264f3-eda3-5c7d-b91e-05b943df2dd7" :answer/id #uuid "0cf264f3-eda3-5c7d-b91e-05b943df2dd7" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "x\ge -3" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-023bbc6a-3c52-5565-bf3a-b9068e2f0a1d" :answer/id #uuid "023bbc6a-3c52-5565-bf3a-b9068e2f0a1d" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "x\ge 3" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-2a356c0a-5c85-5ef6-89f7-71357f55c704" :answer/id #uuid "2a356c0a-5c85-5ef6-89f7-71357f55c704" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "x\ge 5" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-51d31921-a1aa-55dd-9c26-0657fbe6c246" :answer/id #uuid "51d31921-a1aa-55dd-9c26-0657fbe6c246" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "x\le -5" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-fd30a97e-f59d-55a7-a079-e8fc6782015c" :answer/id #uuid "fd30a97e-f59d-55a7-a079-e8fc6782015c" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "x\le 3" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186193912 :tutorial/content "Suppose that we wish to find the solution to the inequality

$$
2x + 6 < 12.
$$

An inequality like this one can be solved just like an equation, using the addition and multiplication principles.

First, we apply the addition principle, subtracting $6$ from both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}2x+6 & <12 \\ 2x+6-6 & <12-6 \\ 2x+0 & <6 \\ 2x & <6\end{aligned}
$$

Second, we apply the multiplication principle, dividing both sides by $2{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}2x & <6 \\ \frac{2x}{2} & <\frac{6}{2} \\ \frac{\cancel{2}x}{\cancel{2}} & <3 \\ x & <3\end{aligned}
$$

The solution is $x < 3$ In other words, any value less than $3$ satisfies the inequality.

Let's see another example." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186192903 :activity/expected-seconds 420.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id 17592186119796 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-445c4dee-b549-5e10-93bb-06205e66703c"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186119795 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-d4f26408-d253-562e-8b0f-c05af2f72107" "question-dbe20736-69a2-5914-aaf4-587bd8fc1776"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-d4f26408-d253-562e-8b0f-c05af2f72107" :question/id #uuid "d4f26408-d253-562e-8b0f-c05af2f72107" :question/math-academy-id "q-32688" :question/problem "Suppose that a $3\times 3$ matrix $C$ is reduced to row echelon form using the following elementary row operations, applied in the order in which they appear:
