circle:

- The **circumference** of a circle is used to describe the perimeter of the circle, as shown in the left diagram below.

- An **arc** is a part of the circumference which is enclosed between two points on a circle. In the right diagram below, we have the arc $\overset{\frown}{AB}.$

![](images/5c/5c918b32007a68beecfdef486e9cd5d0818a2122ad672415608f761f7f7953e7.png)

If an arc is denoted using only two letters, we are referring to the *shortest* arc. However, to avoid ambiguity, we can use three letters. For example, in the diagram below, $\overset{\frown}{ACB}$ is the arc to the left and $\overset{\frown}{ADB}$ is the arc to the right.

![](images/f6/f6329cc70c467e968628d2d82a0839253ee443881371893d6d7721724e9ae02a.png)" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186176974 :tutorial/content "Finally, we have two more elements of a circle to remember:

- A **circular sector** is the region bounded by an arc of the circle and two radii which connect the center of the circle with the endpoints of the arc. In the left diagram below, we have the circular sector $OCD.$

- A **circular segment** is the region bounded by an arc of the circle and the chord that connects the endpoints of the arc. In the right diagram below, we have the circular segment $PQ.$

![](images/84/848e64be2b80b78d88da42473f6778d4012f7ec52ae6950f4ca3635b5b154ca6.png)" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186176115 :activity/expected-seconds 420.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id 17592186161998 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-328730e5-b32c-5f55-aef8-1fdf6d6f55ce"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-328730e5-b32c-5f55-aef8-1fdf6d6f55ce" :question/id #uuid "328730e5-b32c-5f55-aef8-1fdf6d6f55ce" :question/math-academy-id "q-94622" :question/problem "Find the median of the random variable $Y$ if the probability density function of $Y$ is given by

$$
f(y)=\{\begin{aligned}{e}^{-y},\, & y\ge 0, \\ 0,\, & \text{otherwise.}\end{aligned}
$$" :question/worked-solution "The median of a random variable $Y$ is the number $m$ such that

$$
P(Y\le m)=\frac{1}{2}.
$$

In our case, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(Y\le m) & ={\int }_{0}^{m}{e}^{-y}\,\text{d}y \\  & =-{e}^{-y}{|}_{0}^{m} \\  & =1-{e}^{-m}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the median is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}1-{e}^{-m} & =\frac{1}{2} \\ {e}^{-m} & =\frac{1}{2} \\ -m & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{2}) \\ -m & =-\operatorname{ln}⁡2 \\ m & =\operatorname{ln}⁡2.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-a0c67064-cabf-594b-8138-f2a53ecff042"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "e2b4a0b2-77c3-5ed8-8555-0cfe3f01b758" :question/math-academy-id "q-94668" :question/problem "Find, to three decimal places, the interquartile range of the random variable $X$ if the cumulative distribution function of $X$ is given by

$$
F(x)=\{\begin{aligned}0, & x<0, \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{16}, & 0\le x\le 4, \\ 1, & x>4.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/worked-solution "To find the interquartile range, we first need to find the lower quartile and the upper quartile.

The lower quartile of a random variable $X$ is the number ${q}_{1}$ such that

$$
P(X\le {q}_{1})=\frac{1}{4},
$$

and the upper quartile is the number ${q}_{3}$ such that

$$
P(X\le {q}_{3})=\frac{3}{4}.
$$

First, we find the lower quartile:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\le {q}_{1}) & =\frac{1}{4} \\ F({q}_{1}) & =\frac{1}{4} \\ \frac{{q}_{1}^{2}}{16} & =\frac{1}{4} \\ {q}_{1}^{2} & =4 \\ {q}_{1} & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we find the upper quartile:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\le {q}_{3}) & =\frac{3}{4} \\ F({q}_{3}) & =\frac{3}{4} \\ \frac{{q}_{3}^{2}}{16} & =\frac{3}{4} \\ {q}_{3}^{2} & =12 \\ {q}_{3} & =2\sqrt{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the interquartile range is

$$
IQR={q}_{3}-{q}_{1}=2\sqrt{3}-2≈1.464
$$

rounded to three decimal places." :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-cdc675dd-7a38-5eec-ad05-1b9e422a82c4"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} $$" :question/worked-solution "The $100p$th percentile of a random variable $Y$ is the number ${y}_{p}$ such that

$$
P(Y\le {y}_{p})=p.
$$

In our case, we want to find the $60$th percentile, which corresponds to the decimal $p=0.6.$ We have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(Y\le {y}_{0.6}) & ={\int }_{1}^{{y}_{0.6}}\frac{1}{{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={-\frac{1}{y}|}_{1}^{{y}_{0.6}} \\  & =1-\frac{1}{{y}_{0.6}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the $60$th percentile is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}1-\frac{1}{{y}_{0.6}} & =0.6 \\ \frac{1}{{y}_{0.6}} & =0.4 \\ {y}_{0.6} & =\frac{1}{0.4} \\ {y}_{0.6} & =\frac{5}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-b021d4b8-9d31-550f-8894-f27be8d6ecdd"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id random variable $X$ if the probability distribution function of $X$ is given by

$$
f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{16}\sqrt{x},\, & 0\le x\le 4, \\ 0,\, & \text{otherwise.}\end{aligned}
$$" :question/worked-solution "The $100p$th percentile of a random variable $X$ is the number ${x}_{p}$ such that

$$
P(X\le {x}_{p})=p.
$$

In our case, we want to find the $72.9$th percentile, which corresponds to the decimal $p=0.729.$ We have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\le {x}_{0.729}) & ={\int }_{0}^{{x}_{0.729}}\frac{3}{16}\sqrt{x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\frac{{x}^{\frac{3}{2}}}{8}|}_{0}^{{x}_{0.729}} \\  & =\frac{{x}_{0.729}^{\frac{3}{2}}}{8}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the $72.9$th percentile is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{x}_{0.729}^{\frac{3}{2}}}{8} & =0.729 \\ {x}_{0.729}^{\frac{1}{2}} & =\sqrt[3]{(8)(0.729)} \\ {x}_{0.729}^{\frac{1}{2}} & =(2)(0.9) \\ {x}_{0.729} & =(1.8)^{2} \\ {x}_{0.729} & =3.24.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-4d9539fc-eb18-57bd-a7aa-1b80040b3b7f"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-4d9539fc-eb18-57bd-a7aa-1b80040b3b7f" :answer-field/id #uuid "4d9539fc-eb18-57bd-a7aa-1b80040b3b7f" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-1aed5558-3986-50d7-b1f2-81753d74b873" :answer-field/choices ["answer-9a4f0b16-dcc0-5510-825c-f040ca9cf4a6" "answer-92f9b85f-813a-5ae6-862a-7c2bae09fbfa" "answer-3978a119-ff81-5c74-849d-d9dd5d8e9158" "answer-1aed5558-3986-50d7-b1f2-81753d74b873" "answer-8b6cb7e1-9231-5421-81e5-f17c6d73d937"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-9a4f0b16-dcc0-5510-825c-f040ca9cf4a6" :answer/id #uuid "9a4f0b16-dcc0-5510-825c-f040ca9cf4a6" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "1.8" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-92f9b85f-813a-5ae6-862a-7c2bae09fbfa" :answer/id #uuid "92f9b85f-813a-5ae6-862a-7c2bae09fbfa" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "2.56" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-3978a119-ff81-5c74-849d-d9dd5d8e9158" :answer/id #uuid "3978a119-ff81-5c74-849d-d9dd5d8e9158" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "3.14" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-1aed5558-3986-50d7-b1f2-81753d74b873" :answer/id #uuid "1aed5558-3986-50d7-b1f2-81753d74b873" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "3.24" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-8b6cb7e1-9231-5421-81e5-f17c6d73d937" :answer/id #uuid "8b6cb7e1-9231-5421-81e5-f17c6d73d937" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "7.29" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-c3057bfc-a8d8-5a19-9075-be23799b04aa" :question/id #uuid "c3057bfc-a8d8-5a19-9075-be23799b04aa" :question/math-academy-id "q-125715" :question/problem "Find the interquartile range of the random variable $X$ if the cumulative distribution function of $X$ is given by

$$
F(x)=\{\begin{aligned}0, & x<1, \\ 1-\frac{1}{{x}^{6}}, & x\ge 1.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/worked-solution "To find the interquartile range, we first need to find the lower quartile and the upper quartile.

The lower quartile of a random variable $X$ is the number ${q}_{1}$ such that

$$
P(X\le {q}_{1})=\frac{1}{4},
$$

and the upper quartile is the number ${q}_{3}$ such that

$$
P(X\le {q}_{3})=\frac{3}{4}.
$$

First, we find the lower quartile:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\le {q}_{1}) & =\frac{1}{4} \\ F({q}_{1}) & =\frac{1}{4} \\ 1-\frac{1}{{q}_{1}^{6}} & =\frac{1}{4} \\ \frac{1}{{q}_{1}^{6}} & =\frac{3}{4} \\ \frac{1}{{q}_{1}} & =\sqrt[6]{\frac{3}{4}} \\ {q}_{1} & =\sqrt[6]{\frac{4}{3}}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we find the upper quartile:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\le {q}_{3}) & =\frac{3}{4} \\ F({q}_{3}) & =\frac{3}{4} \\ 1-\frac{1}{{q}_{3}^{6}} & =\frac{3}{4} \\ \frac{1}{{q}_{3}^{6}} & =\frac{1}{4} \\ \frac{1}{{q}_{1}} & =\sqrt[6]{\frac{1}{4}} \\ {q}_{1} & =\sqrt[6]{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the interquartile range is

$$
\begin{aligned}IQR & ={q}_{3}-{q}_{1} \\  & =\sqrt[6]{4}-\sqrt[6]{\frac{4}{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-87f1f10e-3dae-5b47-be1d-ec0989a80ffb"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186064143 :question/problem "Find the derivative of the function $y = x^{x^3}.$" :question/worked-solution "We have the function 

$$
y = x^{x^3}.
$$

First, we take the natural logarithm of both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{{x}^{3}}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & ={x}^{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to $x{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡x) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =({x}^{3})^{′}\cdot (\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+({x}^{3})\cdot {(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)}^{′} \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =3{x}^{2}\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡x+{x}^{3}\cdot \frac{1}{x} \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =3{x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡x+{x}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve for $y'{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =y(3{x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡x+{x}^{2})\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $y=x^{x^3}{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & ={x}^{{x}^{3}}(3{x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡x+{x}^{2}) \\  & ={x}^{{x}^{3}}({x}^{2}(3\operatorname{ln}⁡x+1)) \\  & ={x}^{{x}^{3}+2}(3\operatorname{ln}⁡x+1)\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186064307 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-73c29bd9-9c93-5235-9a81-b902322f8bb3" "question-9798e200-13a6-549b-86eb-d44d6cb98aeb" "question-22063a8c-2673-5c08-b0b7-4fcd50355c5f" "question-cdcbfec1-c9f8-5550-af44-736f646a25ea"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186064144 :question/problem "Find the derivative of the function $y = (x^2-1)^x.$" :question/worked-solution "We have the function 

$$
y = (x^2-1)^x.
$$

First, we take the natural logarithm of both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(({x}^{2}-1)^{x}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}-1)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to $x{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}-1)) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x)\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}-1)+x\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}-1)) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =1\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}-1)+x\cdot (\frac{1}{{x}^{2}-1}\cdot 2x) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}-1)+\frac{2{x}^{2}}{{x}^{2}-1}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve for $\dfrac {\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x}{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =y(\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}-1)+\frac{2{x}^{2}}{{x}^{2}-1})\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $y = (x^2-1)^x{:}$

$$

{{field-1}}$)$" :question/worked-solution "We have the function 

$$
y=e{x}^{2-5{x}^{2}}.

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(e{x}^{2-5{x}^{2}}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡e+\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2-5{x}^{2}}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =1+(2-5{x}^{2})\operatorname{ln}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(1+(2-5{x}^{2})\operatorname{ln}⁡x) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =0+(2-5{x}^{2})^{′}\cdot (\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+(2-5{x}^{2})\cdot {(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)}^{′} \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =(-10x)\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡x+(2-5{x}^{2})\cdot \frac{1}{x} \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =-10x\operatorname{ln}⁡x+\frac{2-5{x}^{2}}{x} \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =-10x\operatorname{ln}⁡x-5x+\frac{2}{x}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =y(-10x\operatorname{ln}⁡x-5x+\frac{2}{x})\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =e{x}^{2-5{x}^{2}}\cdot (-10x\operatorname{ln}⁡x-5x+\frac{2}{x}) \\  & =e{x}^{1-5{x}^{2}}\cdot x(-10x\operatorname{ln}⁡x-5x+\frac{2}{x}) \\  & =e{x}^{1-5{x}^{2}}\cdot (-10{x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡x-5{x}^{2}+2)\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-834f15be-62e7-5d6a-9efc-72702ab37e17"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-834f15be-62e7-5d6a-9efc-72702ab37e17" :answer-field/id #uuid "834f15be-62e7-5d6a-9efc-72702ab37e17" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-0b8d60af-e149-5616-afdf-10d5747154fa" :answer-field/choices ["answer-0b8d60af-e149-5616-afdf-10d5747154fa"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-0b8d60af-e149-5616-afdf-10d5747154fa" :answer/id #uuid "0b8d60af-e149-5616-afdf-10d5747154fa" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "2-5x^2-10x^2\ln x" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-358ad886-8781-5867-add0-1dfbbd99e7fd" :question/id #uuid "358ad886-8781-5867-add0-1dfbbd99e7fd" :question/math-academy-id "q-138791" :question/problem "Consider the function $y={x}^{5{x}^{2}-2}.$ Its derivative is given by

Find the function $g(x).$" :question/worked-solution "We have the function 

$$
y={x}^{5{x}^{2}-2}.

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{5{x}^{2}-2}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =(5{x}^{2}-2)\operatorname{ln}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

$$

{{field-1}}$)$" :question/worked-solution "We have the function 

$$
y={x}^{\operatorname{sec}⁡x}.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{\operatorname{sec}⁡x}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{sec}⁡x\,\operatorname{ln}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{sec}⁡x\operatorname{ln}⁡x) \\ \frac{1}{y}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =(\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}\operatorname{sec}⁡x)\operatorname{ln}⁡x+\operatorname{sec}⁡x(\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}\operatorname{ln}⁡x) \\ \frac{1}{y}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =(\operatorname{sec}⁡x\operatorname{tan}⁡x)\operatorname{ln}⁡x+\operatorname{sec}⁡x\cdot \frac{1}{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve for $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =y(\operatorname{ln}⁡x\,\operatorname{sec}⁡x\operatorname{tan}⁡x+\frac{\operatorname{sec}⁡x}{x})\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $y={x}^{\operatorname{sec}⁡x}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & ={x}^{\operatorname{sec}⁡x}\cdot (\operatorname{ln}⁡x\,\operatorname{sec}⁡x\operatorname{tan}⁡x+\frac{\operatorname{sec}⁡x}{x}) \\  & ={x}^{\operatorname{sec}⁡x}\cdot \frac{\operatorname{sec}⁡x}{x}\cdot (x\operatorname{ln}⁡x\,\operatorname{tan}⁡x+1) \\  & ={x}^{\operatorname{sec}⁡x-1}\operatorname{sec}⁡x\cdot (x\operatorname{ln}⁡x\operatorname{tan}⁡x+1).\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-a32a9416-0150-598e-ac86-6202b9e0f123"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-a32a9416-0150-598e-ac86-6202b9e0f123" :answer-field/id #uuid "a32a9416-0150-598e-ac86-6202b9e0f123" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-016328d0-e890-5f0f-acd5-5481d9b4f783" :answer-field/choices ["answer-016328d0-e890-5f0f-acd5-5481d9b4f783"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-016328d0-e890-5f0f-acd5-5481d9b4f783" :answer/id #uuid "016328d0-e890-5f0f-acd5-5481d9b4f783" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "1+x\tan x\ln x" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-73c29bd9-9c93-5235-9a81-b902322f8bb3" :question/id #uuid "73c29bd9-9c93-5235-9a81-b902322f8bb3" :question/math-academy-id "q-138837" :question/problem "Consider the function $y=(\operatorname{tan}⁡x)^{x}.$ Its derivative is given by  

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=(\operatorname{tan}⁡x)^{x}\cdot g(x).
$$

Find the function $g(x).$" :question/worked-solution "We have the function 

$$
y=(\operatorname{tan}⁡x)^{x}.
$$

First, we take the natural logarithm of both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡((\operatorname{tan}⁡x)^{x}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{tan}⁡x)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{tan}⁡x)) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x)\cdot (\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{tan}⁡x))+(x)\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{tan}⁡x)) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =1\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{tan}⁡x)+x\cdot (\frac{1}{\operatorname{tan}⁡x}\cdot {sec}^{2}⁡x) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{tan}⁡x)+x\operatorname{csc}⁡x\operatorname{sec}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve for $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =y(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{tan}⁡x)+x\operatorname{csc}⁡x\operatorname{sec}⁡x)\end{aligned}
$$

{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "The slope of the tangent to the curve at $x=\frac{e}{3}$ equals the function's derivative at the corresponding point.

We have the function 

$$
y=(\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x))^{{x}^{2}}.
$$

First, we take the natural logarithm of both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡((\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x))^{{x}^{2}}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & ={x}^{2}\,\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x))\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}\,\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x))) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =({x}^{2})^{′}\cdot (\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x)))+({x}^{2})\cdot {(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x)))}^{′} \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =2x\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x))+{x}^{2}\cdot (\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x)}\cdot \frac{1}{x}) \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =2x\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x))+\frac{x}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x)}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve for ${y}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =y(2x\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x))+\frac{x}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x)})\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $y=(\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x))^{{x}^{2}}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =(\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x))^{{x}^{2}}(2x\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x))+\frac{x}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x)})\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of $y=(\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x))^{{x}^{2}}$ at $x=\frac{e}{3}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}m={y}^{′}{|}_{x=e/3} & =(\operatorname{ln}⁡(e))^{(e/3)^{2}}(2(\frac{e}{3})\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡(e))+\frac{(\frac{e}{3})}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(e)}) \\  & =(1)^{(e/3)^{2}}(2(\frac{e}{3})\operatorname{ln}⁡(1)+\frac{(\frac{e}{3})}{1}) \\  & =1\cdot (0+\frac{e}{3}) \\  & =\frac{e}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-36d45e39-f71d-51b2-ae6d-2faee3a34b79"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-36d45e39-f71d-51b2-ae6d-2faee3a34b79" :answer-field/id #uuid "36d45e39-f71d-51b2-ae6d-2faee3a34b79" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-9bdcbb96-5ec9-5007-b256-214fc5f8397c" :answer-field/choices ["answer-9bdcbb96-5ec9-5007-b256-214fc5f8397c"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-9bdcbb96-5ec9-5007-b256-214fc5f8397c" :answer/id #uuid "9bdcbb96-5ec9-5007-b256-214fc5f8397c" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{e}{3}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-a8502904-ea72-54be-8bde-7a62b1b58e76" :question/id #uuid "a8502904-ea72-54be-8bde-7a62b1b58e76" :question/math-academy-id "q-138863" :question/problem "Find the slope of the tangent to the curve $y=(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)^{5x}$ at $x=e.$" :question/worked-solution "The slope of the tangent to the curve at $x=e$ equals the function's derivative at the corresponding point.

We have the function 

$$
y=(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)^{5x}.
$$

First, we take the natural logarithm of both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡((\operatorname{ln}⁡x)^{5x}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =5x\,\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(5x\,\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =(5x)^{′}\cdot (\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x))+(5x)\cdot {(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x))}^{′} \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =5\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+5x\cdot (\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}\cdot \frac{1}{x}) \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =5\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+\frac{5}{\operatorname{ln}⁡x} \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =5(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡x})\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve for ${y}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =y(5(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}))\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $y=(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)^{5x}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =5(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)^{5x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡x})\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of $y=(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)^{5x}$ at $x=e$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}{|}_{x=e} & =5(\operatorname{ln}⁡e)^{5\cdot e}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡e)+\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡e}) \\  & =5(1)^{5e}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(1)+\frac{1}{1}) \\  & =5.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-ba9151a4-b3b8-572e-a482-a0acf45515d6"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-ba9151a4-b3b8-572e-a482-a0acf45515d6" :answer-field/id #uuid "ba9151a4-b3b8-572e-a482-a0acf45515d6" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-958860f4-6bc6-5bdf-97ca-7bb1fc4df790" :answer-field/choices ["answer-8b404956-da94-552b-947d-159dfaef39dd" "answer-958860f4-6bc6-5bdf-97ca-7bb1fc4df790" "answer-7035e9b8-2a3c-533d-bcf2-3bfb073ccc28" "answer-6fd19c25-5aab-572e-808f-2654216bf71a" "answer-a0be53dd-9f2c-5eb8-a506-84c246e69f71"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-8b404956-da94-552b-947d-159dfaef39dd" :answer/id #uuid "8b404956-da94-552b-947d-159dfaef39dd" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-958860f4-6bc6-5bdf-97ca-7bb1fc4df790" :answer/id #uuid "958860f4-6bc6-5bdf-97ca-7bb1fc4df790" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "5" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-7035e9b8-2a3c-533d-bcf2-3bfb073ccc28" :answer/id #uuid "7035e9b8-2a3c-533d-bcf2-3bfb073ccc28" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "5e" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-6fd19c25-5aab-572e-808f-2654216bf71a" :answer/id #uuid "6fd19c25-5aab-572e-808f-2654216bf71a" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "6" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-a0be53dd-9f2c-5eb8-a506-84c246e69f71" :answer/id #uuid "a0be53dd-9f2c-5eb8-a506-84c246e69f71" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "e" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186065395 :tutorial/content "**Logarithmic differentiation** is a technique to compute derivatives that are difficult to find using the usual rules of differentiation, such as the product, quotient, and chain rules.

Let's consider the following function.

$$
y = x^x
$$

We aim to compute $\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d x}.$ However, in this case, we note the following:

- Both the base and the exponent are functions of $x.$

- This means we cannot apply the power rule since the exponent is not a fixed number.

- We also cannot apply the rules for differentiating exponentials since the base is not a fixed number.

So instead, we'll use logarithmic differentiation. We proceed as follows:

**Step 1.** We take the natural logarithm of both sides and apply the power rule for logarithms:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & ={x}^{x} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡{x}^{x} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2.** We differentiate both sides of the above equation with respect to $x$ using implicit differentiation and the product rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x\operatorname{ln}⁡x) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x)\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡x+x\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡x) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =1\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡x+x\cdot (\frac{1}{x}) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡x+1\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3.** Now, we solve for $\dfrac {\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x}.$ This gives

$$
\dfrac {\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} =  y\left( \ln x + 1 \right).
$$

**Step 4.** Finally, we substitute back our original expression for $y=x^x{:}$

$$
\dfrac {\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} = x^x \left( \ln x + 1 \right)
$$

$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186178954 :answer-field/correct 17592186178958 :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id 17592186179889 :activity/expected-seconds 420.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id 17592186180636 :step/math-academy-id 637169 :db/ensure [:step/validate]} {:db/id 17592186180637 :step/math-academy-id 637170 :db/ensure [:step/validate]} {:db/id 17592186180638 :step/math-academy-id 637173 :db/ensure [:step/validate]} {:db/id 17592186162009 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-c8c9dba6-d928-5ac1-ba3e-1db8d33cfb50"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-c8c9dba6-d928-5ac1-ba3e-1db8d33cfb50" :question/id #uuid "c8c9dba6-d928-5ac1-ba3e-1db8d33cfb50" :question/math-academy-id "q-94793" :question/problem "Consider the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}2 & 7 \\ 7 & 2\end{aligned}].$ Which of the following statements are true?

I. The eigenvalues of $A$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=-5$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=9$

II. ${x}^{T}\,A\,x$ is positive-definite

III. $A$ is indefinite" :question/worked-solution "Given a quadratic form $Q(x)={x}^{T}Ax,$ we have the following theorem:

- $Q$ is positive-definite if and only if all the eigenvalues of $A$ are positive,

- $Q$ is positive semi-definite if and only if all the eigenvalues of $A$ are non-negative (note that positive semi-definite quadratic forms include all positive-definite quadratic forms),

- $Q$ is negative-definite if and only if all the eigenvalues of $A$ are negative,

- $Q$ is negative semi-definite if and only if all the eigenvalues of $A$ are non-positive (note that negative semi-definite quadratic forms include all negative-definite quadratic forms), and

- $Q$ is indefinite if and only if $A$ has both positive and negative eigenvalues.

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. Computing the characteristic equation of $A,$ we obtain

$$

$$

- Statement II is false, while statement III is true. Since $A$ has both positive and negative eigenvalues, the quadratic form ${x}^{T}\,A\,x$ (as well as the matrix $A$) is indefinite.

Consider the differential equation 

$$
y'' - 4y = 4e^{2x}
$$

for which the corresponding homogeneous equation has the fundamental solutions $y_1 = e^{2x}$ and $y_2 = e^{-2x}.$ 

Let’s work through this example using the method of variation of parameters.

We seek a particular solution of the form

$$
y_p = u_1 y_1 + u_2 y_2
$$

subject to the standard constraints:

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}^{′}{y}_{1}^{′}+{u}_{2}^{′}{y}_{2}^{′}=4{e}^{2x} \\ {u}_{1}^{′}{y}_{1}+{u}_{2}^{′}{y}_{2}=0\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

First, let's verify that the fundamental solutions $y_1$ and $y_2$ are independent by computing the Wronskian:

$$
\begin{aligned}W({y}_{1},{y}_{2}) & =|\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} & {y}_{2} \\ {y}_{1}^{′} & {y}_{2}^{′}\end{aligned}| \\  & ={y}_{1}{y}_{2}^{′}-{y}_{1}^{′}{y}_{2} \\  & =({e}^{2x})({e}^{-2x})^{′}-({e}^{2x})^{′}({e}^{-2x}) \\  & =({e}^{2x})(-2{e}^{-2x})-(2{e}^{2x})({e}^{-2x}) \\  & =-2-2 \\  & =-4 \\  & \ne 0\end{aligned}
$$

Since $W \neq 0,$ the functions are linearly independent. 

Substituting $y_1, y_2$ and their derivatives into our constraints gives the system:

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}^{′}{({e}^{2x})}^{′}+{u}_{2}^{′}{({e}^{-2x})}^{′}=4{e}^{2x} \\ {u}_{1}^{′}{e}^{2x}+{u}_{2}^{′}{e}^{-2x}=0\end{aligned}\,⟹\,\{\begin{aligned}2{u}_{1}^{′}{e}^{2x}-2{u}_{2}^{′}{e}^{-2x}=4{e}^{2x} \\ {u}_{1}^{′}{e}^{2x}+{u}_{2}^{′}{e}^{-2x}=0\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

We start by solving for $u_2'$ from the second equation to get

$$
u_2' = -\dfrac{u_1'e^{2x}}{e^{-2x}}=-u_1'e^{4x}.
$$

Substituting this into the first equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}2{u}_{1}^{′}{e}^{2x}-2{u}_{2}^{′}{e}^{-2x} & =4{e}^{2x} \\ 2{u}_{1}^{′}{e}^{2x}-2(-{u}_{1}^{′}{e}^{4x}){e}^{-2x} & =4{e}^{2x} \\ 2{u}_{1}^{′}{e}^{2x}+2{u}_{1}^{′}{e}^{2x} & =4{e}^{2x} \\ 4{u}_{1}^{′}{e}^{2x} & =4{e}^{2x} \\ {u}_{1}^{′} & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have

$$
u_2' = -(1)e^{4x} = -e^{4x}.
$$

Next, we integrate $u_1'$ and $u_2'$ with respect to $x$ (taking constants as $0$):

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\int {u}_{1}^{′}\,\text{d}x=\int 1\,\text{d}x=x, \\ {u}_{2} & =\int {u}_{2}^{′}\,\text{d}x=\int -{e}^{4x}\,\text{d}x=-\frac{1}{4}{e}^{4x}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our particular solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p} & ={u}_{1}{y}_{1}+{u}_{2}{y}_{2} \\  & =(x){e}^{2x}+(-\frac{1}{4}{e}^{4x}){e}^{-2x} \\  & =x{e}^{2x}-\frac{1}{4}{e}^{2x}.\end{aligned}
$$

The general solution is $y = y_c + y_p,$ where $y_c = C_1 e^{2x} + C_2 e^{-2x}.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =({C}_{1}{e}^{2x}+{C}_{2}{e}^{-2x})+(x{e}^{2x}-\frac{1}{4}{e}^{2x}) \\  & =({C}_{1}-\frac{1}{4}){e}^{2x}+{C}_{2}{e}^{-2x}+x{e}^{2x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, replacing constants $C_1 - \dfrac{1}{4}$ with $A$ and $C_2$ with $B,$ we get

$$
\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{y(x) = A e^{2x} + B e^{-2x} + xe^{2x}}
$$

where $A$ and $B$ are arbitrary constants." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186148655 :tutorial/content "In variation of parameters for a second-order linear equation, we seek a particular solution of the form

$$
y_p = u_1y_1 + u_2y_2,
$$

where $y_1$ and $y_2$ are linearly independent solutions of the corresponding homogeneous equation, and $u_1$ and $u_2$ are unknown functions.

At first, it may seem natural to differentiate $y_p$ directly:

$$
y_p' = (u_1y_1+u_2y_2)' = u_1'y_1 + u_1y_1' + u_2'y_2 + u_2y_2'.
$$

This expression contains the *extra terms* $u_1'y_1$ and $u_2'y_2,$ which will also appear (after differentiating again) in the expression for $y_p''$.

If we substitute $y=y_p$ into the differential equation, we will obtain *one* equation involving *two* unknown derivatives $u_1'$ and $u_2',$ so we need a second equation to determine them.

To create a second equation, we *choose* to impose the condition

$$
u_1'y_1 + u_2'y_2 = 0.
$$

This is not a property of $u_1$ and $u_2$ that we already know, but it is an additional constraint that we enforce to make the system solvable.

Now, observe what happens to the formula for $y_p'.$ Starting from the product rule expansion,

$$
y_p' = u_1'y_1 + u_1y_1' + u_2'y_2 + u_2y_2',
$$

and using the constraint $u_1'y_1+u_2'y_2=0,$ we obtain

$$
y_p' = u_1y_1' + u_2y_2'.
$$

So, the commonly stated "derivative condition"

$$
y_p' = u_1y_1' + u_2y_2'
$$

is simply the product-rule derivative of $y_p$ *after* we impose $u_1'y_1+u_2'y_2=0.$

This constraint has two key benefits:

1\. *It produces a solvable system.* Substituting $y_p$ into the differential equation gives one equation in $u_1'$ and $u_2'.$  The constraint $u_1'y_1 + u_2'y_2=0$ gives a second equation.

2\. *It simplifies the computation of $y_p''.$* Since the $u_1'y_1$ and $u_2'y_2$ terms vanish, the expression for $y_p''$ becomes simpler, and the final system for $u_1'$ and $u_2'$ is easier to solve.

This is why variation of parameters uses the constraint $u_1'y_1 + u_2'y_2 = 0,$ and why it leads to the simplified expression $y_p' = u_1y_1' + u_2y_2'.$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186147706 :activity/expected-seconds 480.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id 17592186064275 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-e241dd2f-cf9d-55b1-810e-b45db1f40880" "question-3bf93bdf-40a6-507b-8e4d-2fa269000a75" "question-354ae055-47d1-5393-8d47-099f76806cac" "question-c4cdcaf7-2982-5947-b7f9-f0933f5cb1a5" "question-6b9e1a36-03a5-51c4-becb-f3f4b938141f"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186064118 :question/problem "The function $f(x)$ is defined for every real number $x$ and is given by

$a=$ {{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "To calculate the limit, we multiply the numerator and the denominator by the conjugate of the denominator. We get

{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "To calculate the limit, we multiply the numerator and the denominator by the conjugate of the numerator. We get

![](images/20/20b2fd99ae051c3447e4c3530fee053b248393147a8295d3a9451524d7534f52.svg)

The function $f(x)$ seems to have a point discontinuity at $x=4.$ However, by selecting a particular value for $a,$ we can remove the point discontinuity and make the function continuous.

We can find this value of $a$ by forcing the limit of the function to be equal to the value of the function at $x=4\mathbin{:}$

$$
\lim\limits_{x\to 4} f(x) = f(4)
$$

Remember that $\lim\limits_{x\to 4} f(x)$ represents the value that $f(x)$ approaches as $x$ gets closer and closer, but not equal, to $4.$ So, when evaluating $\lim\limits_{x\to 4} f(x),$ we need to use the function definition for $x \neq 4.$

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 4}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to 4}(3x+a) \\  & =3(4)+a \\  & =12+a\end{aligned}
$$

At $x=4,$ the function is defined as $f(x)=13.$ So $f(4)=13,$ and we can solve the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 4}f(x) & =f(4) \\ 12+a & =13 \\ a & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, to make $f(x)$ continuous at $x=4,$ we need to choose $a=1.$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186064432 :activity/expected-seconds 540.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} [:db/retract 17592186189604 :answer-field/choices 17592186189605] [:db/retract 17592186189604 :answer-field/choices 17592186189606] [:db/retract 17592186189604 :answer-field/choices 17592186189607] [:db/retract 17592186189604 :answer-field/choices 17592186189608] [:db/retract 17592186189604 :answer-field/choices 17592186189609] {:db/id 17592186192627 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-8301710f-dfbb-5680-866d-b67f486e14d7" "question-a4783dad-574a-5127-8f16-79c4f5746713"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186192581 :question/worked-solution "The inequality $x \geq 1$ corresponds to all numbers greater than or equal to $1.$ A number line for this inequality is shown below:

![](images/82/829c0bd7c365ef7e5b1d3bee70a632b34cd644349a7528b688abdfd57575a1ab.png)

From the segment on the number line, we have the following:

- The left endpoint $1$ *is* included in the interval.

- There is no right endpoint - it continues forever. So, we write the interval with infinity as the right endpoint, not included.

Therefore, using interval notation, we represent $x \geq 1$ as

$$
x \in [1,\infty).
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186192628 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-df8b3cd8-e582-5e68-8862-832cf8d8a7f7" "question-05484b4a-57a2-55c2-9049-f423ce09e86a"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186192582 :question/problem "What inequality corresponds the interval $x\in\left[5, \infty\right)?$" :question/worked-solution "The statement $x\in\left[5, \infty\right)$ means that $x$ lies between $5$ and $\infty,$ where 

- the left endpoint $5$ *is* included, and

- the right endpoint $\infty$ is *not* included.

Therefore, the inequality represented by this interval is 

$$
5 \leq   x <     \infty.
$$

However, since all numbers are smaller than infinity, it suffices to write 

$$
5 \leq   x
$$

or, equivalently, 

$$
x \geq 5.
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186192629 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-7495bbc7-a548-574a-82ac-70b0b5806589" "question-0b34c9dd-15c6-517b-a545-622b3797f82a"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186192583 :question/worked-solution "The inequality $x \leq 1$ corresponds to all numbers less than or equal to $1.$ A number line for this interval is shown below:

,-7)$ corresponds to the inequality" :question/worked-solution "The statement $x\in (-\infty ,-7)$ means that $x$ lies between $-\infty $ and $-7,$ where 

- the left endpoint $-\infty $ is *not* included, and

- the right endpoint $-7$ is *not* included.

Therefore, the inequality represented by this interval is 

$$
-\infty <x<-7.
$$

However, since all numbers are greater than negative infinity, it suffices to write 

$$
x<-7.
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-17aef558-2ba7-5da3-b0f3-5fde99d8b14a"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-17aef558-2ba7-5da3-b0f3-5fde99d8b14a" :answer-field/id #uuid "17aef558-2ba7-5da3-b0f3-5fde99d8b14a" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-ba6abd59-760c-5139-8f9d-3e2306642a11" :answer-field/choices ["answer-ba6abd59-760c-5139-8f9d-3e2306642a11" "answer-cf64deaf-eb4c-5e28-a5cb-c0d8a5ca27d3" "answer-7bb20d81-b551-56ae-b425-39c6bd43e715" "answer-50cdcef6-9c18-58ca-95d8-1aabfed4067b" "answer-912382eb-e86d-53d1-a4f9-37de67d559dd"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-ba6abd59-760c-5139-8f9d-3e2306642a11" :answer/id #uuid "ba6abd59-760c-5139-8f9d-3e2306642a11" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "x<-7" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-cf64deaf-eb4c-5e28-a5cb-c0d8a5ca27d3" :answer/id #uuid "cf64deaf-eb4c-5e28-a5cb-c0d8a5ca27d3" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "x<7" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-7bb20d81-b551-56ae-b425-39c6bd43e715" :answer/id #uuid "7bb20d81-b551-56ae-b425-39c6bd43e715" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "x>-7" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-50cdcef6-9c18-58ca-95d8-1aabfed4067b" :answer/id #uuid "50cdcef6-9c18-58ca-95d8-1aabfed4067b" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "x\ge 7" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-912382eb-e86d-53d1-a4f9-37de67d559dd" :answer/id #uuid "912382eb-e86d-53d1-a4f9-37de67d559dd" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "x\le -7" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186193939 :tutorial/content "Consider the following inequality: 

$$
x > 0
$$

We can represent this inequality using a number line as follows:

![](images/79/79664d125db14d5b8534d592d232839659a6d0efbd527379207b50d71f9e7454.png)

How do we represent this inequality using interval notation?

Note the following:

- The left endpoint $x=0$ is *not* included. Therefore, we use a parenthesis $($ for this endpoint.

- The interval continues forever in the positive direction. To denote this, we must introduce the **infinity** symbol $\infty.$ Infinity is not a number but a concept that means *larger than any number*.

- We use a right parenthesis $)$ in conjunction with the $\infty$ symbol.

Therefore, we can express the inequality $x > 0$ in interval notation as follows:

$$
x \in (0, \infty)
$$

**Watch Out!** Whenever $\infty$ appears in an interval, it is *always* associated with a right parenthesis. Infinity is *never* associated with a bracket, even if the other endpoint is." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186193940 :tutorial/content "Now, consider the following inequality: 

$$
x \lt 0
$$

We can represent this inequality using a number line as follows:

![](images/52/52be4b1ae3d32f2d3bb1dbf9f4faa1f288cff5736870064533b958ac89a76dad.png)

To represent this inequality using interval notation, we note the following:

- The right endpoint $x=0$ is *not* included. Therefore, we use a parenthesis $)$ for this endpoint.

- The interval continues forever in the negative direction. To denote this, we use the **negative infinity** symbol $-\infty.$ We use a left parenthesis $($ in conjunction with the negative infinity symbol.

Therefore, we can express the inequality $x < 0$ in interval notation as follows:

$$
x \in (-\infty, 0)
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186192906 :activity/expected-seconds 420.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id 17592186124608 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-dfe98e1c-3b93-5422-932b-6229fbfa5965"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186124610 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-adb4921d-df66-5c35-baf2-cc613e0cb3d4"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186124451 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-d66b6ff3-5c30-5d09-a1a7-0b4d573341bb"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186125256 :question/problem "Let $f(x,y)$ be a differentiable function such that

$$
f(1,1)=1,\,{f}_{x}(x,y)=3{x}^{2}{y}^{4},\,{f}_{y}(x,y)=4{x}^{3}{y}^{3}.
$$

Using a linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(1,1),$ estimate the value of $f(1.02,0.97).$" :question/worked-solution "The linear approximation of the function $f$ at the point $(a,b)$ is given by

$$
f(x,y)≈f(a,b)+∇f(a,b)\cdot ⟨x-a,y-b⟩.
$$

So, the linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(1,1)$ is:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ≈f(1,1)+∇f(1,1)\cdot ⟨x-1,y-1⟩ \\  & ≈f(1,1)+⟨{f}_{x}(1,1),{f}_{y}(1,1)⟩\cdot ⟨x-1,y-1⟩ \\  & ≈1+⟨{f}_{x}(1,1),{f}_{y}(1,1)⟩\cdot ⟨x-1,y-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we find ${f}_{x}(1,1)$ and ${f}_{y}(1,1)$ using the given partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(1,1) & =3(1)^{2}(1)^{4}=3 \\ {f}_{y}(1,1) & =4(1)^{3}(1)^{3}=4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
f(x,y)≈1+⟨3,4⟩\cdot ⟨x-1,y-1⟩
$$

Finally, we can estimate $f(1.02,0.97)$ by evaluating the linear approximation at $x=1.02$ and $y=0.97,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(1.02,0.97) & ≈1+⟨3,4⟩\cdot ⟨1.02-1,0.97-1⟩ \\  & =1+⟨3,4⟩\cdot ⟨0.02,-0.03⟩ \\  & =1+0.06-0.12 \\  & =0.94\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186124136 :answer-field/correct 17592186124139 :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "question-dfe98e1c-3b93-5422-932b-6229fbfa5965" :question/id #uuid "dfe98e1c-3b93-5422-932b-6229fbfa5965" :question/math-academy-id "q-129635" :question/problem "Let $f(x,y)$ be a differentiable function such that

$$
f(-1,0)=2,\,{f}_{x}(x,y)=4x,\,{f}_{y}(x,y)=6y.
$$

Using a linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(-1,0),$ estimate the value of $f(-1.01,0.01).$" :question/worked-solution "The linear approximation of the function $f$ at the point $(a,b)$ is given by

$$
f(x,y)≈f(a,b)+∇f(a,b)\cdot ⟨x-a,y-b⟩.
$$

So, the linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(-1,0)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ≈f(-1,0)+∇f(-1,0)\cdot ⟨x-(-1),y-0⟩ \\  & ≈f(-1,0)+⟨{f}_{x}(-1,0),{f}_{y}(-1,0)⟩\cdot ⟨x+1,y⟩ \\  & ≈2+⟨{f}_{x}(-1,0),{f}_{y}(-1,0)⟩\cdot ⟨x+1,y⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we find ${f}_{x}(-1,0)$ and ${f}_{y}(-1,0)$ using the given partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(-1,0) & =4(-1)=-4 \\ {f}_{y}(-1,0) & =6(0)=0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
f(x,y)≈2+⟨-4,0⟩\cdot ⟨x+1,y⟩.
$$

Finally, we can estimate $f(-1.01,0.01)$ by evaluating the linear approximation at $x=-1.01$ and $y=0.01,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(-1.01,0.01) & ≈2+⟨-4,0⟩\cdot ⟨-1.01+1,0.01⟩ \\  & =2+⟨-4,0⟩\cdot ⟨-0.01,0.01⟩ \\  & =2-4(-0.01)+0(0.01) \\  & =2+0.04+0 \\  & =2.04\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-668268b9-6681-52bb-9c91-25df63005244"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-668268b9-6681-52bb-9c91-25df63005244" :answer-field/id #uuid "668268b9-6681-52bb-9c91-25df63005244" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-85f1f3d8-db96-5275-8e07-2c90cff21efb" :answer-field/choices ["answer-dfeb2cf6-4561-587e-8a37-967f5082634f" "answer-6f236c61-9ea2-5adb-8fa9-d16d1df7ed78" "answer-147497f8-477a-5c9c-9f25-9681d0be79d3" "answer-85f1f3d8-db96-5275-8e07-2c90cff21efb" "answer-23cf49ce-832f-57a1-9d20-ff6549700eab"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-dfeb2cf6-4561-587e-8a37-967f5082634f" :answer/id #uuid "dfeb2cf6-4561-587e-8a37-967f5082634f" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "1.96" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-6f236c61-9ea2-5adb-8fa9-d16d1df7ed78" :answer/id #uuid "6f236c61-9ea2-5adb-8fa9-d16d1df7ed78" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "1.98" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-147497f8-477a-5c9c-9f25-9681d0be79d3" :answer/id #uuid "147497f8-477a-5c9c-9f25-9681d0be79d3" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "2.02" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-85f1f3d8-db96-5275-8e07-2c90cff21efb" :answer/id #uuid "85f1f3d8-db96-5275-8e07-2c90cff21efb" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "2.04" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-23cf49ce-832f-57a1-9d20-ff6549700eab" :answer/id #uuid "23cf49ce-832f-57a1-9d20-ff6549700eab" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "2.07" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-adb4921d-df66-5c35-baf2-cc613e0cb3d4" :question/id #uuid "adb4921d-df66-5c35-baf2-cc613e0cb3d4" :question/math-academy-id "q-98350" :question/problem "Let be $f(x,y,z)$ a differentiable function such that

$$
\begin{aligned} & f(0,2,1)=8, & \, & {f}_{x}(x,y,z)=\frac{2{e}^{x}}{\sqrt{{e}^{x}+y+z}}, \\  & {f}_{y}(x,y,z)=\frac{2}{\sqrt{{e}^{x}+y+z}}, & \, & {f}_{z}(x,y,z)=\frac{2}{\sqrt{{e}^{x}+y+z}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Using a linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(0,2,1),$ estimate the value of $f(-0.01,1.98,1.05).$" :question/worked-solution "The linear approximation of the function $f$ at the point $(a,b,c)$ is given by

$$
f(x,y,z)≈f(a,b,c)+∇f(a,b,c)\cdot ⟨x-a,y-b,z-c⟩.
$$

So, the linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(0,2,1)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & ≈f(0,2,1)+∇f(0,2,1)\cdot ⟨x-0,y-2,z-1⟩ \\  & =8+⟨{f}_{x}(0,2,1),{f}_{y}(0,2,1),{f}_{z}(0,2,1)⟩\cdot ⟨x,y-2,z-1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we find ${f}_{x}(0,2,1)$, ${f}_{y}(0,2,1)$ and ${f}_{z}(0,2,1),$ using the given partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(0,2,1) & =\frac{2{e}^{0}}{\sqrt{{e}^{0}+2+1}}=1 \\ {f}_{y}(0,2,1) & =\frac{2}{\sqrt{{e}^{0}+2+1}}=1 \\ {f}_{z}(0,2,1) & =\frac{2}{\sqrt{{e}^{0}+2+1}}=1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
f(x,y,z)≈8+⟨1,1,1⟩\cdot ⟨x,y-2,z-1⟩.
$$

Finally, we can estimate $f(-0.01,1.98,1.05)$ by evaluating the linear approximation at $x=-0.01,y=1.98$ and $z=1.05,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(-0.01,1.98,1.05) & ≈8+⟨1,1,1⟩\cdot ⟨-0.01,1.98-2,1.05-1⟩ \\  & =8+⟨1,1,1⟩\cdot ⟨-0.01,-0.02,0.05⟩ \\  & =8-0.01-0.02+0.05 \\  & =8.02\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-e18cb7ab-d012-533c-946a-99ec38759650"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id the linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(1,0,2).$" :question/worked-solution "The linear approximation of the function $f$ at the point $(a,b,c)$ is given by

$$
f(x,y,z)≈f(a,b,c)+∇f(a,b,c)\cdot ⟨x-a,y-b,z-c⟩.
$$

So, the linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(1,0,2)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & ≈f(1,0,2)+∇f(1,0,2)\cdot ⟨x-1,y,z-2⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

From the definition of $f,$ we have that $f(1,0,2)=2.$ Computing the partial derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x} & =2xz\,⇒\,{f}_{x}(1,0,2)=4, \\ {f}_{y} & =-2y\,⇒\,{f}_{y}(1,0,2)=0, \\ {f}_{z} & ={x}^{2}\,⇒\,{f}_{z}(1,0,2)=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the gradient of the function at the point $(1,0,2)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(1,0,2) & =⟨{f}_{x}(1,0,2),{f}_{y}(1,0,2),{f}_{z}(1,0,2)⟩ \\  & =⟨4,0,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the linear approximation of the function $f$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & ≈f(1,0,2)+∇f(1,0,2)\cdot ⟨x-1,y,z-2⟩ \\  & ≈2+⟨4,0,1⟩\cdot ⟨x-1,y,z-2⟩ \\  & ≈2+4(x-1)+0(y)+(z-2) \\  & ≈-4+4x+z.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-531515dc-d792-550d-b5bf-9db7ffa81bdf"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id $$
{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}f({x}_{i})\cdot Δx,
$$

    

where $Δx=\frac{b-a}{n}$ and ${x}_{i}=a+iΔx.$

In the definite integral

$$
{\int }_{1}^{5}(\operatorname{arctan}⁡(x)+2)\,\text{d}x,
$$

the function is $f(x)=\operatorname{arctan}⁡(x)+2,$ the lower bound is $a=1,$ and the upper bound is $b=5.$ So, we have

$$
Δx=\frac{5-1}{n}=\frac{4}{n},
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{5}(\operatorname{arctan}⁡(x)+2)\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}f({x}_{i})\cdot Δx \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}[f(1+i\cdot \frac{4}{n})\cdot \frac{4}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}[f(1+\frac{4i}{n})\cdot \frac{4}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}[(\operatorname{arctan}⁡(\,1+\frac{4i}{n}\,)+2)\,\cdot \frac{4}{n}].\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-bacd6074-8287-5758-9454-33c120a66361" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-f2252516-11cb-503e-94e5-fbb51ee360c4" :answer-field/id #uuid "f2252516-11cb-503e-94e5-fbb51ee360c4"] ["answer-2c9696ed-0cf7-51a5-ab03-f99476ed2805" :answer/id #uuid "2c9696ed-0cf7-51a5-ab03-f99476ed2805"] ["answer-2c9696ed-0cf7-51a5-ab03-f99476ed2805" :answer/type :answer.type/math] ["answer-2c9696ed-0cf7-51a5-ab03-f99476ed2805" :answer/value "1+\frac{4i}{n}"] ["answer-field-f2252516-11cb-503e-94e5-fbb51ee360c4" :answer-field/key "field-1"] ["answer-field-f2252516-11cb-503e-94e5-fbb51ee360c4" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank] ["answer-field-f2252516-11cb-503e-94e5-fbb51ee360c4" :answer-field/correct "answer-2c9696ed-0cf7-51a5-ab03-f99476ed2805"] ["answer-field-f2252516-11cb-503e-94e5-fbb51ee360c4" :answer-field/choices "answer-2c9696ed-0cf7-51a5-ab03-f99476ed2805"] ["question-bacd6074-8287-5758-9454-33c120a66361" :question/answer-fields "answer-field-f2252516-11cb-503e-94e5-fbb51ee360c4"] [17592186096631 :knowledge-point/questions "question-bacd6074-8287-5758-9454-33c120a66361"] [17592186233960 :question/worked-solution "The definite integral can be defined in terms of the limit of a left Riemann sum as

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=1}^{n}f({x}_{k})\cdot Δx,
$$

where ${x}_{k}=a+kΔx$ and $Δx=\frac{b-a}{n}.$

In the definite integral

$$
{\int }_{1}^{2}{x}^{5}\,\text{d}x,
$$

the function is $f(x)={x}^{5},$ the lower bound is $a=1$ and the upper bound is $b=2.$ So, we have

$$

$$"] ["question-d07197e2-a19c-5121-ad34-53964d711400" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-ba7def75-76e7-58e1-a7fd-65e719e06d6a" :answer-field/id #uuid We can do this using a left Riemann sum with $n=4$ subintervals, as shown below:

![](images/1b/1b25a722d5527db77cd7dd5fb581c0ffed9b9324913d390e2633211360b6a8ab.png)

A better approximation can be found by taking more subintervals. For instance, taking $n=8$ subintervals gives:

![](images/17/17f6c8e458b2e6fbd887728cbbcc7cb64a670598256f76cad69d9e5a9c3cf7b5.png)

As we continue to increase $n,$ our approximation gets better and better. In fact, we can get an *exact* value for the area by taking the limit of the Riemann sum as $n\to\infty.$

Let's write down that limit. First, we need to express the left Riemann sum using sigma notation. Using $n$ subintervals between the endpoints $a=0$ and $b=1,$ we express

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ≈{\sum }_{k=0}^{n-1}f({x}_{k})Δx \\  & ={\sum }_{k=0}^{n-1}f(0+k\cdot Δx)Δx \\  & ={\sum }_{k=0}^{n-1}f(k\cdot Δx)Δx \\  & ={\sum }_{k=0}^{n-1}({(k\cdot Δx)}^{2}+1)Δx \\  & ={\sum }_{k=0}^{n-1}({k}^{2}\cdot \frac{1}{{n}^{2}}+1)\cdot \frac{1}{n} \\  & ={\sum }_{k=0}^{n-1}(\frac{{k}^{2}}{{n}^{2}}+1)\cdot \frac{1}{n}.\end{aligned}
$$

In the above, we used the fact that $x_k = 0 + k\Delta x = k\Delta x$ and $\Delta x = \dfrac{1 - 0}{n} = \dfrac 1 n,$ as we've seen before.

The exact area is found by computing the limit as $n\to\infty.$ So instead of using an approximation symbol $(\approx),$ we can now use an equality symbol and write

$$
A = \lim_{n\to\infty}\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\left(\dfrac{k^2}{n^2} + 1\right)\cdot \dfrac{1}{n}.
$$

The formula above is a bit clunky, so instead of writing it using limits and sigma notation, we introduce a new notation called the **definite integral**, defined as

$$
\mathcal{A} = \lim_{n\to\infty}\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\left(\dfrac{k^2}{n^2} + 1\right)\cdot \dfrac{1}{n}= \int_0^1 (x^2 + 1)\, \textrm{d}x.
$$

In our example, 

$$
\displaystyle \int_0^1 (x^2+1)\, \textrm{d}x
$$

can be interpreted as the exact area under the graph of $y = f(x) = x^2+1$ between $x=0,$ $x=1,$ and the $x$-axis."] [17592186097911 :tutorial/content "In general, for a function $f(x)$ defined on $[a,b],$ the **definite integral** of $f(x)$ between $x=a$ and $x=b$ can be defined using the limit of a left  Riemann sum as

$$
\int_a^b f(x)\textrm{d}x = \lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\sum_{k=0}^{n-1} f(x_k)\Delta x,
$$

    

where $\Delta x = \dfrac{b-a}{n}$ and $x_k = a + k\Delta x.$

The limit $x=a$ is referred to as the **lower limit**, whereas $x=b$ is called the **upper limit**."] [17592186097447 :step/math-academy-id 631552] [17592186097449 :step/math-academy-id 631553] [17592186097448 :step/math-academy-id 631554] [17592186097450 :step/math-academy-id 631557] [17592186097451 :step/math-academy-id 631560] [17592186097452 :step/math-academy-id 631563] [17592186097453 :step/math-academy-id 631564] [17592186096875 :activity/expected-seconds 960.0] [17592186128903 :question/worked-solution "The function has discontinuities due to vertical asymptotes at $x=\pm 1.$ Note that

which is enough to conclude that there is a discontinuity due to a vertical asymptote at $x=1.$

![](images/2b/2b1f430a78861fce15c689843d0e4af5376e0f600b650b0a614257d86365cd29.svg)"] [17592186128906 :question/worked-solution "Infinite discontinuities coincide with the vertical asymptotes of $y=f(x).$ The only possible way that $y=f(x)$ can have vertical asymptotes is if either $\dfrac{1}{x-5}$ or $\dfrac{1}{x-4}$ grow without bound within their respective subdomains.

- We first compute the asymptotes of $\dfrac{1}{x-5}.$ Setting the denominator equal to zero, we get

$$
x-5=0\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad x=5.
$$

Although this branch of the function is defined for $x < 5$, we do have that

$$
\lim_{x\to 5^{-}}\left(\dfrac{1}{x-5}\right) = -\infty,
$$

and therefore we conclude that $x=5$ is indeed an infinite discontinuity.

- Next, we compute the asymptotes of $\dfrac{1}{x-4}.$ Setting the denominator equal to zero, we get

$$
x-4=0\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad x=4.
$$

However, this branch of the function is defined for $x \geq 5,$ which does not contain the neighborhood of $x=4.$ So $x=4$ cannot be a vertical asymptote, and therefore $x=4$ cannot be an infinite discontinuity.

"Infinite discontinuities coincide with the vertical asymptotes of $y=f(x).$ 

To find the vertical asymptotes, let's start by factoring the expression in the denominator. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{1}{{x}^{2}-5x} \\  & =\frac{1}{x(x-5)}.\end{aligned}
$$

There are no common factors in the numerator and denominator, so we can find the vertical asymptotes by setting the denominator to zero:

$$
x(x-5)=0\,⟹\,x=0,5.
$$

$$
f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{5-x}, & x<5 \\ \frac{1}{8-x}, & x\ge 5,\,x\ne 8\end{aligned}
$$

 has an infinite discontinuity are

$x=$
{{field-1}}$\,$ and $\,$ $x=$
{{field-2}}."] ["question-bccf9705-1345-5b91-b48e-5b2d9522eb17" :question/worked-solution "Infinite discontinuities coincide with the vertical asymptotes of $y=f(x).$ The only possible way that $y=f(x)$ can have vertical asymptotes is if either $\frac{1}{5-x}$ or $\frac{1}{8-x}$ grow without bound within its respective subdomain.

- We first compute the asymptotes of $\frac{1}{5-x}.$ Setting the denominator equal to zero, we get

$$
5-x=0\,⟹\,x=5.
$$

Although this branch of the function is defined for $x<5,$ which excludes $x=5,$ we have that

$$
{lim}_{x\to {5}^{-}}(\frac{1}{5-x})=+\infty ,
$$

and therefore we conclude that $x=5$ is an infinite discontinuity.

- Next, we compute the asymptotes of $\frac{1}{8-x}.$ Setting the denominator equal to zero, we get

$$
8-x=0\,⟹\,x=8.
$$

Although this branch of the function is defined for $5\le x<8$ and $x>8,$ which excludes $x=8,$ we have that

$$
{lim}_{x\to {8}^{-}}(\frac{1}{8-x})=\infty \,,\,{lim}_{x\to {8}^{+}}(\frac{1}{8-x})=-\infty ,
$$

and therefore we conclude that $x=8$ is an infinite discontinuity.

Therefore, from left to right, the function $y=f(x)$ has infinite discontinuities at 

$$
x=5\,\text{and}\,x=8.
$$

This matches up with what we see in the graph of $y=f(x),$ shown below.

["question-28d2bedc-f4b0-58dc-80a4-886e3d716859" :question/math-academy-id "q-340259"] ["question-28d2bedc-f4b0-58dc-80a4-886e3d716859" :question/problem "The function $f(x)$ defined by

f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}-\frac{3}{x+3}, & x\ne -3 \\ 2, & x=-3\end{aligned}

has an  infinite discontinuity at $x=${{field-1}}."] ["question-28d2bedc-f4b0-58dc-80a4-886e3d716859" :question/worked-solution "Infinite discontinuities coincide with the vertical asymptotes of $y=f(x).$ The only possible way that $y=f(x)$ can have vertical asymptotes is if  $-\frac{3}{x+3}$ grows without bound within its respective subdomain.

$$
x+3=0\,⟹\,x=-3.
$$

Although both branches of the function are defined for $x\ne -3,$ we have that

$$

$$

and therefore we conclude that $x=-3$ is indeed an infinite discontinuity.

f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-1, & x\le 1 \\ \frac{2}{x-1}, & x>1\end{aligned}
$$

has an  infinite discontinuity at $x=${{field-1}}."] ["question-af7b8af8-e50c-5536-8725-7ed61d38a3dd" :question/worked-solution "Infinite discontinuities coincide with the vertical asymptotes of $y=f(x).$ The only possible way that $y=f(x)$ can have vertical asymptotes is if either ${x}^{2}-1$ or $\frac{2}{x-1}$ grows without bound within its respective subdomain.

- We first compute the asymptotes of ${x}^{2}-1.$ Since ${x}^{2}-1$ is a polynomial, therefore it cannot grow without bound due to a vertical asymptote. So this function cannot have an infinite discontinuity.

- Next, we compute the asymptotes of $\frac{2}{x-1}.$ Setting the denominator equal to zero, we get

$$
x-1=0\,⟹\,x=1.
$$

Although this branch of the function is defined for $x>1$, we have that

$$
{lim}_{x\to {1}^{+}}(\frac{2}{x-1})=\infty ,
$$

and therefore we conclude that $x=1$ is indeed an infinite discontinuity.

Therefore, the only point where the function $y=f(x)$ has an infinite discontinuity is  $x=1.$

This matches up with what we see in the graph of $y=f(x),$ shown below.

"question-fdd8bd57-2d2f-5ace-b80e-0473ac5a0a46"] [17592186130330 :tutorial/content "Let's take a look at the function $y=\dfrac 1 x$ below.

![](images/cc/cc9593860b0c134d0d99635b37eeac4f16a712a7af9e1c6474fcf1f885e8451e.png)

The function has a vertical asymptote at $x=0.$ There is also a discontinuity in the function at $x=0,$ since we cannot draw the points on the curve without taking our pen off the paper to cross the asymptote.

So, we say that $y = \dfrac 1 x$ has a **discontinuity due to a vertical asymptote** at $x=0.$ Discontinuities due to vertical asymptotes are also called **infinite discontinuities**.

Notice that here, both one-sided limits are infinite:

$$
\lim_{x\to 0^-} \left(\dfrac 1 x\right) =-\infty\qquad\text{and}\qquad\lim_{x\to 0^+} \left(\dfrac 1 x \right)=\infty.
$$

In general, a function $y=f(x)$ has a discontinuity due to a vertical asymptote at $x=c$ if either one-sided limit is infinite:

$$
\lim_{x\to c^-} f(x) =\pm \infty\qquad\text{or}\qquad\lim_{x\to c^+} f(x) =\pm \infty.
$$

Note that we only need a single limit to become infinite to conclude that there is an infinite discontinuity at $x=c.$"] [17592186129349 :activity/expected-seconds 540.0] ["question-779dfcc0-3a36-5636-a5d6-b4ea61af4fcc" :question/id #uuid "779dfcc0-3a36-5636-a5d6-b4ea61af4fcc"] ["question-779dfcc0-3a36-5636-a5d6-b4ea61af4fcc" :question/math-academy-id "q-339135"] ["question-779dfcc0-3a36-5636-a5d6-b4ea61af4fcc" :question/problem "Evaluate the following limit:

{{field-1}}"] ["question-779dfcc0-3a36-5636-a5d6-b4ea61af4fcc" :question/worked-solution "Let's sketch the graph of $y=\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(x):$

![](images/24/24f07da42a537ded7916fc2440dcf3ee1ccdfc81c7b027b47e97814fec059f5a.png)

The domain of $\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(x)$ is $x\in [-1,1].$  

Now, substituting $x=0$ directly into the limit, we have

Let's begin by recalling the graph of $y=\arcsin(x).$

![](images/df/df22eea4331c47da3047381ca672fd80ebf75118054316fe88c0e2d96dae0d34.png)

Using the graph, we note the following:

- The domain of $\arcsin(x)$ is $x \in [-1,1].$

- For every value $a \in (-1,1),$ we have

$$
\lim_\limits{x\to a} \arcsin(x) = \arcsin(a).
$$

 
In other words, we can evaluate the limit using direct substitution. For example,

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 1/2}\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(x) & =\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

- For any value $a$ that does *not* lie in the domain of $\arcsin(x),$ the limit

$$
\lim_\limits{x\to a} \arcsin(x)
$$

 
does *not* exist.

- At the point $x=-1,$ the limit does *not* exist because the left-sided limit does not exist. However, the right-sided limit *does* exist and is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (-1)^{+}}\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(x) & =\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(-1) \\  & =-\frac{\pi }{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Similarly, at the point $x=1,$ the limit does *not* exist because the right-sided limit does not exist. However, the left-sided limit *does* exist and is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {1}^{-}}\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(x) & =\operatorname{arcsin}⁡(1) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

The limit properties of $y=\arccos(x)$ are similar. Let's discuss them briefly."] [17592186185363 :tutorial/content "Let's recall the graph of $y=\arccos(x).$

![](images/9d/9dcc5a116c2a564547283783a7df7b1cd3a9ab3b76ac24dc2695c4cb367796d5.png)

From the graph, we note the following:

- The domain is $x \in [-1,1].$

- For every value $a \in (-1,1),$ we have

$$
\lim_\limits{x\to a} \arccos(x) = \arccos(a).
$$

- For any value $a$ that does *not* lie in the domain of $\arccos(x),$ the limit

$$
\lim_\limits{x\to a} \arccos(x)
$$

 
does *not* exist.

- The right-sided limit at $x=-1$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (-1)^{+}}\operatorname{arccos}⁡(x) & =\operatorname{arccos}⁡(-1) \\  & =\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

- Similarly, the left-sided limit at $x=1$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {1}^{-}}\operatorname{arccos}⁡(x) & =\operatorname{arccos}⁡(1) \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

- For every value $a,$ we have

$$
\lim_\limits{x\to a} \arctan(x) = \arctan(a).
$$

- The limit as $x\to-\infty$ is given by

$$

- The limit as $x\to\infty$ is given by

$$

$$

We can use the algebra of limits to evaluate expressions involving inverse trigonometric functions. Let's see some examples."] [17592186185360 :tutorial/content "We can deduce limits at infinity of transformed inverse trigonometric functions by sketching their graphs.

For example, let's consider the following limit:

$$
\lim_\limits{x \to \, \infty} \dfrac{2}{\pi}\arctan \left(x-\pi\right)
$$

To evaluate this limit, we first sketch the graph of  $y =\arctan \left(x-\pi\right){:}$  

![](images/51/51a0b9a210147b3791ce20a2f65320e20618826671ea6c7c31a27f8647595079.png)

The domain of   $\arctan \left(x-\pi\right)$ is $(-\infty,\infty).$   Moreover, from the graph, we see that 

$$
\lim\limits_{x\to \infty} \arctan \left(x-\pi\right)=\color{blue}{\dfrac{\pi}{2} }  .
$$

Therefore, by the algebra of limits, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \,\infty }\frac{2}{\pi }\operatorname{arctan}⁡(x-\pi ) & =\frac{2}{\pi }\cdot {lim}_{x\to \,\infty }\operatorname{arctan}⁡(x-\pi ) \\  & =\frac{2}{\pi }\cdot (\frac{\pi }{2}) \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Limits at infinity involving the inverse sine and cosine functions usually do not exist. $$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({e}^{2y}\operatorname{tan}⁡({x}^{2}))\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({e}^{2y}\operatorname{tan}⁡({x}^{2}))\,j \\  & =2x{e}^{2y}{sec}^{2}⁡({x}^{2})\,i+2{e}^{2y}\operatorname{tan}⁡({x}^{2})\,j \\ ∇f(\frac{\sqrt{\pi }}{2},0) & =2(\frac{\sqrt{\pi }}{2}){e}^{0}{sec}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})\,i+2{e}^{0}\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})\,j \\  & =2\sqrt{\pi }\,i+2\,j\end{aligned}
$$

:question/worked-solution "The tangent plane to a surface is horizontal if and only if the normal vector to the tangent plane is vertical. So, let's first find the general expression of a normal vector to the surface.

Remember that the Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the surface $z=f(x,y)$ at the point $(x_0, y_0, z_0)$ on the surface can be written as

$$
z - z_0 = (x-x_0)\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}(x_0,y_0) + (y-y_0)\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}(x_0,y_0)
$$

where $\left\langle \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}(x_0,y_0), \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}(x_0,y_0), -1 \right\rangle$ represents a normal vector to the tangent plane.

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({y}^{2}+xy) \\  & =y \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{2}+xy) \\  & =2y+x\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, a normal vector to the tangent plane is 

$$
\left\langle y, \: 2y+x, \: -1 \right\rangle.
$$

We want to find where this normal vector is vertical. This means that the $x$- and $y$-components of the vector must be $0\mathbin{:}$

![](images/ec/ec631b90dd9a037263e163bc32ebd982de5f60ee813622ae7b4f1a6b153fe856.svg) 

From the first equation, we get $y=0.$ Substituting this into the second equation, we obtain 

$$
2(0) +x = 0 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad x = 0.
$$

Finally, substituting $x=0$ and $y=0$ into our function, we get

$$
z = 0^2+(0)(0)= 0.
$$

Therefore, the point where the tangent plane is horizontal is $(0,0,0).$"] ["question-bbe6eb83-f049-5d99-ba2d-54fe9f07632a" :question/id #uuid "bbe6eb83-f049-5d99-ba2d-54fe9f07632a"] ["question-bbe6eb83-f049-5d99-ba2d-54fe9f07632a" :question/math-academy-id "q-129449"] ["question-bbe6eb83-f049-5d99-ba2d-54fe9f07632a" :question/problem "Determine the equation of the tangent plane to the surface $z={y}^{2}-{x}^{2}y$ at the point $(1,0,0).$"] ["question-bbe6eb83-f049-5d99-ba2d-54fe9f07632a" :question/worked-solution "The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the surface $z=f(x,y)$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ on the surface can be written as

$$
z-{z}_{0}=(x-{x}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}).
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({y}^{2}-{x}^{2}y) \\  & =-2xy \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{2}-{x}^{2}y) \\  & =2y-{x}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the partial derivatives at $(x,y)=(1,0):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}(1,0) & =-2(1)(0)=0 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y}(1,0) & =2(0)-{1}^{2}=-1\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write down the equation of the tangent plane:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-0 & =(x-1)\frac{∂f}{∂x}(1,0)+(y-0)\frac{∂f}{∂y}(1,0) \\ z & =0(x-1)-y \\ z & =-y \\ y+z & =0\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-bbe6eb83-f049-5d99-ba2d-54fe9f07632a" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-828b7774-44b4-512b-b1f3-ad49b7de67b9" :answer-field/id #uuid to the hypersurface $w={x}^{2}+yz$ at the point $(-1,1,1,2).$"] ["question-5d1f491f-4f62-54c6-804f-2430afabf623" :question/worked-solution "The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the hypersurface $w=f(x,y,z)$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0},{w}_{0})$ on the hypersurface can be written as

$$
w-{w}_{0}=(x-{x}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})+(z-{z}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂z}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0}).
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+yz)=2x \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+yz)=z \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}({x}^{2}+yz)=y\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the partial derivatives at $(x,y,z)=(-1,1,1):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}(-1,1,1) & =2(-1)=-2 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y}(-1,1,1) & =1 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z}(-1,1,1) & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write down the equation of the tangent hyperplane:

$$
\begin{aligned}w-2 & =(x-(-1))\frac{∂f}{∂x}(-1,1,1)+(y-1)\frac{∂f}{∂y}(-1,1,1)+(z-1)\frac{∂f}{∂z}(-1,1,1) \\ w-2 & =-2(x+1)+(y-1)+(z-1) \\ w-2 & =-2x+y+z-4 \\ 2x-y-z+w+2 & =0\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-5d1f491f-4f62-54c6-804f-2430afabf623" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-f8cc4165-06fc-5353-97db-60ce6554a423" :answer-field/id #uuid plane to the surface $z=f(x,y)$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ on the surface can be written as

$$
z-{z}_{0}=(x-{x}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),
$$

where $⟨\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),-1⟩$ represents a normal vector to the tangent plane.

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x\operatorname{ln}⁡y)=\operatorname{ln}⁡y \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(x\operatorname{ln}⁡y)=\frac{x}{y}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Hence, the normal vector to the tangent plane is 

$$
⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡y,\,\frac{x}{y},\,-1⟩.
$$

Note that the tangent plane is horizontal if and only if the normal vector is vertical. This means that the $x$- and $y$-components of the vector must be $0:$

$$
\{\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=0 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y}=0\end{aligned}\,⟹\,\{\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y=0 \\ \frac{x}{y}=0\end{aligned}
$$

 

From the first equation we get $y=1,$ while the second equation gives $x=0.$ 

Finally, substituting $x=0$ and $y=1$ into our function, we get

$$
z=0\operatorname{ln}⁡1=0.
$$

$$
z-{z}_{0}=(x-{x}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),

where $⟨\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),-1⟩$ represents a normal vector to the tangent plane.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(xy-3x+2y-5)=y-3 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(xy-3x+2y-5)=x+2\end{aligned}
$$

 

Hence, the normal vector to the tangent plane is 

$$
⟨y-3,\,x+2,\,-1⟩.
$$

Note that the tangent plane is horizontal if and only if the normal vector is vertical. This means that the $x$- and $y$-components of the vector must be $0:$

$$

$$

 

From the second equation we get $x=-2,$ while the first equation gives $y=3.$ 

Finally, substituting $x=-2$ and $y=3$ into our function, we get

$$
z=(-2)(3)-3(-2)+2(3)-5=1.
$$

"question-540d859a-8179-5e53-b6ff-389c30bf0b61"] [17592186130386 :tutorial/content "Similar to tangent lines for single variable functions, we can think of the **tangent plane** to a surface at a point as the plane that "touches" the surface at that point.

The equation of the tangent plane to a surface $z=f(x,y)$ at the point $(x_0,y_0,z_0),$ where $z_0=f(x_0,y_0),$ can be found using the formula

$$
z - z_0 = (x-x_0)\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}(x_0,y_0) + (y-y_0)\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}(x_0,y_0).
$$

For example, consider the surface 

$$
z = 4-x^2-y^2.
$$

Let's find the equation of the tangent plane to the surface at the point $(0,\sqrt{2},2),$ as shown below.

![](images/03/03df90a94615238e2126338f64d1f51fcefc379068a8cdc366b33b998cd69f45.png)

 

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(4-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2})=-2x \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(4-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2})=-2y\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the partial derivatives at $(x,y) = (0,\sqrt{2})\mathbin{:}$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}(0,\sqrt{2}) & =-2(0)=0 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y}(0,\sqrt{2}) & =-2(\sqrt{2})=-2\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write down the equation of the tangent plane:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-2 & =(x-0)\frac{∂f}{∂x}(0,\sqrt{2})+(y-\sqrt{2})\frac{∂f}{∂y}(0,\sqrt{2}) \\ z-2 & =0(x-0)-2\sqrt{2}(y-\sqrt{2}) \\ z-2 & =-2\sqrt{2}y+4 \\ 2\sqrt{2}y+z-6 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So, we get that the Cartesian equation of the tangent plane is $2\sqrt{2}y + z - 6 = 0.$

$$

$$

Finally, let's swap the left and right-hand sides so that the variable is on the left-hand side. Remember, we also need to flip the inequality.

$$
y>-5
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}-1 & \le 5x+14 \\ -1-14 & \le 5x+14-14 \\ -15 & \le 5x+0 \\ -15 & \le 5x\end{aligned}
$$

Second, we apply the multiplication principle, dividing both sides by $5:$

$$
\begin{aligned}-15 & \le 5x \\ -\frac{15}{5} & \le \frac{5x}{5} \\ -3 & \le \frac{\cancel{5}x}{\cancel{5}} \\ -3 & \le x\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, let's swap the left and right-hand sides so that the variable is on the left-hand side. Remember, we also need to flip the inequality.

$$
x\ge -3
$$

"question-a7f55f36-a99e-57a6-94a7-d395d5c39a69"] [17592186193912 :tutorial/content "Suppose that we wish to find the solution to the inequality

$$
2x + 6 < 12.
$$

An inequality like this one can be solved just like an equation, using the addition and multiplication principles.

First, we apply the addition principle, subtracting $6$ from both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}2x+6 & <12 \\ 2x+6-6 & <12-6 \\ 2x+0 & <6 \\ 2x & <6\end{aligned}
$$

Second, we apply the multiplication principle, dividing both sides by $2{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}2x & <6 \\ \frac{2x}{2} & <\frac{6}{2} \\ \frac{\cancel{2}x}{\cancel{2}} & <3 \\ x & <3\end{aligned}
$$

The solution is $x < 3$ In other words, any value less than $3$ satisfies the inequality.

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & 6 & 0 \\ 1 & -3 & 2 \\ 3 & -6 & 3\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(\frac{1}{3}){R}_{1} & ⟺ & \,\overset{{E}_{1}}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ \frac{1}{3} & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}}\cdot A \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-3 & 6 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 2 \\ 3 & -6 & 3\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+{R}_{1} & ⟺ & \,\overset{{E}_{2}}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}}\cdot {E}_{1}\cdot A \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-3 & 6 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =U\end{aligned}
$$

$$
P(Y\le m)=\frac{1}{2}.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}P(Y\le m) & ={\int }_{0}^{m}{e}^{-y}\,\text{d}y \\  & =-{e}^{-y}{|}_{0}^{m} \\  & =1-{e}^{-m}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}1-{e}^{-m} & =\frac{1}{2} \\ {e}^{-m} & =\frac{1}{2} \\ -m & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{2}) \\ -m & =-\operatorname{ln}⁡2 \\ m & =\operatorname{ln}⁡2.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-328730e5-b32c-5f55-aef8-1fdf6d6f55ce" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-a0c67064-cabf-594b-8138-f2a53ecff042" :answer-field/id #uuid :question/problem "Find, to three decimal places, the interquartile range of the random variable $X$ if the cumulative distribution function of $X$ is given by

$$
F(x)=\{\begin{aligned}0, & x<0, \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{16}, & 0\le x\le 4, \\ 1, & x>4.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-e2b4a0b2-77c3-5ed8-8555-0cfe3f01b758" :question/worked-solution "To find the interquartile range, we first need to find the lower quartile and the upper quartile.

The lower quartile of a random variable $X$ is the number ${q}_{1}$ such that

$$
P(X\le {q}_{1})=\frac{1}{4},
$$

and the upper quartile is the number ${q}_{3}$ such that

$$
P(X\le {q}_{3})=\frac{3}{4}.
$$

First, we find the lower quartile:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\le {q}_{1}) & =\frac{1}{4} \\ F({q}_{1}) & =\frac{1}{4} \\ \frac{{q}_{1}^{2}}{16} & =\frac{1}{4} \\ {q}_{1}^{2} & =4 \\ {q}_{1} & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we find the upper quartile:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\le {q}_{3}) & =\frac{3}{4} \\ F({q}_{3}) & =\frac{3}{4} \\ \frac{{q}_{3}^{2}}{16} & =\frac{3}{4} \\ {q}_{3}^{2} & =12 \\ {q}_{3} & =2\sqrt{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the interquartile range is

$$
IQR={q}_{3}-{q}_{1}=2\sqrt{3}-2≈1.464
$$

rounded to three decimal places."] ["question-e2b4a0b2-77c3-5ed8-8555-0cfe3f01b758" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-cdc675dd-7a38-5eec-ad05-1b9e422a82c4" $$

$$"] ["question-7f1b2358-54f2-52cf-a9df-c46a72812503" :question/worked-solution "The $100p$th percentile of a random variable $Y$ is the number ${y}_{p}$ such that

$$
P(Y\le {y}_{p})=p.
$$

In our case, we want to find the $60$th percentile, which corresponds to the decimal $p=0.6.$ We have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(Y\le {y}_{0.6}) & ={\int }_{1}^{{y}_{0.6}}\frac{1}{{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={-\frac{1}{y}|}_{1}^{{y}_{0.6}} \\  & =1-\frac{1}{{y}_{0.6}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the $60$th percentile is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}1-\frac{1}{{y}_{0.6}} & =0.6 \\ \frac{1}{{y}_{0.6}} & =0.4 \\ {y}_{0.6} & =\frac{1}{0.4} \\ {y}_{0.6} & =\frac{5}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-7f1b2358-54f2-52cf-a9df-c46a72812503" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-b021d4b8-9d31-550f-8894-f27be8d6ecdd" :answer-field/id #uuid ["question-c3057bfc-a8d8-5a19-9075-be23799b04aa" :question/math-academy-id "q-125715"] ["question-c3057bfc-a8d8-5a19-9075-be23799b04aa" :question/problem "Find the interquartile range of the random variable $X$ if the cumulative distribution function of $X$ is given by

$$
F(x)=\{\begin{aligned}0, & x<1, \\ 1-\frac{1}{{x}^{6}}, & x\ge 1.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-c3057bfc-a8d8-5a19-9075-be23799b04aa" :question/worked-solution "To find the interquartile range, we first need to find the lower quartile and the upper quartile.

The lower quartile of a random variable $X$ is the number ${q}_{1}$ such that

$$
P(X\le {q}_{1})=\frac{1}{4},
$$

and the upper quartile is the number ${q}_{3}$ such that

$$
P(X\le {q}_{3})=\frac{3}{4}.
$$

First, we find the lower quartile:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\le {q}_{1}) & =\frac{1}{4} \\ F({q}_{1}) & =\frac{1}{4} \\ 1-\frac{1}{{q}_{1}^{6}} & =\frac{1}{4} \\ \frac{1}{{q}_{1}^{6}} & =\frac{3}{4} \\ \frac{1}{{q}_{1}} & =\sqrt[6]{\frac{3}{4}} \\ {q}_{1} & =\sqrt[6]{\frac{4}{3}}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we find the upper quartile:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\le {q}_{3}) & =\frac{3}{4} \\ F({q}_{3}) & =\frac{3}{4} \\ 1-\frac{1}{{q}_{3}^{6}} & =\frac{3}{4} \\ \frac{1}{{q}_{3}^{6}} & =\frac{1}{4} \\ \frac{1}{{q}_{1}} & =\sqrt[6]{\frac{1}{4}} \\ {q}_{1} & =\sqrt[6]{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the interquartile range is

$$
\begin{aligned}IQR & ={q}_{3}-{q}_{1} \\  & =\sqrt[6]{4}-\sqrt[6]{\frac{4}{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-c3057bfc-a8d8-5a19-9075-be23799b04aa" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-87f1f10e-3dae-5b47-be1d-ec0989a80ffb" :answer-field/id #uuid
