x^{x^3}.$"] [17592186064143 :question/worked-solution "We have the function 

$$
y = x^{x^3}.
$$

First, we take the natural logarithm of both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{{x}^{3}}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & ={x}^{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to $x{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡x) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =({x}^{3})^{′}\cdot (\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+({x}^{3})\cdot {(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)}^{′} \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =3{x}^{2}\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡x+{x}^{3}\cdot \frac{1}{x} \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =3{x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡x+{x}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve for $y'{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =y(3{x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡x+{x}^{2})\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $y=x^{x^3}{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & ={x}^{{x}^{3}}(3{x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡x+{x}^{2}) \\  & ={x}^{{x}^{3}}({x}^{2}(3\operatorname{ln}⁡x+1)) \\  & ={x}^{{x}^{3}+2}(3\operatorname{ln}⁡x+1)\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186064144 :question/problem "Find the derivative of the function $y = (x^2-1)^x.$"] [17592186064144 :question/worked-solution "We have the function 

$$
y = (x^2-1)^x.
$$

First, we take the natural logarithm of both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(({x}^{2}-1)^{x}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}-1)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to $x{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}-1)) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x)\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}-1)+x\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}-1)) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =1\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}-1)+x\cdot (\frac{1}{{x}^{2}-1}\cdot 2x) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}-1)+\frac{2{x}^{2}}{{x}^{2}-1}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve for $\dfrac {\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x}{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =y(\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}-1)+\frac{2{x}^{2}}{{x}^{2}-1})\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $y = (x^2-1)^x{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =({x}^{2}-1)^{x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}-1)+\frac{2{x}^{2}}{{x}^{2}-1}) \\  & =({x}^{2}-1)^{x}(\frac{({x}^{2}-1)\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}-1)}{{x}^{2}-1}+\frac{2{x}^{2}}{{x}^{2}-1}) \\  & =({x}^{2}-1)^{x-1}(({x}^{2}-1)\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}-1)+2{x}^{2})\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186064145 :question/problem "Find the derivative of the function $y = (\sin x)^{\cos x}.$"] [17592186064145 :question/worked-solution "We have the function 

$$
y = (\sin x)^{\cos x}.
$$

First, we take the natural logarithm of both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡((\operatorname{sin}⁡x)^{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to $x{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)^{′}\cdot (\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{sin}⁡x))+(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)\cdot {(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{sin}⁡x))}^{′} \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =(-\operatorname{sin}⁡x)\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)+\operatorname{cos}⁡x\cdot (\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡x) \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\operatorname{cot}⁡x-\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve for $y'{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =y(\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\operatorname{cot}⁡x-\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{sin}⁡x))\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $y = (\sin x)^{\cos x}{:}$

["question-cdcbfec1-c9f8-5550-af44-736f646a25ea" :question/problem "Consider the function $y=({x}^{2}+3x)^{x}.$ Its derivative is given by 

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=({x}^{2}+3x)^{x-1}\cdot g(x).
$$

Find the function $g(x).$"] ["question-cdcbfec1-c9f8-5550-af44-736f646a25ea" :question/worked-solution "We have the function 

$$
y=({x}^{2}+3x)^{x}.
$$

First, we take the natural logarithm of both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(({x}^{2}+3x)^{x}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+3x)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+3x)) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x)\cdot (\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+3x))+(x)\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+3x)) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =1\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+3x)+x\cdot (\frac{1}{{x}^{2}+3x}\cdot 2x+3) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+3x)+\frac{2{x}^{2}+3x}{{x}^{2}+3x}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve for $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =y(\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+3x)+\frac{2{x}^{2}+3x}{{x}^{2}+3x})\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $y=({x}^{2}+3x)^{x}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =({x}^{2}+3x)^{x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+3x)+\frac{2{x}^{2}+3x}{{x}^{2}+3x}) \\  & =({x}^{2}+3x)^{x}(\frac{({x}^{2}+3x)\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+3x)}{{x}^{2}+3x}+\frac{2{x}^{2}+3x}{{x}^{2}+3x}) \\  & =({x}^{2}+3x)^{x-1}(({x}^{2}+3x)\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+3x)+(2{x}^{2}+3x)).\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, $g(x)=({x}^{2}+3x)\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+3x)+(2{x}^{2}+3x).$"] ["question-cdcbfec1-c9f8-5550-af44-736f646a25ea" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] {{field-1}}"] ["question-650ff22d-86ac-5784-9e2d-04a2cd40b0db" :question/worked-solution "The slope of the tangent to the curve at $x=\frac{e}{3}$ equals the function's derivative at the corresponding point.

We have the function 

$$
y=(\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x))^{{x}^{2}}.
$$

First, we take the natural logarithm of both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡((\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x))^{{x}^{2}}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & ={x}^{2}\,\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x))\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}\,\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x))) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =({x}^{2})^{′}\cdot (\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x)))+({x}^{2})\cdot {(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x)))}^{′} \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =2x\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x))+{x}^{2}\cdot (\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x)}\cdot \frac{1}{x}) \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =2x\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x))+\frac{x}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x)}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve for ${y}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =y(2x\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x))+\frac{x}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x)})\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $y=(\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x))^{{x}^{2}}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =(\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x))^{{x}^{2}}(2x\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x))+\frac{x}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x)})\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of $y=(\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x))^{{x}^{2}}$ at $x=\frac{e}{3}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}m={y}^{′}{|}_{x=e/3} & =(\operatorname{ln}⁡(e))^{(e/3)^{2}}(2(\frac{e}{3})\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡(e))+\frac{(\frac{e}{3})}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(e)}) \\  & =(1)^{(e/3)^{2}}(2(\frac{e}{3})\operatorname{ln}⁡(1)+\frac{(\frac{e}{3})}{1}) \\  & =1\cdot (0+\frac{e}{3}) \\  & =\frac{e}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-650ff22d-86ac-5784-9e2d-04a2cd40b0db" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-36d45e39-f71d-51b2-ae6d-2faee3a34b79" :answer-field/id #uuid "36d45e39-f71d-51b2-ae6d-2faee3a34b79"] ["answer-9bdcbb96-5ec9-5007-b256-214fc5f8397c" :answer/id #uuid "9bdcbb96-5ec9-5007-b256-214fc5f8397c"] ["answer-9bdcbb96-5ec9-5007-b256-214fc5f8397c" :answer/type :answer.type/math] ["answer-9bdcbb96-5ec9-5007-b256-214fc5f8397c" :answer/value "\frac{e}{3}"] ["answer-field-36d45e39-f71d-51b2-ae6d-2faee3a34b79" :answer-field/key "field-1"] ["answer-field-36d45e39-f71d-51b2-ae6d-2faee3a34b79" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank] ["answer-field-36d45e39-f71d-51b2-ae6d-2faee3a34b79" :answer-field/correct "answer-9bdcbb96-5ec9-5007-b256-214fc5f8397c"] ["answer-field-36d45e39-f71d-51b2-ae6d-2faee3a34b79" :answer-field/choices "answer-9bdcbb96-5ec9-5007-b256-214fc5f8397c"] ["question-650ff22d-86ac-5784-9e2d-04a2cd40b0db" :question/answer-fields "answer-field-36d45e39-f71d-51b2-ae6d-2faee3a34b79"] [17592186064308 :knowledge-point/questions "question-650ff22d-86ac-5784-9e2d-04a2cd40b0db"] ["question-a8502904-ea72-54be-8bde-7a62b1b58e76" :question/id #uuid "a8502904-ea72-54be-8bde-7a62b1b58e76"] ["question-a8502904-ea72-54be-8bde-7a62b1b58e76" :question/math-academy-id "q-138863"] ["question-a8502904-ea72-54be-8bde-7a62b1b58e76" :question/problem "Find the slope of the tangent to the curve $y=(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)^{5x}$ at $x=e.$"] ["question-a8502904-ea72-54be-8bde-7a62b1b58e76" :question/worked-solution "The slope of the tangent to the curve at $x=e$ equals the function's derivative at the corresponding point.

We have the function 

$$
y=(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)^{5x}.
$$

First, we take the natural logarithm of both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡((\operatorname{ln}⁡x)^{5x}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =5x\,\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(5x\,\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =(5x)^{′}\cdot (\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x))+(5x)\cdot {(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x))}^{′} \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =5\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+5x\cdot (\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}\cdot \frac{1}{x}) \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =5\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+\frac{5}{\operatorname{ln}⁡x} \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =5(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡x})\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =y(5(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}))\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $y=(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)^{5x}:$

$$

$$

Therefore, the slope of $y=(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)^{5x}$ at $x=e$ is

$$

"question-a8502904-ea72-54be-8bde-7a62b1b58e76"] [17592186065395 :tutorial/content "**Logarithmic differentiation** is a technique to compute derivatives that are difficult to find using the usual rules of differentiation, such as the product, quotient, and chain rules.

Let's consider the following function.

$$
y = x^x
$$

We aim to compute $\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d x}.$ However, in this case, we note the following:

- Both the base and the exponent are functions of $x.$

- This means we cannot apply the power rule since the exponent is not a fixed number.

- We also cannot apply the rules for differentiating exponentials since the base is not a fixed number.

So instead, we'll use logarithmic differentiation. We proceed as follows:

**Step 1.** We take the natural logarithm of both sides and apply the power rule for logarithms:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & ={x}^{x} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡{x}^{x} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2.** We differentiate both sides of the above equation with respect to $x$ using implicit differentiation and the product rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x\operatorname{ln}⁡x) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x)\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡x+x\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡x) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =1\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡x+x\cdot (\frac{1}{x}) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡x+1\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3.** Now, we solve for $\dfrac {\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x}.$ This gives

$$
\dfrac {\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} =  y\left( \ln x + 1 \right).
$$

**Step 4.** Finally, we substitute back our original expression for $y=x^x{:}$

$$
\dfrac {\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} = x^x \left( \ln x + 1 \right)
$$

If the coin landed heads up $16$ times, how many times did it land tails up?"] ["question-1e6db99f-016f-5b3d-be15-91b5ecbdbcbd" :question/worked-solution "We start with the ratio $4:9$ and write it as a fraction:

$$
\frac{4}{9}
$$

In this fraction, the numerator represents the number of heads, and the denominator represents the total number of tosses.

We can make a numerator of $16$ by multiplying the numerator and denominator by $4:$

$$
\frac{4\times 4}{9\times 4}=\frac{16}{36}
$$

Therefore, the coin was tossed $36$ times in total. 
So, the number of tails is

$$
36-16=20.

"question-8ad1d634-a638-5b7b-9104-1b08e0a11215"] [17592186180235 :question/worked-solution "We are given that the ratio of red roses to the total number of roses is $\frac{3}{10}.$

\frac{3\times 9}{10\times 9}=\frac{27}{90}
$$

$$"] [17592186180235 :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] [17592186178954 :answer-field/correct 17592186178958] [17592186180636 :step/math-academy-id 637169] [17592186180637 :step/math-academy-id 637170] [17592186180638 :step/math-academy-id 637173] [17592186179889 :activity/expected-seconds 420.0] ["question-c8c9dba6-d928-5ac1-ba3e-1db8d33cfb50" :question/id #uuid "c8c9dba6-d928-5ac1-ba3e-1db8d33cfb50"] ["question-c8c9dba6-d928-5ac1-ba3e-1db8d33cfb50" :question/math-academy-id "q-94793"] ["question-c8c9dba6-d928-5ac1-ba3e-1db8d33cfb50" :question/problem "Consider the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}2 & 7 \\ 7 & 2\end{aligned}].$ Which of the following statements are true?

I. The eigenvalues of $A$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=-5$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=9$

II. ${x}^{T}\,A\,x$ is positive-definite

III. $A$ is indefinite"] ["question-c8c9dba6-d928-5ac1-ba3e-1db8d33cfb50" :question/worked-solution "Given a quadratic form $Q(x)={x}^{T}Ax,$ we have the following theorem:

- $Q$ is positive-definite if and only if all the eigenvalues of $A$ are positive,

- $Q$ is positive semi-definite if and only if all the eigenvalues of $A$ are non-negative (note that positive semi-definite quadratic forms include all positive-definite quadratic forms),

- $Q$ is negative-definite if and only if all the eigenvalues of $A$ are negative,

- $Q$ is negative semi-definite if and only if all the eigenvalues of $A$ are non-positive (note that negative semi-definite quadratic forms include all negative-definite quadratic forms), and

- $Q$ is indefinite if and only if $A$ has both positive and negative eigenvalues.

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. Computing the characteristic equation of $A,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}|A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}2-\lambda  & 7 \\ 7 & 2-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (2-\lambda )(2-\lambda )-49 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-4\lambda -45 & =0 \\ \lambda  & =-5,\,9.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is false, while statement III is true. Since $A$ has both positive and negative eigenvalues, the quadratic form ${x}^{T}\,A\,x$ (as well as the matrix $A$) is indefinite.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only.""] ["question-c8c9dba6-d928-5ac1-ba3e-1db8d33cfb50" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] "$5-3(x+1)=$"] [17592186188950 :question/worked-solution "Notice that the expression we need to subtract from $5$ must be expanded using the distributive law. 

So first, let's write some big brackets around the expression in parentheses, keeping the minus sign *outside*.

$$
5-[3(x+1)]
$$

Next, we expand the expression inside the brackets using the distributive law. This gives

$$
5-[3x+3].
$$

Now, we remove the brackets by distributing the negative sign. This gives

$$
5-3x-3.
$$

Finally, we collect like terms:

$$
\begin{aligned}5-3x-3 & = \\ (5-3)-3x & = \\ 2-3x & \end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186188950 :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-503a5a0c-6d91-57c6-948d-dc1e42b752c7" :answer/id #uuid "503a5a0c-6d91-57c6-948d-dc1e42b752c7"] At first, it may seem natural to differentiate $y_p$ directly:

$$
y_p' = (u_1y_1+u_2y_2)' = u_1'y_1 + u_1y_1' + u_2'y_2 + u_2y_2'.

This expression contains the *extra terms* $u_1'y_1$ and $u_2'y_2,$ which will also appear (after differentiating again) in the expression for $y_p''$.

If we substitute $y=y_p$ into the differential equation, we will obtain *one* equation involving *two* unknown derivatives $u_1'$ and $u_2',$ so we need a second equation to determine them.

To create a second equation, we *choose* to impose the condition

$$

This is not a property of $u_1$ and $u_2$ that we already know, but it is an additional constraint that we enforce to make the system solvable.

$$
y_p' = u_1'y_1 + u_1y_1' + u_2'y_2 + u_2y_2',

and using the constraint $u_1'y_1+u_2'y_2=0,$ we obtain

$$
y_p' = u_1y_1' + u_2y_2'.
$$

So, the commonly stated "derivative condition"

$$
y_p' = u_1y_1' + u_2y_2'
$$

is simply the product-rule derivative of $y_p$ *after* we impose $u_1'y_1+u_2'y_2=0.$

{{field-1}}"] ["question-060bce41-c046-5d08-898b-cfb8261e7661" :question/worked-solution "From the definition of $f(x),$

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to -1}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to -1}{log}_{5}⁡(2x+k) \\  & ={log}_{5}⁡(k-2).\end{aligned}
$$

In order for $f(x)$ to be continuous at $x=-1,$ we must have

$$

\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 0}g(x) & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{x}{\sqrt{x-b}-\sqrt{2{x}^{2}-b}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}(\frac{x}{\sqrt{x-b}-\sqrt{2{x}^{2}-b}}\cdot \frac{\sqrt{x-b}+\sqrt{2{x}^{2}-b}}{\sqrt{x-b}+\sqrt{2{x}^{2}-b}}) \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{x(\sqrt{x-b}+\sqrt{2{x}^{2}-b})}{(\sqrt{x-b})^{2}-(\sqrt{2{x}^{2}-b})^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{x(\sqrt{x-b}+\sqrt{2{x}^{2}-b})}{x-2{x}^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{x(\sqrt{x-b}+\sqrt{2{x}^{2}-b})}{x(1-2x)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{\cancel{x}(\sqrt{x-b}+\sqrt{2{x}^{2}-b})}{\cancel{x}(1-2x)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{\sqrt{x-b}+\sqrt{2{x}^{2}-b}}{1-2x} \\  & =2\sqrt{-b}.\end{aligned}
$$

In order for $g(x)$ to be continuous at $x=0,$ we must have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 0}g(x) & =g(0) \\ 2\sqrt{-b} & =10 \\ \sqrt{-b} & =5 \\ -b & =25 \\ b & =-25.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, setting $b=-25$ removes the point discontinuity."] ["question-1326dade-f2c7-5d3e-a020-cedd74fc345f" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-77bbd51e-5904-5d45-8bc3-de4505ff154f" :answer-field/id #uuid "77bbd51e-5904-5d45-8bc3-de4505ff154f"] ["answer-24ede090-0e98-526f-95c9-95e8850bcb72" :answer/id #uuid "24ede090-0e98-526f-95c9-95e8850bcb72"] ["answer-24ede090-0e98-526f-95c9-95e8850bcb72" :answer/type :answer.type/math] ["answer-24ede090-0e98-526f-95c9-95e8850bcb72" :answer/value "-25"] ["answer-field-77bbd51e-5904-5d45-8bc3-de4505ff154f" :answer-field/key "field-1"] ["answer-field-77bbd51e-5904-5d45-8bc3-de4505ff154f" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank] ["answer-field-77bbd51e-5904-5d45-8bc3-de4505ff154f" :answer-field/correct "answer-24ede090-0e98-526f-95c9-95e8850bcb72"] ["answer-field-77bbd51e-5904-5d45-8bc3-de4505ff154f" :answer-field/choices "answer-24ede090-0e98-526f-95c9-95e8850bcb72"] ["question-1326dade-f2c7-5d3e-a020-cedd74fc345f" :question/answer-fields "answer-field-77bbd51e-5904-5d45-8bc3-de4505ff154f"] [17592186064150 :knowledge-point/questions "question-1326dade-f2c7-5d3e-a020-cedd74fc345f"] [17592186065391 :tutorial/content "Consider the function $f(x)$ below.

The function $f(x)$ seems to have a point discontinuity at $x=4.$ However, by selecting a particular value for $a,$ we can remove the point discontinuity and make the function continuous.

We can find this value of $a$ by forcing the limit of the function to be equal to the value of the function at $x=4\mathbin{:}$

$$
\lim\limits_{x\to 4} f(x) = f(4)
$$

Remember that $\lim\limits_{x\to 4} f(x)$ represents the value that $f(x)$ approaches as $x$ gets closer and closer, but not equal, to $4.$ So, when evaluating $\lim\limits_{x\to 4} f(x),$ we need to use the function definition for $x \neq 4.$

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 4}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to 4}(3x+a) \\  & =3(4)+a \\  & =12+a\end{aligned}
$$

At $x=4,$ the function is defined as $f(x)=13.$ So $f(4)=13,$ and we can solve the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 4}f(x) & =f(4) \\ 12+a & =13 \\ a & =1\end{aligned}
$$

$$
x > 0
$$

We can represent this inequality using a number line as follows:

![](images/79/79664d125db14d5b8534d592d232839659a6d0efbd527379207b50d71f9e7454.png)

How do we represent this inequality using interval notation?

Note the following:

- The left endpoint $x=0$ is *not* included. Therefore, we use a parenthesis $($ for this endpoint.

- The interval continues forever in the positive direction. To denote this, we must introduce the **infinity** symbol $\infty.$ Infinity is not a number but a concept that means *larger than any number*.

- We use a right parenthesis $)$ in conjunction with the $\infty$ symbol.

Therefore, we can express the inequality $x > 0$ in interval notation as follows:

$$
x \in (0, \infty)
$$

**Watch Out!** Whenever $\infty$ appears in an interval, it is *always* associated with a right parenthesis. Infinity is *never* associated with a bracket, even if the other endpoint is."] [17592186193940 :tutorial/content "Now, consider the following inequality:

Using a linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(1,1),$ estimate the value of $f(1.02,0.97).$"] [17592186125256 :question/worked-solution "The linear approximation of the function $f$ at the point $(a,b)$ is given by

$$
f(x,y)≈f(a,b)+∇f(a,b)\cdot ⟨x-a,y-b⟩.
$$

So, the linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(1,1)$ is:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ≈f(1,1)+∇f(1,1)\cdot ⟨x-1,y-1⟩ \\  & ≈f(1,1)+⟨{f}_{x}(1,1),{f}_{y}(1,1)⟩\cdot ⟨x-1,y-1⟩ \\  & ≈1+⟨{f}_{x}(1,1),{f}_{y}(1,1)⟩\cdot ⟨x-1,y-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we find ${f}_{x}(1,1)$ and ${f}_{y}(1,1)$ using the given partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(1,1) & =3(1)^{2}(1)^{4}=3 \\ {f}_{y}(1,1) & =4(1)^{3}(1)^{3}=4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
f(x,y)≈1+⟨3,4⟩\cdot ⟨x-1,y-1⟩
$$

Finally, we can estimate $f(1.02,0.97)$ by evaluating the linear approximation at $x=1.02$ and $y=0.97,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(1.02,0.97) & ≈1+⟨3,4⟩\cdot ⟨1.02-1,0.97-1⟩ \\  & =1+⟨3,4⟩\cdot ⟨0.02,-0.03⟩ \\  & =1+0.06-0.12 \\  & =0.94\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186125256 :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] [17592186124136 :answer-field/correct 17592186124139] ["question-dfe98e1c-3b93-5422-932b-6229fbfa5965" :question/id #uuid "dfe98e1c-3b93-5422-932b-6229fbfa5965"] ["question-dfe98e1c-3b93-5422-932b-6229fbfa5965" :question/math-academy-id "q-129635"] ["question-dfe98e1c-3b93-5422-932b-6229fbfa5965" :question/problem "Let $f(x,y)$ be a differentiable function such that

Using a linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(-1,0),$ estimate the value of $f(-1.01,0.01).$"] ["question-dfe98e1c-3b93-5422-932b-6229fbfa5965" :question/worked-solution "The linear approximation of the function $f$ at the point $(a,b)$ is given by

$$
f(x,y)≈f(a,b)+∇f(a,b)\cdot ⟨x-a,y-b⟩.
$$

So, the linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(-1,0)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ≈f(-1,0)+∇f(-1,0)\cdot ⟨x-(-1),y-0⟩ \\  & ≈f(-1,0)+⟨{f}_{x}(-1,0),{f}_{y}(-1,0)⟩\cdot ⟨x+1,y⟩ \\  & ≈2+⟨{f}_{x}(-1,0),{f}_{y}(-1,0)⟩\cdot ⟨x+1,y⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we find ${f}_{x}(-1,0)$ and ${f}_{y}(-1,0)$ using the given partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(-1,0) & =4(-1)=-4 \\ {f}_{y}(-1,0) & =6(0)=0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
f(x,y)≈2+⟨-4,0⟩\cdot ⟨x+1,y⟩.
$$

Finally, we can estimate $f(-1.01,0.01)$ by evaluating the linear approximation at $x=-1.01$ and $y=0.01,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(-1.01,0.01) & ≈2+⟨-4,0⟩\cdot ⟨-1.01+1,0.01⟩ \\  & =2+⟨-4,0⟩\cdot ⟨-0.01,0.01⟩ \\  & =2-4(-0.01)+0(0.01) \\  & =2+0.04+0 \\  & =2.04\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-dfe98e1c-3b93-5422-932b-6229fbfa5965" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-668268b9-6681-52bb-9c91-25df63005244" :answer-field/id #uuid $$
f(x,y,z)≈f(a,b,c)+∇f(a,b,c)\cdot ⟨x-a,y-b,z-c⟩.
$$

So, the linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(0,2,1)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & ≈f(0,2,1)+∇f(0,2,1)\cdot ⟨x-0,y-2,z-1⟩ \\  & =8+⟨{f}_{x}(0,2,1),{f}_{y}(0,2,1),{f}_{z}(0,2,1)⟩\cdot ⟨x,y-2,z-1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we find ${f}_{x}(0,2,1)$, ${f}_{y}(0,2,1)$ and ${f}_{z}(0,2,1),$ using the given partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(0,2,1) & =\frac{2{e}^{0}}{\sqrt{{e}^{0}+2+1}}=1 \\ {f}_{y}(0,2,1) & =\frac{2}{\sqrt{{e}^{0}+2+1}}=1 \\ {f}_{z}(0,2,1) & =\frac{2}{\sqrt{{e}^{0}+2+1}}=1\end{aligned}

Therefore, we have

$$
f(x,y,z)≈8+⟨1,1,1⟩\cdot ⟨x,y-2,z-1⟩.
$$

Finally, we can estimate $f(-0.01,1.98,1.05)$ by evaluating the linear approximation at $x=-0.01,y=1.98$ and $z=1.05,$ as follows:

$$

$$"] ["question-adb4921d-df66-5c35-baf2-cc613e0cb3d4" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-e18cb7ab-d012-533c-946a-99ec38759650" :answer-field/id #uuid ["question-d66b6ff3-5c30-5d09-a1a7-0b4d573341bb" :question/math-academy-id "q-129750"] ["question-d66b6ff3-5c30-5d09-a1a7-0b4d573341bb" :question/problem "Let $f(x,y,z)={x}^{2}z-{y}^{2}.$ Find the linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(1,0,2).$"] ["question-d66b6ff3-5c30-5d09-a1a7-0b4d573341bb" :question/worked-solution "The linear approximation of the function $f$ at the point $(a,b,c)$ is given by

$$
f(x,y,z)≈f(a,b,c)+∇f(a,b,c)\cdot ⟨x-a,y-b,z-c⟩.
$$

So, the linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(1,0,2)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & ≈f(1,0,2)+∇f(1,0,2)\cdot ⟨x-1,y,z-2⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

From the definition of $f,$ we have that $f(1,0,2)=2.$ Computing the partial derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x} & =2xz\,⇒\,{f}_{x}(1,0,2)=4, \\ {f}_{y} & =-2y\,⇒\,{f}_{y}(1,0,2)=0, \\ {f}_{z} & ={x}^{2}\,⇒\,{f}_{z}(1,0,2)=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the gradient of the function at the point $(1,0,2)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(1,0,2) & =⟨{f}_{x}(1,0,2),{f}_{y}(1,0,2),{f}_{z}(1,0,2)⟩ \\  & =⟨4,0,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the linear approximation of the function $f$ is

$$

:question/worked-solution "The definite integral can be defined in terms of the limit of a left Riemann sum as

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}f({x}_{i})\cdot Δx,
$$

 

where $Δx=\frac{b-a}{n}$ and ${x}_{i}=a+iΔx.$

In the definite integral

$$
{\int }_{1}^{10}{x}^{1/2}\,\text{d}x,
$$

the function is $f(x)={x}^{1/2},$ the lower bound is $a=1,$ and the upper bound is $b=10.$ So, we have

$$
Δx=\frac{10-1}{n}=\frac{9}{n},
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{10}{x}^{1/2}\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}f({x}_{i})\cdot Δx \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}[f(1+i\cdot \frac{9}{n})\cdot \frac{9}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}[f(1+\frac{9i}{n})\cdot \frac{9}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}[{(\,1+\frac{9i}{n}\,)}^{\,1/2}\,\cdot \frac{9}{n}].\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186318563 :answer-field/correct 17592186317738] [17592186234108 :question/problem "Find the function $f(x)$ and the value of $b,$ given that ${\int }_{-\pi }^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=0}^{n-1}[{cos}^{2}(-\pi +\frac{\pi k}{n})\cdot \frac{\pi }{n}].$"] [17592186234108 :question/worked-solution "A definite integral can be defined as the limit of a left Riemann sum as follows:

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=0}^{n-1}f({x}_{k})\cdot Δx
$$

where $Δx=\frac{b-a}{n}$ and ${x}_{k}=a+kΔx.$

Notice that we're given that the lower limit $a=-\pi .$ 

Comparing the given summation with the general expression above, we see that $Δx=\frac{\pi }{n}.$ Therefore, 

$$
\frac{\pi }{n}=\frac{b-(-\pi )}{n}\,⟹\,b=0.

Consequently, ${x}_{k}=-\pi +\frac{\pi k}{n}$ and $f({x}_{k})={cos}^{2}{x}_{k}.$

We can do this using a left Riemann sum with $n=4$ subintervals, as shown below:

![](images/1b/1b25a722d5527db77cd7dd5fb581c0ffed9b9324913d390e2633211360b6a8ab.png)

A better approximation can be found by taking more subintervals. For instance, taking $n=8$ subintervals gives:

![](images/17/17f6c8e458b2e6fbd887728cbbcc7cb64a670598256f76cad69d9e5a9c3cf7b5.png)

As we continue to increase $n,$ our approximation gets better and better. In fact, we can get an *exact* value for the area by taking the limit of the Riemann sum as $n\to\infty.$

Let's write down that limit. First, we need to express the left Riemann sum using sigma notation. Using $n$ subintervals between the endpoints $a=0$ and $b=1,$ we express

$$
\begin{aligned}A & \approx {\sum }_{k=0}^{n-1}f({x}_{k})Δx \\  & ={\sum }_{k=0}^{n-1}f(0+k\cdot Δx)Δx \\  & ={\sum }_{k=0}^{n-1}f(k\cdot Δx)Δx \\  & ={\sum }_{k=0}^{n-1}({(k\cdot Δx)}^{2}+1)Δx \\  & ={\sum }_{k=0}^{n-1}({k}^{2}\cdot \frac{1}{{n}^{2}}+1)\cdot \frac{1}{n} \\  & ={\sum }_{k=0}^{n-1}(\frac{{k}^{2}}{{n}^{2}}+1)\cdot \frac{1}{n}.\end{aligned}
$$

In the above, we used the fact that $x_k = 0 + k\Delta x = k\Delta x$ and $\Delta x = \dfrac{1 - 0}{n} = \dfrac 1 n,$ as we've seen before.

The exact area is found by computing the limit as $n\to\infty.$ So instead of using an approximation symbol $(\approx),$ we can now use an equality symbol and write

$$
A = \lim_{n\to\infty}\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\left(\dfrac{k^2}{n^2} + 1\right)\cdot \dfrac{1}{n}.
$$

The formula above is a bit clunky, so instead of writing it using limits and sigma notation, we introduce a new notation called the **definite integral**, defined as

$$
\mathcal{A} = \lim_{n\to\infty}\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\left(\dfrac{k^2}{n^2} + 1\right)\cdot \dfrac{1}{n}= \int_0^1 (x^2 + 1)\, \textrm{d}x.
$$

In our example, 

$$
\displaystyle \int_0^1 (x^2+1)\, \textrm{d}x

can be interpreted as the exact area under the graph of $y = f(x) = x^2+1$ between $x=0,$ $x=1,$ and the $x$-axis."] [17592186097911 :tutorial/content "In general, for a function $f(x)$ defined on $[a,b],$ the **definite integral** of $f(x)$ between $x=a$ and $x=b$ can be defined using the limit of a left  Riemann sum as

Let's see an example."] [17592186128997 :question/worked-solution "The tangent plane to a surface is horizontal if and only if the normal vector to the tangent plane is vertical. So, let's first find the general expression of a normal vector to the surface.

Remember that the Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the surface $z=f(x,y)$ at the point $(x_0, y_0, z_0)$ on the surface can be written as

$$
z - z_0 = (x-x_0)\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}(x_0,y_0) + (y-y_0)\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}(x_0,y_0)
$$

where $\left\langle \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}(x_0,y_0), \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}(x_0,y_0), -1 \right\rangle$ represents a normal vector to the tangent plane.

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({y}^{2}+xy) \\  & =y \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{2}+xy) \\  & =2y+x\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, a normal vector to the tangent plane is 

$$
\left\langle y, \: 2y+x, \: -1 \right\rangle.
$$

Therefore, the points where the tangent plane is horizontal are $(-1,-1,1)$ and $(1,-1,-3).$"] [17592186130386 :tutorial/content "Similar to tangent lines for single variable functions, we can think of the **tangent plane** to a surface at a point as the plane that "touches" the surface at that point.

The equation of the tangent plane to a surface $z=f(x,y)$ at the point $(x_0,y_0,z_0),$ where $z_0=f(x_0,y_0),$ can be found using the formula

$$
z - z_0 = (x-x_0)\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}(x_0,y_0) + (y-y_0)\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}(x_0,y_0).
$$

For example, consider the surface 

$$
z = 4-x^2-y^2.
$$

Let's find the equation of the tangent plane to the surface at the point $(0,\sqrt{2},2),$ as shown below.

$$

Next, we evaluate the partial derivatives at $(x,y) = (0,\sqrt{2})\mathbin{:}$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}(0,\sqrt{2}) & =-2(0)=0 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y}(0,\sqrt{2}) & =-2(\sqrt{2})=-2\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write down the equation of the tangent plane:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-2 & =(x-0)\frac{∂f}{∂x}(0,\sqrt{2})+(y-\sqrt{2})\frac{∂f}{∂y}(0,\sqrt{2}) \\ z-2 & =0(x-0)-2\sqrt{2}(y-\sqrt{2}) \\ z-2 & =-2\sqrt{2}y+4 \\ 2\sqrt{2}y+z-6 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So, we get that the Cartesian equation of the tangent plane is $2\sqrt{2}y + z - 6 = 0.$

![](images/d5/d51bdbe8820472334f7e1d942c027b6ad8164eaece58220f3f2e5cdb51544f05.png)"] [17592186130382 :tutorial/content "Earlier, we claimed that function $f(x)$ is differentiable at $x_0$ *if the function admits a unique tangent line* at $x_0.$ Let's now justify this claim.

Recall that a function $f(x)$ is differentiable at $x=x_0$ with derivative $f'(x_0)$ if and only if the following limit exists:

$$
f'(x_0) = \lim_{x\to x_0}\dfrac {f(x) - f(x_0)} {x-x_0}
$$

We can rewrite this limit as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {x}_{0}}(\frac{f(x)-f({x}_{0})}{x-{x}_{0}})-{f}^{'}({x}_{0}) & =0 \\ {lim}_{x\to {x}_{0}}(\frac{f(x)-f({x}_{0})}{x-{x}_{0}}-{f}^{'}({x}_{0})) & =0 \\ {lim}_{x\to {x}_{0}}\frac{f(x)-f({x}_{0})-(x-{x}_{0}){f}^{'}({x}_{0})}{x-{x}_{0}} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

In order for the above limit to hold true, the numerator must approach zero. So, near $x_0,$ we must have

$$
f(x) - f(x_0) - (x-x_0)f'(x_0) \approx 0,
$$

which can be rewritten as

$$
f(x) - f(x_0) \approx (x-x_0)f'(x_0).

This corresponds to the following equation of the tangent line at $x_0\mathbin{:}$

$$

First, we take the natural logarithm of both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\ln y &= \ln (x^{x^{3}}) \\

\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to $x{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}

\frac{1}{y} \cdot y^{′} &= (x^{3})^{′} \cdot (\ln x) + (x^{3}) \cdot (\ln x)^{′} \\
\frac{1}{y} \cdot y^{′} &= 3x^{2} \cdot \ln x + x^{3} \cdot \frac{1}{x} \\
\frac{y^{′}}{y} &= 3x^{2}\ln x + x^{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve for $y'{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}
y^{′} &= y(3x^{2}\ln x + x^{2})
\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute

$$
y=x^{x^3}{:}
$$

$$

y^{′} &= x^{x^{3}}(3x^{2}\ln x + x^{2}) \\
&= x^{x^{3}}(x^{2}(3\ln x + 1)) \\
&= x^{x^{3} + 2}(3\ln x + 1)
\end{aligned}

Let's consider the following function.

$$
y = x^x
$$

We aim to compute

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d x}
$$

However, in this case, we note the following:

- Both the base and the exponent are functions of $x$.
- This means we cannot apply the power rule since the exponent is not a fixed number.
- We also cannot apply the rules for differentiating exponentials since the base is not a fixed number.

So instead, we'll use logarithmic differentiation. We proceed as follows:

**Step 1.** We take the natural logarithm of both sides and apply the power rule for logarithms:

$$
\begin{aligned}
y &= x^{x} \\
\ln y &= \ln x^{x} \\
\ln y &= x\ln x
\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2.** We differentiate both sides of the above equation with respect to $x$ using implicit differentiation and the product rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{d}{dx}(\ln y) &= \frac{d}{dx}(x\ln x) \\
\frac{1}{y} \cdot \frac{dy}{dx} &= \frac{d}{dx}(x) \cdot \ln x + x \cdot \frac{d}{dx}(\ln x) \\
\frac{1}{y} \cdot \frac{dy}{dx} &= 1 \cdot \ln x + x \cdot (\frac{1}{x}) \\
\frac{1}{y} \cdot \frac{dy}{dx} &= \ln x + 1
\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3.** Now, we solve for

$$
\dfrac {\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x}
$$

This gives

$$
\dfrac {\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} = y\left(\ln x + 1 \right)
$$

**Step 4.** Finally, we substitute back our original expression for $y=x^x{:}$

$$
\dfrac {\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} = x^x \left(\ln x + 1 \right)
$$

$$
y'' - 3y' + 2y = f(x)
$$

where we assume that the forcing function $f$ is not identically zero.

The corresponding homogeneous equation is

$$
y'' - 3y' + 2y = 0.
$$

Substituting $y = e^{\lambda x}$ into the equation and solving the resulting quadratic in $\lambda,$ we find that the complementary solution is

$$
y_c(x) = Ae^x + Be^{2x}
$$

where $A$ and $B$ are constants, and the fundamental solutions $y_1(x)$ and $y_2(x)$ are

$$
y_1(x) = e^{x}, \qquad y_2(x) = e^{2x}.
$$

Note that the Wronskian 

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{x} & {e}^{2x} \\ ({e}^{x})^{'} & ({e}^{2x})^{'}\end{aligned}
$$

is nonzero for all $x,$ and so the set 

$$
S = \{y_1, y_2\}
$$

 
is a linearly independent set of fundamental solutions. 

Now, suppose we wish to seek a particular solution using variation of parameters. By allowing the constants $A$ and $B$ to vary, we can introduce new functions $u_1(x)$ and $u_2(x),$ and seek a particular solution of the form

$$
y_p(x) = u_1y_1+ u_2y_2.
$$

But we have a problem! Differentiating $y_p=u_1y_1+u_2y_2,$ we get terms involving $u'_1$ and $u'_2.$ Substituting into the ODE produces a single equation involving both $u'_1$ and $u'_2,$ so we need a second equation.

To help with this issue, we will seek a solution that satisfies the following constraint:

$$

\int_1^3(4-x)\,\textrm{d}x$ as the limit of a left Riemann sum." :question/worked-solution "The definite integral can be defined in terms of the limit of a left Riemann sum as

$$
\int_a^b f(x)\textrm{d}x = \lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\sum_{k=0}^{n-1} f(x_k)\Delta x,
$$

    

where $\Delta x = \dfrac{b-a}{n}$ and $x_k = a + k\Delta x.$

In the definite integral

$$
\displaystyle \int_1^3(4-x)\,\textrm{d}x,
$$

the function is $f(x) = 4-x,$ the lower bound is $a=1,$ and the upper bound is $b=3.$ So, we have

$$
\Delta x = \dfrac{3-1}{n} = \dfrac 2 n,
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{3}(4-x)\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=0}^{n-1}f({x}_{k})\,Δx \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=0}^{n-1}[f(1+k\cdot \frac{2}{n})\,\cdot \frac{2}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=0}^{n-1}[f(1+\frac{2k}{n})\,\cdot \frac{2}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=0}^{n-1}[(4-(1+\frac{2k}{n}))\,\cdot \frac{2}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=0}^{n-1}[(3-\frac{2k}{n})\,\cdot \frac{2}{n}].\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186097264 :question/id #uuid "9b0d7120-9669-5715-9447-51eb9dde3961" :question/math-academy-id "q-49179"} {:db/id 17592186097268 :question/id #uuid "9edba8fa-85df-5a13-ac73-844331e577d2" :question/math-academy-id "q-49190"} {:db/id 17592186233193 :question/id #uuid "dc7d253b-e356-5891-bf20-62f635e76a71" :question/math-academy-id "q-113886"} {:db/id 17592186233960 :question/id #uuid "7bb0589a-33d3-5697-b41b-737b35b84cc9" :question/math-academy-id "q-346174" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186096631 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "cdc82e49-5df6-5096-a8fd-e00017fb1e3a" :knowledge-point/title "Expressing a Definite Integral as the Limit of a Left Riemann Sum"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "c858a40c-f20b-55e5-b84b-e3d282235b1d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "1+\frac{9i}{n}" :db/id 17592186232938}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "c858a40c-f20b-55e5-b84b-e3d282235b1d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "1+\frac{9i}{n}" :db/id 17592186232938} :answer-field/id #uuid "d4e64ce4-dc0f-5c7f-8d0a-bb5a34372b24" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492 :db/ident :answer-field.type/blank} :db/id 17592186232937}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "Express ${\int }_{1}^{10}{x}^{1/2}\,\text{d}x$ as the limit of a left Riemann sum.

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}f({x}_{i})\cdot Δx,
$$

In the definite integral

$$
{\int }_{1}^{5}{e}^{x-1}\,\text{d}x,
$$

the function is $f(x)={e}^{x-1},$ the lower bound is $a=1,$ and the upper bound is $b=5.$ So, we have

$$
Δx=\frac{5-1}{n}=\frac{4}{n},
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{5}{e}^{x-1}\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}f({x}_{i})\cdot Δx \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}[f(1+i\cdot \frac{4}{n})\,\cdot \frac{4}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}[f(1+\frac{4i}{n})\cdot \frac{4}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}[{e}^{1+4i/n-1}\cdot \frac{4}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{i=0}^{n-1}[{e}^{4i/n}\cdot \frac{4}{n}].\end{aligned}

\dfrac{5k}{n}\right)^2\cdot \dfrac 5 n\right].$" :question/worked-solution "A definite integral can be defined as the limit of a left Riemann sum as follows:

$$
\int_a^b f(x) \, \textrm d x = \lim_{n\to\infty}\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}f\left(x_k\right)\cdot \Delta x
$$

where $\Delta x = \dfrac{b-a}{n}$ and $x_k = a + k\Delta x.$

Notice that we're given that the lower limit $a = 3.$ 

Comparing the given summation with the general expression above, we see that $\Delta x = \dfrac{5}{n}.$ Therefore, 

$$
\dfrac{5}{n} = \dfrac{b-3}{n} \quad \Longrightarrow \quad b = 8.
$$

Consequently, $x_k = 3 + \dfrac{5k}{n}$ and $f(x_k) = x_{k}^2.$

Hence,

$$
\int_{3}^{8} x^2 \, \textrm d x =\lim_{n\to\infty}\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\left[\left(3 + \dfrac{5k}{n}\right)^2\cdot \dfrac 5 n\right].
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is $f(x)= x^2$ and $b = 8.$"} {:db/id 17592186097262 :question/id #uuid "6798d466-87fa-5086-ac4a-cf1eac1b223b" :question/math-academy-id "q-49141"} {:db/id 17592186097270 :question/id #uuid "6781de8f-ac38-5841-ac31-a697903fa191" :question/math-academy-id "q-49231"} {:db/id 17592186233800 :question/id #uuid "48a37973-85e7-5045-857e-c973f50df713" :question/math-academy-id "q-315828"} {:db/id 17592186234108 :question/id #uuid "b0c16e42-a6fd-5291-a75a-a545c6a864c6" :question/math-academy-id "q-49233" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186096632 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "4f663b0b-9b5e-512c-92bb-0ea84d5baac5" :knowledge-point/title "Expressing the Limit of a Left Riemann Sum as a Definite Integral"}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486 :db/ident :question.difficulty/hard} :question/problem "Find the function $f(x)$ and the value of $b,$ given that ${\int }_{-\pi }^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=0}^{n-1}[{cos}^{2}(-\pi +\frac{\pi k}{n})\cdot \frac{\pi }{n}].$" :question/worked-solution "A definite integral can be defined as the limit of a left Riemann sum as follows:

$$

$$

where $x_k = a + k\Delta x$ and $\Delta x =  \dfrac{b-a}{n}.$

In the definite integral

$$
\displaystyle \int_1^2 x^2\,\textrm d x,
$$

the function is $f(x) = x^2,$ the lower bound is $a=1$ and the upper bound is $b=2.$ So, we have

$$
\Delta x = \dfrac{2-1}{n} = \dfrac 1 n.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{2}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=1}^{n}f({x}_{k})\,Δx \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=1}^{n}[f(1+k\cdot \frac{1}{n})\cdot \frac{1}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=1}^{n}[f(1+\frac{k}{n})\cdot \frac{1}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=1}^{n}[{(1+\frac{k}{n})}^{2}\,\cdot \frac{1}{n}].\end{aligned}

:question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "What is ${\int }_{-2}^{3}-2{x}^{3}\text{d}x$ expressed as the limit of a right Riemann sum?" :question/worked-solution "The definite integral can be defined in terms of the limit of a right Riemann sum as

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=1}^{n}f({x}_{k})\cdot Δx,
$$

where ${x}_{k}=a+kΔx$ and $Δx=\frac{b-a}{n}.$

In the definite integral

$$
{\int }_{-2}^{3}-2{x}^{3}\text{d}x,
$$

the function is $f(x)=-2{x}^{3},$ the lower bound is $a=-2$ and the upper bound is $b=3.$ So, we have

$$
Δx=\frac{3-(-2)}{n}=\frac{5}{n}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-2}^{3}-2{x}^{3}\text{d}x & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=1}^{n}f({x}_{k})\cdot Δx \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=1}^{n}[f(-2+k\cdot \frac{5}{n})\cdot \frac{5}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=1}^{n}[f(-2+\frac{5k}{n})\cdot \frac{5}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=1}^{n}[-2{(-2+\frac{5k}{n})}^{3}\cdot \frac{5}{n}].\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186393271 :question/id #uuid "d76772d8-d5b1-522d-b84a-c52ac6da6060" :question/math-academy-id "q-73182"} {:db/id 17592186048413} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186097447 :step/content {:db/id 17592186097910 :tutorial/content "Suppose that we want to approximate the area $\mathcal A$ bound by the curve $y= x^2+1$ and the lines $x=0,$ $x=1,$ and the $x$-axis. We can do this using a left Riemann sum with $n=4$ subintervals, as shown below:

![](images/1b/1b25a722d5527db77cd7dd5fb581c0ffed9b9324913d390e2633211360b6a8ab.png)

A better approximation can be found by taking more subintervals. For instance, taking $n=8$ subintervals gives:

![](images/17/17f6c8e458b2e6fbd887728cbbcc7cb64a670598256f76cad69d9e5a9c3cf7b5.png)

As we continue to increase $n,$ our approximation gets better and better. In fact, we can get an *exact* value for the area by taking the limit of the Riemann sum as $n\to\infty.$

Let's write down that limit. First, we need to express the left Riemann sum using sigma notation. Using $n$ subintervals between the endpoints $a=0$ and $b=1,$ we express

$$

$$
A = \lim_{n\to\infty}\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\left(\dfrac{k^2}{n^2} + 1\right)\cdot \dfrac{1}{n}.

$$

To find the vertical asymptotes, let's start by factoring the expression in the denominator. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
f(x) &= \frac{1}{x^{2} - 5x + 6} \\
&= (1)/((x - 3)(x - 2))
\end{aligned}
$$

There are no common factors in the numerator and denominator, so we can find the vertical asymptotes by setting the denominator to zero:

$$
(x-3)(x-2) = 0 \qquad \Longrightarrow\qquad x=2,3
$$

Therefore, the function has infinite discontinuities at $x=2$ and $x=3$."} {:db/id 17592186048163} {:db/id 17592186129803 :question/id #uuid "770f10a1-d24d-558b-b9a1-ca455011df31" :question/math-academy-id "q-48239"} {:db/id 17592186129804 :question/id #uuid "0a0611d4-19df-5c7d-b621-28aa5ba7bd94" :question/math-academy-id "q-48241"} {:db/id 17592186129091 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186128905 :question/id #uuid "26d318a3-0b3f-50be-9802-92b10b83d119" :question/math-academy-id "e-3587"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "ea5bdd3b-810c-56e6-acfd-4de0e0cfc4e8" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186129805 :question/id #uuid "a0878e3d-eb31-5ffd-95cf-f0f7adba1115" :question/math-academy-id "q-48246"} {:db/id 17592186129806 :question/id #uuid "0dc10b7d-a82b-5014-b6d1-42e5dbd1375a" :question/math-academy-id "q-48251"} {:db/id 17592186234351 :question/id #uuid "e3cc6eed-e52f-5a0b-bc51-e9a47cb4eee9" :question/math-academy-id "q-73427"}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding Infinite Discontinuities of Rational Functions With Common Factors"} {:db/id 17592186128905 :question/id #uuid "26d318a3-0b3f-50be-9802-92b10b83d119" :question/math-academy-id "e-3587" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186129091 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "ea5bdd3b-810c-56e6-acfd-4de0e0cfc4e8" :knowledge-point/title "Finding Infinite Discontinuities of Rational Functions With Common Factors"}] :question/problem "Find all the points where the function $f(x) = \dfrac{x^2+x-6}{x^2-4}$ has infinite discontinuities." :question/worked-solution "Infinite discontinuities coincide with the vertical asymptotes of $y=f(x)$.

To find the vertical asymptotes, let's start by factoring the expressions in the numerator and denominator. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
f(x) &= \frac{x^{2} + x - 6}{x^{2} - 4} \\
&= ((x - 2)(x + 3))/((x - 2)(x + 2)) \\
&= ((x - 2)(x + 3))/((x - 2)(x + 2)) \\
&= \frac{x + 3}{x + 2}
\end{aligned}
$$

To find the vertical asymptotes, we set the denominator equal to zero and solve:

$$
x+2 = 0 \qquad \Longrightarrow\qquad x=-2
$$

Therefore, the function has an infinite discontinuity at $x=-2$."} {:db/id 17592186129805 :question/id #uuid "a0878e3d-eb31-5ffd-95cf-f0f7adba1115" :question/math-academy-id "q-48246"} {:db/id 17592186129806 :question/id #uuid "0dc10b7d-a82b-5014-b6d1-42e5dbd1375a" :question/math-academy-id "q-48251"} {:db/id 17592186234351 :question/id #uuid "e3cc6eed-e52f-5a0b-bc51-e9a47cb4eee9" :question/math-academy-id "q-73427"} {:db/id 17592186129092 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186128906 :question/id #uuid "83f4e413-e2f4-53dd-9893-fdf8e2df2642" :question/math-academy-id "e-3588"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "4317f5b8-cc60-5695-b5bb-47744cecc4cf" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049534}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186129633 :question/id #uuid "e0e8d7b9-750d-5053-9cfe-e5211a2c2e3d" :question/math-academy-id "q-38219"} {:db/id 17592186129661 :question/id #uuid "a7ec8526-7c03-5480-8d03-a5cda5bfb1ab" :question/math-academy-id "q-38556"}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding Infinite Discontinuities of a Piecewise Function"} {:db/id 17592186128906 :question/id #uuid "83f4e413-e2f4-53dd-9893-fdf8e2df2642" :question/math-academy-id "e-3588" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186129092 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "4317f5b8-cc60-5695-b5bb-47744cecc4cf" :knowledge-point/title "Finding Infinite Discontinuities of a Piecewise Function"}] :question/problem "Find all of the points where $f(x)$ below has infinite discontinuities.

${\frac{1}{x - 5},\begin{vmatrix}x < 5 \\ \frac{1}{x - 4},\end{vmatrix}x \ge 5$." :question/worked-solution "Infinite discontinuities coincide with the vertical asymptotes of $y=f(x)$. The only possible way that $y=f(x)$ can have vertical asymptotes is if either

$$
\dfrac{1}{x-5}
$$

or

$$
\dfrac{1}{x-4}
$$

grow without bound within their respective subdomains.

- We first compute the asymptotes of $\dfrac{1}{x-5}$. Setting the denominator equal to zero, we get
$x-5=0\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad x=5$.
Although this branch of the function is defined for $x < 5$, we do have that
$\lim_{x\to 5^{-}}\left(\dfrac{1}{x-5}\right) = -\infty$,
and therefore we conclude that $x=5$ is indeed an infinite discontinuity.
- Next, we compute the asymptotes of $\dfrac{1}{x-4}$. Setting the denominator equal to zero, we get
$x-4=0\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad x=4$.
However, this branch of the function is defined for $x \geq 5$, which does not contain the neighborhood of $x=4$. So $x=4$ cannot be a vertical asymptote, and therefore $x=4$ cannot be an infinite discontinuity.

Therefore, the function $f(x)$ only has a single infinite discontinuity, and it is at $x=5$.

This matches up with what we see in the graph of $y=f(x)$, shown below.

$$
y=\dfrac 1 x
$$

below.

![](images/cc/cc9593860b0c134d0d99635b37eeac4f16a712a7af9e1c6474fcf1f885e8451e.png)

The function has a vertical asymptote at $x=0$. There is also a discontinuity in the function at $x=0$, since we cannot draw the points on the curve without taking our pen off the paper to cross the asymptote.

So, we say that

$$
y = \dfrac 1 x
$$

has a **discontinuity due to a vertical asymptote** at $x=0$. Discontinuities due to vertical asymptotes are also called **infinite discontinuities**.

Notice that here, both one-sided limits are infinite:

$$
\lim_{x\to 0^-} \left(\dfrac 1 x\right) =-\infty\qquad\text{and}\qquad\lim_{x\to 0^+} \left(\dfrac 1 x \right)=\infty
$$

In general, a function $y=f(x)$ has a discontinuity due to a vertical asymptote at $x=c$ if either one-sided limit is infinite:

$$
\lim_{x\to c^-} f(x) =\pm \infty\qquad\text{or}\qquad\lim_{x\to c^+} f(x) =\pm \infty
$$

Note that we only need a single limit to become infinite to conclude that there is an infinite discontinuity at $x=c$." :tutorial/id #uuid "ce83f36f-d7f8-546f-b887-1e6818a75bfb" has a **discontinuity due to a vertical asymptote** at $x=0$. Discontinuities due to vertical asymptotes are also called **infinite discontinuities**.

Notice that here, both one-sided limits are infinite:

$$
\lim_{x\to 0^-} \left(\dfrac 1 x\right) =-\infty\qquad\text{and}\qquad\lim_{x\to 0^+} \left(\dfrac 1 x \right)=\infty
$$

In general, a function $y=f(x)$ has a discontinuity due to a vertical asymptote at $x=c$ if either one-sided limit is infinite:

$$
\lim_{x\to c^-} f(x) =\pm \infty\qquad\text{or}\qquad\lim_{x\to c^+} f(x) =\pm \infty
$$

Note that we only need a single limit to become infinite to conclude that there is an infinite discontinuity at $x=c$." :tutorial/id #uuid "ce83f36f-d7f8-546f-b887-1e6818a75bfb" {{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "First, let's sketch the graph of $y=\operatorname{arctan}(2x+7):$

![](images/37/371cbb841c67494626038fc93747a1d0a2b2245f422364911f1a859f4711868d.png)

The domain of $\operatorname{arctan}(2x+7)$ is $(-\infty ,\infty ).$ Moreover, from the graph, we see that

$$
{lim}_{x\to -\infty }\operatorname{arctan}(2x+7)=-\frac{\pi }{2}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
{lim}_{x\to \,-\infty }\frac{5}{2\pi }(\operatorname{arctan}(2x+7))=\frac{5}{2\pi }\cdot (-\frac{\pi }{2})=-\frac{5}{4}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186233953 :question/id #uuid "ecbfd230-3cf4-56df-961c-5ee65b48f356" :question/math-academy-id "q-344536" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186184239 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "4bcc5d54-e7fd-5be5-9d00-4240d03e21cb" :knowledge-point/title "Finding Limits at Infinity"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "fa252a79-6198-5339-b8cd-9b165faf3c53" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186232921}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "fa252a79-6198-5339-b8cd-9b165faf3c53" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186232921} :answer-field/id #uuid "fa58ccf0-ef3f-5aee-9f0d-b90bf4397dde" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492 :db/ident :answer-field.type/blank} :db/id 17592186232920}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "Evaluate the following limit:

$$
{lim}_{x\to -\infty }\operatorname{arctan}(x+1)=-\frac{\pi }{2}.

$$

trigonometric functions. 

Let's begin by recalling the graph of $y=\arcsin(x).$

![](images/df/df22eea4331c47da3047381ca672fd80ebf75118054316fe88c0e2d96dae0d34.png)

Using the graph, we note the following:

- The domain of $\arcsin(x)$ is $x \in [-1,1].$

- For every value $a \in (-1,1),$ we have

$$
\lim_\limits{x\to a} \arcsin(x) = \arcsin(a).
$$

 
In other words, we can evaluate the limit using direct substitution. For example,

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 1/2}\operatorname{arcsin}(x) & =\operatorname{arcsin}(\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

- For any value $a$ that does *not* lie in the domain of $\arcsin(x),$ the limit

$$
\lim_\limits{x\to a} \arcsin(x)
$$

 
does *not* exist.

- At the point $x=-1,$ the limit does *not* exist because the left-sided limit does not exist. However, the right-sided limit *does* exist and is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (-1)^{+}}\operatorname{arcsin}(x) & =\operatorname{arcsin}(-1) \\  & =-\frac{\pi }{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Similarly, at the point $x=1,$ the limit does *not* exist because the right-sided limit does not exist. However, the left-sided limit *does* exist and is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {1}^{-}}\operatorname{arcsin}(x) & =\operatorname{arcsin}(1) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

The limit properties of $y=\arccos(x)$ are similar. Let's discuss them briefly." :tutorial/id #uuid "f1bc1975-006b-5be4-ad5c-88888abb00d5" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6599 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid deduce limits at infinity of transformed inverse trigonometric functions by sketching their graphs.

For example, let's consider the following limit:

$$
\lim_\limits{x \to \, \infty} \dfrac{2}{\pi}\arctan \left(x-\pi\right)
$$

To evaluate this limit, we first sketch the graph of  $y =\arctan \left(x-\pi\right){:}$ 

![](images/51/51a0b9a210147b3791ce20a2f65320e20618826671ea6c7c31a27f8647595079.png)

The domain of   $\arctan \left(x-\pi\right)$ is $(-\infty,\infty).$   Moreover, from the graph, we see that 

$$
\lim\limits_{x\to \infty} \arctan \left(x-\pi\right)=\color{blue}{\dfrac{\pi}{2} }  .
$$

Therefore, by the algebra of limits, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \,\infty }\frac{2}{\pi }\operatorname{arctan}(x-\pi ) & =\frac{2}{\pi }\cdot {lim}_{x\to \,\infty }\operatorname{arctan}(x-\pi ) \\  & =\frac{2}{\pi }\cdot (\frac{\pi }{2}) \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Limits at infinity involving the inverse sine and cosine functions usually do not exist. Let's see an example." :tutorial/id #uuid "24cdcba9-d6c5-5719-a086-34fe417cc42f" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6600 :tutorial/title "Limits of Inverse Trigonometric Function at Infinity"} :step/id #uuid "66882814-9d8d-500a-b199-d60870f60cec" :step/math-academy-id 39815 :step/next {:db/id 17592186185043}} {:db/id 17592186185045 :step/content {:db/id 17592186184240 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186183923 :question/id #uuid "7ce46ca9-cfff-5e8b-89b9-a2a7b34921fd" :question/math-academy-id "e-10537"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "5a58f115-f368-5171-af73-37084085b42a" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048465}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186184518} {:db/id 17592186184519} {:db/id 17592186233509} {:db/id 17592186233510} {:db/id 17592186233892} {:db/id 17592186233954} {:db/id 17592186275308} {:db/id 17592186297278} {:db/id 17592186297280} {:db/id 17592186314786} {:db/id 17592186314787} {:db/id 17592186314788} {:db/id 17592186317512}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding a Limit Involving Trigonometric Functions and Their Inverses"} :step/id #uuid "f8205256-4d92-59b5-babd-ec4ae58b06b8" :step/math-academy-id 39823} {:db/id 17592186185051 :step/content {:db/id 17592186185362 :tutorial/content "The graph of $y=\arctan x$ is shown below.

From the graph, we note the following:

- The domain is $x \in (-\infty, \infty).$

- For every value $a,$ we have

$$
\lim_\limits{x\to a} \arctan(x) = \arctan(a).
$$

- The limit as $x\to-\infty$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to -\infty }\operatorname{arctan}(x) & =-\frac{\pi }{2}.\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \infty }\operatorname{arctan}(x) & =\frac{\pi }{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

\lim_\limits{x \to \, \infty} \dfrac{2}{\pi}\arctan \left(x-\pi\right)
$$

To evaluate this limit, we first sketch the graph of  $y =\arctan \left(x-\pi\right){:}$ 

![](images/51/51a0b9a210147b3791ce20a2f65320e20618826671ea6c7c31a27f8647595079.png)

The domain of   $\arctan \left(x-\pi\right)$ is $(-\infty,\infty).$   Moreover, from the graph, we see that 

$$
\lim\limits_{x\to \infty} \arctan \left(x-\pi\right)=\color{blue}{\dfrac{\pi}{2} }  .
$$

Therefore, by the algebra of limits, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \,\infty }\frac{2}{\pi }\operatorname{arctan}(x-\pi ) & =\frac{2}{\pi }\cdot {lim}_{x\to \,\infty }\operatorname{arctan}(x-\pi ) \\  & =\frac{2}{\pi }\cdot (\frac{\pi }{2}) \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Limits at infinity involving the inverse sine and cosine functions usually do not exist. Let's see an example." :tutorial/id #uuid "24cdcba9-d6c5-5719-a086-34fe417cc42f" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6600 :tutorial/title "Limits of Inverse Trigonometric Function at Infinity"} {:db/id 17592186185051 :step/content {:db/id 17592186185362 :tutorial/content "The graph of $y=\arctan x$ is shown below.

- The domain is $x \in (-\infty, \infty).$

- For every value $a,$ we have

$$
\lim_\limits{x\to a} \arctan(x) = \arctan(a).
$$

- The limit as $x\to-\infty$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to -\infty }\operatorname{arctan}(x) & =-\frac{\pi }{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

- The limit as $x\to\infty$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \infty }\operatorname{arctan}(x) & =\frac{\pi }{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can use the algebra of limits to evaluate expressions involving inverse trigonometric functions. $(1,1,2)?$" :question/worked-solution "At a given point, a function $g(x,y,z)$ increases most rapidly in the direction of its gradient at that point.

So, we compute $∇g(x,y,z)$ and evaluate it at the point $(1,1,2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇g(x,y,z) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}({y}^{2}+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\pi x+\pi z)),\,\frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{2}+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\pi x+\pi z)),\,\frac{∂}{∂z}({y}^{2}+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\pi x+\pi z))⟩ \\  & =⟨2\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(2\pi x+\pi z),\,2y,\,\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(2\pi x+\pi z)⟩ \\ ∇g(1,1,2) & =⟨2\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(2\pi \cdot 1+\pi \cdot 2),\,2\cdot 1,\,\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(2\pi \cdot 1+\pi \cdot 2)⟩ \\  & =⟨2\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(4\pi ),\,2,\,\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(4\pi )⟩ \\  & =⟨2\pi ,\,2,\,\pi ⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the function increases most rapidly in the direction of $⟨2\pi ,\,2,\,\pi ⟩.$"} {:db/id 17592186265872 :question/id #uuid "234c72df-7b34-5698-b613-f1acebf8fd8e" :question/math-academy-id direction of the vector $v=⟨1,-\sqrt{2}⟩?$" :question/worked-solution "The rate of change of $g(x,y)$ at the point $(-1,1)$ in the direction of $v$ is equal to the directional derivative ${g}_{u}^{′}(-1,1).$ 

First, we find the unit vector $u$ in the direction of $v:$

$$
\begin{aligned}‖v‖ & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+(-\sqrt{2})^{2}}=\sqrt{3} \\ u & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}⟨1,-\sqrt{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we find the gradient $∇g(x,y)$ and evaluate it at the point $(-1,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇g(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{x}{y}+\frac{y}{x}),\,\frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{x}{y}+\frac{y}{x})⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{1}{y}-\frac{y}{{x}^{2}},\,\frac{1}{x}-\frac{x}{{y}^{2}}⟩ \\ ∇g(-1,1) & =⟨\frac{1}{1}-\frac{1}{(-1)^{2}},\frac{1}{(-1)}-\frac{(-1)}{{1}^{2}}⟩ \\  & =⟨0,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the directional derivative ${g}_{u}^{′}(-1,1)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{g}_{u}^{′}(-1,1) & =∇g(-1,1)\cdot u \\  & =⟨0,0⟩\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}⟨1,-\sqrt{2}⟩ \\  & =\frac{0(1)+0(-\sqrt{2})}{\sqrt{3}} \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186323791 :question/id #uuid "a13cba05-5f4a-5d75-8f65-f72eb54e0d73" :question/math-academy-id "q-36300" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186124460 :knowledge-point/id #uuid which the function decreases most rapidly?" :question/worked-solution "At a given point, a function $f(x,y)$ decreases most rapidly in the opposite direction of its gradient at that point.

In our case, we compute $-∇f(x,y)$ and evaluate it at the point $(1,3):$

$$
\begin{aligned}-∇\,f(x,y) & =-\frac{∂}{∂x}(2xy+{e}^{3x-y})\text{ }i-\frac{∂}{∂y}(2xy+{e}^{3x-y})\text{ }j \\  & =-(2y+3{e}^{3x-y})\text{ }i-(2x-{e}^{3x-y})\text{ }j \\ -∇\,f(1,3) & =-(2\cdot 3+3\cdot {e}^{3\cdot 1-3})\text{ }i-(2\cdot 1-{e}^{3\cdot 1-3})\text{ }j \\  & =-9\text{ }i-\text{ }j\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the rate of change of $f(x,y)$ at the point $(1,3)$ in the direction of $-∇f(1,3)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}‖-∇\,f(1,3)‖ & =‖-9\text{ }i-\text{ }j‖ \\  & =\sqrt{(-9)^{2}+(-1)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{82}.\end{aligned}

:question/problem "Consider the function $g(x,y)=\frac{{e}^{y}}{yx}.$ What is the rate of change of $g(x,y)$ at the point $(1,1)$ in the direction of the vector $v=⟨2,4⟩?$" :question/worked-solution "The rate of change of $g(x,y)$ at the point $(1,1)$ in the direction of $v$ is equal to the directional derivative ${g}_{u}^{′}(1,1).$ 

First, we find the unit vector $u$ in the direction of $v:$

$$
\begin{aligned}‖v‖ & =\sqrt{{2}^{2}+{4}^{2}}=\sqrt{20}=2\sqrt{5} \\ u & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{5}}⟨2,4⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}⟨1,2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we find the gradient $∇g(x,y)$ and evaluate it at the point $(1,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇g(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{{e}^{y}}{yx}),\,\frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{{e}^{y}}{yx})⟩ \\  & =⟨-\frac{{e}^{y}}{{x}^{2}y},\,\frac{{e}^{y}(y-1)}{x{y}^{2}}⟩ \\ ∇g(1,1) & =⟨-\frac{{e}^{1}}{{1}^{2}\cdot 1},\,\frac{{e}^{1}\cdot (1-1)}{1\cdot {1}^{2}}⟩ \\  & =⟨-e,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the directional derivative ${g}_{u}^{′}(1,1)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{g}_{u}^{′}(1,1) & =∇g(1,1)\cdot u \\  & =⟨-e,0⟩\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}⟨1,2⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}(-e\cdot 1+0\cdot 2) \\  & =-\frac{e}{\sqrt{5}} \\  & =-\frac{e\sqrt{5}}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "371188b1-b7ec-57b7-b295-164f4505e38f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "i-2\,j" :db/id 17592186263494} :topic/math-academy-id 1938} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186125299 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125736 :tutorial/content "Let's consider a surface $z=f(x,y)$ and a unit vector $\mathbf{u} = \left\langle  u_1, u_2 \right\rangle.$

The **directional derivative of $f$** at the point $(x_0,y_0)$ in the direction of $\mathbf{u}$ is

$$
f'_{\mathbf u}(x_0,y_0) = \lim\limits_{t \to 0}\dfrac{f(\mathbf x_0 + t \mathbf u) - f(\mathbf x_0)}{t}.
$$

The directional derivative of $f$ is the rate of change of the function $f$ in the direction of $\mathbf{u}.$ We'll discuss this idea more later in the lesson.

It turns out that if $f$ is differentiable, we can write $f'_{\mathbf u}$ in terms of partial derivatives $f_x$ and $f_y,$ as follows:

$$
f'_{\mathbf u}(x_0,y_0) = \nabla f (x_0,y_0) \cdot \mathbf u.
$$

At the end of the lesson, we'll derive this formula. But for now, let's get some practice using it.

For example, let's find the directional derivative of the function $f(x, y) = x^2 + y^2$ at the point $(x_0,y_0)=(1,2)$ in the direction of the vector $\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{i} + \mathbf{j}.$

First, we find the unit vector $\mathbf{u}$ in the direction of $\mathbf{v} \mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}‖v‖ & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}}=\sqrt{2} \\ u & =\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(i+j)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we compute the gradient $\nabla f(x,y)$ and evaluate it at the point $(1,2)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\,f(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,j \\  & =2x\,i+2y\,j \\ ∇\,f(1,2) & =(2\cdot 1)\,i+(2\cdot 2)\,j \\  & =2i+4j\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the directional derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{u}^{′}(1,2) & =∇\,f(1,2)\cdot u \\  & =(2\,i+4\,j)\cdot (\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}i+\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}j) \\  & =\frac{2\cdot 1+4\cdot 1}{\sqrt{2}} \\  & =\frac{6}{\sqrt{2}} \\  & =3\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "925cfc95-04b9-5e98-bec4-99d0e4ae3a54" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2503 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "7b456d3e-c653-5713-8112-18d37fb77751" :step/math-academy-id 11245 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125300}} {:db/id 17592186125300 :step/content {:db/id 17592186124458 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186124262 :question/id #uuid "bf35c502-5a22-5953-9158-b2464d28c09f" :question/math-academy-id "e-3377"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "fd2b430e-fd5d-57ba-bc28-f7c113eda07a" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048954} {:db/id 17592186050143} {:db/id 17592186050988}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186124962} {:db/id 17592186125029} {:db/id 17592186235525} {:db/id 17592186265867} {:db/id 17592186265868} {:db/id 17592186265869} {:db/id 17592186323790} {:db/id 17592186354470} {:db/id 17592186446241} {:db/id 17592186446242}] :knowledge-point/title "Calculating a Directional Derivative"} :step/id #uuid "e45885a4-1bb2-5e1b-b77d-8445bc691679" :step/math-academy-id 11246 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125301}} {:db/id 17592186125301 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125737 :tutorial/content "From the formula for the directional derivative, we get that if  $z = f (x, y)$ is a differentiable function and $\mathbf u$ is a unit vector, then

$$
\eqalign{
f'_{\mathbf u} &= \nabla f \cdot \mathbf u \[3pt]
                      &= |\nabla f| |\mathbf u| \cos\theta\[3pt]
                      & = |\nabla f| \cos\theta,
}
$$

where $\theta$ is the angle between the vectors $\nabla f$ and $\mathbf u,$ as depicted below.

![](images/50/50c82908d5fd619c1c3c45f2aa3ff26929b8f369233c08d0688a091d2d3c123c.png)

 

It follows that $f'_{\mathbf u}$ is maximized when $\theta =0.$ In other words, $f'_{\mathbf u}$ is maximized when $\mathbf u$ and $\nabla f$ point in the same direction. Thus, the maximum value of $f'_{\mathbf u}$ is $|\nabla f|.$

A similar argument shows that $f'_{\mathbf u}$ reaches its minimum value $- |\nabla f|$ when $\theta = \pi;$ that is, when $\nabla f$ and $\mathbf u$ point in opposite directions.

As a result, we get the following theorem:

*A differentiable function $f$ increases most rapidly in the direction of the gradient and decreases most rapidly in the opposite direction to that of its gradient.*

For functions of more than two variables, the same theorem holds." :tutorial/id #uuid "5e4c2cac-e80c-51dd-8138-681fa98ae521" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2505 :tutorial/title "The Gradient as the :step/content {:db/id 17592186125738 :tutorial/content "For a surface $z = f(x,y),$ the partial derivative $f_x(x_0,y_0)$ gives us the rate of change of $f$ in the direction of the vector $\mathbf{i} = \langle 1,0\rangle.$ But this is just a special case of the directional derivative, because

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{i}^{′}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}) & =∇({x}_{0},{y}_{0})\cdot ⟨1,0⟩ \\  & =⟨{f}_{x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),{f}_{y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0})⟩\cdot ⟨1,0⟩ \\  & ={f}_{x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}).\end{aligned}
$$

Similarly, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{j}^{′}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}) & =∇({x}_{0},{y}_{0})\cdot ⟨0,1⟩ \\  & =⟨{f}_{x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),{f}_{y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0})⟩\cdot ⟨0,1⟩ \\  & ={f}_{y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}).\end{aligned}
$$

So, the directional derivative generalizes the notion of a partial derivative. 

Now, recall that the partial derivatives $f_x$ and $f_y$ represent the rate of change of $f$ in the direction of vectors $\mathbf i$ and $\mathbf j,$ respectively. As for a general directional derivative, we obtain the following property:

*The directional derivative $f'_\mathbf{u}(x_0,y_0)$ represents the rate of change of the function $f(x,y)$ at the point $(x_0,y_0)$ in the direction of $\mathbf{u}.$*" :tutorial/id #uuid "40fa091e-c99f-5d19-8681-e9656e23dc2e" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2508 :tutorial/title "The Directional Derivative as a Generalization of the Partial Derivative"} :step/id #uuid "d49395bc-14f6-5290-8963-de30d5d2fe22" :step/math-academy-id 11285 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125503}} {:db/id 17592186125305 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125739 :tutorial/content "Consider a surface $S$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ and suppose that the point $P$ with coordinates $(x_0,y_0, f(x_0,y_0))$ lies on $S.$ We wish to derive a formula for the directional derivative $f'_\mathbf{u}(x_0,y_0),$ where $\mathbf u = \langle u_1, u_2 \rangle$ is a unit vector.

Geometrically, $f'_{\mathbf u}(x_0,y_0)$ can be constructed in the following way:

- Define a vertical plane $\Pi$ that's parallel to $\mathbf u$ and passes through $P.$

- Define the curve $C$ as the intersection of the surface $S$ and the plane $\Pi.$

- Then, the directional derivative $f'_{\mathbf u}$ is the slope of the tangent to $C$ at $P.$

The geometric interpretation of $f'_{\mathbf u}$ is similar to that of the partial derivatives $f_x$ and $f_y.$ The only difference here is that we are not restricting the plane $\Pi$ to be parallel to the coordinate axes.

Now, since $f'_{\mathbf u}$ is tangent to $C$ and is in the direction of $\mathbf u$ at $P,$ the vector 

$$
\mathbf v = \langle u_1, u_2, f'_{\mathbf u}\rangle
$$

is tangent to our surface $S$ at $P.$

![](images/59/59cb8fa410b9194c298d8f477ab0d0cff3e27765bc45c14cb9b5ea9210288184.png)

Recall that $\langle f_x (x_0,y_0), f_y(x_0,y_0), -1\rangle$ is known to be a normal vector to the surface at $P.$ Since this vector must be perpendicular to $\mathbf v,$ the dot product of the two vectors must be zero, which means that

$$
\eqalign{
\langle u_1, u_2, f'_{\mathbf u}\rangle \cdot \langle f_x (x_0,y_0), f_y(x_0,y_0), -1\rangle &=0 \[5pt]
u_1 f_x (x_0,y_0) + u_2 f_y (x_0,y_0) - f'_{\mathbf u} &=0 \[5pt]
f'_{\mathbf u} = \nabla f (x_0,y_0) \cdot \mathbf u. }
$$

We can interpret this formula as the projection of $\nabla f (x_0,y_0)$ onto the direction of $\mathbf u,$ as shown below.

![](images/82/82e7dece2597e15172600ff598090241facb834a7248ed54286fa777c25a6ebd.png)" :tutorial/id #uuid "baa62c26-a25a-5293-a28f-128d45e61d68" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2509 :tutorial/title "Deriving the Formula For the Directional Derivative"} :step/id #uuid "61d92228-7cc0-5d7f-93a0-5595777edad8" :step/math-academy-id 11286} {:db/id 17592186125503 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125825 :tutorial/content "What is the directional derivative of the function $\mathbf{f}$ at $(x_0,y_0)$ in the direction of the gradient? 

Let's apply our formula. First, we find the unit vector $\mathbf{u}$ in the direction of $\nabla\! f\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}u & =\frac{∇\,f({x}_{0},{y}_{0})}{‖∇\,f({x}_{0},{y}_{0})‖}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the directional derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{u}^{′}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}) & =∇\,f({x}_{0},{y}_{0})\cdot \frac{∇\,f({x}_{0},{y}_{0})}{‖∇\,f({x}_{0},{y}_{0})‖} \\  & =\frac{∇\,f({x}_{0},{y}_{0})\cdot ∇\,f({x}_{0},{y}_{0})}{‖∇\,f({x}_{0},{y}_{0})‖} \\  & =\frac{‖∇\,f({x}_{0},{y}_{0}){‖}^{2}}{‖∇\,f({x}_{0},{y}_{0})‖} \\  & =‖∇\,f({x}_{0},{y}_{0})‖.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we conclude the following:

*The directional derivative in the direction of the gradient equals the norm of the gradient. Furthermore, the norm of the gradient can be interpreted as the rate of change of the function in the direction of the gradient.*" :tutorial/id #uuid "f8d8fbab-9897-5441-9c15-b0bc1455ed67" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4469 :tutorial/title "The Rate of Change in the Direction of the Gradient"} :step/id #uuid "c95e7b32-1764-5c4a-a384-792d274c2f3a" :step/math-academy-id 27522 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125303}}] :activity/title "Directional Derivatives" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186124730} {:db/id 17592186125299 :step/content {:db/id 17592186125736 :tutorial/content "Let's consider a surface $z=f(x,y)$ and a unit vector $\mathbf{u} = \left\langle  u_1, u_2 \right\rangle.$

The **directional derivative of $f$** at the point $(x_0,y_0)$ in the direction of $\mathbf{u}$ is

$$
f'_{\mathbf u}(x_0,y_0) = \lim\limits_{t \to 0}\dfrac{f(\mathbf x_0 + t \mathbf u) - f(\mathbf x_0)}{t}.
$$

The directional derivative of $f$ is the rate of change of the function $f$ in the direction of $\mathbf{u}.$ We'll discuss this idea more later in the lesson.

It turns out that if $f$ is differentiable, we can write $f'_{\mathbf u}$ in terms of partial derivatives $f_x$ and $f_y,$ as follows:

$$
f'_{\mathbf u}(x_0,y_0) = \nabla f (x_0,y_0) \cdot \mathbf u.
$$

At the end of the lesson, we'll derive this formula. But for now, let's get some practice using it.

For example, let's find the directional derivative of the function $f(x, y) = x^2 + y^2$ at the point $(x_0,y_0)=(1,2)$ in the direction of the vector $\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{i} + \mathbf{j}.$

First, we find the unit vector $\mathbf{u}$ in the direction of $\mathbf{v} \mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}‖v‖ & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}}=\sqrt{2} \\ u & =\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(i+j)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we compute the gradient $\nabla f(x,y)$ and evaluate it at the point $(1,2)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\,f(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,j \\  & =2x\,i+2y\,j \\ ∇\,f(1,2) & =(2\cdot 1)\,i+(2\cdot 2)\,j \\  & =2i+4j\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{u}^{′}(1,2) & =∇\,f(1,2)\cdot u \\  & =(2\,i+4\,j)\cdot (\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}i+\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}j) \\  & =\frac{2\cdot 1+4\cdot 1}{\sqrt{2}} \\  & =\frac{6}{\sqrt{2}} \\  & =3\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "925cfc95-04b9-5e98-bec4-99d0e4ae3a54" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2503 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "7b456d3e-c653-5713-8112-18d37fb77751" :step/math-academy-id 11245 :step/next {:db/id 17592186125300}} {:db/id 17592186125736 :tutorial/content "Let's consider a surface $z=f(x,y)$ and a unit vector $\mathbf{u} = \left\langle  u_1, u_2 \right\rangle.$

$$
\eqalign{

![](images/50/50c82908d5fd619c1c3c45f2aa3ff26929b8f369233c08d0688a091d2d3c123c.png)

*A differentiable function $f$ increases most rapidly in the direction of the gradient and decreases most rapidly in the opposite direction to that of its gradient.*

![](images/59/59cb8fa410b9194c298d8f477ab0d0cff3e27765bc45c14cb9b5ea9210288184.png)

Recall that $\langle f_x (x_0,y_0), f_y(x_0,y_0), -1\rangle$ is known to be a normal vector to the surface at $P.$ Since this vector must be perpendicular to $\mathbf v,$ the dot product of the two vectors must be zero, which means that

$$
\eqalign{
\langle u_1, u_2, f'_{\mathbf u}\rangle \cdot \langle f_x (x_0,y_0), f_y(x_0,y_0), -1\rangle &=0 \[5pt]
u_1 f_x (x_0,y_0) + u_2 f_y (x_0,y_0) - f'_{\mathbf u} &=0 \[5pt]
f'_{\mathbf u} = \nabla f (x_0,y_0) \cdot \mathbf u. }
$$

We can interpret this formula as the projection of $\nabla f (x_0,y_0)$ onto the direction of $\mathbf u,$ as shown below.

![](images/82/82e7dece2597e15172600ff598090241facb834a7248ed54286fa777c25a6ebd.png)" :tutorial/id #uuid "baa62c26-a25a-5293-a28f-128d45e61d68" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2509 :tutorial/title "Deriving the Formula For the Directional Derivative"} {:db/id 17592186125825 :tutorial/content "What is the directional derivative of the function $\mathbf{f}$ at $(x_0,y_0)$ in the direction of the gradient? 

Let's apply our formula. First, we find the unit vector $\mathbf{u}$ in the direction of $\nabla\! f\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}u & =\frac{∇\,f({x}_{0},{y}_{0})}{‖∇\,f({x}_{0},{y}_{0})‖}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the directional derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{u}^{′}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}) & =∇\,f({x}_{0},{y}_{0})\cdot \frac{∇\,f({x}_{0},{y}_{0})}{‖∇\,f({x}_{0},{y}_{0})‖} \\  & =\frac{∇\,f({x}_{0},{y}_{0})\cdot ∇\,f({x}_{0},{y}_{0})}{‖∇\,f({x}_{0},{y}_{0})‖} \\  & =\frac{‖∇\,f({x}_{0},{y}_{0}){‖}^{2}}{‖∇\,f({x}_{0},{y}_{0})‖} \\  & =‖∇\,f({x}_{0},{y}_{0})‖.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we conclude the following:

*The directional derivative in the direction of the gradient equals the norm of the gradient. Furthermore, the norm of the gradient can be interpreted as the rate of change of the function in the direction of the gradient.*" :tutorial/id #uuid "f8d8fbab-9897-5441-9c15-b0bc1455ed67"
