point $(1,1)$ in the direction of the vector $v=⟨2,4⟩?$" :question/worked-solution "The rate of change of $g(x,y)$ at the point $(1,1)$ in the direction of $v$ is equal to the directional derivative ${g}_{u}^{′}(1,1).$ 

First, we find the unit vector $u$ in the direction of $v:$

$$
\begin{aligned}‖v‖ & =\sqrt{{2}^{2}+{4}^{2}}=\sqrt{20}=2\sqrt{5} \\ u & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{5}}⟨2,4⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}⟨1,2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we find the gradient $∇g(x,y)$ and evaluate it at the point $(1,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}∇g(x,y) & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{{e}^{y}}{yx}),\,\frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{{e}^{y}}{yx})⟩ \\  & =⟨-\frac{{e}^{y}}{{x}^{2}y},\,\frac{{e}^{y}(y-1)}{x{y}^{2}}⟩ \\ ∇g(1,1) & =⟨-\frac{{e}^{1}}{{1}^{2}\cdot 1},\,\frac{{e}^{1}\cdot (1-1)}{1\cdot {1}^{2}}⟩ \\  & =⟨-e,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the directional derivative ${g}_{u}^{′}(1,1)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{g}_{u}^{′}(1,1) & =∇g(1,1)\cdot u \\  & =⟨-e,0⟩\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}⟨1,2⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}(-e\cdot 1+0\cdot 2) \\  & =-\frac{e}{\sqrt{5}} \\  & =-\frac{e\sqrt{5}}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "0a60e94a-7f5d-54b3-9400-bd9ba416bdb2" :step/next {:db/id 17592186501277}} {:db/id 17592186501275 :step/content {:db/id 17592186323875 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "8837b541-d3d8-5ebe-8ea8-af61591cb6fa" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2\sqrt{2}" :db/id 17592186322232} {:answer/id #uuid "b6f03f12-e1ac-5472-a11e-f1f87bcd9621" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\sqrt{3}" :db/id 17592186322572} {:answer/id #uuid "c1717e43-53c5-54f5-8c5f-68df4b9cfd08" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186322650} {:answer/id #uuid "d2a54f97-4039-5587-a94f-458a55a1776d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\sqrt{2}" :db/id 17592186322792} {:answer/id #uuid "f7ef68e3-e12b-57d6-890b-83987a1922bd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186323097}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186322792} :answer-field/id #uuid "4a40605a-36ce-555d-abab-e5a81e672aeb" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186323308}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "3a0c033d-5079-51f1-a44e-c13c59694293" :question/math-academy-id "q-37083" :question/problem "Consider the function $f(x,y)=(x+y)\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y).$ What is the rate of change of $f(x,y)$ at the point $(2,-1)$ in the direction in which the function decreases most rapidly?" :question/worked-solution "At a given point, a function $f(x,y)$ decreases most rapidly in the opposite direction of its gradient at that point.

In our case, we compute $-∇f(x,y)$ and evaluate it at the point $(2,-1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}-∇\,f(x,y) & =-\frac{∂}{∂x}((x+y)\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y))\text{ }i-\frac{∂}{∂y}((x+y)\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y))\text{ }j \\  & =(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)+1)\text{ }i+(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)+1)\text{ }j \\ -∇\,f(2,-1) & =-(\operatorname{ln}⁡(2-1)+1)i-(\operatorname{ln}⁡(2-1)+1)j \\  & =-i-j\end{aligned}

$$

the point $(1,2, 3).$" :question/worked-solution "The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the surface $z=f(x,y)$ at the point $(x_0, y_0, z_0)$ on the surface can be written as

$$
z - z_0 = (x-x_0)\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}(x_0,y_0) + (y-y_0)\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}(x_0,y_0).
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+xy) \\  & =2x+y \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+xy) \\  & =x\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the partial derivatives at $(x,y) = (1,2)\mathbin{:}$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}(1,2) & =2(1)+2=4 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y}(1,2) & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write down the equation of the tangent plane:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-3 & =(x-1)\frac{∂f}{∂x}(1,2)+(y-2)\frac{∂f}{∂y}(1,2) \\ z-3 & =4(x-1)+1(y-2) \\ z-3 & =4x+y-6 \\ -4x-y+z+3 & =0 \\ 4x+y-z-3 & =0\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186129610 :question/id #uuid "ab92392f-12a1-569b-997c-793bd45fc373" :question/math-academy-id "q-37595" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186129177 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "4de868c0-80b7-5cbb-9dc2-ba04493471fc" :knowledge-point/title "Calculating the Equation of a Tangent Plane"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0caeec29-3446-59d6-929a-da0cd6def940" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "8x+4y-z-5=0" :db/id 17592186321249} {:answer/id #uuid "218b3d6e-723a-57b0-b05e-f5ef5d66c924" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "-x+6y-z-3=0" :db/id 17592186321400} {:answer/id #uuid "52bcf9a2-7660-5058-a7d1-f5e4ac1fb320" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "-8x+3y-z-3=0" :db/id 17592186321799} {:answer/id #uuid "8a0d0dc7-0e7f-5b67-b3b1-975d12d46b91" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "3x+4y-z-5=0" :db/id 17592186322249} {:answer/id #uuid "937cdd9e-46a7-5faa-9ab8-81f2619665b9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "4x+4y-z-5=0" :db/id 17592186322318}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "0caeec29-3446-59d6-929a-da0cd6def940" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "8x+4y-z-5=0" :db/id 17592186321249} :answer-field/id #uuid "7eb1e71a-8aff-588b-b599-a3d0d8de5885" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186323421}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485 :db/ident :question.difficulty/easy} :question/problem "Find the equation of the tangent plane to the surface $z={y}^{2}{e}^{2x}-1$ at the point $(0,2,3).$" :question/worked-solution "The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the surface $z=f(x,y)$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ on the surface can be written as

$$

:question/worked-solution "The tangent plane to a surface is horizontal if and only if the normal vector to the tangent plane is vertical. So, let's first find the general expression of a normal vector to the surface.

Remember that the Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the surface $z=f(x,y)$ at the point $(x_0, y_0, z_0)$ on the surface can be written as

$$
z - z_0 = (x-x_0)\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}(x_0,y_0) + (y-y_0)\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}(x_0,y_0)
$$

where $\left\langle \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}(x_0,y_0), \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}(x_0,y_0), -1 \right\rangle$ represents a normal vector to the tangent plane.

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({y}^{2}+xy) \\  & =y \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{2}+xy) \\  & =2y+x\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, a normal vector to the tangent plane is 

$$
\left\langle y, \: 2y+x, \: -1 \right\rangle.
$$

We want to find where this normal vector is vertical. This means that the $x$- and $y$-components of the vector must be $0\mathbin{:}$

![](images/df/df6542baabd72b24ce115cb79c912c7b19fd3bd1b663467956445553b60a68c1.png) 

From the first equation, we get $y=0.$ Substituting this into the second equation, we obtain 

$$
2(0) +x = 0 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad x = 0.
$$

Finally, substituting $x=0$ and $y=0$ into our function, we get

$$
z = 0^2+(0)(0)= 0.
$$

Therefore, the point where the tangent plane is horizontal is $(0,0,0).$"} {:db/id 17592186129624 :question/id #uuid "92e52e05-2a21-5219-b9c8-0556f35cdaa8" :question/math-academy-id "q-37982"} {:db/id 17592186129625 :question/id #uuid "9f0c2107-2927-516f-9a87-f35b56581e57" :question/math-academy-id "q-37993"} {:db/id 17592186265747 :question/id #uuid "614f0c59-2007-5d79-93a8-aaee2f0fc248" :question/math-academy-id "q-129554"} {:db/id 17592186265748 :question/id #uuid "12830aeb-cb43-530e-902c-e52ba9d7524f" :question/math-academy-id "q-129557" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "4831fde7-328b-5f95-8b4f-bd555404f79f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(-1,-1,4)" :db/id 17592186263624} {:answer/id #uuid "5b9d3b86-7aec-5970-92c9-47d3d544786f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(1,0,3)" :db/id 17592186263789} {:answer/id #uuid "94d3b3cb-73a3-5f94-abc9-28adc6612ba0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(0,1,1)" :db/id 17592186264274} {:answer/id #uuid "9d20a40f-b237-5738-bfa6-76f889ea8789" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(\frac{2}{3},-1,\frac{7}{3})" :db/id 17592186264345} {:answer/id #uuid "a54e3749-cf7d-5ffc-ac93-9256ee36c08f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(-\frac{1}{3},0,\frac{1}{9})" :db/id 17592186264415}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186264345} :answer-field/id #uuid "38b8a09a-7de4-5c87-b2a5-460a354244c2" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186265348}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/problem "At which point on the surface $z=3{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}$ is the tangent plane perpendicular to the vector  $v=⟨4,-2,-1⟩?$" :question/worked-solution "The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the surface $z=f(x,y)$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ on the surface can be written as

$$
z-{z}_{0}=(x-{x}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),
$$

where $⟨\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),-1⟩$ represents a normal vector to the tangent plane.

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(3{x}^{2}+{y}^{2})=6x \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(3{x}^{2}+{y}^{2})=2y\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the normal vector to the tangent plane is 

$$
⟨6x,\,2y,\,-1⟩.
$$

Our tangent plane should be perpendicular to $⟨4,-2,-1⟩.$ So, the normal vector of that plane must be parallel to that vector. In other words, for some constant $c$, we must have

$$
c\cdot ⟨6x,\,2y,\,-1⟩=⟨4,-2,-1⟩.
$$

Equating the corresponding coordinates, we obtain the following system:

$$
{\begin{aligned}6cx=4 \\ 2cy=-2 \\ -c=-1\end{aligned}
$$

From the third equation, we get $c=1.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain 

$$
6(1)x=4\,⟹\,x=\frac{2}{3}.
$$

And substituting $c=1$ into the second equation, we have 

$$
2(1)y=-2\,⟹\,y=-1.
$$

Finally, substituting $x=\frac{2}{3}$ and $y=-1$ into our function, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}z & =3{(\frac{2}{3})}^{2}+(-1)^{2} \\  & =\frac{4}{3}+1 \\  & =\frac{7}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent plane is perpendicular to the vector $v$ at $(\frac{2}{3},-1,\frac{7}{3}).$"} {:db/id 17592186323964 :question/id #uuid "5c9333a9-b5d6-5ec8-b1f3-0c62768fb8b7" :question/math-academy-id "q-37986" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "464dff10-0c59-5dad-80a1-2ee16d60dbfa" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(2\pi ,-\pi ,2\pi )" :db/id 17592186321703} {:answer/id #uuid "48223b68-6d40-5d37-8bb5-b27364a9cf80" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(2\pi ,\pi ,-1)" :db/id 17592186321715} {:answer/id #uuid "a226c677-0c51-577f-b0f5-1b3064cc6815" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(\pi ,2,-2\pi )" :db/id 17592186322427} {:answer/id #uuid "adf98dbd-c12a-5550-9749-ddcc015f00fd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(2\pi ,\pi ,12\pi )" :db/id 17592186322512} {:answer/id #uuid "d80a3e3a-b37d-53fa-b4ba-7e5d51839fdf" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(-2,6,8\pi )" :db/id 17592186322836}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186322427} :answer-field/id #uuid "5baf0726-2cff-5a6b-904f-2992e085ab37" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186323351}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/problem "At which points on the surface $z=2\operatorname{sin}⁡x-xy$ is the tangent plane perpendicular to the vector  $v\,=\,⟨8,2\pi ,2⟩?$" :question/worked-solution "The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the surface $z=f(x,y)$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ on the surface can be written as

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

z-{z}_{0}=(x-{x}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),
$$

where $⟨\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),-1⟩$ represents a normal vector to the tangent plane.

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}-7)=2x \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}-7)=4y\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the normal vector to the tangent plane is 

$$
⟨2x,\,4y,\,-1⟩.
$$

Our tangent plane should be perpendicular to $⟨6,-8,-1⟩.$ So, the normal vector of that plane must be parallel to that vector. In other words, for some constant $c$, we must have

$$
c\cdot ⟨2x,\,4y,\,-1⟩=⟨6,-8,-1⟩.
$$

Equating the corresponding coordinates, we obtain the following system:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}2cx=6 \\ 4cy=-8 \\ -c=-1\end{aligned}
$$

From the third equation, we get $c=1.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain 

$$
2(1)x=6\,⟹\,x=3.
$$

And substituting $c=1$ into the second equation, we have 

$$
4(1)y=-8\,⟹\,y=-2.
$$

Finally, substituting $x=3$ and $y=-2$ into our function, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}z & ={3}^{2}+2(-2)^{2}-7 \\  & =9+8-7 \\  & =10.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent plane is perpendicular to the vector $v$ at $(3,-2,10).$"} {:db/id 17592186435553 :question/id #uuid "e0b70f07-48f3-5e91-bb4d-83ea4566f9c8" :question/math-academy-id "q-129560" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "6521128c-8b33-54da-8c83-d27bef687244" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(-1,1,-3)" :db/id 17592186435529} {:answer/id #uuid "6a9c4d22-52c4-582f-b256-0ddd6fa135ad" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(\frac{1}{2},1,-\frac{3}{2})" :db/id 17592186435530} {:answer/id #uuid "84cf53e7-7029-5a30-8dd0-ad54d0eb0064" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(1,0,2)" :db/id 17592186435533} {:answer/id #uuid "bcd79e5d-b439-5f83-a72f-40d75fd4cdd8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(2,-1,-9)" :db/id 17592186435537} {:answer/id #uuid "d89ebc6c-8c25-5ee8-a102-c0421505fca3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(-\frac{1}{2},-\frac{1}{2},\frac{9}{4})" :db/id 17592186435540}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186435540} :answer-field/id #uuid "e1008d1e-ad25-59f1-8249-03f1bd3c30fe" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186435547}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/problem "At which point on the surface $z=4-2{x}^{2}-5{y}^{2}$ is the tangent plane perpendicular to the vector $v=⟨-2,-5,1⟩?$" :question/worked-solution "The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the surface $z=f(x,y)$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ on the surface can be written as

where $⟨\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),-1⟩$ represents a normal vector to the tangent plane.

$$
c\cdot ⟨-4x,\,-10y,\,-1⟩=⟨-2,-5,1⟩.
$$

Equating the corresponding coordinates, we obtain the following system:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}-4cx=-2 \\ -10cy=-5 \\ -c=1\end{aligned}
$$

$$
-4(-1)x=-2\,⟹\,x=-\frac{1}{2}.

$$
-10(-1)y=-5\,⟹\,y=-\frac{1}{2}.

$$

$(1,-1,1,5).$" :question/worked-solution "The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the surface $w=f(x,y,z)$ at the point $(x_0, y_0, z_0,w_0)$ on the hypersurface can be written as

$$
w - w_0 = (x-x_0)\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}(x_0,y_0,z_0) + (y-y_0)\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}(x_0,y_0,z_0) + (z-z_0)\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial z}(x_0,y_0,z_0).
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}-2xyz)=2x-2yz \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}-2xyz)=2y-2xz \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}-2xyz)=2z-2xy\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the partial derivatives at $(x,y,z) = (1,-1,1)\mathbin{:}$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}(1,-1,1) & =2(1)-2(-1)(1)=4 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y}(1,-1,1) & =2(-1)-2(1)(1)=-4 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z}(1,-1,1) & =2(1)-2(1)(-1)=4\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write down the equation of the tangent hyperplane:

$$
\begin{aligned}w-5 & =(x-1)\frac{∂f}{∂x}(1,-1,1)+(y+1)\frac{∂f}{∂y}(1,-1,1)+(z-1)\frac{∂f}{∂z}(1,-1,1)\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting and simplifying, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}w-5 & =4(x-1)-4(y+1)+4(z-1) \\ w-5 & =4x-4y+4z-12 \\ -4x+4y-4z+w+7 & =0 \\ 4x-4y+4z-w-7 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186129612 :question/id #uuid "bf18ba79-26dd-5213-bc52-5eab8640b606" :question/math-academy-id "q-37604"} {:db/id 17592186129857 :question/id #uuid 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "Find the equation of the tangent hyperplane to the hypersurface $w=4x\operatorname{arctan}⁡(yz)$ at the point $(-1,1,1,-\pi ).$" :question/worked-solution "The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the hypersurface $w=f(x,y,z)$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0},{w}_{0})$ on the hypersurface can be written as

$$
w-{w}_{0}=(x-{x}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})+(z-{z}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂z}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0}).
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(4x\operatorname{arctan}⁡(yz))=4\operatorname{arctan}⁡(yz) \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(4x\operatorname{arctan}⁡(yz))=\frac{4xz}{1+{y}^{2}{z}^{2}} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(4x\operatorname{arctan}⁡(yz))=\frac{4xy}{1+{y}^{2}{z}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the partial derivatives at $(x,y,z)=(-1,1,1):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}(-1,1,1) & =4\operatorname{arctan}⁡(1\cdot 1)=\pi  \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y}(-1,1,1) & =\frac{4(-1)(1)}{1+({1}^{2})({1}^{2})}=-2 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z}(-1,1,1) & =\frac{4(-1)(1)}{1+({1}^{2})({1}^{2})}=-2\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write down the equation of the tangent hyperplane:

$$
\begin{aligned}w-(-\pi ) & =(x-(-1))\frac{∂f}{∂x}(-1,1,1)+(y-1)\frac{∂f}{∂y}(-1,1,1)+(z-1)\frac{∂f}{∂z}(-1,1,1) \\ w+\pi  & =\pi (x+1)-2(y-1)-2(z-1) \\ w+\pi  & =\pi x-2y-2z+4+\pi  \\ \pi x-2y-2z-w+4 & =0\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186342093 :question/id #uuid "de6bd964-56b9-511c-9d67-ed8d06732a08" :question/math-academy-id "q-73851" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "62fcc3f3-ddff-52b4-b6ee-b406a0ffec98" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\pi x-\pi y-z+w+\pi =0" :db/id 17592186340008} {:answer/id #uuid "93a5ca28-3798-5c54-9d92-aa2d41eb6d90" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\pi x-\pi y+z+w-\pi =0" :db/id 17592186340453} {:answer/id #uuid "9f8794dd-7491-5377-b367-530775903444" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\pi x+\pi y+z-w+3\pi =0" :db/id 17592186340570} {:answer/id #uuid "f6251148-2e5e-526a-995c-c61130894b01" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\pi x+\pi y-z+w-\pi =0" :db/id 17592186341302} {:answer/id #uuid "fa7d3452-6743-53e2-bd9c-8cfa857fa7bf" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\pi x+\pi y+z+w-3\pi =0" :db/id 17592186341343}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186341343} :answer-field/id #uuid "a31f7eac-9e1f-5aaa-97e4-e132312fc936" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186341668}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "Find the equation of the tangent hyperplane to the hypersurface $w=\operatorname{sin}⁡(xyz)$ at the point $(1,1,\pi ,0).$" :question/worked-solution "The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the hypersurface $w=f(x,y,z)$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0},{w}_{0})$ on the hypersurface can be written as

$$
w-{w}_{0}=(x-{x}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})+(z-{z}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂z}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0}).
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(xyz))=yz\operatorname{cos}⁡(xyz) \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(xyz))=xz\operatorname{cos}⁡(xyz) \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(xyz))=xy\operatorname{cos}⁡(xyz)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the partial derivatives at $(x,y,z)=(1,1,\pi ):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}(1,1,\pi ) & =(1)(\pi )\operatorname{cos}⁡(1\cdot 1\cdot \pi )=-\pi  \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y}(1,1,\pi ) & =(1)(\pi )\operatorname{cos}⁡(1\cdot 1\cdot \pi )=-\pi  \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z}(1,1,\pi ) & =(1)(1)\operatorname{cos}⁡(1\cdot 1\cdot \pi )=-1\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write down the equation of the tangent hyperplane:

$({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0},{w}_{0})$ on the hypersurface can be written as

$$
w-{w}_{0}=(x-{x}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})+(z-{z}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂z}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0}).
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-{z}^{2}))=\frac{2x}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-{z}^{2}} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-{z}^{2}))=\frac{2y}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-{z}^{2}} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-{z}^{2}))=-\frac{2z}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-{z}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the partial derivatives at $(x,y,z)=(1,-1,1):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}(1,-1,1) & =\frac{2(1)}{(1)^{2}+(-1)^{2}-(1)^{2}}=2 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y}(1,-1,1) & =\frac{2(-1)}{(1)^{2}+(-1)^{2}-(1)^{2}}=-2 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z}(1,-1,1) & =-\frac{2(1)}{(1)^{2}+(-1)^{2}-(1)^{2}}=-2\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write down the equation of the tangent hyperplane:

$$
\begin{aligned}w-0 & =(x-1)\frac{∂f}{∂x}(1,-1,1)+(y+1)\frac{∂f}{∂y}(1,-1,1)+(z-1)\frac{∂f}{∂z}(1,-1,1) \\ w & =2(x-1)-2(y+1)-2(z-1) \\ w & =2x-2-2y-2-2z+2 \\ -2x+2y+2z+w+2 & =0 \\ 2x-2y-2z-w-2 & =0\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186435550 :question/id #uuid "6b798538-8660-5c1f-9d93-5bdad8bdb40c" :question/math-academy-id "q-129477" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "18541d05-49d2-5f19-b579-6b534b3bcfd4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x+2y+z+w-2=0" :db/id 17592186435522} {:answer/id #uuid "1e19600e-76b4-5880-a603-02783cbb324e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x+y-2z-w+1=0" :db/id 17592186435523} {:answer/id #uuid "36b42409-fb4f-52cb-a983-864ab8cc5f71" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2x+y+z-w-3=0" :db/id 17592186435525} {:answer/id #uuid "b3f12775-7dc0-5662-9058-bbd97ad38d1d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3x-2y-z+w-2=0" :db/id 17592186435536} {:answer/id #uuid "ca2e0787-ad3a-5c7f-add5-4e016dc6c7a7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x+2y-3z+w+2=0" :db/id 17592186435538}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186435523} :answer-field/id #uuid "49b834ec-93e3-593b-87ef-065fbe59d9c9" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186435544}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "Find the equation of the tangent hyperplane to the hypersurface $w=x+y-{z}^{2}$ at the point $(1,0,1,0).$" :question/worked-solution "The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the hypersurface $w=f(x,y,z)$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0},{w}_{0})$ on the hypersurface can be written as

$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x+y-{z}^{2})=1 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(x+y-{z}^{2})=1 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(x+y-{z}^{2})=-2z\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the partial derivatives at $(x,y,z)=(1,0,1):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}(1,0,1) & =1 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y}(1,0,1) & =1 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z}(1,0,1) & =-2(1)=-2\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write down the equation of the tangent hyperplane:

$$
\begin{aligned}w-0 & =(x-1)\frac{∂f}{∂x}(1,0,1)+(y-0)\frac{∂f}{∂y}(1,0,1)+(z-1)\frac{∂f}{∂z}(1,0,1) \\ w & =(x-1)+y-2(z-1) \\ w & =x+y-2z+1 \\ x+y-2z-w+1 & =0\end{aligned}

$$
w-{w}_{0}=(x-{x}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})+(z-{z}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂z}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0}).
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2x{y}^{2}+y{z}^{2}-3{x}^{2}z)=2{y}^{2}-6xz \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2x{y}^{2}+y{z}^{2}-3{x}^{2}z)=4xy+{z}^{2} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(2x{y}^{2}+y{z}^{2}-3{x}^{2}z)=2yz-3{x}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the partial derivatives at $(x,y,z)=(2,-2,1):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}(2,-2,1) & =2(-2)^{2}-6(2)(1)=-4 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y}(2,-2,1) & =4(2)(-2)+(1)^{2}=-15 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z}(2,-2,1) & =2(-2)(1)-3(2)^{2}=-16\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}w-2 & =(x-2)\frac{∂f}{∂x}(2,-2,1)+(y+2)\frac{∂f}{∂y}(2,-2,1)+(z-1)\frac{∂f}{∂z}(2,-2,1) \\ w-2 & =-4(x-2)-15(y+2)-16(z-1) \\ w-2 & =-4x+8-15y-30-16z+16 \\ 4x+15y+16z+w+4 & =0\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186048642} {:db/id 17592186049809 :topic/difficulty 1.0543168393207591 :topic/encompasses [{:db/id 17592186428468 :encompassing/rationale "Initial Codex estimate from captured target-band crossing frequency. :topic/math-academy-id 1980} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186130044 :step/content {:db/id 17592186130382 :tutorial/content "Earlier, we claimed that function $f(x)$ is differentiable at $x_0$ *if the function admits a unique tangent line* at $x_0.$ Let's now justify this claim.

Recall that a function $f(x)$ is differentiable at $x=x_0$ with derivative $f'(x_0)$ if and only if the following limit exists:

$$
f'(x_0) = \lim_{x\to x_0}\dfrac {f(x) - f(x_0)} {x-x_0}
$$

We can rewrite this limit as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {x}_{0}}(\frac{f(x)-f({x}_{0})}{x-{x}_{0}})-{f}^{'}({x}_{0}) & =0 \\ {lim}_{x\to {x}_{0}}(\frac{f(x)-f({x}_{0})}{x-{x}_{0}}-{f}^{'}({x}_{0})) & =0 \\ {lim}_{x\to {x}_{0}}\frac{f(x)-f({x}_{0})-(x-{x}_{0}){f}^{'}({x}_{0})}{x-{x}_{0}} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

In order for the above limit to hold true, the numerator must approach zero. So, near $x_0,$ we must have

$$
f(x) - f(x_0) - (x-x_0)f'(x_0) \approx 0,
$$

which can be rewritten as

$$
f(x) - f(x_0) \approx (x-x_0)f'(x_0).
$$

This corresponds to the following equation of the tangent line at $x_0\mathbin{:}$

$$
y -y_0 = (x-x_0)\dfrac{\textrm d f}{\textrm d x}(x_0)
$$

From here, we can say that a function $f(x)$ is differentiable at $x_0$ *if the function admits a unique tangent line* at $x_0.$

We'll now use a similar idea to define the differentiability of a multivariable function at a point $P$ in terms of tangent planes." :tutorial/id #uuid "48f4e466-1052-5e98-b9a0-d345e3139cb2" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3914 :tutorial/title "Defining the Differentiability of Single Variable Functions in Terms of Tangent Lines"} :step/id #uuid "41594163-d4dc-5179-be5c-4adec6fac7bc" :step/math-academy-id 23115 :step/next {:db/id 17592186130045}} {:db/id 17592186130045 :step/content {:db/id 17592186130383 :tutorial/content "Earlier, we claimed that function $f(x,y)$ is differentiable at $(x_0,y_0)$ *if the function admits a unique tangent plane* at $(x_0,y_0).$ Let's now justify this claim.

Assume that $f(x,y)$ is a differentiable function of two variables. Since $f(x,y)$ is differentiable at $(x_0,y_0),$ then there exists a vector $\nabla f = \langle f_1, f_2\rangle$ such that

$$
\lim_{(x,y)\to (x_0,y_0)}\dfrac {f(x,y) - f(x_0,y_0) - \langle x-x_0, y-y_0\rangle \cdot \langle f_1, f_2\rangle} {||\langle x-x_0,y-y_0\rangle||} = 0. \qquad (\ast)
$$

For the above limit to hold, the numerator must approach zero. So, near $(x_0,y_0),$ we must have

$$
f(x,y) - f(x_0,y_0) - \langle x-x_0, y-y_0\rangle \cdot \langle f_1, f_2\rangle \approx 0,
$$

which can be rewritten as

$$
f(x,y) - f(x_0,y_0) \approx \langle x-x_0, y-y_0\rangle \cdot \langle f_1, f_2\rangle.
$$

Expanding the dot product, we get

$$
f(x,y) \approx  f(x_0,y_0) + (x-x_0)\cdot f_1+ (y-y_0)\cdot f_2.
$$

We now need to show that $f_1$ and $f_2$ are the partial derivatives.

- Let $y=y_0$ in the first equation $(\ast)$ above. This gives

$$
\lim_{x\to x_0}\dfrac {f(x,y_0) - f(x_0,y_0) - (x-x_0) f_1} {x-x_0} = 0,
$$

which is the definition of the partial derivative with respect to $x.$ So, we have $f_1 = \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}(x_0,y_0).$

- Similarly, letting $x = x_0$ gives $f_2 = \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}(x_0,y_0).$

Therefore, the function $f(x,y)$ can be linearized as

$$
f(x,y)\approx f(x_0,y_0) + (x-x_0)\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}(x_0,y_0) + (y-y_0)\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}(x_0,y_0).
$$

By setting $z=f(x,y)$ and $z_0 = f(x_0,y_0),$ we get the equation of the tangent plane:

$$
z - z_0 = (x-x_0)\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}(x_0,y_0) + (y-y_0)\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}(x_0,y_0)
$$

From here, we can say that a function $f(x,y)$ is differentiable at $(x_0,y_0)$ *if the function admits a unique tangent plane* at $(x_0, y_0).$

Finally, note that we have also shown that 

$$
\nabla f = \left\langle \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}, \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y} \right\rangle.
$$

The vector $\nabla f$ is known as the **gradient vector**." :tutorial/id #uuid "3e6cb319-460f-5a22-888e-e3f886ea9b0b" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3915 :tutorial/title "Defining the Differentiability of Multivariable Functions in Terms of Tangent Planes"} :step/id #uuid "c0a78a51-4800-5622-8fa8-92069e9e72f6" :step/math-academy-id 23116} {:db/id 17592186130046 :step/content {:db/id 17592186129177 "a126e19a-f8b5-5040-9719-0bc0a4c611e3" :step/math-academy-id 23123 :step/next {:db/id 17592186130044}} {:db/id 17592186130049 :step/content {:db/id 17592186130384 :tutorial/content "Recall that the equation of the tangent plane to the surface $z = f(x,y)$ at $(x_0,y_0,z_0)$ can be given as

$$
z - z_0 = (x-x_0)\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}(x_0,y_0) + (y-y_0)\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}(x_0,y_0).
$$

Slightly rewriting the equation, we obtain

$$
{\color{blue}\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}(x_0,y_0)} \cdot (x-x_0) + {\color{blue}\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}(x_0,y_0)} \cdot (y-y_0) + ({\color{blue}-1}) \cdot (z - z_0) = 0,
$$

which immediately gives us a normal vector to the tangent plane:

$$
\left\langle {\color{blue}\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}(x_0,y_0)}, \:\: {\color{blue}\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}(x_0,y_0)}, \:\: {\color{blue}-1} \right\rangle
$$

A normal vector to the tangent plane to the surface is called a **normal vector to the surface**." :tutorial/id #uuid "c5ebd9d6-c219-583a-8bca-87268b8aa8bc" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3919 :tutorial/title "Finding a Normal Vector to a Surface"} :step/id #uuid "828fdb16-4d33-565c-9b6f-4db12aed5567" :step/math-academy-id 23133 :step/next {:db/id 17592186130047}} {:db/id 17592186130050 :step/content {:db/id 17592186130385 :tutorial/content "Until now, we considered only functions of the form 

![](images/48/4838bea41cd622ef69be5caaafac89df818d35cf108730686d68d7b7a12265ac.svg)

of two independent variables. But what about the case of functions 

![](images/72/72e701a6fcd4514adb9731764fc74a1cb3f0b73f548680db162cd2c8a025e0d6.svg)

with three variables? Can we define a tangent plane to such a function?

The answer is yes! Analogously to the case with two variables, a function of three variables ![](images/72/72e701a6fcd4514adb9731764fc74a1cb3f0b73f548680db162cd2c8a025e0d6.svg) is differentiable at ![](images/f4/f46650c560f32308db30c404d86da2d5921654805cca770cd2bc3627e55dbf86.svg) if it admits a **unique tangent hyperplane** at ![](images/3f/3fe19998bf33d149c699a01ca363c2691041b3ecfd52c47a167053b4097dbb57.svg) where ![](images/7e/7e2db5c48c69709e3c1d04d4834af7cc0b2ff0df186cf1713e207c164a8e41e5.svg) The equation of the **tangent hyperplane** is given by

![](images/f4/f433839875810dc7417400a22bad7b8a63c0eb1033954a8e91e7049f3ada361a.svg)

Notice that we use the term *hyperplane*. The graphs of functions of three variables live in four-dimensional space. The equation above describes an object (a so-called hyperplane) in four-dimensional space that can be considered an analog to a *plane* in three-dimensional space." :tutorial/id #uuid "d6f087f4-e5d4-59f8-90f7-a5a9484a0c6f" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3920 :tutorial/title "The Equation of a Tangent Hyperplane"} :step/id #uuid "773e70e4-737a-5fa4-92ed-0e1d04815ea8" :step/math-academy-id 23134 :step/next {:db/id 17592186130051}} {:db/id 17592186130051 :step/content {:db/id 17592186129180 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186128999 :question/id #uuid "ed1a3960-c2c4-57e7-8fd1-daf5d98bf052" :question/math-academy-id "e-6185"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "cc56f7a5-65a7-53a9-9eb6-ae7b91a1bdd0" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186129612} {:db/id 17592186129857} {:db/id 17592186265736} {:db/id 17592186265737} {:db/id 17592186265738} {:db/id 17592186265739} {:db/id 17592186342093} {:db/id 17592186342094} {:db/id 17592186342095} {:db/id 17592186342096} {:db/id 17592186385585} {:db/id 17592186407513} {:db/id 17592186435550} {:db/id 17592186435551}] :knowledge-point/title "Calculating the Equation of a Tangent Hyperplane"} :step/id #uuid "ca4b822d-4434-5d75-8400-5106f71e78a9" :step/math-academy-id 23135 :step/next {:db/id 17592186130049}} {:db/id 17592186130052 :step/content {:db/id 17592186130386 :tutorial/content "Similar to tangent lines for single variable functions, we can think of the **tangent plane** to a surface at a point as the plane that "touches" the surface at that point.

The equation of the tangent plane to a surface $z=f(x,y)$ at the point $(x_0,y_0,z_0),$ where $z_0=f(x_0,y_0),$ can be found using the formula

$$
z - z_0 = (x-x_0)\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}(x_0,y_0) + (y-y_0)\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}(x_0,y_0).
$$

For example, consider the surface 

$$
z = 4-x^2-y^2.
$$

Let's find the equation of the tangent plane to the surface at the point $(0,\sqrt{2},2),$ as shown below.

![](images/03/03df90a94615238e2126338f64d1f51fcefc379068a8cdc366b33b998cd69f45.png)

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(4-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2})=-2x \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(4-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2})=-2y\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the partial derivatives at $(x,y) = (0,\sqrt{2})\mathbin{:}$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}(0,\sqrt{2}) & =-2(0)=0 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y}(0,\sqrt{2}) & =-2(\sqrt{2})=-2\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write down the equation of the tangent plane:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-2 & =(x-0)\frac{∂f}{∂x}(0,\sqrt{2})+(y-\sqrt{2})\frac{∂f}{∂y}(0,\sqrt{2}) \\ z-2 & =0(x-0)-2\sqrt{2}(y-\sqrt{2}) \\ z-2 & =-2\sqrt{2}y+4 \\ 2\sqrt{2}y+z-6 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So, we get that the Cartesian equation of the tangent plane is $2\sqrt{2}y + z - 6 = 0.$

![](images/d5/d51bdbe8820472334f7e1d942c027b6ad8164eaece58220f3f2e5cdb51544f05.png)" :tutorial/id #uuid "bced0695-3ebd-5b62-b7ff-9c8f2500fc2a" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3921 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "0355e3e0-f89b-5dca-97bc-21791fa4aed2" :step/math-academy-id 23153 :step/next {:db/id 17592186130067}} {:db/id 17592186130067 :step/content {:db/id 17592186130396 :tutorial/content "A surface $z = f(x,y)$ is differentiable at a point $P$ if and only if it admits a *unique* tangent plane at $P.$ Intuitively, this means that, in the neighborhood of $P,$ the surface $z=f(x,y)$ can be approximated as a plane.

Note that this is analogous to the case of functions of one variable. A function $y = f(x)$ is differentiable at a point $P$ if and only if it admits a *unique* tangent *line* at $P.$ This is the same as saying that, in the neighborhood of $P,$ the curve $y=f(x)$ can be approximated as a straight line.  

We'll explore these ideas in more depth at the end of the lesson. For now, let's get some practice at computing tangent planes." :tutorial/id #uuid "015c4e8e-c1ba-5672-8228-ff0869681d6d" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4231 :tutorial/title "A Note on Differentiability"} :step/id #uuid "0296b5b5-c2ce-56c6-a8e4-ad0af71e0dde" :step/math-academy-id 25668 :step/next {:db/id 17592186130046}}] :activity/title "Tangent Planes to Surfaces" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186129328} {:db/id 17592186130052 :step/content {:db/id 17592186130386 :tutorial/content "Similar to tangent lines for single variable functions, we can think of the **tangent plane** to a surface at a point as the plane that "touches" the surface at that point.

The equation of the tangent plane to a surface $z=f(x,y)$ at the point $(x_0,y_0,z_0),$ where $z_0=f(x_0,y_0),$ can be found using the formula

$$
z - z_0 = (x-x_0)\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}(x_0,y_0) + (y-y_0)\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}(x_0,y_0).
$$

For example, consider the surface 

$$
z = 4-x^2-y^2.
$$

Let's find the equation of the tangent plane to the surface at the point $(0,\sqrt{2},2),$ as shown below.

![](images/03/03df90a94615238e2126338f64d1f51fcefc379068a8cdc366b33b998cd69f45.png)

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(4-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2})=-2x \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(4-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2})=-2y\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the partial derivatives at $(x,y) = (0,\sqrt{2})\mathbin{:}$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}(0,\sqrt{2}) & =-2(0)=0 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y}(0,\sqrt{2}) & =-2(\sqrt{2})=-2\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write down the equation of the tangent plane:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-2 & =(x-0)\frac{∂f}{∂x}(0,\sqrt{2})+(y-\sqrt{2})\frac{∂f}{∂y}(0,\sqrt{2}) \\ z-2 & =0(x-0)-2\sqrt{2}(y-\sqrt{2}) \\ z-2 & =-2\sqrt{2}y+4 \\ 2\sqrt{2}y+z-6 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So, we get that the Cartesian equation of the tangent plane is $2\sqrt{2}y + z - 6 = 0.$

![](images/d5/d51bdbe8820472334f7e1d942c027b6ad8164eaece58220f3f2e5cdb51544f05.png)" :tutorial/id #uuid "bced0695-3ebd-5b62-b7ff-9c8f2500fc2a" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3921 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "0355e3e0-f89b-5dca-97bc-21791fa4aed2" :step/math-academy-id 23153 :step/next {:db/id 17592186130067}} {:db/id 17592186130044 :step/content {:db/id 17592186130382 :tutorial/content "Earlier, we claimed that function $f(x)$ is differentiable at $x_0$ *if the function admits a unique tangent line* at $x_0.$ Let's now justify this claim.

Recall that a function $f(x)$ is differentiable at $x=x_0$ with derivative $f'(x_0)$ if and only if the following limit exists:

$$
f'(x_0) = \lim_{x\to x_0}\dfrac {f(x) - f(x_0)} {x-x_0}
$$

We can rewrite this limit as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {x}_{0}}(\frac{f(x)-f({x}_{0})}{x-{x}_{0}})-{f}^{'}({x}_{0}) & =0 \\ {lim}_{x\to {x}_{0}}(\frac{f(x)-f({x}_{0})}{x-{x}_{0}}-{f}^{'}({x}_{0})) & =0 \\ {lim}_{x\to {x}_{0}}\frac{f(x)-f({x}_{0})-(x-{x}_{0}){f}^{'}({x}_{0})}{x-{x}_{0}} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

In order for the above limit to hold true, the numerator must approach zero. So, near $x_0,$ we must have

$$
f(x) - f(x_0) - (x-x_0)f'(x_0) \approx 0,
$$

which can be rewritten as

$$
f(x) - f(x_0) \approx (x-x_0)f'(x_0).
$$

This corresponds to the following equation of the tangent line at $x_0\mathbin{:}$

$$
y -y_0 = (x-x_0)\dfrac{\textrm d f}{\textrm d x}(x_0)
$$

From here, we can say that a function $f(x)$ is differentiable at $x_0$ *if the function admits a unique tangent line* at $x_0.$

We'll now use a similar idea to define the differentiability of a multivariable function at a point $P$ in terms of tangent planes." :tutorial/id #uuid "48f4e466-1052-5e98-b9a0-d345e3139cb2" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3914 :tutorial/title "Defining the Differentiability of Single Variable Functions in Terms of Tangent Lines"} :step/id #uuid "41594163-d4dc-5179-be5c-4adec6fac7bc" :step/math-academy-id 23115 :step/next {:db/id 17592186130045}} {:db/id 17592186130382 :tutorial/content "Earlier, we claimed that function $f(x)$ is differentiable at $x_0$ *if the function admits a unique tangent line* at $x_0.$ Let's now justify this claim.

We'll now use a similar idea to define the differentiability of a multivariable function at a point $P$ in terms of tangent planes." :tutorial/id #uuid "48f4e466-1052-5e98-b9a0-d345e3139cb2" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3914 :tutorial/title "Defining the Differentiability of Single Variable Functions in Terms of Tangent Lines"} {:db/id 17592186130045 :step/content {:db/id 17592186130383 :tutorial/content "Earlier, we claimed that function $f(x,y)$ is differentiable at $(x_0,y_0)$ *if the function admits a unique tangent plane* at $(x_0,y_0).$ Let's now justify this claim.

Assume that $f(x,y)$ is a differentiable function of two variables. Since $f(x,y)$ is differentiable at $(x_0,y_0),$ then there exists a vector $\nabla f = \langle f_1, f_2\rangle$ such that

$$
\lim_{(x,y)\to (x_0,y_0)}\dfrac {f(x,y) - f(x_0,y_0) - \langle x-x_0, y-y_0\rangle \cdot \langle f_1, f_2\rangle} {||\langle x-x_0,y-y_0\rangle||} = 0. \qquad (\ast)
$$

For the above limit to hold, the numerator must approach zero. So, near $(x_0,y_0),$ we must have

$$
f(x,y) - f(x_0,y_0) - \langle x-x_0, y-y_0\rangle \cdot \langle f_1, f_2\rangle \approx 0,
$$

which can be rewritten as

$$
f(x,y) - f(x_0,y_0) \approx \langle x-x_0, y-y_0\rangle \cdot \langle f_1, f_2\rangle.
$$

Expanding the dot product, we get

$$
f(x,y) \approx  f(x_0,y_0) + (x-x_0)\cdot f_1+ (y-y_0)\cdot f_2.
$$

We now need to show that $f_1$ and $f_2$ are the partial derivatives.

- Let $y=y_0$ in the first equation $(\ast)$ above. This gives

$$
\lim_{x\to x_0}\dfrac {f(x,y_0) - f(x_0,y_0) - (x-x_0) f_1} {x-x_0} = 0,
$$

which is the definition of the partial derivative with respect to $x.$ So, we have $f_1 = \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}(x_0,y_0).$

- Similarly, letting $x = x_0$ gives $f_2 = \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}(x_0,y_0).$

Therefore, the function $f(x,y)$ can be linearized as

$$
f(x,y)\approx f(x_0,y_0) + (x-x_0)\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}(x_0,y_0) + (y-y_0)\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}(x_0,y_0).
$$

By setting $z=f(x,y)$ and $z_0 = f(x_0,y_0),$ we get the equation of the tangent plane:

$$
z - z_0 = (x-x_0)\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}(x_0,y_0) + (y-y_0)\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}(x_0,y_0)
$$

From here, we can say that a function $f(x,y)$ is differentiable at $(x_0,y_0)$ *if the function admits a unique tangent plane* at $(x_0, y_0).$

Finally, note that we have also shown that 

$$
\nabla f = \left\langle \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}, \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y} \right\rangle.
$$

The vector $\nabla f$ is known as the **gradient vector**." :tutorial/id #uuid "3e6cb319-460f-5a22-888e-e3f886ea9b0b" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3915 :tutorial/title "Defining the Differentiability of Multivariable Functions in Terms of Tangent Planes"} :step/id #uuid "c0a78a51-4800-5622-8fa8-92069e9e72f6" :step/math-academy-id 23116} {:db/id 17592186130383 :tutorial/content "Earlier, we claimed that function $f(x,y)$ is differentiable at $(x_0,y_0)$ *if the function admits a unique tangent plane* at $(x_0,y_0).$ Let's now justify this claim.

$$

Let's find the equation of the tangent plane to the surface at the point $(0,\sqrt{2},2),$ as shown below.

![](images/03/03df90a94615238e2126338f64d1f51fcefc379068a8cdc366b33b998cd69f45.png)

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(4-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2})=-2x \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(4-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2})=-2y\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the partial derivatives at $(x,y) = (0,\sqrt{2})\mathbin{:}$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}(0,\sqrt{2}) & =-2(0)=0 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y}(0,\sqrt{2}) & =-2(\sqrt{2})=-2\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write down the equation of the tangent plane:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-2 & =(x-0)\frac{∂f}{∂x}(0,\sqrt{2})+(y-\sqrt{2})\frac{∂f}{∂y}(0,\sqrt{2}) \\ z-2 & =0(x-0)-2\sqrt{2}(y-\sqrt{2}) \\ z-2 & =-2\sqrt{2}y+4 \\ 2\sqrt{2}y+z-6 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So, we get that the Cartesian equation of the tangent plane is $2\sqrt{2}y + z - 6 = 0.$

$$
z-{z}_{0}=(x-{x}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),
$$

where $⟨\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),-1⟩$ represents a normal vector to the tangent plane.

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}-2x+{y}^{2}+6y+10) \\  & =2x-2 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}-2x+{y}^{2}+6y+10) \\  & =2y+6\end{aligned}
$$

 

Hence, the normal vector to the tangent plane is 

$$
⟨2x-2,\,2y+6,\,-1⟩.
$$

Note that the tangent plane is horizontal if and only if the normal vector is vertical. This means that the $x$- and $y$-components of the vector must be $0:$

$$
{\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=0 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y}=0\end{aligned}\,⟹\,{\begin{aligned}2x-2=0 \\ 2y+6=0\end{aligned}
$$

 

From the first equation, we get $x=1$ while the second equation gives $y=-3.$ 

Finally, substituting $x=1$ and $y=-3$ into our function, we get

$$
z={1}^{2}-2(1)+(-3)^{2}+6(-3)+10=0.
$$

Therefore, the point where the tangent plane is horizontal is $(1,-3,0).$"} :step/id #uuid "0eadd7d5-26a1-573f-b533-83cfbfb498b9" :step/next {:db/id 17592186407516}} {:db/id 17592186407515 :step/content {:db/id 17592186323964 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "464dff10-0c59-5dad-80a1-2ee16d60dbfa" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(2\pi ,-\pi ,2\pi )" :db/id 17592186321703} {:answer/id #uuid "48223b68-6d40-5d37-8bb5-b27364a9cf80" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(2\pi ,\pi ,-1)" :db/id 17592186321715} {:answer/id #uuid "a226c677-0c51-577f-b0f5-1b3064cc6815" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(\pi ,2,-2\pi )" :db/id 17592186322427} {:answer/id #uuid "adf98dbd-c12a-5550-9749-ddcc015f00fd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(2\pi ,\pi ,12\pi )" :db/id 17592186322512} {:answer/id #uuid "d80a3e3a-b37d-53fa-b4ba-7e5d51839fdf" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(-2,6,8\pi )" :db/id 17592186322836}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186322427} :answer-field/id #uuid "5baf0726-2cff-5a6b-904f-2992e085ab37" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186323351}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "5c9333a9-b5d6-5ec8-b1f3-0c62768fb8b7" :question/math-academy-id "q-37986" :question/problem "At which points on the surface $z=2\operatorname{sin}⁡x-xy$ is the tangent plane perpendicular to the vector  $v\,=\,⟨8,2\pi ,2⟩?$" :question/worked-solution "The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the surface $z=f(x,y)$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ on the surface can be written as

$$
z-{z}_{0}=(x-{x}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),
$$

where $⟨\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),-1⟩$ represents a normal vector to the tangent plane.

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡x-xy) \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡x-y \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡x-xy) \\  & =-x\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the normal vector to the tangent plane is 

$$
⟨2\operatorname{cos}⁡x-y,\,-x,\,-1⟩
$$

Our tangent plane should be perpendicular to $⟨8,2\pi ,2⟩.$ So, the normal vector of that plane must be parallel to that vector. In other words, for some constant $c$, we must have

$$
c\cdot ⟨2\operatorname{cos}⁡x-y,\,-x,\,-1⟩=⟨8,2\pi ,2⟩.
$$

Equating the corresponding coordinates, we obtain the following system:

$$
{\begin{aligned}2c\operatorname{cos}⁡x-cy=8 \\ -xc=2\pi  \\ -c=2\end{aligned}
$$

From the third equation, we get $c=-2.$ Substituting this into the second equation, we obtain 

$$
-x(-2)=2\pi \,⟹\,x=\pi .
$$

And substituting $c=-2$ and $x=\pi $ into the first equation, we have 

$$
2(-2)\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi -(-2)y=8\,⟹\,y=2.
$$

Finally, substituting $x=\pi $ and $y=2$ into our function, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}z & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡x-xy \\  & =3\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi -(\pi )(2) \\  & =-2\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent plane is perpendicular to the vector  $v$ at $(\pi ,2,-2\pi ).$"} :step/id #uuid "2b51d9b4-6f4d-519a-946f-18af30633fc4" :step/next {:db/id 17592186407518}} {:db/id 17592186407516 :step/content {:db/id 17592186265748 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "4831fde7-328b-5f95-8b4f-bd555404f79f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(-1,-1,4)" :db/id 17592186263624} {:answer/id #uuid "5b9d3b86-7aec-5970-92c9-47d3d544786f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(1,0,3)" :db/id 17592186263789} {:answer/id #uuid "94d3b3cb-73a3-5f94-abc9-28adc6612ba0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(0,1,1)" :db/id 17592186264274} {:answer/id #uuid "9d20a40f-b237-5738-bfa6-76f889ea8789" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(\frac{2}{3},-1,\frac{7}{3})" :db/id 17592186264345} {:answer/id #uuid "a54e3749-cf7d-5ffc-ac93-9256ee36c08f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(-\frac{1}{3},0,\frac{1}{9})" :db/id 17592186264415}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186264345} :answer-field/id #uuid "38b8a09a-7de4-5c87-b2a5-460a354244c2" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186265348}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "12830aeb-cb43-530e-902c-e52ba9d7524f" :question/math-academy-id "q-129557" :question/problem "At which point on the surface $z=3{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}$ is the tangent plane perpendicular to the vector  $v=⟨4,-2,-1⟩?$" :question/worked-solution "The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the surface $z=f(x,y)$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ on the surface can be written as

$$

$$

where $⟨\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),-1⟩$ represents a normal vector to the tangent plane.

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(3{x}^{2}+{y}^{2})=6x \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(3{x}^{2}+{y}^{2})=2y\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the normal vector to the tangent plane is 

$$
⟨6x,\,2y,\,-1⟩.
$$

Our tangent plane should be perpendicular to $⟨4,-2,-1⟩.$ So, the normal vector of that plane must be parallel to that vector. In other words, for some constant $c$, we must have

$$
c\cdot ⟨6x,\,2y,\,-1⟩=⟨4,-2,-1⟩.
$$

Equating the corresponding coordinates, we obtain the following system:

$$
{\begin{aligned}6cx=4 \\ 2cy=-2 \\ -c=-1\end{aligned}
$$

From the third equation, we get $c=1.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain 

$$
6(1)x=4\,⟹\,x=\frac{2}{3}.
$$

$$
2(1)y=-2\,⟹\,y=-1.
$$

Finally, substituting $x=\frac{2}{3}$ and $y=-1$ into our function, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}z & =3{(\frac{2}{3})}^{2}+(-1)^{2} \\  & =\frac{4}{3}+1 \\  & =\frac{7}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent plane is perpendicular to the vector $v$ at $(\frac{2}{3},-1,\frac{7}{3}).$"} :step/id #uuid "32cd70ef-6665-5a4e-a0ab-b70e5098e66f"} {:db/id 17592186407517 :step/content {:db/id 17592186342093 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "62fcc3f3-ddff-52b4-b6ee-b406a0ffec98" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\pi x-\pi y-z+w+\pi =0" :db/id 17592186340008} {:answer/id #uuid "93a5ca28-3798-5c54-9d92-aa2d41eb6d90" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\pi x-\pi y+z+w-\pi =0" :db/id 17592186340453} {:answer/id #uuid "9f8794dd-7491-5377-b367-530775903444" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\pi x+\pi y+z-w+3\pi =0" :db/id 17592186340570} {:answer/id #uuid "f6251148-2e5e-526a-995c-c61130894b01" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\pi x+\pi y-z+w-\pi =0" :db/id 17592186341302} {:answer/id #uuid "fa7d3452-6743-53e2-bd9c-8cfa857fa7bf" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\pi x+\pi y+z+w-3\pi =0" :db/id 17592186341343}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186341343} :answer-field/id #uuid "a31f7eac-9e1f-5aaa-97e4-e132312fc936" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186341668}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "de6bd964-56b9-511c-9d67-ed8d06732a08" :question/math-academy-id "q-73851" :question/problem "Find the equation of the tangent hyperplane to the hypersurface $w=\operatorname{sin}⁡(xyz)$ at the point $(1,1,\pi ,0).$" :question/worked-solution "The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the hypersurface $w=f(x,y,z)$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0},{w}_{0})$ on the hypersurface can be written as

$$
w-{w}_{0}=(x-{x}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})+(z-{z}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂z}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0}).
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(xyz))=yz\operatorname{cos}⁡(xyz) \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(xyz))=xz\operatorname{cos}⁡(xyz) \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(xyz))=xy\operatorname{cos}⁡(xyz)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the partial derivatives at $(x,y,z)=(1,1,\pi ):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}(1,1,\pi ) & =(1)(\pi )\operatorname{cos}⁡(1\cdot 1\cdot \pi )=-\pi  \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y}(1,1,\pi ) & =(1)(\pi )\operatorname{cos}⁡(1\cdot 1\cdot \pi )=-\pi  \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z}(1,1,\pi ) & =(1)(1)\operatorname{cos}⁡(1\cdot 1\cdot \pi )=-1\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write down the equation of the tangent hyperplane:

$$
\begin{aligned}w-0 & =(x-1)\frac{∂f}{∂x}(1,1,\pi )+(y-1)\frac{∂f}{∂y}(1,1,\pi )+(z-\pi )\frac{∂f}{∂z}(1,1,\pi ) \\ w & =-\pi (x-1)-\pi (y-1)-(z-\pi ) \\ w & =-\pi x+\pi -\pi y+\pi -z+\pi  \\ \pi x+\pi y+z+w-3\pi  & =0\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "536015a5-6f9f-597a-ae46-2c87559ba2b3" :step/next {:db/id 17592186407514}} {:db/id 17592186407518 :step/content {:db/id 17592186407513 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2cf0dc93-d9d4-5f21-8930-dd5004fc42a6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2x-2y-2z-w-2=0" :db/id 17592186407507} {:answer/id #uuid "5110fa49-48ce-56a6-b93d-b9d08b07b745" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2x+2y+2z-w-2=0" :db/id 17592186407508} {:answer/id #uuid "728a521d-8a62-5203-8384-b89408abe64b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2x-2y-2z+w-2=0" :db/id 17592186407509} {:answer/id #uuid "72b11d02-8ab8-5c20-a244-f44e993b6792" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2x+2y-2z-w+2=0" :db/id 17592186407510} {:answer/id #uuid "e0e8ca25-16b2-54a8-b96c-ad5665775b39" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2x-2y+2z+w-8=0" :db/id 17592186407511}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186407507} :answer-field/id #uuid "75cea473-3250-5a97-b3ad-a51baa102dcf" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186407512}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "8ca7d6fc-55d0-503c-8138-64f03d668ed2" :question/math-academy-id "q-73850" :question/problem "Find the equation of the tangent hyperplane to the hypersurface $w=\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-{z}^{2})$ at the point $(1,-1,1,0).$" :question/worked-solution "The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the hypersurface $w=f(x,y,z)$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0},{w}_{0})$ on the hypersurface can be written as

$$
w-{w}_{0}=(x-{x}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})+(z-{z}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂z}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0}).
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-{z}^{2}))=\frac{2x}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-{z}^{2}} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-{z}^{2}))=\frac{2y}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-{z}^{2}} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-{z}^{2}))=-\frac{2z}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-{z}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the partial derivatives at $(x,y,z)=(1,-1,1):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}(1,-1,1) & =\frac{2(1)}{(1)^{2}+(-1)^{2}-(1)^{2}}=2 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y}(1,-1,1) & =\frac{2(-1)}{(1)^{2}+(-1)^{2}-(1)^{2}}=-2 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z}(1,-1,1) & =-\frac{2(1)}{(1)^{2}+(-1)^{2}-(1)^{2}}=-2\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write down the equation of the tangent hyperplane:

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}w-0 & =(x-1)\frac{∂f}{∂x}(1,1,\pi )+(y-1)\frac{∂f}{∂y}(1,1,\pi )+(z-\pi )\frac{∂f}{∂z}(1,1,\pi ) \\ w & =-\pi (x-1)-\pi (y-1)-(z-\pi ) \\ w & =-\pi x+\pi -\pi y+\pi -z+\pi  \\ \pi x+\pi y+z+w-3\pi  & =0\end{aligned}

$$
w-{w}_{0}=(x-{x}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})+(z-{z}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂z}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0}).

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2x{y}^{2}+y{z}^{2}-3{x}^{2}z)=2{y}^{2}-6xz \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2x{y}^{2}+y{z}^{2}-3{x}^{2}z)=4xy+{z}^{2} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(2x{y}^{2}+y{z}^{2}-3{x}^{2}z)=2yz-3{x}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the partial derivatives at $(x,y,z)=(2,-2,1):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}(2,-2,1) & =2(-2)^{2}-6(2)(1)=-4 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y}(2,-2,1) & =4(2)(-2)+(1)^{2}=-15 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z}(2,-2,1) & =2(-2)(1)-3(2)^{2}=-16\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write down the equation of the tangent hyperplane:

$$
\begin{aligned}w-2 & =(x-2)\frac{∂f}{∂x}(2,-2,1)+(y+2)\frac{∂f}{∂y}(2,-2,1)+(z-1)\frac{∂f}{∂z}(2,-2,1) \\ w-2 & =-4(x-2)-15(y+2)-16(z-1) \\ w-2 & =-4x+8-15y-30-16z+16 \\ 4x+15y+16z+w+4 & =0\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "0af89c86-dd82-51d3-8a60-9428fdaf17c3" :step/next {:db/id 17592186435556}} {:db/id 17592186435555 :step/content {:db/id 17592186435553 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "6521128c-8b33-54da-8c83-d27bef687244" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(-1,1,-3)" :db/id 17592186435529} {:answer/id #uuid "6a9c4d22-52c4-582f-b256-0ddd6fa135ad" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(\frac{1}{2},1,-\frac{3}{2})" :db/id 17592186435530} {:answer/id #uuid "84cf53e7-7029-5a30-8dd0-ad54d0eb0064" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(1,0,2)" :db/id 17592186435533} {:answer/id #uuid "bcd79e5d-b439-5f83-a72f-40d75fd4cdd8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(2,-1,-9)" :db/id 17592186435537} {:answer/id #uuid "d89ebc6c-8c25-5ee8-a102-c0421505fca3" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(-\frac{1}{2},-\frac{1}{2},\frac{9}{4})" :db/id 17592186435540}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186435540} :answer-field/id #uuid "e1008d1e-ad25-59f1-8249-03f1bd3c30fe" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186435547}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "e0b70f07-48f3-5e91-bb4d-83ea4566f9c8" :question/math-academy-id "q-129560" :question/problem "At which point on the surface $z=4-2{x}^{2}-5{y}^{2}$ is the tangent plane perpendicular to the vector $v=⟨-2,-5,1⟩?$" :question/worked-solution "The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the surface $z=f(x,y)$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ on the surface can be written as

$$
z-{z}_{0}=(x-{x}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),
$$

where $⟨\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),-1⟩$ represents a normal vector to the tangent plane.

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(4-2{x}^{2}-5{y}^{2})=-4x \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(4-2{x}^{2}-5{y}^{2})=-10y\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the normal vector to the tangent plane is 

$$
⟨-4x,\,-10y,\,-1⟩.
$$

Our tangent plane should be perpendicular to $⟨-2,-5,1⟩.$ So, the normal vector of that plane must be parallel to that vector. In other words, for some constant $c$, we must have

$$
c\cdot ⟨-4x,\,-10y,\,-1⟩=⟨-2,-5,1⟩.
$$

Equating the corresponding coordinates, we obtain the following system:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}-4cx=-2 \\ -10cy=-5 \\ -c=1\end{aligned}
$$

From the third equation, we get $c=-1.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain 

$$
-4(-1)x=-2\,⟹\,x=-\frac{1}{2}.
$$

And substituting $c=-1$ into the second equation, we have 

$$
-10(-1)y=-5\,⟹\,y=-\frac{1}{2}.
$$

Finally, substituting $x=-\frac{1}{2}$ and $y=-\frac{1}{2}$ into our function, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}z & =4-2{(-\frac{1}{2})}^{2}-5{(-\frac{1}{2})}^{2} \\  & =4-\frac{1}{2}-\frac{5}{4} \\  & =\frac{9}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent plane is perpendicular to the vector $v$ at $(-\frac{1}{2},-\frac{1}{2},\frac{9}{4}).$"} :step/id #uuid "52566cd2-c610-5b7e-a93b-8dfb407f2200"} {:db/id 17592186435556 :step/content {:db/id 17592186435550 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "18541d05-49d2-5f19-b579-6b534b3bcfd4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x+2y+z+w-2=0" :db/id 17592186435522} {:answer/id #uuid "1e19600e-76b4-5880-a603-02783cbb324e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x+y-2z-w+1=0" :db/id 17592186435523} {:answer/id #uuid "36b42409-fb4f-52cb-a983-864ab8cc5f71" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2x+y+z-w-3=0" :db/id 17592186435525} {:answer/id #uuid "b3f12775-7dc0-5662-9058-bbd97ad38d1d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3x-2y-z+w-2=0" :db/id 17592186435536} {:answer/id #uuid "ca2e0787-ad3a-5c7f-add5-4e016dc6c7a7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x+2y-3z+w+2=0" :db/id 17592186435538}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186435523} :answer-field/id #uuid "49b834ec-93e3-593b-87ef-065fbe59d9c9" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186435544}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "6b798538-8660-5c1f-9d93-5bdad8bdb40c" :question/math-academy-id "q-129477" :question/problem "Find the equation of the tangent hyperplane to the hypersurface $w=x+y-{z}^{2}$ at the point $(1,0,1,0).$" :question/worked-solution "The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the hypersurface $w=f(x,y,z)$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0},{w}_{0})$ on the hypersurface can be written as

First, we find the partial derivatives:

Next, we evaluate the partial derivatives at $(x,y)=(0,0):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}(0,0) & ={e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡(0+0)}\operatorname{cos}⁡(0+0)=1 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y}(0,0) & ={e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡(0+0)}\operatorname{cos}⁡(0+0)=1\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$v=⟨6,-8,-1⟩?$" :question/worked-solution "The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the surface $z=f(x,y)$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ on the surface can be written as

$$

$$

Hence, the normal vector to the tangent plane is 

$$
⟨2x,\,4y,\,-1⟩.
$$

Our tangent plane should be perpendicular to $⟨6,-8,-1⟩.$ So, the normal vector of that plane must be parallel to that vector. In other words, for some constant $c$, we must have

$$

$$

$$
\{\begin{aligned}2cx=6 \\ 4cy=-8 \\ -c=-1\end{aligned}

$$
2(1)x=6\,⟹\,x=3.

$$
4(1)y=-8\,⟹\,y=-2.

$$
\begin{bmatrix}-11 & \le - 8y + 5 \\ -11 - 5 & \le - 8y + 5 - 5 \\ -16 & \le - 8y + 0 \\ -16 & \le - 8y\end{bmatrix}
$$

Then, we apply the multiplication principle, dividing both sides by $-8$.

Remember, when multiplying or dividing an inequality by a negative number, we need to flip the inequality sign:

$$
\begin{bmatrix}-16 & \le- 8y \\ \frac{-16}{-8} & \ge\frac{-8y}{-8} \\ 2 & \ge\frac{-8y}{-8} \\ 2 & \gey\end{bmatrix}
$$

Finally, let's swap the left and right-hand sides so that the variable is on the left-hand side. Remember, we also need to flip the inequality.

$$
y \le 2
$$

$$
y \le 2
$$"} {:db/id 17592186192940 :question/id #uuid "35329721-2939-524f-be67-6cedc7694b45" :question/math-academy-id "q-101931"} {:db/id 17592186193308 :question/id #uuid "6434fada-1355-5a49-aa0d-b3f9327d3f1a" :question/math-academy-id "q-3016"} {:db/id 17592186048483} {:db/id 17592186049736} {:activity/first-step {:db/id 17592186193766} :activity/id #uuid "baef8b1d-be2f-50d5-a6ff-93120a166f8f" :activity/scope {:db/id 17592186050503 :topic/id #uuid "4e9c2678-4be0-55d7-9838-e4f11d55dccf" :topic/math-academy-id 4021} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186193766 :step/content {:db/id 17592186193912 :tutorial/content "Suppose that we wish to find the solution to the inequality

First, we apply the addition principle, subtracting $6$ from both sides:

$$
\begin{bmatrix}2x + 6 & < 12 \\ 2x + 6 - 6 & < 12 - 6 \\ 2x + 0 & < 6 \\ 2x & < 6\end{bmatrix}
$$

Second, we apply the multiplication principle, dividing both sides by $2{:}$

$$
\begin{bmatrix}2x & < 6 \\ \frac{2x}{2} & < \frac{6}{2} \\ \frac{2x}{2} & < 3 \\ x & < 3\end{bmatrix}
$$

17592186120656 :step/content {:db/id 17592186121029 :tutorial/content "Recall that LU factorization involves writing a matrix $A$ as a product of two matrices $L$ and $U,$ where

- ![](images/2e/2e6c0b6fdaf90e3a3e23ed91ffe09cb360bb39325b9a630f1b7219b3188a25db.svg) is a *unit lower triangular matrix* (a lower triangular matrix that has only $1$'s on the main diagonal), and

- ![](images/0c/0c5d7337e47a53dfa5bdce8c6f4a96bb1e52ef6054349011a6cc38f29701cc61.svg) is an *upper triangular matrix*.

For example, suppose we're given the matrix ![](images/22/22dba4fe66ac5478f5d81a68342a01809a360de8e722e809998655e7740bafe8.svg) To perform LU factorization, we need to write $A$ as 

![](images/d4/d4c92b2e8252619f9a1511d166be884b9a2bdb4311eea8e408e8fe75eed6f36c.svg)

As usual, to find the matrices $L$ and $U,$ we can reduce the matrix $A$ to *echelon form* while simultaneously performing the same elementary row operations on the identity matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & -2 \\ 0 & 2 & -3 \\ -2 & 2 & 7\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+2{R}_{1} & ⇔ & \,\overset{{E}_{1}}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}}\cdot A \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & -2 \\ 0 & 2 & -3 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}]=U\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix is upper triangular, so it is our matrix $U.$ Now, since $E_1A=U,$ we can invert $E_1$ to arrive at the desired LU factorization:

$$
\begin{aligned}{E}_{1}A & =U \\ A & ={E}_{1}^{-1}U \\ A & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}U \\ A & ={{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{L}{{[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & -2 \\ 0 & 2 & -3 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{U}\end{aligned}
$$

**Caution:** In order to get a unit lower triangular matrix at the end, we have the following restriction while reducing a matrix $A$ to its *echelon form*:

- we can only add multiples of higher rows to lower rows ($R_j:=R_j+k R_i$ where $i < j$), and

- the other elementary row operations (swapping or multiplying a row by a number) are not allowed." :tutorial/id #uuid "5f8c6994-f448-5679-8d2e-5591b86c2a97" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3178 For example, suppose we're given the matrix ![](images/22/22dba4fe66ac5478f5d81a68342a01809a360de8e722e809998655e7740bafe8.svg) To perform LU factorization, we need to write $A$ as

As usual, to find the matrices $L$ and $U,$ we can reduce the matrix $A$ to *echelon form* while simultaneously performing the same elementary row operations on the identity matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & -2 \\ 0 & 2 & -3 \\ -2 & 2 & 7\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+2{R}_{1} & ⇔ & \,\overset{{E}_{1}}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}}\cdot A \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & -2 \\ 0 & 2 & -3 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}]=U\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix is upper triangular, so it is our matrix $U.$ Now, since $E_1A=U,$ we can invert $E_1$ to arrive at the desired LU factorization:

$$

$$

**Caution:** In order to get a unit lower triangular matrix at the end, we have the following restriction while reducing a matrix $A$ to its *echelon form*:

$$
{a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 1 \\ -4\end{aligned}],\,x=[\begin{aligned}-6 \\ -2 \\ 10\end{aligned}].
$$" :question/worked-solution "First, we verify whether ${a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}$ are linearly independent. So, we start by creating a matrix whose columns are made up of our vectors, and then we reduce the matrix to row echelon form:

$$
\begin{aligned} & [\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -4 \\ 2 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & -4\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-2){R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}-{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -4 \\ 0 & -3 & 9 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, the pivot columns correspond to the linearly independent vectors ${a}_{1}$ and ${a}_{2}$ that form the basis of our span.

Now, the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace spanned by the linearly independent columns of a matrix $A$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x=A({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}\,{A}^{T}\,x.
$$

In our case, we have

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {a}_{1} & {a}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]\,⟹\,{A}^{T}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 1 \\ 2 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we get the following projection:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 1 \\ 2 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 1 \\ 2 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-6 \\ -2 \\ 10\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot {[\begin{aligned}6 & 6 \\ 6 & 9\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 \\ 6\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{18}[\begin{aligned}9 & -6 \\ -6 & 6\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 \\ 6\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -2 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186392354 :question/id #uuid "5c071401-3e46-54b6-b9cb-b8280a1a58b2" :question/math-academy-id "q-40630"} {:db/id 17592186489238 :question/id #uuid "86358ef9-78e9-5caa-a7a3-a7c614e96d69" :question/math-academy-id "q-40628" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2f402a3a-4f08-5c72-a337-37b1173065e9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 5 \\ 4\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186488572} {:answer/id #uuid "69d00f66-bac7-5a07-842c-86c8ae454700" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 4 \\ 5\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186488678} {:answer/id #uuid "795fe3b9-08f5-5072-9238-46b50ec1f87a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186488709} {:answer/id #uuid "924789e2-65b9-582c-b2a0-b829c5928e12" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 3 \\ 3\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186488762} {:answer/id #uuid "94182863-ea1a-5c03-b764-976abf2d1657" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 7 \\ 8\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186488768}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186488678} :answer-field/id #uuid "5ae069ad-82b0-5089-9f78-df2bcd3c3331" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186489064}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "Verify whether the vectors ${a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}$ are linearly independent, and find the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace spanned by the vectors $\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}\},$ where

\begin{aligned} & [\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & -1 & -2 \\ 2 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}-{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & [\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & -1 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}↔{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & -2 \\ 2 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & -0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}-2{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & -2 \\ 0 & 3 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, the pivot columns correspond to the linearly independent vectors ${a}_{1}$ and ${a}_{2}$ that form the basis of our span.

Now, the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace spanned by the linearly independent columns of a matrix $A$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x=A({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}\,{A}^{T}\,x.
$$

In our case, we have

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {a}_{1} & {a}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\,⇒\,{A}^{T}=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 2 \\ 1 & -1 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we get the following projection:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 2 \\ 1 & -1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 2 \\ 1 & -1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}3 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {[\begin{aligned}9 & 3 \\ 3 & 3\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}8 \\ 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{6}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -1 & 3\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}8 \\ 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}

{:db/id 17592186049970 :topic/id #uuid "22979210-8cd9-5db4-861d-faf167d0a850" :topic/math-academy-id 2124} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186134674 :step/content {:db/id 17592186135049 :tutorial/content "We've already seen how to find the orthogonal projection of a vector onto a subspace in the case when the subspace is defined using an orthogonal basis. In this lesson, we'll learn how to do the same thing in the case of non-orthogonal bases.

For example, consider the following vectors:
![](images/28/28ce7470231775d8889555d0dd9f37ee9215044762a40335bd43578b121486a3.svg)
How can we find the orthogonal projection $\mathbf{x}_S$ of the vector $\mathbf{x}$ onto the subspace $S = \textrm{Span}\{ \mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2 \}?$ Notice that since $\mathbf a_1\cdot \mathbf a_2 \neq 0,$ the vectors $\mathbf{a}_1$ and $\mathbf{a}_2$ are not orthogonal.

As usual, we would like to write $\mathbf{x}$ as 

$$
\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{x}_S + \mathbf{x}_{S^\perp},
$$

where $\mathbf{x}_S = k_1 \mathbf{a}_1 + k_2 \mathbf{a}_2 \in S$ and $\mathbf{x}_{S^\perp} \!\in S^\perp.$

![](images/3a/3a5576fcaf9e0be6fc14978eb91dcbaceee75cbfddaa537fdb05d34b8e31e2e0.png)

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{{S}^{⊥}} & =x-{x}_{S} \\  & =x-({k}_{1}{a}_{1}+{k}_{2}{a}_{2}) \\  & =x-{k}_{1}{a}_{1}-{k}_{2}{a}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $\mathbf{x}_{S^\perp} \in S^\perp,$ that is, $\mathbf{x}_{S^\perp} \perp S,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{{S}^{⊥}}⊥{a}_{1} \\ {x}_{{S}^{⊥}}⊥{a}_{2}\end{aligned}\,⟹\,\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{{S}^{⊥}}\cdot {a}_{1}=0 \\ {x}_{{S}^{⊥}}\cdot {a}_{2}=0.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we substitute the expression for $\mathbf{x}_{S^\perp}$ into the system to get
![](images/f1/f1e3c7ae9e966ebcab88901c9e44a5449cb98716f43fc526d306e0af5186923b.svg)

We can write this system in an equivalent matrix form as follows:
![](images/47/472c41e1e509d2db9c41dfa95127382eeba7ab5fbaa4172d680c39335694ef2e.svg)

If we denote 
![](images/26/2650c1020d413a7c988279cc698ab4b7c4caff427615d49b35ef4e9a42651ff0.svg)
and ![](images/9b/9b50884bd0af404e71f9d7734e9bc054fc9439aba02780cf2beb5fa0a6ac1f32.svg) then we obtain

$$
A^TA\mathbf{k} = A^T\mathbf{x}
	\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
	\mathbf{k}=(A^TA)^{-1}A^T\mathbf{x}.
$$

Also, we note that  $\mathbf{x}_S = k_1 \mathbf{a}_1 + k_2 \mathbf{a}_2$ can be expressed as $\textrm{proj}_{S}\,\mathbf{x}	= A\mathbf{k}.$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =Ak \\  & =A({A}^{T}A)^{-1}{A}^{T}x.\end{aligned}
$$

This is a formula for the orthogonal projection!

Now, we return to our example. Using the formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 3 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 3 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 \\ 4 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}6 & 8 \\ 8 & 11\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}10 \\ 14\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}11 & -8 \\ -8 & 6\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}10 \\ 14\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 4 \\ 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

**Note**: Pay attention to the order in which we carried out the multiplication. Carrying out the operations in the order shown above can save us a lot of work!" :tutorial/id #uuid "0a9a954f-9338-5c3f-a9db-9b39a1a60c0b" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3626 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "f3cce71c-fd0d-5040-949b-813f3fdcbdd7" :step/math-academy-id 20246 :step/next {:db/id 17592186134676}} {:db/id 17592186134675 :step/content {:db/id 17592186133788 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186133597 :question/id #uuid "b8bbe0e1-8bf1-5b3a-a77e-6350ea77e83f" :question/math-academy-id "e-5575"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "ad9f55b2-ce37-507f-8cb6-7d4e30e6868a" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186134296} {:db/id 17592186134301} {:db/id 17592186272103} {:db/id 17592186275452} {:db/id 17592186326787} {:db/id 17592186326854} {:db/id 17592186366111} {:db/id 17592186382580} {:db/id 17592186388723} {:db/id 17592186388960} {:db/id 17592186388967} {:db/id 17592186388974} {:db/id 17592186392354} {:db/id 17592186489238} {:db/id 17592186489280}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Orthogonal Projection of a Vector Onto a Subspace"} :step/id #uuid "8e0f305d-efdf-586e-b799-66fe2b5a8f6a" :step/math-academy-id 20247 :step/next {:db/id 17592186134678}} {:db/id 17592186134676 :step/content {:db/id 17592186135050 :tutorial/content "If $\{ \mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2 , \ldots, \mathbf{a}_n \}$ is a set of *linearly independent* vectors, then the orthogonal projection of a vector $\mathbf{x}$ onto the subspace $S = \textrm{span}\{ \mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2 , \ldots, \mathbf{a}_n \}$ is given by

$$
\textrm{proj}_{S} \: \mathbf{x} = A(A^T\!A)^{-1}\!A^T\,\mathbf{x},
$$

 
where $A$ is the matrix whose columns are the vectors of $\mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2 , \ldots, \mathbf{a}_n,$ that is,

$$
\textrm{proj}_{\mathbf{a}} \, \mathbf{x} = \dfrac{\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{x}}{\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{a}} \: \mathbf{a}.

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{a}\,x & =\frac{(a\cdot x)}{(a\cdot a)}\,a \\  & =[\frac{({a}^{T}x)}{({a}^{T}a)}]a \\  & =a[\frac{({a}^{T}x)}{({a}^{T}a)}] \\  & =a[({a}^{T}a)^{-1}{a}^{T}x] \\  & =a\,({a}^{T}a)^{-1}{a}^{T}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's compare the above with the formula that we use when we want to project onto an arbitrary subspace:

$$
\textrm{proj}_{S} \: \mathbf{x} = A(A^T\!A)^{-1}\!A^T\,\mathbf{x}
$$
