In this lesson, we'll learn how to do the same thing in the case of non-orthogonal bases.

For example, consider the following vectors:
![](images/28/28ce7470231775d8889555d0dd9f37ee9215044762a40335bd43578b121486a3.svg)
How can we find the orthogonal projection $\mathbf{x}_S$ of the vector $\mathbf{x}$ onto the subspace $S = \textrm{Span}\{ \mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2 \}?$ Notice that since $\mathbf a_1\cdot \mathbf a_2 \neq 0,$ the vectors $\mathbf{a}_1$ and $\mathbf{a}_2$ are not orthogonal.

As usual, we would like to write $\mathbf{x}$ as 

$$
\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{x}_S + \mathbf{x}_{S^\perp},
$$

where $\mathbf{x}_S = k_1 \mathbf{a}_1 + k_2 \mathbf{a}_2 \in S$ and $\mathbf{x}_{S^\perp} \!\in S^\perp.$

![](images/3a/3a5576fcaf9e0be6fc14978eb91dcbaceee75cbfddaa537fdb05d34b8e31e2e0.png)

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{{S}^{⊥}} & =x-{x}_{S} \\  & =x-({k}_{1}{a}_{1}+{k}_{2}{a}_{2}) \\  & =x-{k}_{1}{a}_{1}-{k}_{2}{a}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $\mathbf{x}_{S^\perp} \in S^\perp,$ that is, $\mathbf{x}_{S^\perp} \perp S,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{{S}^{⊥}}⊥{a}_{1} \\ {x}_{{S}^{⊥}}⊥{a}_{2}\end{aligned}\,⟹\,\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{{S}^{⊥}}\cdot {a}_{1}=0 \\ {x}_{{S}^{⊥}}\cdot {a}_{2}=0.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we substitute the expression for $\mathbf{x}_{S^\perp}$ into the system to get
![](images/f1/f1e3c7ae9e966ebcab88901c9e44a5449cb98716f43fc526d306e0af5186923b.svg)

We can write this system in an equivalent matrix form as follows:
![](images/47/472c41e1e509d2db9c41dfa95127382eeba7ab5fbaa4172d680c39335694ef2e.svg)

If we denote 
![](images/26/2650c1020d413a7c988279cc698ab4b7c4caff427615d49b35ef4e9a42651ff0.svg)
and ![](images/9b/9b50884bd0af404e71f9d7734e9bc054fc9439aba02780cf2beb5fa0a6ac1f32.svg) then we obtain

$$
A^TA\mathbf{k} = A^T\mathbf{x}
	\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
	\mathbf{k}=(A^TA)^{-1}A^T\mathbf{x}.
$$

Also, we note that  $\mathbf{x}_S = k_1 \mathbf{a}_1 + k_2 \mathbf{a}_2$ can be expressed as $\textrm{proj}_{S}\,\mathbf{x}	= A\mathbf{k}.$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =Ak \\  & =A({A}^{T}A)^{-1}{A}^{T}x.\end{aligned}
$$

This is a formula for the orthogonal projection!

Now, we return to our example. Using the formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 3 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 3 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 \\ 4 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}6 & 8 \\ 8 & 11\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}10 \\ 14\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}11 & -8 \\ -8 & 6\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}10 \\ 14\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 4 \\ 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

**Note**: Pay attention to the order in which we carried out the multiplication. {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "e47080dd-98d4-5498-967c-b6d64e7e3867" :question/math-academy-id "q-40629" :question/problem "Verify whether the vectors ${a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}$ are linearly independent, and find the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace spanned by the vectors $\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}\},$ where

$$
{a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -2 \\ -1\end{aligned}],\,x=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$" :question/worked-solution "First, we verify whether ${a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}$ are linearly independent. So, we start by creating a matrix whose columns are made up of our vectors, and then we reduce the matrix to row echelon form:

$$
\begin{aligned} & [\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & -1 & -2 \\ 2 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}-{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & [\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & -1 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}↔{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & -2 \\ 2 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & -0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}-2{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & -2 \\ 0 & 3 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, the pivot columns correspond to the linearly independent vectors ${a}_{1}$ and ${a}_{2}$ that form the basis of our span.

Now, the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace spanned by the linearly independent columns of a matrix $A$ is given by

$$

"Which elements of a circle are depicted below?

![](images/70/7032918db2c75bcf0c0ebad952f617b54523311095529f7ee5ca90714d9b4d90.png)" :question/worked-solution "Here, we have the following:

- a circular segment which is enclosed between the chord $\overline{CD}$ and the corresponding arc $\overset{\frown}{CD}$,
- a circular sector $OAC$, which is formed by the two radii $\overline{OA}$ and $\overline{OC}$ and the corresponding arc $\overset{\frown}{AC}$, and
- an arc $\overset{\frown}{AB}$."} {:db/id 17592186049856} {:db/id 17592186176521 :question/id #uuid "42aa5ad2-58a4-5aa3-8327-ee26908656a0" :question/math-academy-id "q-53518"} {:db/id 17592186176522 :question/id #uuid "e070724d-3872-5f23-ba81-350932e0d8ba" :question/math-academy-id "q-53519"} {:db/id 17592186175897 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186175764 :question/id #uuid "11cc1b43-3faf-5687-aca8-12c3e60befca" :question/math-academy-id "e-3170"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "938c4422-a8ae-56c4-b728-31776db43653" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186176520 :question/id #uuid "66cefdd9-5395-5b62-bd79-e0f614e9014a" :question/math-academy-id "q-53485"} {:db/id 17592186176523 :question/id #uuid "09edd0cb-b198-5fdf-b5ac-91ddd49fd23d" :question/math-academy-id "q-53529"}] :knowledge-point/title "Completing a True Statement Regarding Circles"} {:db/id 17592186175764 :question/id #uuid "11cc1b43-3faf-5687-aca8-12c3e60befca" :question/math-academy-id "e-3170" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186175897 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "938c4422-a8ae-56c4-b728-31776db43653" :knowledge-point/title "Completing a True Statement Regarding Circles"}] :question/problem "What should be substituted into the blank spaces in the following sentence to make it a true statement?

> "*If $A$ and $B$ are two points on a circle, then $\overline{AB}$ is a $\textrm{_________}$ of the circle. Additionally, if we consider the region bounded by $\overline{AB}$ and the corresponding arc $\overset{\frown}{AB}$, then we obtain a circular $\textrm{_________}$.*"" :question/worked-solution "First, $\overline{AB}$ is a line segment whose endpoints lie on a circle. So, $\overline{AB}$ is a *chord* of the circle.

The region enclosed between $\overline{AB}$ and the corresponding arc $\overset{\frown}{AB}$ is a circular *segment*.

Therefore, the correct mathematical statement is the following:

> "*If $A$ and $B$ are two points on a circle, then $\overline{AB}$ is a **chord** of the circle. Additionally, if we consider the region bounded by $\overline{AB}$ and the corresponding arc $\overset{\frown}{AB}$, then we obtain a circular **segment**.*""} {:db/id 17592186176520 :question/id #uuid "66cefdd9-5395-5b62-bd79-e0f614e9014a" :question/math-academy-id "q-53485"} {:db/id 17592186176523 :question/id #uuid "09edd0cb-b198-5fdf-b5ac-91ddd49fd23d" :question/math-academy-id "q-53529"} {:db/id 17592186049988} {:activity/first-step {:db/id 17592186176598} :activity/id #uuid "ec9d4c2b-1a22-5786-bdab-76e3e5ac092b" :activity/scope {:db/id 17592186049135 :topic/id #uuid "dd916270-3c49-5d1a-a09d-9c318a1004ba" :topic/math-academy-id 3565} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186176598 :step/content {:db/id 17592186176967 :tutorial/content "Let's consider yet more important parts of a circle:

- The **circumference** of a circle is used to describe the perimeter of the circle, as shown in the left diagram below.
- An **arc** is a part of the circumference which is enclosed between two points on a circle. In the right diagram below, we have the arc $\overset{\frown}{AB}$.

![](images/5c/5c918b32007a68beecfdef486e9cd5d0818a2122ad672415608f761f7f7953e7.png)

If an arc is denoted using only two letters, we are referring to the *shortest* arc. However, to avoid ambiguity, we can use three letters. For example, in the diagram below, $\overset{\frown}{ACB}$ is the arc to the left and $\overset{\frown}{ADB}$ is the arc to the right.

"c80985c0-d51a-5f21-9b71-21587d8d82cc" :topic/math-academy-id 3024} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186162882 :step/content {:db/id 17592186163239 :tutorial/content "If $X$ is a continuous random variable and $0 \leq p \leq 1,$ then the $100p$th **percentile** is a number $x_p$ such that

$$
P(X \leq x_p) = p.
$$

- In terms of CDF, the *cumulative distribution function* $F(x)$ of $X,$ the $100p$th percentile $x_p$ is a number on the $x$-axis such that

$$
F(x_p) = p.
$$

- In terms of PDF, the *probability density function* $f(x)$ of $X,$ the $100p$th percentile $x_p$ is a number on the $x$-axis such that the area under the graph of $y=f(x)$ to the left of $x$ is equal to $p \mathbin{:}$

$$
\int_{-\infty}^{x_p} f(x) \, \text{d}x = p.
$$

For example, let's find the $4$th percentile of the random variable $X$ if the probability density function of $X$ is given by

![](images/69/69a9f969e3caaa3cc3d896b5a8b6ed566cff3517743519f0c1088e588c3967e7.svg)

The $4$th percentile corresponds to the decimal $p={\color{red}0.04}$ since $100 \cdot 0.04 = 4.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\le {x}_{0.04}) & ={\int }_{0}^{{x}_{0.04}}\frac{1}{2}x\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\frac{{x}^{2}}{4}|}_{0}^{{x}_{0.04}} \\  & =\frac{{{x}_{0.04}}^{2}}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the $4$th percentile is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{{x}_{0.04}}^{2}}{4} & =0.04 \\ {{x}_{0.04}}^{2} & =0.16 \\ {x}_{0.04} & =0.4.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we took the positive root because $0 \leq x_{0.04} \leq 2.$

There are a few special percentiles:

- the $25$th percentile is called the **lower quartile**. This is the number $q_1$ such that

$$
P(X \leq q_1) = 0.25.
$$

- the $50$th percentile is called the **median**. This is the number $m$ such that

$$
P(X \leq m) = 0.5.
$$

- the $75$th percentile is called the **upper quartile**. This is the number $q_3$ such that

$$
P(X \leq q_3) = 0.75.
$$

- the **interquartile range** is the difference between the upper and lower quartiles, that is,

$$
IQR = q_3 - q_1.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "e91993d1-ae51-5742-8eeb-e76348c0b8af" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4942 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "b587e6fa-53fb-5f03-9ffa-373892fc4d10" :step/math-academy-id - the $50$th percentile is called the **median**. This is the number $m$ such that

$$
P(X \leq m) = 0.5.
$$

- the $75$th percentile is called the **upper quartile**. This is the number $q_3$ such that

$$
P(X \leq q_3) = 0.75.
$$

- the **interquartile range** is the difference between the upper and lower quartiles, that is,

$$
IQR = q_3 - q_1.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "e91993d1-ae51-5742-8eeb-e76348c0b8af" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4942 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "b587e6fa-53fb-5f03-9ffa-373892fc4d10" :step/math-academy-id 30817 :step/next {:db/id 17592186162883}} {:db/id 17592186163239 :tutorial/content "If $X$ is a continuous random variable and $0 \leq p \leq 1,$ then the $100p$th **percentile** is a number $x_p$ such that

$$
P(X \leq x_p) = p.
$$

- In terms of CDF, the *cumulative distribution function* $F(x)$ of $X,$ the $100p$th percentile $x_p$ is a number on the $x$-axis such that

$$
F(x_p) = p.
$$

- In terms of PDF, the *probability density function* $f(x)$ of $X,$ the $100p$th percentile $x_p$ is a number on the $x$-axis such that the area under the graph of $y=f(x)$ to the left of $x$ is equal to $p \mathbin{:}$

$$
\int_{-\infty}^{x_p} f(x) \, \text{d}x = p.
$$

For example, let's find the $4$th percentile of the random variable $X$ if the probability density function of $X$ is given by

![](images/69/69a9f969e3caaa3cc3d896b5a8b6ed566cff3517743519f0c1088e588c3967e7.svg)

The $4$th percentile corresponds to the decimal $p={\color{red}0.04}$ since $100 \cdot 0.04 = 4.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\le {x}_{0.04}) & ={\int }_{0}^{{x}_{0.04}}\frac{1}{2}x\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\frac{{x}^{2}}{4}|}_{0}^{{x}_{0.04}} \\  & =\frac{{{x}_{0.04}}^{2}}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the $4$th percentile is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{{x}_{0.04}}^{2}}{4} & =0.04 \\ {{x}_{0.04}}^{2} & =0.16 \\ {x}_{0.04} & =0.4.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we took the positive root because $0 \leq x_{0.04} \leq 2.$

There are a few special percentiles:

- the $25$th percentile is called the **lower quartile**. This is the number $q_1$ such that

$$
P(X \leq q_1) = 0.25.
$$

- the $50$th percentile is called the **median**. This is the number $m$ such that

$$
P(X \leq m) = 0.5.
$$

- the $75$th percentile is called the **upper quartile**. This is the number $q_3$ such that

$$
P(X \leq q_3) = 0.75.
$$

- the **interquartile range** is the difference between the upper and lower quartiles, that is,

$$
IQR = q_3 - q_1.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "e91993d1-ae51-5742-8eeb-e76348c0b8af" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4942 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186162883 :step/content {:db/id 17592186161997 17592186045485 :db/ident :question.difficulty/easy} :question/problem "$$
A=[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 \\ -1 & -2 \\ 1 & 2 \\ -3 & -6\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0 \\ 3 \\ -1\end{aligned}].
$$

Consider the matrix $A$ and vector $b$ shown above. If the general least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ is 

$$
[\begin{aligned}a \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}b \\ c\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R,
$$

what is the value of $6a+\frac{b}{c}?$" :question/worked-solution "The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

$$
{A}^{T}\,Ax={A}^{T}b
$$

Notice that the columns of $A$ are linearly dependent. So first, let's write down the normal equation in matrix form:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 & 1 & -3 \\ 4 & -2 & 2 & -6\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 4 \\ -1 & -2 \\ 1 & 2 \\ -3 & -6\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 & 1 & -3 \\ 4 & -2 & 2 & -6\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0 \\ 3 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}15 & 30 \\ 30 & 60\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}10 \\ 20\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system corresponding to the above matrix equation using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}15 & 30 & 10 \\ 30 & 60 & 20\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-2){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}15 & 30 & 10 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we have 

$$
{x}_{1}=\frac{2}{3}-2{x}_{2}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{3}-2{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{3} \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
6a+\frac{b}{c}=6\cdot \frac{2}{3}+\frac{(-2)}{1}=2.

A=[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 1 \\ -1 & 2 & -1 \\ 2 & -2 & 0\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Consider the matrix $A$ and vector $b$ shown above. If the general least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}2 \\ b \\ c\end{aligned}]+{x}_{3}[\begin{aligned}a \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}\in R
$$

what is the value of $a+2b+c?$" :question/worked-solution "The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

$$
{A}^{T}\,Ax={A}^{T}b
$$

Notice that the columns of $A$ are linearly dependent. So first, let's write down the normal equation in matrix form:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 2 \\ -2 & 2 & -2 \\ 1 & -1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 1 \\ -1 & 2 & -1 \\ 2 & -2 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 2 \\ -2 & 2 & -2 \\ 1 & -1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}6 & -8 & 2 \\ -8 & 12 & -4 \\ 2 & -4 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2 \\ -2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system corresponding to the final matrix equation using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}6 & -8 & 2 & 0 \\ -8 & 12 & -4 & 2 \\ 2 & -4 & 2 & -2\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}↔{R}_{3}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & -4 & 2 & -2 \\ -8 & 12 & -4 & 2 \\ 6 & -8 & 2 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+4{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-3){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & -4 & 2 & -2 \\ 0 & -4 & 4 & -6 \\ 0 & 4 & -4 & 6\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-1){R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & -4 & 2 & -2 \\ 0 & -4 & 4 & -6 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has two pivot columns (the $1$st and $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we have 

$$
{x}_{2}=\frac{3}{2}+{x}_{3}.
$$

Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

$$
2{x}_{1}-4(\frac{3}{2}+{x}_{3})+2{x}_{3}=-2\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=2+{x}_{3}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}2+{x}_{3} \\ \frac{3}{2}+{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ \frac{3}{2} \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{3}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
a+2b+c=1+2\cdot \frac{3}{2}+0=4.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186269136 :question/id #uuid "ef71613a-c794-54f5-9a74-68efbe48ffea" :question/math-academy-id "q-137034"} {:db/id 17592186326894 :question/id #uuid "d34cdae0-7b23-59fc-a8bc-f0d99444106f" :question/math-academy-id "q-40921" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "027310f9-ee0d-507a-bc28-d9da862bc3bf" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186323994} {:answer/id #uuid "13cbf72a-775b-5500-b4ce-fd7dee8abc45" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "5" :db/id 17592186324150} {:answer/id #uuid "6058f5f8-765c-528f-b9e3-77d370e52e5f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4" :db/id 17592186324776} {:answer/id #uuid "df18dbbf-d1af-5d62-9ba8-07e3f6047abf" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3" :db/id 17592186325920} {:answer/id #uuid "df1f5f2f-9dda-564b-8601-3ba072795d25" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186325921}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186323994} :answer-field/id #uuid "58847018-c5c9-5b9a-9650-5b07e75b721b" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186326372}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 & 2 \\ 1 & -1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 & 1 \\ 2 & -1 & 1 \\ 2 & -1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 & 2 \\ 1 & -1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2 \\ 4\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}12 & -6 & 0 \\ -6 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}12 \\ -6 \\ 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system corresponding to the above matrix equation using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}12 & -6 & 0 & 12 \\ -6 & 3 & 0 & -6 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & 2\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:=2{R}_{2}+{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}12 & -6 & 0 & 12 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & 2\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}↔{R}_{3}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}12 & -6 & 0 & 12 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}:=(1/6){R}_{1} \\ {R}_{2}:=(1/2){R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has two pivot columns (the $1$st and $3$rd). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable.  

From the third row, we have

$$
{x}_{3}=1,
$$

and from the first row we obtain

$$
2{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}=2\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=1+\frac{{x}_{2}}{2}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}1+\frac{{x}_{2}}{2} \\ {x}_{2} \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2} \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

$$
2a-3b-6c=2(\frac{1}{2})-3(1)-6(0)=-2.

$$

Therefore, we have

$$

17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "$$
{\begin{aligned}-{x}_{1}+4{x}_{2}=2 \\ {x}_{1}-4{x}_{2}=2 \\ 2{x}_{1}-8{x}_{2}=4\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the system of linear equations shown above. If the general least-squares solution of the system is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}a \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}b \\ c\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R
$$

what is the value of $3a+\frac{b}{c}?$" :question/worked-solution "First, we write our system in matrix form as $Ax=b,$ where 

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 4 \\ 1 & -4 \\ 2 & -8\end{aligned}],\,x=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2 \\ 4\end{aligned}].
$$

The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

$$
{A}^{T}\,Ax={A}^{T}b
$$

Notice that the columns of $A$ are linearly dependent. So first, let's write down the normal equation in matrix form:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 2 \\ 4 & -4 & -8\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 & 4 \\ 1 & -4 \\ 2 & -8\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 2 \\ 4 & -4 & -8\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2 \\ 4\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}6 & -24 \\ -24 & 96\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}8 \\ -32\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system corresponding to the final matrix equation using Gaussian elimination, as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}6 & -24 & 8 \\ -24 & 96 & -32\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+4{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}6 & -24 & 8 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we have 

$$
{x}_{1}=\frac{4}{3}+4{x}_{2}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{4}{3}+4{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{4}{3} \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
3a+\frac{b}{c}=3\cdot \frac{4}{3}+\frac{4}{1}=8.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186134374 :question/id #uuid "00e4806c-b4ce-579d-8d0e-03b84320da38" :question/math-academy-id "q-41919"} {:db/id 17592186269137 :question/id #uuid "26d67fbf-4de7-566c-9152-9d1736d17888" :question/math-academy-id "q-137061"} {:db/id 17592186269138 :question/id #uuid "cb576d6c-dcbf-591c-a5dd-97e97349a8f0" :question/math-academy-id "q-137095" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "71872f14-7cc4-5fb9-8cf7-9ffe96aefe19" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "8" :db/id 17592186267142} {:answer/id #uuid "725897a0-9e77-57f9-b8a9-68f56715093b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "5" :db/id 17592186267146} {:answer/id #uuid "828574ad-8b28-58c3-ac93-daffbb878a55" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3" :db/id 17592186267291} {:answer/id #uuid "9d160852-1af1-56d1-8d23-a808bbfc6b00" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "6" :db/id 17592186267556} {:answer/id #uuid "edbdca09-407a-5b44-b814-062fce5150c1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186268256}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186267291} :answer-field/id #uuid "b1b80840-f020-56db-8303-eb251d19e950" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186268722}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "$$

\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}-2{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}=1 \\ -2{x}_{1}+4{x}_{2}-2{x}_{3}=-1\end{aligned}\,\,[\begin{aligned}5 & -10 & 5 \\ -10 & a & b \\ 5 & -10 & 5\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ c \\ 3\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the system of linear equations and its corresponding normal equation shown above. What is the value of $a+b+c?$" :question/worked-solution "First, we write our system in matrix form as $Ax=b,$ where 

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 1 \\ -2 & 4 & -2\end{aligned}],\,x=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}].
$$

The normal equation corresponding to $Ax=b$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,Ax & ={A}^{T}b \\ [\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ -2 & 4 \\ 1 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 1 \\ -2 & 4 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ -2 & 4 \\ 1 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}5 & -10 & 5 \\ -10 & 20 & -10 \\ 5 & -10 & 5\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -6 \\ 3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
a+b+c=20+(-10)+(-6)=4.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186483345 :question/id #uuid "0200c257-e4df-57c1-8eaf-e14f946ede8a" :question/math-academy-id "q-41913"} {:db/id 17592186049282} {:db/id 17592186049503} {:db/id 17592186049845} :topic/math-academy-id 2167} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186134698 :step/content {:db/id 17592186135060 :tutorial/content "Let's consider the following inconsistent system of equations:

![](images/6b/6bcdc34077d88eac5ed89d408a1d2525b617a4f427b13433757df918585d380f.svg)

Since the system is inconsistent, we cannot find an exact solution. However, as we've previously seen, we can attempt to find the so-called least-squares solution, which is a vector ${\hat{\mathbf{x}}}$ such that

$$
\|  A{\hat{\mathbf{x}}} - \mathbf{b} \|
$$

is as small as possible. 

As before, the least-squares solution can be found by solving the corresponding normal equation, given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A\overset{^}{x} & ={A}^{T}b.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, note the following: 

- Previously, we solved the normal equation by left-multiplying the normal equation by $(A^T A)^{-1}.$

- However, in this case, the second column of $A$ is a multiple of the first.

- So, the columns of $A$ are linearly dependent.

- Therefore, $A^T A$ is not invertible.

To solve the normal equation in this case, we proceed as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A\overset{^}{x} & ={A}^{T}b \\ [\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ -4 & 8\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -4 \\ -2 & 8\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ -4 & 8\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}5 & -20 \\ -20 & 80\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-5 \\ 20\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the last equation by Gaussian elimination, we obtain the general solution

![](images/b9/b93bd5cb988f208eb26115bfaa08e81be989ee79cf3655612c1a0522a5566d95.svg)

Notice that our solution is not unique! The second term of the least-squares solution (highlighted in blue) represents vectors from the null space of $A.$ 

In general, if a matrix $A$ has collinear columns, then the least-squares solution to $A\mathbf x = \mathbf b$ is not unique." :tutorial/id #uuid "2f2e227a-264e-5e00-8c12-ea534f4b351f" - Therefore, $A^T A$ is not invertible.

To solve the normal equation in this case, we proceed as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A\overset{^}{x} & ={A}^{T}b \\ [\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ -4 & 8\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -4 \\ -2 & 8\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ -4 & 8\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}5 & -20 \\ -20 & 80\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-5 \\ 20\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the last equation by Gaussian elimination, we obtain the general solution

Notice that our solution is not unique! The second term of the least-squares solution (highlighted in blue) represents vectors from the null space of $A.$

Since the system is inconsistent, we cannot find an exact solution. However, as we've previously seen, we can attempt to find the so-called least-squares solution, which is a vector ${\hat{\mathbf{x}}}$ such that

- So, the columns of $A$ are linearly dependent.

- Therefore, $A^T A$ is not invertible.

17592186415138}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "01d4a87d-4b65-5a4c-9736-928bedaa6703" :question/math-academy-id "q-137086" :question/problem "$$
\{\begin{aligned}-{x}_{1}+3{x}_{2}=3 \\ -2{x}_{1}+6{x}_{2}=1 \\ {x}_{1}-3{x}_{2}=-5\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the system of linear equations shown above. If the general least-squares solution of the system is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}a \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}b \\ c\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R
$$

what is the value of $12a+\frac{b}{c}?$" :question/worked-solution "First, we write our system in matrix form as $Ax=b,$ where 

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 3 \\ -2 & 6 \\ 1 & -3\end{aligned}],\,x=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1 \\ -5\end{aligned}].
$$

The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

$$
{A}^{T}\,Ax={A}^{T}b
$$

Notice that the columns of $A$ are linearly dependent. So first, let's write down the normal equation in matrix form:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}-1 & -2 & 1 \\ 3 & 6 & -3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 & 3 \\ -2 & 6 \\ 1 & -3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & -2 & 1 \\ 3 & 6 & -3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1 \\ -5\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}6 & -18 \\ -18 & 54\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-10 \\ 30\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system corresponding to the final matrix equation using Gaussian elimination, as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}6 & -18 & -10 \\ -18 & 54 & 30\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+3{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}6 & -18 & -10 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we have 

$$
{x}_{1}=-\frac{5}{3}+3{x}_{2}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-\frac{5}{3}+3{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{5}{3} \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
12a+\frac{b}{c}=12\cdot (-\frac{5}{3})+\frac{3}{1}=-17.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "40c07ba2-e36f-5f6c-9e19-b8d5be6314d0" :step/next {:db/id 17592186415145}} {:db/id 17592186415145 :step/content {:db/id 17592186415141 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "29e85101-f9b2-5d74-83c6-aabdd8fc2745" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "-1" :db/id 17592186415114} {:answer/id #uuid "2baff1db-5ead-50b2-af5a-abe277ae4820" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2" :db/id 17592186415115} {:answer/id #uuid "2ccd28ea-578f-5414-8332-a6408e6df178" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "1" :db/id 17592186415116} {:answer/id #uuid "2e8878bb-5944-584d-9b48-2add56ecc5fb" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4" :db/id 17592186415117} {:answer/id #uuid "8cd78f8e-e662-5c98-aa4d-0c408cd252ed" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "3" :db/id 17592186415126}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186415126} :answer-field/id #uuid "a27c023d-32d0-5cf3-ade4-1f1674089f41" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186415135}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "4a92698e-17e4-57b8-8191-7aa9adc0e63f" :question/math-academy-id "q-137092" :question/problem "$$

$$

A=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & 0 \\ -2 & 2 & 2\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2 \\ -2\end{aligned}].
$$

 

Consider the matrix $A$ and vector $b$ shown above. If the general least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ a \\ b\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}c \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R
$$

what is the value of $a+3b+c?$" :question/worked-solution "The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

$$
{A}^{T}\,Ax={A}^{T}b
$$

Notice that the columns of $A$ are linearly dependent. So first, let's write down the normal equation in matrix form:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & -2 \\ -1 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & 0 \\ -2 & 2 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & -2 \\ -1 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2 \\ -2\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}6 & -6 & -4 \\ -6 & 6 & 4 \\ -4 & 4 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -2 \\ -4\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system corresponding to the above matrix equation using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}6 & -6 & -4 & 2 \\ -6 & 6 & 4 & -2 \\ -4 & 4 & 4 & -4\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}↔{R}_{3}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-4 & 4 & 4 & -4 \\ -6 & 6 & 4 & -2 \\ 6 & -6 & -4 & 2\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}:=\frac{1}{4}{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 1 & -1 \\ -6 & 6 & 4 & -2 \\ 6 & -6 & -4 & 2\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-6){R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+6{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & -2 & 4 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & -4\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+{R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & -2 & 4 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has two pivot columns (the $1$st and $3$rd). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we have 

$$
{x}_{3}=-2,
$$

Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

$$
-{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}+(-2)=-1\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=-1+{x}_{2}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-1+{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2} \\ -2\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0 \\ -2\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 & 2 \\ 1 & -1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 & 1 \\ 2 & -1 & 1 \\ 2 & -1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 & 2 \\ 1 & -1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2 \\ 4\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}12 & -6 & 0 \\ -6 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}12 \\ -6 \\ 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system corresponding to the above matrix equation using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}12 & -6 & 0 & 12 \\ -6 & 3 & 0 & -6 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & 2\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:=2{R}_{2}+{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}12 & -6 & 0 & 12 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & 2\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}↔{R}_{3}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}12 & -6 & 0 & 12 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}:=(1/6){R}_{1} \\ {R}_{2}:=(1/2){R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has two pivot columns (the $1$st and $3$rd). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable.  

From the third row, we have

$$
{x}_{3}=1,
$$

and from the first row we obtain

$$
2{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}=2\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=1+\frac{{x}_{2}}{2}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}1+\frac{{x}_{2}}{2} \\ {x}_{2} \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2} \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
2a-3b-6c=2(\frac{1}{2})-3(1)-6(0)=-2.

#uuid "85d7c223-d931-53ec-98fb-80a06e5b2764" :question/math-academy-id "q-41904" :question/problem "$$
A=[\begin{aligned}4 & -2 \\ -2 & 1 \\ -4 & 2 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2 \\ -1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].
$$

Consider the matrix $A$ and vector $b$ shown above. If the general least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ is

$$
[\begin{aligned}a \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}b \\ c\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R,
$$

what is the value of $15a+\frac{b}{c}?$" :question/worked-solution "The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

$$
{A}^{T}\,Ax={A}^{T}b
$$

Notice that the columns of $A$ are linearly dependent. So first, let's write down the normal equation in matrix form:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}4 & -2 & -4 & 2 \\ -2 & 1 & 2 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}4 & -2 \\ -2 & 1 \\ -4 & 2 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}4 & -2 & -4 & 2 \\ -2 & 1 & 2 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2 \\ -1 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}40 & -20 \\ -20 & 10\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}4 \\ -2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system corresponding to the above matrix equation using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}10 & -5 & 1 \\ -10 & 5 & -1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}10 & -5 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we have 

$$
{x}_{1}=\frac{1}{10}+\frac{1}{2}{x}_{2}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{10}+\frac{1}{2}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{10} \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2} \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
15a+\frac{b}{c}=15\cdot \frac{1}{10}+\frac{(\frac{1}{2})}{1}=2.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "e72361cd-94e3-52fd-91cb-f7e78d6bf3a8" :step/next {:db/id 17592186500394}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "3c20af83-4b36-5128-89ee-a2b0f277470a" :answer/type {:db/id #uuid "44425e0c-c9f0-5589-a298-071f456fd0c5" :knowledge-point/title "Differentiating X Raised to the Power of a Function"}] :question/problem "Find the derivative of the function $y = x^{x^3}$." :question/worked-solution "We have the function

$$
y = x^{x^3}
$$

First, we take the natural logarithm of both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\ln y &= \ln (x^{x^{3}}) \\
\ln y &= x^{3}\ln x
\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to $x{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{d}{dx}(\ln y) &= \frac{d}{dx}(x^{3}\ln x) \\
\frac{1}{y} \cdot y^{′} &= (x^{3})^{′} \cdot (\ln x) + (x^{3}) \cdot (\ln x)^{′} \\
\frac{1}{y} \cdot y^{′} &= 3x^{2} \cdot \ln x + x^{3} \cdot \frac{1}{x} \\
\frac{y^{′}}{y} &= 3x^{2}\ln x + x^{2}
\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve for $y'{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}
y^{′} &= y(3x^{2}\ln x + x^{2})
\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute

$$
y=x^{x^3}{:}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
y^{′} &= x^{x^{3}}(3x^{2}\ln x + x^{2}) \\
&= x^{x^{3}}(x^{2}(3\ln x + 1)) \\
&= x^{x^{3} + 2}(3\ln x + 1)
\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186048813} {:db/id 17592186049470} {:db/id 17592186049879} {:db/id 17592186050310} {:db/id 17592186064619 :question/id #uuid "1e0a189a-c99c-5fc1-ae14-4487d0580d0d" :question/math-academy-id "q-2296"} {:db/id 17592186064649 :question/id #uuid "fc650cb2-e28d-509d-8d13-55b4dd6b8629" :question/math-academy-id "q-2520"} {:db/id 17592186424278 :question/id #uuid "09ef39a3-aa47-5850-a2b1-1c368b15a626" :question/math-academy-id "q-2523" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "05f33a63-c291-5841-be1b-4faff432cabd" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x+2\operatorname{ln}⁡x+2" :db/id 17592186424260} {:answer/id #uuid "438050ca-5554-5efb-b6ab-495501b5ed22" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "4x+2\operatorname{ln}⁡x-2" :db/id 17592186424262} {:answer/id #uuid "cd4c6e33-c46b-5d45-876e-4d7c5861b00b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2x+\operatorname{ln}⁡x" :db/id 17592186424270} {:answer/id #uuid "e7caf4ba-0364-56de-9d87-fa137b1cb670" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "2x+2x\operatorname{ln}⁡x+1" :db/id 17592186424271} {:answer/id #uuid "fd40483e-6c18-50b5-b937-12944951fb45" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "x+\operatorname{ln}⁡x+2" :db/id 17592186424274}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186424271} :answer-field/id #uuid "4522aec1-18fc-5a98-a19b-f2258fae7499" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186424276}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "Consider the function $y={x}^{(2x+1)}.$ Its derivative is given by

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}={x}^{2x}\cdot g(x).
$$

Find the function $g(x).$" :question/worked-solution "We have the function 

$$
y={x}^{2x+1}.
$$

First, we take the natural logarithm of both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2x+1}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =(2x+1)\operatorname{ln}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}((2x+1)\operatorname{ln}⁡x) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2x+1)\cdot (\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+(2x+1)\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡x) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =2\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡x+(2x+1)\cdot \frac{1}{x} \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡x+\frac{2x+1}{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve for $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =y(\frac{2x+1}{x}+2\operatorname{ln}⁡x)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $y={x}^{2x+1}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & ={x}^{2x+1}(\frac{2x+1}{x}+2\operatorname{ln}⁡x) \\  & ={x}^{2x+1}(\frac{2x+1}{x}+\frac{2x\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{x}) \\  & ={x}^{2x}\cdot x(\frac{2x+1}{x}+\frac{2x\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{x}) \\  & ={x}^{2x}(2x+2x\operatorname{ln}⁡x+1)\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}

\ln y &= x\ln (x^{2} - 1)
\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to $x{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{d}{dx}(\ln y) &= \frac{d}{dx}(x\ln (x^{2} - 1)) \\
\frac{1}{y} \cdot \frac{dy}{dx} &= \frac{d}{dx}(x) \cdot \ln (x^{2} - 1) + x \cdot \frac{d}{dx}(\ln (x^{2} - 1)) \\
\frac{1}{y} \cdot \frac{dy}{dx} &= 1 \cdot \ln (x^{2} - 1) + x \cdot (\frac{1}{x^{2} - 1} \cdot 2x) \\
\frac{1}{y} \cdot \frac{dy}{dx} &= \ln (x^{2} - 1) + \frac{2x^{2}}{x^{2} - 1}
\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve for

$$
\dfrac {\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x}{:}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{dy}{dx} &= y(\ln (x^{2} - 1) + \frac{2x^{2}}{x^{2} - 1})
\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

&= (x^{2} - 1)^{x - 1}((x^{2} - 1)\ln (x^{2} - 1) + 2x^{2})
\end{aligned}

$$
y=(\operatorname{csc}⁡x)^{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}.

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\,(\operatorname{csc}⁡x)^{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{csc}⁡x)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{csc}⁡x)) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)^{′}\cdot (\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{csc}⁡x))+(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)\cdot {(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{csc}⁡x))}^{′} \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =(-\operatorname{sin}⁡x)\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{csc}⁡x)+\operatorname{cos}⁡x\cdot (\frac{1}{\operatorname{csc}⁡x}\cdot (-\operatorname{cot}⁡x\,\operatorname{csc}⁡x)) \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{csc}⁡x)-\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\operatorname{cot}⁡x \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =-(\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{csc}⁡x)+\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\operatorname{cot}⁡x) \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{csc}⁡x)+{cot}^{2}⁡x)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve for ${y}^{′}:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =-y\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{csc}⁡x)+{cot}^{2}⁡x)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $y=(\operatorname{csc}⁡x)^{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =-(\operatorname{csc}⁡x)^{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{csc}⁡x)+{cot}^{2}⁡x) \\  & =-(\operatorname{csc}⁡x)^{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}\frac{1}{\operatorname{csc}⁡x}\,(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{csc}⁡x)+{cot}^{2}⁡x) \\  & =-(\operatorname{csc}⁡x)^{\operatorname{cos}⁡x-1}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{csc}⁡x)+{cot}^{2}⁡x)\end{aligned}

{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "The slope of the tangent to the curve at $x=0$ equals the function's derivative at the corresponding point.

We have the function 

$$
y={(\sqrt{2x+1})}^{{x}^{2}+1}.
$$

First, we take the natural logarithm of both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({(\sqrt{2x+1})}^{{x}^{2}+1}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =({x}^{2}+1)\,\operatorname{ln}⁡(\sqrt{2x+1})\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}\,(({x}^{2}+1)\,\operatorname{ln}⁡(\sqrt{2x+1})) \\ \frac{1}{y}\,{y}^{′} & =({x}^{2}+1)^{′}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\sqrt{2x+1})+({x}^{2}+1)\,{(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\sqrt{2x+1}))}^{′} \\ \frac{1}{y}\,{y}^{′} & =2x\operatorname{ln}⁡(\sqrt{2x+1})+({x}^{2}+1)\,(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2x+1}}\cdot \frac{2}{2\sqrt{2x+1}}) \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x+1)+\frac{{x}^{2}+1}{2x+1}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve for ${y}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =y\,(x\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x+1)+\frac{{x}^{2}+1}{2x+1})\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $y={(\sqrt{2x+1})}^{{x}^{2}+1}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & ={(\sqrt{2x+1})}^{{x}^{2}+1}(x\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x+1)+\frac{{x}^{2}+1}{2x+1})\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of $y={(\sqrt{2x+1})}^{{x}^{2}+1}$ at $x=0$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}m={y}^{′}{|}_{x=0} & ={(\sqrt{2(0)+1})}^{(0)^{2}+1}(0\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡(2(0)+1)+\frac{(0)^{2}+1}{2(0)+1}) \\  & =1\cdot (0\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡(1)+1) \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186413630 :question/id #uuid "fed635cb-d378-5d78-b478-1026e862dee7" :question/math-academy-id "q-341953" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "96beea54-57c3-53ca-9a62-26604472224a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\csc(x)" :db/id 17592186413614}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186413614} :answer-field/id #uuid "33b8438b-3327-575c-ae05-92d222d1ed04" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186413621}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "Given that $y=(\operatorname{cot}⁡(x))^{\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)}$, find ${y}^{′}.$

[{:db/id 17592186065202 :step/content {:db/id 17592186065395 :tutorial/content "**Logarithmic differentiation** is a technique to compute derivatives that are difficult to find using the usual rules of differentiation, such as the product, quotient, and chain rules.

Let's consider the following function.

$$
y = x^x
$$

We aim to compute

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d x}
$$

However, in this case, we note the following:

- Both the base and the exponent are functions of $x$.
- This means we cannot apply the power rule since the exponent is not a fixed number.
- We also cannot apply the rules for differentiating exponentials since the base is not a fixed number.

So instead, we'll use logarithmic differentiation. We proceed as follows:

**Step 1.** We take the natural logarithm of both sides and apply the power rule for logarithms:

$$
\begin{aligned}
y &= x^{x} \\
\ln y &= \ln x^{x} \\
\ln y &= x\ln x
\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2.** We differentiate both sides of the above equation with respect to $x$ using implicit differentiation and the product rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{d}{dx}(\ln y) &= \frac{d}{dx}(x\ln x) \\
\frac{1}{y} \cdot \frac{dy}{dx} &= \frac{d}{dx}(x) \cdot \ln x + x \cdot \frac{d}{dx}(\ln x) \\
\frac{1}{y} \cdot \frac{dy}{dx} &= 1 \cdot \ln x + x \cdot (\frac{1}{x}) \\
\frac{1}{y} \cdot \frac{dy}{dx} &= \ln x + 1
\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3.** Now, we solve for

$$
\dfrac {\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x}
$$

This gives

$$
\dfrac {\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} = y\left(\ln x + 1 \right)
$$

**Step 4.** Finally, we substitute back our original expression for $y=x^x{:}$

$$
\dfrac {\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} = x^x \left(\ln x + 1 \right)
$$

"b4ed5979-35bd-5227-b6d2-7a9f08a0cbdf" :question/math-academy-id "q-138812" :question/problem "Consider the function $y=(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)^{x}.$ Its derivative is given by 

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)^{x}\cdot g(x).
$$

Find the function $g(x).$" :question/worked-solution "We have the function 

$$
y=(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)^{x}.
$$

First, we take the natural logarithm of both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡((\operatorname{cos}⁡x)^{x}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x)\cdot (\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{cos}⁡x))+(x)\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =1\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)+x\cdot (\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}\cdot (-\operatorname{sin}⁡x)) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)-x\operatorname{tan}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve for $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =y(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)-x\operatorname{tan}⁡x)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $y=(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)^{x}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)^{x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)-x\operatorname{tan}⁡x)\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, $g(x)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{cos}⁡x)-x\operatorname{tan}⁡x.$"} :step/id #uuid "2312e57b-a556-5b41-9d0e-0eea036d1a63" :step/next {:db/id 17592186413634}} {:db/id 17592186413632 :step/content {:db/id 17592186413630 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "96beea54-57c3-53ca-9a62-26604472224a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\csc(x)" :db/id 17592186413614}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186413614} :answer-field/id #uuid "33b8438b-3327-575c-ae05-92d222d1ed04" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186413621}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "fed635cb-d378-5d78-b478-1026e862dee7" :question/math-academy-id "q-341953" :question/problem "Given that $y=(\operatorname{cot}⁡(x))^{\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)}$, find ${y}^{′}.$

{{field-1}}$)$" :question/worked-solution "We have the function 

$$
y=(\operatorname{cot}⁡(x))^{\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)}.
$$

First, we take the natural logarithm of both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡((\operatorname{cot}⁡(x))^{\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)\,\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{cot}⁡(x))\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{cot}⁡(x))) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =(\operatorname{cos}⁡(x))^{′}\cdot (\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{cot}⁡(x)))+(\operatorname{cos}⁡(x))\cdot {(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{cot}⁡(x)))}^{′} \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =(-\operatorname{sin}⁡(x))\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{cot}⁡(x))+\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)\cdot (\frac{1}{\operatorname{cot}⁡(x)}\cdot (-{csc}^{2}⁡(x))) \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)\,\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{cot}⁡(x))-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)\,{csc}^{2}⁡(x)}{\operatorname{cot}⁡(x)} \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)\,\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{cot}⁡(x))-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)\,(\frac{1}{{sin}^{2}⁡(x)})}{(\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)}{\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)})} \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)\,\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{cot}⁡(x))-\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)} \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)\,\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{cot}⁡(x))-\operatorname{csc}⁡(x) \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =-(\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)\,\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{cot}⁡(x))+\operatorname{csc}⁡(x))\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve for ${y}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =-y(\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)\,\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{cot}⁡(x))+\operatorname{csc}⁡(x))\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $y=(\operatorname{cot}⁡(x))^{\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =-(\operatorname{cot}⁡(x))^{\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)}\cdot (\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)\,\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{cot}⁡(x))+\operatorname{csc}⁡(x))\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "677687e2-cbea-59cc-ba58-b6532d7f53b5"} {:db/id 17592186413633 :step/content {:db/id 17592186413626 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "28bc056c-eb5f-5687-8409-0974c7956f17" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "(2x+3)\ln(2x+3)+2x" :db/id 17592186413612}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186413612} :answer-field/id #uuid "d44a882d-c0e6-5d33-a2fe-067332daaf5d" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492} :db/id 17592186413625}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/id #uuid "31fc854a-70c5-5387-9f4b-327eb3d213ff" :question/math-academy-id "q-341727" :question/problem "Given that $y=(2x+3)^{x}$, find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}.$

$\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=(2x+3)^{x-1}\cdot ($
{{field-1}}$)$" :question/worked-solution "We have the function 

$$
y=(2x+3)^{x}.
$$

First, we take the natural logarithm of both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡((2x+3)^{x}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x+3)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x+3)) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x)\cdot (\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x+3))+(x)\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x+3)) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =1\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡(2x+3)+x\cdot (\frac{1}{2x+3}\cdot 2) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x+3)+\frac{2x}{2x+3}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve for $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =y(\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x+3)+\frac{2x}{2x+3})\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $y=(2x+3)^{x}:$

\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}\,(({x}^{2}+1)\,\operatorname{ln}⁡(\sqrt{2x+1})) \\ \frac{1}{y}\,{y}^{′} & =({x}^{2}+1)^{′}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\sqrt{2x+1})+({x}^{2}+1)\,{(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\sqrt{2x+1}))}^{′} \\ \frac{1}{y}\,{y}^{′} & =2x\operatorname{ln}⁡(\sqrt{2x+1})+({x}^{2}+1)\,(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2x+1}}\cdot \frac{2}{2\sqrt{2x+1}}) \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x+1)+\frac{{x}^{2}+1}{2x+1}\end{aligned}
$$

\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =y\,(x\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x+1)+\frac{{x}^{2}+1}{2x+1})\end{aligned}

$$

$$
y={(\sqrt{2x+1})}^{{x}^{2}+1}.
$$

First, we take the natural logarithm of both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({(\sqrt{2x+1})}^{{x}^{2}+1}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =({x}^{2}+1)\,\operatorname{ln}⁡(\sqrt{2x+1})\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}\,(({x}^{2}+1)\,\operatorname{ln}⁡(\sqrt{2x+1})) \\ \frac{1}{y}\,{y}^{′} & =({x}^{2}+1)^{′}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\sqrt{2x+1})+({x}^{2}+1)\,{(\operatorname{ln}⁡(\sqrt{2x+1}))}^{′} \\ \frac{1}{y}\,{y}^{′} & =2x\operatorname{ln}⁡(\sqrt{2x+1})+({x}^{2}+1)\,(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2x+1}}\cdot \frac{2}{2\sqrt{2x+1}}) \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x+1)+\frac{{x}^{2}+1}{2x+1}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve for ${y}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =y\,(x\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x+1)+\frac{{x}^{2}+1}{2x+1})\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $y={(\sqrt{2x+1})}^{{x}^{2}+1}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & ={(\sqrt{2x+1})}^{{x}^{2}+1}(x\operatorname{ln}⁡(2x+1)+\frac{{x}^{2}+1}{2x+1})\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of $y={(\sqrt{2x+1})}^{{x}^{2}+1}$ at $x=0$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}m={y}^{′}{|}_{x=0} & ={(\sqrt{2(0)+1})}^{(0)^{2}+1}(0\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡(2(0)+1)+\frac{(0)^{2}+1}{2(0)+1}) \\  & =1\cdot (0\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡(1)+1) \\  & =1.\end{aligned}

Find the function $g(x).$" :question/worked-solution "We have the function 

$$
y={x}^{2x+1}.
$$

First, we take the natural logarithm of both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2x+1}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =(2x+1)\operatorname{ln}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}((2x+1)\operatorname{ln}⁡x) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2x+1)\cdot (\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+(2x+1)\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡x) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =2\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡x+(2x+1)\cdot \frac{1}{x} \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡x+\frac{2x+1}{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve for $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =y(\frac{2x+1}{x}+2\operatorname{ln}⁡x)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $y={x}^{2x+1}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & ={x}^{2x+1}(\frac{2x+1}{x}+2\operatorname{ln}⁡x) \\  & ={x}^{2x+1}(\frac{2x+1}{x}+\frac{2x\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{x}) \\  & ={x}^{2x}\cdot x(\frac{2x+1}{x}+\frac{2x\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{x}) \\  & ={x}^{2x}(2x+2x\operatorname{ln}⁡x+1)\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

3746} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186180636 :step/content {:db/id 17592186180660 :tutorial/content "Sometimes, we can use ratios to find quantities that aren't explicitly given in the ratio.

For instance, suppose that the ratio of boys to girls in the fifth grade is $3: 4.$ If there are $15$ boys, how many students are there in total?

Notice that the "total number of students" doesn't appear in the ratio. However, we can find the number of students by adding the total number of boys and the number of girls.

We start with the ratio ${\color{blue}3}:{\color{red}4}$ and write it as a fraction:

$$
\dfrac{{\color{blue}3}}{{\color{red}4}}
$$

In this fraction, the numerator represents the number of boys and the denominator represents the number of girls.

We know that there are $15$ boys, so we want to make a numerator of $15.$ We can do this by multiplying the numerator and denominator by $5\mathbin{:}$

$$
\dfrac{{\color{blue}3}\times 5}{{\color{red}4}\times 5} = \dfrac{{\color{blue}15}}{{\color{red}20}}
$$

Therefore, since there are $15$ boys in the fifth grade, there must also be $20$ girls. So the total number of students is 

$$
{\color{blue}15} + {\color{red}20} = 35\,.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "ca3cabae-8ebe-5879-b608-9d0ebdb233fb" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2051 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "a4a7f682-c223-50f1-a3eb-6b1f79aad9b0" :step/math-academy-id 7795 :step/next {:db/id 17592186180637}} {:db/id 17592186180637 :step/content {:db/id 17592186179817 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186179494 :question/id #uuid "02ae40ba-a02c-5025-9597-1968322f2421" :question/math-academy-id "e-2279"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "0e44aa33-0aca-5cb2-8c89-6391240beed8" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050174}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186180232} {:db/id 17592186180234} {:db/id 17592186275168} {:db/id 17592186275170} {:db/id 17592186332959} {:db/id 17592186332960}] :knowledge-point/title "Calculating an Amount Given a Ratio"} :step/id #uuid "91f76525-9d6e-5ea9-a6a3-b6249f246583" :step/math-academy-id 7796 :step/next {:db/id 17592186180638}} {:db/id 17592186180638 :step/content {:db/id 17592186179818 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186179495 :question/id #uuid "4aeb615e-16a1-5170-be5e-fe0f63a5d895" :question/math-academy-id "e-2280"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "b5406de3-483e-56c2-b9c6-73de6769552e" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186180233} {:db/id 17592186180235} {:db/id 17592186275169} {:db/id 17592186275171} {:db/id 17592186275172} {:db/id 17592186357529}] :knowledge-point/title "Calculating an Amount Given a Ratio as a Fraction"} :step/id #uuid "5f14a9d9-61a5-5432-ad78-2673e2e5e50e" :step/math-academy-id 7797}] :activity/title "Further Reasoning With Equivalent Ratios" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186179889} {:db/id 17592186180636 :step/content {:db/id 17592186180660 :tutorial/content "Sometimes, we can use ratios to find quantities that aren't explicitly given in the ratio.

We start with the ratio ${\color{blue}3}:{\color{red}4}$ and write it as a fraction:

$$
\dfrac{{\color{blue}3}}{{\color{red}4}}
$$

In this fraction, the numerator represents the number of boys and the denominator represents the number of girls.

We know that there are $15$ boys, so we want to make a numerator of $15.$ We can do this by multiplying the numerator and denominator by $5\mathbin{:}$

$$
\dfrac{{\color{blue}3}\times 5}{{\color{red}4}\times 5} = \dfrac{{\color{blue}15}}{{\color{red}20}}
$$

Therefore, since there are $15$ boys in the fifth grade, there must also be $20$ girls. So the total number of students is 

$$
{\color{blue}15} + {\color{red}20} = 35\,.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "ca3cabae-8ebe-5879-b608-9d0ebdb233fb" :tutorial/math-academy-id 2051 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} {:db/id 17592186180637 :step/content {:db/id 17592186179817 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186179494 :question/id #uuid "02ae40ba-a02c-5025-9597-1968322f2421" :question/math-academy-id "e-2279"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "0e44aa33-0aca-5cb2-8c89-6391240beed8" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050174}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186180232} {:db/id 17592186180234} {:db/id 17592186275168} {:db/id 17592186275170} {:db/id 17592186332959} {:db/id 17592186332960}] :knowledge-point/title "Calculating an Amount Given a Ratio"} :step/id #uuid "91f76525-9d6e-5ea9-a6a3-b6249f246583" :step/math-academy-id 7796 :step/next {:db/id 17592186180638}} {:db/id 17592186180638 :step/content {:db/id 17592186179818 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186179495 :question/id #uuid "4aeb615e-16a1-5170-be5e-fe0f63a5d895" :question/math-academy-id "e-2280"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "b5406de3-483e-56c2-b9c6-73de6769552e" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186180233} {:db/id 17592186180235} {:db/id 17592186275169} {:db/id 17592186275171} {:db/id 17592186275172} {:db/id 17592186357529}] :knowledge-point/title "Calculating an Amount Given a Ratio as a Fraction"} :step/id #uuid "5f14a9d9-61a5-5432-ad78-2673e2e5e50e" :step/math-academy-id 7797} {:db/id 17592186048555 :topic/encompasses [{:db/id 17592186428883 :encompassing/rationale "Initial Codex estimate from captured target-band crossing frequency. - **I.** ${x}^{T}\,Qx,$ where the eigenvalues of $Q$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=-1$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=0$
- **II.** ${x}^{T}\,Rx,$ where the eigenvalues of $R$ are ${\lambda }_{1}={\lambda }_{2}=1$
- **III.** ${x}^{T}\,Sx,$ where the eigenvalues of $S$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=-1$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=2$

Select all that apply." :question/worked-solution "Given a quadratic form $Q(x)={x}^{T}Ax,$ we have the following theorem:

- $Q$ is positive-definite if and only if all the eigenvalues of $A$ are positive,

- $Q$ is positive semi-definite if and only if all the eigenvalues of $A$ are non-negative (note that positive semi-definite quadratic forms include all positive-definite quadratic forms),

- $Q$ is negative-definite if and only if all the eigenvalues of $A$ are negative,

- $Q$ is negative semi-definite if and only if all the eigenvalues of $A$ are non-positive (note that negative semi-definite quadratic forms include all negative-definite quadratic forms), and

- $Q$ is indefinite if and only if $A$ has both positive and negative eigenvalues.

With that in mind, let's examine our quadratic forms in turn.

- Quadratic form I is negative semi-definite. Indeed, all of the eigenvalues of $Q$ are non-positive.

- Quadratic form II is *not* negative semi-definite since all of the eigenvalues of $R$ are positive.

- Quadratic form III is *not* negative semi-definite since some of the eigenvalues of $S$ are positive (for example, ${\lambda }_{2}=2$ is positive).

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only.""} {:db/id 17592186269222 :question/id #uuid "e96bcaa6-6221-5f7c-9daa-4047225c2c05" :question/math-academy-id "q-139457"} {:db/id 17592186269223 :question/id 17592186045485 :db/ident :question.difficulty/easy} :question/problem "Which of the following quadratic forms over ${R}^{2}$ are positive-definite?
- **I.** ${x}^{T}\,Qx,$ where the eigenvalues of $Q$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=0$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=3$
- **II.** ${x}^{T}\,Rx,$ where the eigenvalues of $R$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=-6$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=10$
- **III.** ${x}^{T}\,Sx,$ where the eigenvalues of $S$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=5$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=8$

Select all that apply." :question/worked-solution "Given a quadratic form $Q(x)={x}^{T}Ax,$ we have the following theorem:

- $Q$ is positive-definite if and only if all the eigenvalues of $A$ are positive,

- $Q$ is positive semi-definite if and only if all the eigenvalues of $A$ are non-negative (note that positive semi-definite quadratic forms include all positive-definite quadratic forms),

- $Q$ is negative-definite if and only if all the eigenvalues of $A$ are negative,

- $Q$ is negative semi-definite if and only if all the eigenvalues of $A$ are non-positive (note that negative semi-definite quadratic forms include all negative-definite quadratic forms), and

- $Q$ is indefinite if and only if $A$ has both positive and negative eigenvalues.

With that in mind, let's examine our quadratic forms in turn.

- Quadratic form I is *not* positive-definite since not all of the eigenvalues of $Q$ are positive (for example, ${\lambda }_{1}=0$ is not positive).

- Quadratic form II is *not* positive-definite since not all of the eigenvalues of $R$ are positive (${\lambda }_{1}=-6$ is not positive).

- Quadratic form III is positive-definite. Indeed, all of the eigenvalues of $S$ are positive.

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only.""} {:db/id 17592186360499 :question/id #uuid "13d1d5cf-031d-5ebf-8e4c-d550f344afdd" :question/math-academy-id "q-94795"} {:db/id 17592186491989 :question/id 17592186045486 :db/ident :question.difficulty/hard} :question/problem "$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-5 & 2 & 0 \\ 2 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -8\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrix $A$ shown above.
Which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.

- **I.** ${a}_{11}=-5$ and $det(A)>0$
- **II.** ${x}^{T}\,A\,x$ is negative-definite
- **III.** $A$ is negative-definite" :question/worked-solution "Let ${Δ}_{i}$ for $i=1,2,…,n$  denote the leading principal minors of an $n\times n$ matrix $A.$ Then, according to Sylvester's criterion, the quadratic form ${x}^{T}\,A\,x$ (as well as the matrix $A$) is 

- positive-definite if and only if ${Δ}_{i}>0$ for all $i=1,2,…,n,$

- negative-definite if and only if, for all $i=1,2,…,n,$ we have ${Δ}_{i}<0$ when $i$ is odd, and ${Δ}_{i}>0$ when $i$ is even.

With that in mind, let's examine each of the statements in turn.

- Statement I is false. Indeed, ${a}_{11}=-5$ but 

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & =|\begin{aligned}-5 & 2 & 0 \\ 2 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -8\end{aligned}| \\  & =(-8)\cdot |\begin{aligned}-5 & 2 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}| \\  & =(-8)\cdot 1 \\  & =-8<0.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statements II and III are true. Notice the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{Δ}_{1} & ={a}_{11}=-5<0 \\ {Δ}_{2} & =|\begin{aligned}-5 & 2 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}|=1>0 \\ {Δ}_{3} & =|A|=-8<0\end{aligned}
$$

So, by Sylvester's criterion, the form ${x}^{T}\,A\,x,$ and the matrix $A,$ are negative-definite.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only.""} {:db/id 17592186360503 :question/id #uuid "7d5f731a-8eca-5400-88d7-dd10fc541120" :question/math-academy-id "q-94805" :knowledge-point/_questions 17592186045486 :db/ident :question.difficulty/hard} :question/problem "$$
A=[\begin{aligned}8 & -3 & 0 \\ -3 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrix $A$ shown above.
Which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.

- **I.** ${a}_{11}=8$ and $det(A)<0$
- **II.** ${x}^{T}\,A\,x$ is positive-definite
- **III.** $A$ is negative-definite" :question/worked-solution "Let ${Δ}_{i}$ for $i=1,2,…,n$  denote the leading principal minors of an $n\times n$ matrix $A.$ Then, according to Sylvester's criterion, the quadratic form ${x}^{T}\,A\,x$ (as well as the matrix $A$) is 

- positive-definite if and only if ${Δ}_{i}>0$ for all $i=1,2,…,n,$

- negative-definite if and only if, for all $i=1,2,…,n,$ we have ${Δ}_{i}<0$ when $i$ is odd, and ${Δ}_{i}>0$ when $i$ is even.

With that in mind, let's examine each of the statements in turn.

- Statement I is false. Indeed, ${a}_{11}=8$ but 

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & =|\begin{aligned}8 & -3 & 0 \\ -3 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}| \\  & =3\cdot |\begin{aligned}8 & -3 \\ -3 & 2\end{aligned}| \\  & =3\cdot 7 \\  & =21>0.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is true, while statement III is false. Notice the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{Δ}_{1} & ={a}_{11}=8>0 \\ {Δ}_{2} & =|\begin{aligned}8 & -3 \\ -3 & 2\end{aligned}|=7>0 \\ {Δ}_{3} & =|A|=21>0\end{aligned}
$$

So, by Sylvester's criterion, the form ${x}^{T}\,A\,x,$ and the matrix $A,$ are positive-definite.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only.""} {:db/id 17592186360504 :question/id #uuid "b0bcde67-e6f1-5859-87e0-ff664264d2ea" :question/math-academy-id "q-94806"} {:db/id 17592186491984 :question/id
